The same model can make a useless agent or a reliable one. What differs
is everything around it: what it's told, what it can see and do, when it
stops, and how anyone knows it's finished. That surrounding code is the
**harness**. Claude Code's documentation puts it in one sentence: the
harness is "the layer around the model that provides the tools and
manages the context the model sees" ([post
50](/posts/how-coding-agents-work/)). This post is about engineering that
layer, and it ends with a measurement of the single most valuable part of
it: a check of whether the work is done.

## Table of contents

## The parts of a harness

- **Instructions and context**: the system prompt, the task, project files,
  and what's retrieved or remembered ([posts 35](/posts/context-engineering-compaction-clearing-memory/)
  and [42](/posts/agent-memory/)).
- **Tools**: their definitions, their implementations, and their error
  messages, which are the model's only window onto what went wrong.
- **The loop controller**: what happens after each model reply: run a tool,
  ask the user, check the work, stop.
- **State**: the transcript, plus anything kept outside it (files, a
  database, checkpoints) so a run can be resumed or inspected.
- **Verification**: whatever decides that the task is done.
- **Budgets**: limits on steps, tokens, time and money, and what happens when
  one runs out.
- **Observability**: traces of every step ([post
  62](/posts/evaluating-and-observing-agents/)).

The model is one component among these, and often not the one to improve
first.

## Loop design

**Stopping.** The simplest loop stops at the first reply without a tool
call (post 40). That trusts the
model to know when it's done. Alternatives: a dedicated "finish" tool whose
arguments are the final answer (so stopping is an explicit act with a
structured output), or stopping only when a check passes, the subject of
the rest of this post.

**Retries.** Two different failures need two different responses. A tool
or API error (a timeout, a rate limit) is retried by the harness, with
backoff, without bothering the model. A *model* error (malformed tool
arguments, a call to a tool that doesn't exist) goes back to the model as
an error message it can act on: the error text is a prompt, and a
specific one ("expression contains a letter; only numbers and + - * / are
allowed") gets fixed where a generic one doesn't.

**Budgets.** Every loop needs limits: steps, tokens, wall-clock time, cost.
The interesting question is what happens at the limit. Returning nothing
wastes the work done; returning the best partial result, saving state so a
person or a later run can continue, or escalating are all better than
silence. And budgets should be measured, not guessed: the distribution
of steps successful runs actually take says where the limit belongs.

## Graphs

A loop has one shape. When a task has known stages (plan, then search,
then draft, then review), branches (route by request type) or points where
a person must approve, it's clearer as a **graph**: nodes for steps, edges
for what can follow what, shared typed state, and a checkpoint after each
step. [Post 49](/posts/langchain-and-langgraph-from-the-inside/) built the
same agent as a loop and as a LangGraph graph: the graph cost a few more
lines and a fraction of a millisecond per run, and bought pausing before a
tool call, resuming, and a history of every step.

The trade is between flexibility and control. A loop lets the model decide
the order of everything; a graph fixes some order in code. Anthropic's
guide to building agents (2024) frames this as **workflows**, where code
orchestrates the model along predefined paths (prompt chaining, routing,
parallelization, an evaluator that feeds back to a generator), versus
**agents**, where the model directs its own process, and advises using the
simplest that works. Fixed structure where the task's shape is known,
model autonomy where it isn't.

## The definition of done

An agent that decides for itself when it's finished will sometimes
decide wrong: it stops early, reports success on unfinished work, or
answers from memory instead of checking. The fix is to make "done" a
**check the harness runs**, not a claim the model makes. For code, the
check is the test suite; for a data task, a schema validation or a
reconciliation; for a document, a list of required sections. The best
checks need no knowledge of the right answer, only of what a right answer
must satisfy, so they can run in production, not just in evaluation.

Here is the experiment. Post 62's calculator agent was right 93% of the
time, and its traces showed that some right answers didn't come from the
calculator it was told to use, and some wrong ones were mental
arithmetic. A check the harness can run without knowing the answer: the
final number must equal the calculator's most recent result. If it
doesn't, the harness tells the agent and lets it continue; if the budget
runs out first, the harness returns the agent's last answer anyway, the
best partial result rather than nothing. The same model, problems and
random seeds, with and without the check, up to eight model calls per run,
every transcript kept:

```python

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

# Two harnesses around the same model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct) and tool (a
# calculator), on post 62's 20 warehouse problems, 3 runs each.
#   plain: stop at the first reply that doesn't call a tool (post 62).
#   checked: a definition of done the harness can verify without knowing
#   the answer: the reply's final number must equal the calculator's most
#   recent result. If not, the harness says so and the agent continues; if
#   the budget runs out, it returns the last answer anyway (unverified).
# Up to 8 model calls per run; the step at which each run finished is kept,
# so success under any smaller budget can be read off afterwards.
PATH = ("/Users/tanle/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/"
        "snapshots/989aa7980e4cf806f80c7fef2b1adb7bc71aa306")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(PATH)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(PATH, dtype=torch.float16).to("mps").eval()
TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "calculator", "description": "Evaluate an arithmetic "
          "expression with + - * / and parentheses, and return the number.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"expression": {"type": "string"}},
                         "required": ["expression"]}}}]
def calculator(expression):
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[\d\s+\-*/().]+", expression or ""):
        return "error: only numbers and + - * / ( ) are allowed"
    return str(round(eval(expression), 6))

rng = random.Random(0)                                  # the same 20 problems as post 62
tasks = []
for _ in range(20):
    a, b, c, d = rng.randint(1000, 9999), rng.randint(100, 999), rng.randint(3, 9), rng.randint(100, 999)
    tasks.append((f"A warehouse holds {a} boxes. It ships out {b} boxes, then receives {c} deliveries of "
                  f"{d} boxes each. How many boxes does it hold now?", a - b + c * d))

def last_number(text):
    nums = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*", text)
    return int(nums[-1].replace(",", "")) if nums else None

@torch.no_grad()
def run(question, seed, checked, max_calls=8):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "Use the calculator tool for every arithmetic step. "
                 "End with: Answer: <number>"}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    last, calls, answer, given = None, 0, None, []    # given: (call number, answer) for every answer the agent gives
    while calls < max_calls:
        prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=TOOLS, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)
        ids = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to("mps")
        out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=1.0, top_k=0,
                             repetition_penalty=1.1)
        text = tok.decode(out[0, ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)
        calls += 1
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
        tool_calls = re.findall(r"<tool_call>\s*(\{.*?\})\s*</tool_call>", text, re.S)
        if tool_calls:
            for c in tool_calls:
                try:
                    r = calculator(json.loads(c)["arguments"]["expression"])
                except (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError):
                    r = "error: malformed tool call"
                if not r.startswith("error"):
                    last = float(r)
                messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": r})
            continue
        answer = last_number(text)
        given.append((calls, answer))
        if not checked or (answer is not None and last is not None and answer == last):
            return answer, calls, messages, given
        messages.append({"role": "user", "content": f"Your answer {answer} is not the calculator's last result. "
                         "Use the calculator for each step, then give its final result as the answer."})
    return answer, calls, messages, given                # budget exhausted: the last answer, unverified

log = {}
for name in ("plain", "checked"):
    rows = []
    for i, (q, truth) in enumerate(tasks):
        for k in range(3):
            ans, calls, msgs, given = run(q, seed=100 * i + k, checked=name == "checked")
            rows.append({"task": i, "right": ans == truth, "calls": calls, "answer": ans, "truth": truth, "given": given,
                         "transcript": [m["content"][:400] for m in msgs[1:]]})
    log[name] = rows
    print(f"{name:8s} right {np.mean([r['right'] for r in rows]):.0%}", flush=True)
json.dump(log, open("runs.json", "w"))

print(f"\n{'harness':8s} " + " ".join(f"{'budget ' + str(b):>10s}" for b in (2, 3, 4, 6, 8)) + "   (share right)")
for name, rows in log.items():
    def at_budget(r, b):
        # Cut at b calls, the harness returns the run's answer if it finished
        # by then, else the last answer the agent had given (unverified).
        if r["calls"] <= b:
            return r["answer"]
        earlier = [a for c, a in r["given"] if c <= b]
        return earlier[-1] if earlier else None
    print(f"{name:8s} " + " ".join(f"{np.mean([at_budget(r, b) == r['truth'] for r in rows]):>10.0%}"
                                   for b in (2, 3, 4, 6, 8)))
for name, rows in log.items():
    calls = [r["calls"] for r in rows]
    print(f"{name}: model calls per run, mean {np.mean(calls):.1f}, max {max(calls)}; "
          f"used all 8 calls {sum(c == 8 for c in calls)} of {len(rows)}")
plain, checked = log["plain"], log["checked"]
print(f"paired: the check fixed {sum(not p['right'] and c['right'] for p, c in zip(plain, checked))} plain failures "
      f"and broke {sum(p['right'] and not c['right'] for p, c in zip(plain, checked))} plain successes")
```

```text
plain    right 93%
checked  right 97%

harness    budget 2   budget 3   budget 4   budget 6   budget 8   (share right)
plain           93%        93%        93%        93%        93%
checked         93%        92%        92%        95%        97%
plain: model calls per run, mean 1.9, max 2; used all 8 calls 0 of 60
checked: model calls per run, mean 2.5, max 8; used all 8 calls 3 of 60
paired: the check fixed 2 plain failures and broke 0 plain successes
```

The check raised accuracy from 93% to 97%. Because both harnesses use the
same seeds, each pair of runs is identical until the check first objects,
so the comparison is exact: it fixed 2 of the plain harness's 4 failures
and broke none of its successes. The transcripts show what it caught: an
answer worked out in prose (5242 − 623 = 4619, then a wrong sum), sent back
until it came from the calculator. With four failures in sixty runs, that
is a small sample, and the direction is what to take from it.

The transcripts also show what it can't catch. One failure passed the
check in both harnesses: the agent asked the calculator for
8113 − (423 + 7 × 755), subtracting the deliveries instead of adding
them, and answered 2405, exactly the calculator's result. The check
verifies where the answer came from, not whether the question put to the
calculator was right. Another run fixed its mental arithmetic and then
made a different error with the calculator. A check that would catch
these needs to know more about the task: recompute the answer a second,
independent way and compare, or check the expression against the
problem's structure. In code, the test suite plays that role, which is why
coding agents ([post 50](/posts/how-coding-agents-work/)) gain so much from
verification.

The check cost 2.5 model calls per run against 1.9, a third more, and more
than that in tokens, since each extra round rereads a longer context;
three runs used all eight calls. Because the harness returns the last
answer when the budget runs out, a tight budget loses nothing relative to
the plain harness (93% at two calls). An earlier version of this
experiment returned nothing at the limit and lost ten points at a two-call
budget: what a harness does at its limits is part of the design.

## Long-running harnesses

Tasks that take hours outlive any one context window, and two failure
modes dominate, as Anthropic's account of harnesses for long-running
coding agents (2025) describes them: the agent tries to do too much at
once, and a later session looks around, sees progress, and declares the
job done. Its harness answers both with the ideas above, made
persistent:
- An **initializer** session turns the request into a feature list, a JSON
  file of specific, testable requirements, each with a `passes` field that
  starts false, and an instruction that removing or editing tests is
  unacceptable. The definition of done is written down before work starts.
- Each later session starts by getting its bearings (the working
  directory, the git log, a progress file), picks the highest-priority
  feature not yet passing, works on that one, tests it end to end as a
  user would (through browser automation, not just unit tests), and
  leaves a commit and a progress note for the next session.
- Git provides both the record and the undo.

## Evaluation harnesses

The same machinery evaluates agents ([post
61](/posts/evaluating-llms/), [post 62](/posts/evaluating-and-observing-agents/)).
An evaluation harness runs each task in a fresh environment (SWE-bench
builds a container per task), applies the agent's result, runs the check,
and records the trace. Everything above applies, with one more
requirement: the harness itself must be tested, because its bugs become
the results. Post 62's first run reported a dozen failures that were its
own token limit.

## Takeaways

- The harness is everything around the model: context, tools, loop
  control, state, verification, budgets and observability.
- Retry infrastructure errors in the harness; send model errors back to
  the model as specific, actionable messages.
- Measure where budgets belong, and decide what happens at the limit.
- Use a graph when the task's stages, branches or approvals are known;
  a loop when they aren't.
- A definition of done catches what it checks. Measured: requiring the
  answer to be the calculator's last result raised accuracy from 93% to
  97% (2 fixes, no breaks), cost a third more calls, and still passed an
  answer computed from the wrong expression.
- Long-running harnesses write the definition of done down first (a
  feature list with pass flags), work on one item at a time, and leave a
  trail for the next session.

## References

- Anthropic, [_Building effective agents_](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) (2024).
- Anthropic, [_Effective harnesses for long-running agents_](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-harnesses-for-long-running-agents) (2025).
- Jimenez et al., [_SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) (2023).
[Post 61](/posts/evaluating-llms/) treated a model's answer as the thing
to evaluate. An agent's answer is the end of a process: several model
calls, tool calls, intermediate results. That changes what evaluation has
to look at. The final answer can be right because the agent did the work
properly, or by luck; wrong because of a real mistake, or because it
wrote "about twelve thousand" where a number was expected. And the same
agent, asked the same thing twice, can do both. This post covers how to
evaluate all of that, and the instrumentation that makes it possible.

## Table of contents

## Three levels of evaluation

- **Outcome**: did the task end in the right state? The answer is
  correct, the tests pass, the database row exists. This is what users
  care about, and the only level many benchmarks score.
- **Trajectory**: did the agent get there the right way? It called the
  tools it should, in a sensible order, without detours, without actions
  it shouldn't take (deleting a file, emailing a customer) on the way.
  Two agents with the same outcome score can differ completely here, and
  the one that guessed right will fail on the next variation.
- **Tool use**: was each call well formed and appropriate? Right tool,
  valid arguments, result actually used.

Agent benchmarks mostly score outcomes in environments built to make the
outcome checkable. **SWE-bench** (Jimenez et al., 2023) gives an agent a
real GitHub issue and repository and runs the project's own tests on its
patch. **τ-bench** (Yao et al., 2024) puts an agent in a simulated customer
service conversation, with a simulated user and tools over a database,
and checks the database's final state against the goal, along with
information the agent had to tell the user. τ-bench also introduced the
metric this post turns to next, because it asks the question production
cares about: does the agent succeed *every* time? Its strongest agent at
publication succeeded on about 60% of retail tasks in one try, and on
about a quarter in all of eight.

Agent evaluations also need what model evaluations don't: an
environment that resets. An agent with tools changes things (files,
databases, sent messages), so each run needs a fresh sandbox, as
SWE-bench's per-task containers and τ-bench's database resets provide,
or runs contaminate each other and side effects leak into the real
world.

## pass@k and pass^k

Run an agent $k$ times on one task. Two different questions:
- **pass@k**: does *at least one* of the $k$ attempts succeed? Right when
  you can check answers and keep the best, as a coding benchmark with
  unit tests can.
- **pass^k**: do *all* $k$ succeed? Right when every attempt goes to a
  user, as in customer service, where $k$ customers asking the same thing
  should all be helped.

For a task the agent solves with probability $p$ per attempt, they are
$1 - (1 - p)^k$ and $p^k$:

```python
from math import comb

# pass@k: at least one of k attempts succeeds (what a benchmark with
# retries, or a human picking the best of k, cares about). pass^k: all k
# succeed (what a user who asks k times, or k customers, cares about).
# For one task with per-attempt success p: 1 - (1 - p)^k and p^k.
print(f"{'p':>5s} " + " ".join(f"{'pass@' + str(k):>8s}" for k in (1, 4, 8)) + "   " +
      " ".join(f"{'pass^' + str(k):>8s}" for k in (1, 4, 8)))
for p in (0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99):
    print(f"{p:5.2f} " + " ".join(f"{1 - (1 - p) ** k:8.3f}" for k in (1, 4, 8)) + "   " +
          " ".join(f"{p ** k:8.3f}" for k in (1, 4, 8)))

# From n attempts with c successes, unbiased estimates for k <= n
# (Chen et al. 2021 for pass@k; the same counting gives pass^k).
def pass_at(n, c, k): return 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)
def pass_hat(n, c, k): return comb(c, k) / comb(n, k)
print(f"\n5 attempts, 3 succeed: pass@1 {pass_at(5, 3, 1):.2f}, pass@3 {pass_at(5, 3, 3):.2f}, "
      f"pass^3 {pass_hat(5, 3, 3):.2f}")
```

```text
    p   pass@1   pass@4   pass@8     pass^1   pass^4   pass^8
 0.50    0.500    0.938    0.996      0.500    0.062    0.004
 0.80    0.800    0.998    1.000      0.800    0.410    0.168
 0.90    0.900    1.000    1.000      0.900    0.656    0.430
 0.95    0.950    1.000    1.000      0.950    0.815    0.663
 0.99    0.990    1.000    1.000      0.990    0.961    0.923

5 attempts, 3 succeed: pass@1 0.60, pass@3 1.00, pass^3 0.10
```

They move in opposite directions. An agent that succeeds 80% of the time
looks nearly perfect by pass@8 (1.000) and unreliable by pass^8 (0.17):
across eight customers, it fails at least one five times in six. Even 99%
per attempt gives pass^8 of 0.92. τ-bench reported exactly this pattern:
agents whose single-attempt success looked respectable fell sharply as
$k$ grew. Report $k$, and pick the direction that matches the deployment.

From $n$ attempts with $c$ successes, both have unbiased estimates for any
$k \le n$, by counting subsets (pass@k's from Chen et al., 2021, pass^k's
from τ-bench):
$1 - \binom{n-c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$ and $\binom{c}{k}/\binom{n}{k}$. With 3
of 5 successes, pass@3 is 1.0 (any 3 attempts include a success) and
pass^3 is 0.1 (1 of the 10 possible triples is all successes).

## Traces and spans

Trajectory evaluation needs a record of the trajectory, and that is what
**tracing** provides. A **trace** is the record of one request through a
system; it is made of **spans**, each a timed operation with a name,
attributes, and a parent, so they form a tree. Distributed systems have
used this for years, and OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for
it. Its **GenAI semantic conventions** (still marked "development") fix
the names for AI work, so any backend can read any agent's traces:
- an agent run is a span named `invoke_agent {agent name}`;
- each model call is `chat {model}`, with `gen_ai.request.model`,
  `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` and `gen_ai.usage.output_tokens`;
- each tool call is `execute_tool {tool name}`, with `gen_ai.tool.name`,
  `gen_ai.tool.call.id`, and, if you opt in, the arguments and result;
- `gen_ai.operation.name` on every span says which kind it is, and
  `gen_ai.response.finish_reasons` says why a model call stopped;
- model calls are client spans (a call to another service), tool calls
  usually internal ones; a failed operation sets `error.type` and the
  span's error status.

Message contents (prompts, responses, tool arguments and results) are
opt-in, because they may hold personal data; deciding what to record is a
privacy decision as much as a debugging one. Production systems usually
redact personal data before storing contents, and sample traces (keep
all failures and slow runs, a fraction of the rest) to control volume.

## An agent, traced and evaluated

A small agent to evaluate: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with one tool, a
calculator, on 20 word problems that each need two arithmetic steps on
3- and 4-digit numbers, run 5 times each at temperature 0.7. Every model
call and tool call becomes a record shaped like an OpenTelemetry span,
with the GenAI attribute names (plain dictionaries here, to keep the code
self-contained; the OpenTelemetry SDK would add span kinds, wall-clock
timestamps and export to a tracing backend):

```python

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

# A small agent, traced. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct with one tool, a calculator,
# on 20 word problems that each need two arithmetic steps on 3- and 4-digit
# numbers. Each problem is run 5 times (temperature 0.7, and the model's
# default repetition penalty of 1.1, stated explicitly). Every model call
# and tool call is recorded as a span-shaped record with OpenTelemetry's
# GenAI attribute names, including the opt-in message contents and each
# call's finish reason; the evaluation reads nothing else but the answer key.
PATH = ("/Users/tanle/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/"
        "snapshots/989aa7980e4cf806f80c7fef2b1adb7bc71aa306")
MODEL = "qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct"
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(PATH)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(PATH, dtype=torch.float16).to("mps").eval()
TOOLS = [{"type": "function", "function": {"name": "calculator", "description": "Evaluate an arithmetic "
          "expression with + - * / and parentheses, and return the number.",
          "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"expression": {"type": "string"}},
                         "required": ["expression"]}}}]

def calculator(expression):
    if not re.fullmatch(r"[\d\s+\-*/().]+", expression):
        return "error: only numbers and + - * / ( ) are allowed"
    return str(round(eval(expression), 6))                    # safe: the regex admits arithmetic only

rng = random.Random(0)
tasks = []
for _ in range(20):
    a, b, c, d = rng.randint(1000, 9999), rng.randint(100, 999), rng.randint(3, 9), rng.randint(100, 999)
    tasks.append((f"A warehouse holds {a} boxes. It ships out {b} boxes, then receives {c} deliveries of "
                  f"{d} boxes each. How many boxes does it hold now?", a - b + c * d))

def span(trace, name, parent, **attrs):
    s = {"trace_id": trace["id"], "span_id": uuid.uuid4().hex[:16], "parent_id": parent, "name": name,
         "start": time.perf_counter(), "attributes": attrs}
    trace["spans"].append(s)
    return s

def run(question, seed, max_turns=5):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    trace = {"id": uuid.uuid4().hex, "spans": []}
    root = span(trace, "invoke_agent warehouse-helper", None, **{"gen_ai.operation.name": "invoke_agent",
                "gen_ai.agent.name": "warehouse-helper"})
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": "Use the calculator tool for every arithmetic step. "
                 "End with: Answer: <number>"}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    answer = lenient = final = None
    for _ in range(max_turns):
        prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tools=TOOLS, add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=False)
        ids = tok(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to("mps")
        s = span(trace, f"chat {MODEL}", root["span_id"], **{"gen_ai.operation.name": "chat",
                 "gen_ai.provider.name": "local", "gen_ai.request.model": MODEL, "gen_ai.request.temperature": 0.7,
                 "gen_ai.request.max_tokens": 512})
        out = model.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=True, temperature=0.7, top_p=1.0, top_k=0,
                             repetition_penalty=1.1)
        new = out[0, ids.shape[1]:]
        text = tok.decode(new, skip_special_tokens=True)
        s["end"] = time.perf_counter()
        stopped = new[-1].item() in (tok.eos_token_id, tok.convert_tokens_to_ids("<|im_end|>"))
        s["attributes"].update({"gen_ai.usage.input_tokens": ids.shape[1], "gen_ai.usage.output_tokens": len(new),
                                "gen_ai.response.finish_reasons": ["stop" if stopped else "length"],
                                "gen_ai.output.messages": [{"role": "assistant", "content": text}]})
        calls = re.findall(r"<tool_call>\s*(\{.*?\})\s*</tool_call>", text, re.S)
        messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
        if not calls:
            final = text
            m = re.search(r"Answer:\s*\$?(-?[\d,]+)", text)               # the format we asked for
            answer = int(m.group(1).replace(",", "")) if m else None
            nums = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*", text)                        # or just the last number in the reply
            lenient = int(nums[-1].replace(",", "")) if nums else None
            break
        for c in calls:
            try:
                args = json.loads(c)["arguments"]; expr = args["expression"]
            except (ValueError, KeyError, TypeError):
                args, expr = c, None
            # the model emits no call id, so the harness assigns one
            t = span(trace, "execute_tool calculator", root["span_id"], **{"gen_ai.operation.name": "execute_tool",
                     "gen_ai.tool.name": "calculator", "gen_ai.tool.call.id": uuid.uuid4().hex[:8],
                     "gen_ai.tool.call.arguments": args})
            result = calculator(expr) if expr is not None else "error: malformed tool call"
            t["end"] = time.perf_counter()
            if result.startswith("error"):
                t["attributes"]["error.type"] = "invalid_arguments"; t["status"] = "ERROR"
            else:
                t["attributes"]["gen_ai.tool.call.result"] = result
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
    root["end"] = time.perf_counter()
    return trace, answer, lenient, final

results = []
for i, (q, truth) in enumerate(tasks):
    for k in range(5):
        trace, ans, lenient, final = run(q, seed=100 * i + k)
        results.append({"task": i, "truth": truth, "answer": ans, "lenient": lenient, "final": final, "trace": trace})
    print(f"task {i:2d}: {sum(r['answer'] == truth for r in results[-5:])}/5 correct as asked, "
          f"{sum(r['lenient'] == truth for r in results[-5:])}/5 by the last number", flush=True)
json.dump(results, open("traces.json", "w"))
```

The evaluation then reads only the traces and the answer key:

```python

from math import comb

# Evaluating the agent from its traces: every fact below is read from the
# span records (message contents, finish reasons, tool calls); the only
# other input is the answer key.
results = json.load(open("traces.json"))
key = {r["task"]: r["truth"] for r in results}

def facts(r):
    spans = r["trace"]["spans"]
    chats = [s["attributes"] for s in spans if s["attributes"]["gen_ai.operation.name"] == "chat"]
    tools = [s["attributes"] for s in spans if s["attributes"]["gen_ai.operation.name"] == "execute_tool"]
    final = chats[-1]["gen_ai.output.messages"][0]["content"]
    strict = re.search(r"Answer:\s*\$?(-?[\d,]+)", final)
    nums = re.findall(r"-?\d[\d,]*", final)
    return {"final": final, "tools": tools,
            "truncated": any(c["gen_ai.response.finish_reasons"] == ["length"] for c in chats),
            "strict": int(strict.group(1).replace(",", "")) if strict else None,
            "lenient": int(nums[-1].replace(",", "")) if nums else None,
            "tool_has_truth": str(key[r["task"]]) in [t.get("gen_ai.tool.call.result", "").split(".")[0] for t in tools]}
F = [(r, facts(r)) for r in results]

pass_at = lambda n, c, k: 1 - comb(n - c, k) / comb(n, k)
pass_hat = lambda n, c, k: comb(c, k) / comb(n, k)
for name, field in (("as asked ('Answer: <number>')", "strict"), ("by the last number in the reply", "lenient")):
    per = {}
    for r, f in F:
        per.setdefault(r["task"], []).append(f[field] == key[r["task"]])
    print(f"outcome scored {name}, 20 tasks x 5 runs:")
    for k in (1, 3, 5):
        print(f"  pass@{k} {np.mean([pass_at(5, sum(v), k) for v in per.values()]):.2f}   "
              f"pass^{k} {np.mean([pass_hat(5, sum(v), k) for v in per.values()]):.2f}")
    print(f"  tasks solved in all 5 runs: {sum(sum(v) == 5 for v in per.values())} of 20")

def trajectory(f, truth):
    right = f["lenient"] == truth
    if f["truncated"]:
        return "cut off by the token budget" + (" (still right)" if right else "")
    if right:
        return "right, the calculator produced the answer" if f["tool_has_truth"] else "right, the calculator didn't produce it"
    if f["tools"] and not f["tool_has_truth"]:
        return "wrong: asked the calculator the wrong question"
    if f["tool_has_truth"]:
        return "wrong: calculator had it, reply differs"
    return "wrong: no calculator"
cats = {}
for r, f in F:
    c = trajectory(f, key[r["task"]]); cats[c] = cats.get(c, 0) + 1
print("\ntrajectories (100 runs):")
for c, v in sorted(cats.items(), key=lambda x: -x[1]):
    print(f"  {v:3d}  {c}")
calls = [len(f["tools"]) for _, f in F]
print(f"  calculator calls per run: none {calls.count(0)}, one {calls.count(1)}, two or more {sum(c >= 2 for c in calls)}"
      f" (the instructions asked for one per arithmetic step: two)")
print(f"  runs with no 'Answer:' line: {sum(f['strict'] is None for _, f in F)}; of those, replies saying "
      f"'the answer is': {sum(f['strict'] is None and 'answer is' in f['final'].lower() for _, f in F)}")

spans = [s for r in results for s in r["trace"]["spans"]]
by = lambda op: [s for s in spans if s["attributes"]["gen_ai.operation.name"] == op]
dur = lambda ss: np.array([s["end"] - s["start"] for s in ss])
chat, tool, agents = by("chat"), by("execute_tool"), by("invoke_agent")
tin = sum(s["attributes"]["gen_ai.usage.input_tokens"] for s in chat)
tout = sum(s["attributes"]["gen_ai.usage.output_tokens"] for s in chat)
right = sum(f["lenient"] == key[r["task"]] for r, f in F)
print(f"\ndashboard: {len(agents)} runs, {len(chat)} model calls, {len(tool)} tool calls")
print(f"  per run: {len(chat) / len(agents):.1f} model calls, {tin / len(agents):,.0f} tokens in, {tout / len(agents):.0f} out; "
      f"per successful run: {(tin + tout) / right:,.0f} tokens")
print(f"  run latency p50 {np.median(dur(agents)):.1f} s, p95 {np.percentile(dur(agents), 95):.1f} s; "
      f"model call p50 {np.median(dur(chat)):.2f} s; tool call p50 {np.median(dur(tool)) * 1e6:.0f} us")

r, f = next((r, f) for r, f in F if trajectory(f, key[r["task"]]).startswith("wrong: asked"))
print(f"\none trace (task {r['task']}, right answer {key[r['task']]}):")
t0 = r["trace"]["spans"][0]["start"]
for s in r["trace"]["spans"]:
    a = s["attributes"]
    extra = (f"in {a['gen_ai.usage.input_tokens']} out {a['gen_ai.usage.output_tokens']} tokens, "
             f"finish {a['gen_ai.response.finish_reasons'][0]}" if a["gen_ai.operation.name"] == "chat" else
             f"{a.get('gen_ai.tool.call.arguments')} -> {a.get('gen_ai.tool.call.result')}"
             if a["gen_ai.operation.name"] == "execute_tool" else "")
    print(f"{'  ' if s['parent_id'] is None else '      '}{s['name']:38s} {(s['start'] - t0) * 1e3:7.0f} ms  "
          f"+{(s['end'] - s['start']) * 1e3:6.0f} ms  {extra}")
print(f"  final reply: {f['final']!r}")
```

```text
outcome scored as asked ('Answer: <number>'), 20 tasks x 5 runs:
  pass@1 0.15   pass^1 0.15
  pass@3 0.39   pass^3 0.00
  pass@5 0.55   pass^5 0.00
  tasks solved in all 5 runs: 0 of 20
outcome scored by the last number in the reply, 20 tasks x 5 runs:
  pass@1 0.93   pass^1 0.93
  pass@3 1.00   pass^3 0.81
  pass@5 1.00   pass^5 0.70
  tasks solved in all 5 runs: 14 of 20

trajectories (100 runs):
   81  right, the calculator produced the answer
   11  right, the calculator didn't produce it
    4  wrong: no calculator
    3  wrong: asked the calculator the wrong question
    1  cut off by the token budget (still right)
  calculator calls per run: none 14, one 84, two or more 2 (the instructions asked for one per arithmetic step: two)
  runs with no 'Answer:' line: 83; of those, replies saying 'the answer is': 19

dashboard: 100 runs, 186 model calls, 88 tool calls
  per run: 1.9 model calls, 454 tokens in, 81 out; per successful run: 575 tokens
  run latency p50 2.5 s, p95 10.9 s; model call p50 1.55 s; tool call p50 33 us

one trace (task 9, right answer 12975):
  invoke_agent warehouse-helper                0 ms  +  2468 ms  
      chat qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct                   1 ms  +  1594 ms  in 213 out 33 tokens, finish stop
      execute_tool calculator                   1595 ms  +     0 ms  {'expression': '8113-(423+7*755)'} -> 2405
      chat qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct                1596 ms  +   872 ms  in 268 out 12 tokens, finish stop
  final reply: 'The warehouse holds 2405 boxes now.'
```

**The first score was a measurement error, twice.** Scored as instructed,
by an `Answer: <number>` line, the agent passes 15% of runs. Scored by the
last number in its final reply, 93%. Most replies simply said "The
warehouse now holds 7281 boxes"; 19 said "the answer is" without the
colon. The agent did the task and loosely followed the format. And an
earlier version of this experiment, with a 160-token budget per model
call, reported 86% and a dozen "mental arithmetic" failures; the traces
showed that most of those replies had been cut off mid-sentence and
scored by whatever number came last. With 512 tokens and each call's
finish reason recorded (`gen_ai.response.finish_reasons`), one run hit the
limit, and it was still right. The harness's budgets, parser and
sampling settings are part of the evaluation, and they belong in the
trace, so that a surprising score can be checked against what the model
actually said.

**The trajectory separates good answers from lucky ones.** Of the 93
right answers, 81 came out of the calculator. In 11, no calculator
result contained the answer: the model did at least part of the
arithmetic itself and got it right. Those count as successes by outcome
and as process failures by trajectory, and the four runs where unaided
arithmetic went wrong show what the habit costs. Three runs used the
calculator correctly on the wrong expression. The trace above is one: the
agent computed 8113 − (423 + 7 × 755), subtracting the deliveries instead
of adding them, and the calculator faithfully returned 2405. Every span in
that trace is healthy; the error is in what the model asked for, which no
tool-level metric catches.

And one rule went unchecked until the traces were counted. The
instructions asked for the calculator "for every arithmetic step", two
per problem. Only 2 runs made two calls; 84 packed both steps into one
expression. Whether that's a violation depends on what the rule was for,
but an outcome score could never have shown it.

**pass^k is the sobering number.** At 93% of runs right, 14 of the 20 tasks
were solved in all five runs, and pass^5 averages 0.70. (Here that
happens to match $0.93^5$; in general the average of per-task pass^k
differs from the average success rate raised to the $k$, because
failures concentrate in some tasks, and it's the per-task view that a
user meets.) With five runs per task, each task's pass^5 estimate is just
"all five passed or not", and with 20 tasks of one template, these
numbers describe this agent on this problem, nothing broader.

Rule-based categories like these don't scale to open-ended tasks, where
"the right route" can't be written as a check. There, trajectories are
graded by an LLM judge reading the trace against a rubric, with all the
judge biases of [post 61](/posts/evaluating-llms/) and the same need to
calibrate it against people.

**The dashboard lines** come from the same spans: 1.9 model calls and
about 535 tokens per run, 575 tokens per *successful* run (the number to
budget with), and a median run of 2.5 seconds, almost all of it model
time; the tool calls take microseconds. In a real system the tool spans
would hold network calls and database queries, and the same breakdown
would show where the time goes.

## Observability is not evaluation

The same traces serve two purposes that are easy to conflate.
**Evaluation** asks whether the agent is good, on a fixed set of tasks,
before a change ships. **Observability** asks what the agent is doing in
production, on traffic nobody chose: latency and cost per run, how many
model calls and tool calls a run takes, which tools fail, where time
goes. The dashboard lines above are the start of it. In production, the
useful views are distributions, not averages (a p95 run that makes ten
model calls is a different problem from a slow model), cost per
successful task rather than per call, and alerts on shifts: a jump in
calls per run often means an agent has started looping. The two meet in a
loop: production traces of failures become new evaluation tasks.

## Takeaways

- Evaluate agents at three levels: the outcome, the trajectory that
  produced it, and each tool call.
- pass@k (any of $k$ succeeds) and pass^k (all $k$ succeed) diverge
  quickly: 80% per attempt is 1.00 by pass@8 and 0.17 by pass^8. Choose
  the one that matches how answers reach users.
- Traces made of spans are what make trajectory evaluation possible;
  OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions name them (`invoke_agent`, `chat`,
  `execute_tool`) so any tool can read them.
- A small agent scored 15% by the requested answer format and 93% by the
  number it actually gave, after an earlier run's 160-token budget had
  silently truncated replies; its traces showed both problems, which
  right answers skipped the calculator, and which wrong ones asked it the
  wrong question. 14 of 20 tasks were right in all five runs.
- Observability watches production with the same traces; production
  failures become tomorrow's eval tasks.

## References

- Jimenez et al., [_SWE-bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) (2023).
- Yao et al., [_τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12045) (2024).
- Chen et al., [_Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374) (2021).
- OpenTelemetry, [_Semantic conventions for generative AI_](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai) (development status).
Every decision in this series that compared two things (two retrievers,
two fine-tunes, two decoding settings) rested on an evaluation, and most
of them came with a warning about seeds or sample size. This post is
about evaluation itself. The core idea is borrowed from measurement in
any science: an eval is an instrument. It has to measure the thing you
care about (**validity**), give the same answer when nothing changed
(**reliability**), and come with an error bar, or its readings can't be
compared. A language-model judge is an instrument too, and it has to be
calibrated like one.

## Table of contents

## What to measure

Start from the decision the eval serves. "Is model B better than model
A?" is too vague to measure. "On our customers' support questions, does
B give a correct, complete answer more often, without getting slower?" can
be. That framing names the data (your traffic, not a public benchmark),
the property (correctness, completeness) and the constraint (latency).

The metric then depends on what an answer looks like:
- **Exact or programmatic checks**, when the answer is checkable: a
  multiple-choice letter, a number, code that must pass tests, JSON that
  must validate. These are the cheapest and most reliable metrics, and
  [post 31](/posts/grpo-and-verifiable-rewards/) used them as rewards.
- **Reference-based overlap**, such as BLEU or ROUGE, which count n-grams
  shared with a reference answer. They were built for translation and
  summarization, where outputs are close to a reference; for open-ended
  answers they reward wording, not correctness, and a correct answer
  phrased differently scores low.
- **Embedding similarity** to a reference ([post
  8](/posts/embeddings-and-contrastive-learning/)), which tolerates
  rewording but still can't tell a confident wrong answer that shares the
  reference's vocabulary from a right one.
- **Human judgment**, the reference standard for open-ended quality, and
  slow and expensive.
- **An LLM judge**, cheaper than people and scalable, and biased in ways
  measured below.

Perplexity ([post 9](/posts/autoregression-and-perplexity/)) belongs on
this list for base models: it measures how well a model predicts text,
which tracks capability but says nothing about whether answers are
helpful.

## Benchmarks and contamination

Public benchmarks make models comparable: MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2020)
for knowledge across 57 subjects, HELM (Liang et al., 2022) for a broad,
standardized battery, SWE-bench for coding agents, and many more. They
share two weaknesses. They **saturate**: once frontier models score in
the high 90s, a benchmark stops separating them. And they **leak**: a
benchmark's questions published on the web end up in later models'
training data, so a high score may reflect memory rather than ability.
Checks for contamination look for verbatim overlap between benchmark and
training data, or for a model doing much better on a benchmark's public
questions than on freshly written questions of the same kind. The
practical defense is an eval of your own: questions written for your
task, kept out of anything public, and refreshed.

## How many questions?

Suppose two models score around 70% and you want to detect a 2-point
difference. The number of questions this takes is a power calculation,
the same one a clinical trial uses:

```python

from statistics import NormalDist

# How many questions does an eval need? Two models, accuracy around 70%,
# and a difference of 2 points to detect, with a 5% false-alarm rate
# (two-sided) and 80% power.
z = NormalDist().inv_cdf
za, zb = z(0.975), z(0.80)
p1, p2 = 0.70, 0.72
# Unpaired: the two models answer different random questions.
n_unpaired = (za + zb) ** 2 * (p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2)) / (p2 - p1) ** 2
print(f"unpaired (different questions): {math.ceil(n_unpaired):,} questions per model")
# Paired: both answer the same questions, and only the questions they
# disagree on carry information (McNemar). If they disagree on a share d of
# questions, the per-question difference has variance d - (p2 - p1)^2,
# about d. (Independent errors would make them disagree on
# p1 (1 - p2) + p2 (1 - p1) = 41%: the unpaired case.)
for d in (0.30, 0.15, 0.08):
    n = (za + zb) ** 2 * d / (p2 - p1) ** 2
    print(f"paired, models disagree on {d:.0%} of questions: {math.ceil(n):,} questions")

# A 95% confidence interval for one accuracy (Wilson score interval).
def wilson(k, n, conf=0.95):
    q = z(0.5 + conf / 2)
    p = k / n
    centre = (p + q * q / (2 * n)) / (1 + q * q / n)
    half = q * math.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + q * q / (4 * n * n)) / (1 + q * q / n)
    return centre - half, centre + half
print()
for k, n in ((70, 100), (700, 1000), (7000, 10000)):
    lo, hi = wilson(k, n)
    print(f"{k:,} right of {n:,}: accuracy {k / n:.0%}, 95% interval {lo:.1%} to {hi:.1%} "
          f"(about ±{(hi - lo) / 2 * 100:.1f} points)")

# What matters for a comparison is the interval on the difference.
n = 500
unpaired = za * math.sqrt((p1 * (1 - p1) + p2 * (1 - p2)) / n)
paired = za * math.sqrt((0.15 - (p2 - p1) ** 2) / n)
print(f"\n{n} questions, 95% interval on the difference in accuracy: unpaired ±{unpaired * 100:.1f} points, "
      f"paired (disagreeing on 15%) ±{paired * 100:.1f} points")

# Cohen's kappa: agreement between two annotators beyond what chance gives.
# 100 answers labeled good/bad by two people:
#                  B good   B bad
#   A good           45       10
#   A bad             5       40
a = [[45, 10], [5, 40]]
n = sum(map(sum, a))
p_obs = (a[0][0] + a[1][1]) / n
pa_good, pb_good = sum(a[0]) / n, (a[0][0] + a[1][0]) / n
p_chance = pa_good * pb_good + (1 - pa_good) * (1 - pb_good)
kappa = (p_obs - p_chance) / (1 - p_chance)
print(f"\nCohen's kappa: observed agreement {p_obs:.2f}, chance agreement {pa_good:.2f} x {pb_good:.2f} + "
      f"{1 - pa_good:.2f} x {1 - pb_good:.2f} = {p_chance:.3f}, kappa = ({p_obs:.2f} - {p_chance:.3f}) / (1 - {p_chance:.3f}) = {kappa:.2f}")
```

```text
unpaired (different questions): 8,077 questions per model
paired, models disagree on 30% of questions: 5,887 questions
paired, models disagree on 15% of questions: 2,944 questions
paired, models disagree on 8% of questions: 1,570 questions

70 right of 100: accuracy 70%, 95% interval 60.4% to 78.1% (about ±8.8 points)
700 right of 1,000: accuracy 70%, 95% interval 67.1% to 72.8% (about ±2.8 points)
7,000 right of 10,000: accuracy 70%, 95% interval 69.1% to 70.9% (about ±0.9 points)

500 questions, 95% interval on the difference in accuracy: unpaired ±5.6 points, paired (disagreeing on 15%) ±3.4 points

Cohen's kappa: observed agreement 0.85, chance agreement 0.55 x 0.50 + 0.45 x 0.50 = 0.500, kappa = (0.85 - 0.500) / (1 - 0.500) = 0.70
```

With different questions for each model, about 8,000 each. Few evals are
that large, which is why a 2-point gap on a 500-question benchmark is
usually noise: at 500 questions, the 95% interval on the *difference*
between two models is about ±5.6 points unpaired (last line of the
output).

Scoring both models on the **same** questions helps a great deal, because
it cancels the question-to-question variation. Only the questions where
the models disagree carry information about which is better (the logic of
McNemar's test), so the sample size scales with how often they disagree:
1,570 questions if they disagree on 8% of them, 5,887 at 30%. (Two models
with independent errors at 70% and 72% would disagree on 41% of
questions: the unpaired case is the paired one with no shared
difficulty.) At 500 questions and 15% disagreement, the interval on the
difference shrinks from ±5.6 to ±3.4 points. Always compare models on the
same items, and report the paired difference with its interval: if model
B is right and A wrong on $b$ questions, and the reverse on $c$, the
difference is $(b - c)/n$, with a 95% interval of about
$\pm 1.96\sqrt{b + c - (b - c)^2/n}\,/\,n$.

Three things make real intervals wider than these formulas say.
Questions are often **clustered**: several built from one passage or one
template, which fail together, so the effective number of independent
questions is smaller; clustered standard errors account for it (Miller,
2024, argues they're often several times the naive ones). Sampling at a
temperature above zero adds **run-to-run variance**: score each question
several times, or decode greedily, and include that variance in the error
bar. And comparing many variants or many slices of an eval guarantees
some false "wins" at 5% each: correct for the number of comparisons, or
confirm a winner on fresh data.

The middle block is the interval for a single accuracy. At 100 questions,
70% means "somewhere from 60% to 78%"; at 1,000, ±2.8 points; at 10,000,
under a point. The Wilson interval used here behaves better than the
textbook $p \pm 1.96\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$ near 0% and 100% and at small $n$.

## Human evaluation and agreement

When people judge answers, they disagree, and the first thing to measure
is how much. Raw agreement is misleading, because two raters who label
most answers "good" agree often by chance. **Cohen's $\kappa$** corrects for
it:

$$
\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e},
$$

where $p_o$ is the observed agreement and $p_e$ the agreement expected if
each rater labeled at random with their own overall rates. In the worked
example above, two raters agree on 85 of 100 answers, but since each says
"good" about half the time, chance alone would give 50%, and
$\kappa = 0.70$: agreement well beyond chance, short of perfect. A common
rough reading, from Landis and Koch (1977), is that $\kappa$ above about 0.6
is substantial and above 0.8 near-perfect, but the point is less the label
than the use: if your raters reach only $\kappa = 0.4$ on a rubric, the
rubric is ambiguous, and no model, human or LLM, can be scored reliably
against it until it's fixed. Cohen's $\kappa$ is for two raters; with more,
Fleiss' $\kappa$ or Krippendorff's $\alpha$ do the same job. The same
statistic calibrates an LLM judge: compute $\kappa$ between the judge and
human raters on a labeled sample, and trust the judge only if it agrees
with people about as well as people agree with each other.

## LLM-as-judge, measured

Using a strong model to grade answers (Zheng et al., 2023) made
open-ended evaluation cheap. It comes in two forms: **pointwise**, where
the judge scores one answer against a rubric (G-Eval, Liu et al., 2023,
has it reason through rubric steps first, then averages the possible
scores weighted by the probabilities the judge gives each score token),
and **pairwise**, where it picks the better of two, usually with a tie
option. Pairwise is easier for a judge and maps directly
onto arena-style ratings; it is also where the best-known biases show up.

To measure them, a judge needs questions whose right answer is known. A
hundred two-digit multiplications, each wrong answer off by a multiple of
ten, and twenty capital cities, with each country's best-known other city
as the wrong answer, judged by Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, reading its
preference between "A" and "B" from the next-token probabilities (the
same trick G-Eval uses):

```python

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

# Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as a pairwise judge, on questions whose right answer
# is known, so its biases can be measured rather than argued about. The
# judge sees a question and two answers and is asked which is correct; its
# choice is whichever of the tokens "A" and "B" it rates more likely next.
PATH = ("/Users/tanle/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/"
        "snapshots/989aa7980e4cf806f80c7fef2b1adb7bc71aa306")
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(PATH)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(PATH, dtype=torch.float16).to("mps").eval()
A, B = tok.encode("A")[0], tok.encode("B")[0]

@torch.no_grad()
def judge(question, first, second, labels=("A", "B")):
    """Returns 1 if the judge prefers the first-shown answer, else 2.
    labels: the letters printed before the first and second answers."""
    prompt = (f"Question: {question}\n\nAnswer {labels[0]}: {first}\n\nAnswer {labels[1]}: {second}\n\n"
              "Which answer is correct? Reply with a single letter, A or B.")
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], add_generation_prompt=True,
                                  return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True)["input_ids"].to("mps")
    logits = model(ids).logits[0, -1]
    first_letter = A if labels[0] == "A" else B
    second_letter = B if labels[0] == "A" else A
    return 1 if logits[first_letter] > logits[second_letter] else 2

rng = random.Random(0)
items = []                                   # (question, right answer, wrong answer)
for _ in range(100):
    a, b = rng.randint(12, 99), rng.randint(12, 99)
    wrong = a * b + rng.choice([-1, 1]) * rng.randint(1, 9) * 10
    items.append((f"What is {a} x {b}?", str(a * b), str(wrong)))
capitals = [("Australia", "Canberra", "Sydney"), ("Canada", "Ottawa", "Toronto"), ("Brazil", "Brasilia", "Rio de Janeiro"),
            ("Turkey", "Ankara", "Istanbul"), ("Switzerland", "Bern", "Zurich"), ("Morocco", "Rabat", "Casablanca"),
            ("Nigeria", "Abuja", "Lagos"), ("Vietnam", "Hanoi", "Ho Chi Minh City"), ("New Zealand", "Wellington", "Auckland"),
            ("South Africa", "Pretoria", "Johannesburg"), ("Pakistan", "Islamabad", "Karachi"), ("Myanmar", "Naypyidaw", "Yangon"),
            ("Kazakhstan", "Astana", "Almaty"), ("Tanzania", "Dodoma", "Dar es Salaam"), ("Bolivia", "Sucre", "Santa Cruz"),
            ("Ecuador", "Quito", "Guayaquil"), ("India", "New Delhi", "Mumbai"), ("China", "Beijing", "Shanghai"),
            ("Italy", "Rome", "Milan"), ("Germany", "Berlin", "Munich")]
items += [(f"What is the capital of {c}?", r, w) for c, r, w in capitals]

def verbose(wrong):            # a wrong answer with claims of having been checked
    return (f"The answer is {wrong}. I worked this out carefully, checking each step twice, and the result is "
            f"consistent with standard references, so you can rely on {wrong} being correct.")
def padded(ans):               # the same length of padding, with no claims
    return (f"The answer is {ans}. This question asks for one value, and the reply gives that value here in "
            f"a full sentence rather than on its own, followed by this sentence, which adds nothing to {ans}.")

def rate(pairs, labels=("A", "B")):
    """Share of judgments that pick the right answer, over both orders.
    pairs: (question, answer that is right, the other answer)."""
    hits = [judge(q, r, w, labels) == 1 for q, r, w in pairs] + [judge(q, w, r, labels) == 2 for q, r, w in pairs]
    return sum(hits) / len(hits)

subsets = {"multiplication": items[:100], "capitals": items[100:]}
print(f"{len(items)} questions with a known answer: 100 two-digit multiplications, {len(capitals)} capitals\n")
print(f"{'':40s} {'multiplication':>15s} {'capitals':>9s}")
def row(name, f):
    print(f"{name:40s} " + " ".join(f"{f(v):>{w}.0%}" for v, w in zip(subsets.values(), (15, 9))), flush=True)
row("right answer first: judge right", lambda p: sum(judge(q, r, w) == 1 for q, r, w in p) / len(p))
row("right answer second: judge right", lambda p: sum(judge(q, w, r) == 2 for q, r, w in p) / len(p))
row("  same, first answer labeled B", lambda p: sum(judge(q, w, r, ("B", "A")) == 2 for q, r, w in p) / len(p))
row("right in both orders", lambda p: sum(judge(q, r, w) == 1 and judge(q, w, r) == 2 for q, r, w in p) / len(p))
row("chose the same slot both times", lambda p: sum(judge(q, r, w) == judge(q, w, r) for q, r, w in p) / len(p))
print("\nshare of judgments picking the right answer, both orders averaged:")
row("bare right vs bare wrong", lambda p: rate(p))
row("bare right vs wrong + claims of checking", lambda p: rate([(q, r, verbose(w)) for q, r, w in p]))
row("bare right vs wrong + neutral padding", lambda p: rate([(q, r, padded(w)) for q, r, w in p]))
row("right + neutral padding vs bare wrong", lambda p: rate([(q, padded(r), w) for q, r, w in p]))
```

```text
120 questions with a known answer: 100 two-digit multiplications, 20 capitals

                                          multiplication  capitals
right answer first: judge right                      99%       85%
right answer second: judge right                     12%      100%
  same, first answer labeled B                        0%       55%
right in both orders                                 12%       85%
chose the same slot both times                       87%       15%

share of judgments picking the right answer, both orders averaged:
bare right vs bare wrong                             56%       92%
bare right vs wrong + claims of checking              6%       42%
bare right vs wrong + neutral padding                48%       82%
right + neutral padding vs bare wrong                62%       95%
```

The two subsets tell different stories, and the difference is the
lesson. **On capitals, which the judge knows, it is a decent judge**: it
gives the same verdict in both orders 85% of the time, and the right
answer wins in 92% of judgments. **On multiplications, which it can't
check, position takes over**: it picks whichever answer comes first in
87% of pairs, so it's right 99% of the time when the right answer happens
to be first and 12% when it's second. Relabeling the first answer "B"
doesn't change that (0%), so the bias is toward the first position, not
the letter A. (The relabeling does confuse it on capitals, 55%: small
models are sensitive to such details.) A judge's biases come out where
the task exceeds its own ability, which is exactly when you'd most want
to rely on it.

A standard correction follows: judge every pair in both orders and count
only verdicts that agree, treating the rest as ties. Here that leaves 85%
of capital pairs decided, all correctly, and 13% of multiplication pairs,
12 points of them correctly.
It doesn't make the judge know more; it stops it from guessing.

**Claims of authority fool it more than length.** A wrong answer padded
with a neutral sentence of the same length moved the judge only a few
points (from 92% right to 82% on capitals); padding the right answer
instead helped it slightly. But the same wrong answer with two sentences
*claiming* it had been carefully checked dropped the judge to 42% on
capitals, questions it otherwise gets right, and 6% on multiplications.
Zheng et al. found weaker versions of such attacks fooled GPT-3.5 and
Claude-v1 most of the time and GPT-4 rarely: stronger judges resist
better. A third bias, **self-preference** (a judge favoring its own model's
answers), needs two model families to measure and isn't shown here.

A 1.5B model is a deliberately weak judge. Zheng et al. measured GPT-4
giving the same verdict in both orders about two-thirds of the time, on
closely matched answers where ties were allowed, so it's not directly
comparable to these numbers, but it shows strong judges are not immune.
Before trusting a judge, measure it on items with known answers or
against human labels with $\kappa$, check that it can do the task it's
judging, and correct for what you find (swap orders, strip claims and
padding, use a rubric).

## Arenas: ratings from comparisons

Chatbot Arena (Chiang et al., 2024) collects people's votes between two
anonymous models' answers and turns them into a leaderboard. The model
behind the ratings is Bradley–Terry, the same one reward models are built
on ([post 29](/posts/rlhf-from-comparisons/)): model $i$ beats model $j$
with probability $\sigma(r_i - r_j)$. Fitting the ratings to votes, with
intervals from resampling the votes:

```python

# Arena-style ratings: people compare two anonymous models' answers and vote
# for one. The Bradley-Terry model (post 29) says model i beats model j with
# probability sigmoid(r_i - r_j); fit the ratings r by maximum likelihood
# and report them on the Elo-like scale arenas use (400 / ln 10 per unit).
# Four models with known true ratings; votes on random pairs; 95% intervals
# from 200 bootstrap resamples of the votes.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
true = np.array([0.0, 0.10, 0.20, 0.60])               # in logits: small, small, small, large gaps
names = ["model A", "model B", "model C", "model D"]
SCALE = 400 / np.log(10)

def fit(i, j, win, iters=500, lr=0.5):
    """Maximum likelihood by gradient ascent; model A pinned at 0."""
    r = np.zeros(len(true))
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(r[i] - r[j])))
        g = np.zeros_like(r)
        np.add.at(g, i, win - p); np.add.at(g, j, p - win)
        r += lr * g / len(win) * len(true)
        r -= r[0]
    return r

for votes in (500, 5000, 50000):
    i = rng.integers(0, 4, votes); j = (i + rng.integers(1, 4, votes)) % 4
    win = (rng.random(votes) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(true[i] - true[j])))).astype(float)
    r = fit(i, j, win)
    boot = []
    for _ in range(200):
        k = rng.integers(0, votes, votes)
        boot.append(fit(i[k], j[k], win[k]))
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5], axis=0)
    print(f"{votes:,} votes:")
    for n, t, est, a, b in zip(names, true, r, lo, hi):
        print(f"  {n}: true {t * SCALE:5.0f}, estimated {est * SCALE:5.0f}, 95% interval {a * SCALE:5.0f} to {b * SCALE:5.0f}")
```

```text
500 votes:
  model A: true     0, estimated     0, 95% interval     0 to     0
  model B: true    17, estimated    44, 95% interval    -9 to    93
  model C: true    35, estimated    51, 95% interval    -2 to   104
  model D: true   104, estimated   133, 95% interval    73 to   184
5,000 votes:
  model A: true     0, estimated     0, 95% interval     0 to     0
  model B: true    17, estimated    19, 95% interval     5 to    38
  model C: true    35, estimated    33, 95% interval    16 to    53
  model D: true   104, estimated   102, 95% interval    87 to   120
50,000 votes:
  model A: true     0, estimated     0, 95% interval     0 to     0
  model B: true    17, estimated    17, 95% interval    11 to    22
  model C: true    35, estimated    30, 95% interval    25 to    36
  model D: true   104, estimated   100, 95% interval    95 to   105
```

With 500 votes, models A, B and C, truly 17 and 35 points apart, have
overlapping intervals about 100 points wide; their order is not
established. With 5,000 votes the point estimates fall in the true order,
but B's and C's intervals (about ±17) still overlap; with 50,000, they
narrow to about ±5 and separate. (Ratings are relative, here to model A,
so A's own uncertainty is folded into every interval; bootstrapping the
gap between two models directly gives a tighter answer for that pair.) Small gaps at the top of a
leaderboard need very many votes, and a leaderboard without intervals
invites reading noise as ranking. Arena ratings also measure what the
voters prefer, on the prompts they chose to ask, which is not the same as
correctness on your task: style and length sway votes as they sway
judges, which is why the arena now also reports ratings with style
control, a regression that removes the effect of answer length and
formatting from the fit.

## Takeaways

- Treat an eval as an instrument: validity (does it measure the decision
  you face?), reliability, and an error bar.
- Prefer programmatic checks where answers are checkable; n-gram overlap
  rewards wording, not correctness.
- Public benchmarks saturate and leak; keep a private, refreshed eval for
  your own task.
- Detecting a 2-point difference near 70% takes about 8,000 questions per
  model, or 1,500 to 6,000 when both models answer the same questions;
  always compare paired, and widen the interval for clustered questions,
  sampling variance and multiple comparisons.
- Cohen's $\kappa$ separates agreement from chance; low $\kappa$ means a
  broken rubric.
- An LLM judge must be measured, on tasks it can actually do: a 1.5B
  judge was 92% right on capitals but picked the first answer in 87% of
  multiplication pairs it couldn't check, and a claim of "carefully
  checked" made it pick a wrong capital 58% of the time. Judge both
  orders and keep only agreeing verdicts.
- Arena ratings are Bradley–Terry fits whose intervals shrink only with
  many votes; small gaps need tens of thousands.
