- Miller, [_Adding Error Bars to Evals: A Statistical Approach to Language Model Evaluations_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00640) (2024).
The [first post](/posts/learning-is-optimization/) ended with a router that
got 19 of 24 reader questions right. It used one feature: a count of words
like "cache", "batch" and "latency". Its five mistakes all had the same
cause. The feature couldn't see what the question was about, only whether
it used a particular vocabulary.

The obvious fix is to stop hand-picking the vocabulary and give the model
every word as a feature, letting it learn which ones matter. This post makes
that change, and it immediately runs into the central problem of machine
learning. The richer model fits its training questions perfectly and does
*worse* on new ones. We'll see exactly why, watch the weights run away to
infinity, and derive the two standard penalties that stop them. L2 shrinks
every weight. L1 sets most of them to exactly zero. Then we'll find that on
this data, one well-chosen feature matches all of them, and learn how to tell which differences are real when every comparison
reuses the same 200 questions.

This is post 2.1 of the series. Its sibling, 2.2, asks the question this
post only uses accuracy and loss for: how to measure a classifier honestly.

## Table of contents

## From text to features

A model can only multiply numbers, so every input has to become a vector
first. The choices made in that step, called **feature engineering**, decide
what the model is *able* to learn before training starts. A linear model can
only weigh the features it's given.

For text, the standard first representation is a **bag of words**:

1. Split each question into tokens: here, lowercase runs of letters and
   digits.
2. Build a **vocabulary** from the training questions: every distinct token
   gets a column.
3. Represent a question as a 0/1 vector, with a 1 in the column of each word
   it contains.

"Does vLLM use paged attention?" becomes a vector with ones in the columns
for *does*, *vllm*, *use*, *paged* and *attention*, and zeros everywhere
else. Each word is a category with its own dimension, as in **one-hot
encoding**. A question is the one-hot vectors of its words added together
and clipped to 1, a *multi-hot* vector. Word order is thrown away, which is
where the name comes from.

A few decisions hide in those three steps, each of which matters:

- **Presence or counts.** We use 0/1 presence. Counts matter for long
  documents, but a word rarely repeats in a one-sentence question.
- **The vocabulary comes from training data only.** A word that first
  appears in a new question has no column, so it's silently dropped. That's
  correct, since the model has no weight for it, and it has a large
  consequence for the Vietnamese questions in post 2.2.
- **What counts as a token.** Our rule splits "TensorRT-LLM" into
  *tensorrt* and *llm*, and treats "token" and "tokens" as unrelated words.
  Better tokenization (stemming, subwords) is itself feature engineering.
  The [BPE post](/posts/bpe-tokenizer-explained/) covers how language models
  do it.
- **Weighting.** Classic retrieval systems down-weight words that appear
  everywhere, like *the* or *how*, with **TF-IDF**. We keep plain 0/1 and
  let the model learn weights, which turns out to have a cost.

### A real dataset

The router now needs more than 24 questions. This post uses 200 English
reader questions, written by hand for this series and labeled with the part
of the blog that should answer them: 50 each for **serving**,
**architecture**, **agents** and **foundations**. The first post's 24
questions are included. There are also 20 Vietnamese questions, held back
for post 2.2. The file is
[router-questions.csv](/data/notebook-assistant/router-questions.csv), and
every result below comes from it.

For now the router stays binary: serving versus everything else. So a
quarter of the questions are positive. A router that always says "not
serving" is right 75% of the time, a baseline worth keeping in mind.

```python

ROUTES = ["serving", "architecture", "agents", "foundations"]
rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("router-questions.csv")))
english = [r for r in rows if r["lang"] == "en"]
vietnamese = [r for r in rows if r["lang"] == "vi"]

def tokens(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())

def split(seed):
    """30 train / 10 validation / 10 test questions per route."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    train, val, test = [], [], []
    for route in ROUTES:
        group = [r for r in english if r["route"] == route]
        for k, i in enumerate(rng.permutation(len(group))):
            (train if k < 30 else val if k < 40 else test).append(group[i])
    return train, val, test

def featurize(train, *others):
    """Bag of words: one 0/1 column per word seen in *training* questions."""
    vocab = sorted({t for r in train for t in tokens(r["question"])})
    column = {t: j for j, t in enumerate(vocab)}
    out = []
    for rs in (train, *others):
        X = np.zeros((len(rs), len(vocab)))
        for i, r in enumerate(rs):
            for t in set(tokens(r["question"])):
                if t in column:          # words never seen in training are dropped
                    X[i, column[t]] = 1
        y = np.array([r["route"] == "serving" for r in rs], dtype=float)
        out.append((X, y))
    return out, vocab
```

Save this as `router_data.py`. The scripts below import it.

## Three sets, three jobs

Once the model can fit its training data perfectly, as this one will, the
training score says nothing about how it will do on questions it hasn't
seen. So the data is split three ways, and each part has one job.

- The **training set** (120 questions, 30 per route) is what the gradient
  sees.
- The **validation set** (40 questions) is for decisions *about* training:
  how long to train, how strong a penalty to use, which features to keep.
- The **test set** (40 questions) is looked at once, at the end, to report
  how the final model does. If it influences any decision, it stops being a
  test.

The split is **stratified**: each route contributes the same share to every
set. That keeps a random split from putting, say, most of the serving
questions in the test set.

With only 40 validation questions, one question moves accuracy by 2.5 points,
so a single split is noisy. Where it matters, results below are averaged
over **20 random splits**. This is repeated hold-out validation, a close
cousin of $k$-fold **cross-validation**, which rotates every example through
the validation role once. Both answer the same question: how much of a
difference is signal, and how much is which questions happened to land in
which set?

Averaging over splits comes with a trap, and we'll fall into it on purpose
before climbing out. The 20 splits reuse the same 200 questions, so their
results aren't independent. A standard error computed as if they were is too
small. The section [How sure are we?](#how-sure-are-we) measures by how much.

## Overfitting, watched

Train the bag-of-words router with no penalty and record both losses as it
goes. This is the same logistic regression as in post 1, with 379 weights
instead of one:

```python

from router_data import split, featurize

sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def log_loss(p, y):
    p = np.clip(p, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    return -(y * np.log(p) + (1 - y) * np.log(1 - p)).mean()

def train(X, y, lam=0.0, penalty="l2", eta=0.5, steps=4000):
    w, b = np.zeros(X.shape[1]), 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        p = sigmoid(X @ w + b)
        grad_w, grad_b = X.T @ (p - y) / len(y), (p - y).mean()
        if penalty == "l2":                   # weight decay
            w -= eta * (grad_w + lam * w)
        else:                                 # L1: step, then soft-threshold
            w -= eta * grad_w
            w = np.sign(w) * np.maximum(np.abs(w) - eta * lam, 0.0)
        b -= eta * grad_b
    return w, b

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # 1. One split, no penalty: watch training and validation loss diverge.
    (train_set, val_set, _), vocab = featurize(*split(seed=0))
    (Xtr, ytr), (Xva, yva) = train_set, val_set
    print(f"{len(vocab)} words, {len(ytr)} training questions")
    w, b = np.zeros(Xtr.shape[1]), 0.0
    for step in range(1, 25601):
        p = sigmoid(Xtr @ w + b)
        w -= 0.5 * Xtr.T @ (p - ytr) / len(ytr)
        b -= 0.5 * (p - ytr).mean()
        if step in (100, 400, 1600, 3200, 6400, 25600):
            print(f"step {step:5d}: train loss {log_loss(sigmoid(Xtr @ w + b), ytr):.4f}"
                  f"  val loss {log_loss(sigmoid(Xva @ w + b), yva):.4f}"
                  f"  |w| {np.linalg.norm(w):5.2f}")
```

```text
379 words, 120 training questions
step   100: train loss 0.2138  val loss 0.3951  |w|  4.02
step   400: train loss 0.0701  val loss 0.3196  |w|  8.32
step  1600: train loss 0.0175  val loss 0.2880  |w| 13.43
step  3200: train loss 0.0086  val loss 0.2870  |w| 16.01
step  6400: train loss 0.0043  val loss 0.2918  |w| 18.56
step 25600: train loss 0.0011  val loss 0.3117  |w| 23.64
```

Save it as `overfit.py`. Three columns, three stories:

- **Training loss** heads to zero. By step 25,600 the model assigns its
  training labels a probability of about 0.999 (the geometric mean,
  $e^{-0.0011}$).
- **Validation loss** falls until around step 2,500, then *rises*. From that
  point on, every extra step makes the model better at its 120 training
  questions and worse at new ones. That turning point is **overfitting**,
  measured.
- **The weight norm** keeps growing, and it never stops.

The last column is the real diagnosis. It's worth understanding why it
happens, because it's also the key to the fix.

### Why the weights run to infinity

There are 379 features and only 120 questions. With more dimensions than
points, there is often a hyperplane that separates the positives from the
negatives perfectly: some $w$ with $w^\top x_i + b > 0$ for every serving
question and $< 0$ for every other. Here there is: with no penalty, every one
of the 20 splits below reaches 100% training accuracy. The training data is
**linearly separable**. Now take that separating $w$ and scale it by $c > 1$. Every
logit $z_i$ gets $c$ times further from zero, on the correct side, so every
term of the log-loss shrinks:

$$
-\log \sigma(c\,z_i) \;\longrightarrow\; 0 \quad \text{as } c \to \infty \quad (z_i > 0)
$$

So the loss has no minimum at any finite $w$. It only approaches zero as
$\|w\| \to \infty$, and gradient descent obligingly walks off in that
direction forever. In the table, the norm grows by about 2.6 each time the
step count doubles, slowing roughly like $\log t$, which is what theory
predicts for gradient descent on separable data.

Large weights are how this model overfits. A weight of 5 on a word that happened to
appear in two training questions means that word alone moves the log-odds by
5, turning a probability of 0.5 into 0.99. The model becomes certain about
patterns it saw twice. On new questions, some of those certainties are
wrong, and log-loss punishes confident mistakes hardest. That's the rising
validation curve.

The first fix is already visible in the table: **stop early**, around step
2,500, where validation loss bottoms out. Early stopping works, and it's
standard when fine-tuning large models. (Pretraining is different: it usually
passes over the data about once, so it rarely gets the chance to memorize.)
But early stopping controls the weights only indirectly, through the step
count. A penalty controls them directly.

## L2: shrink every weight

Add the size of the weights to the loss:

$$
\mathcal{L}_\text{L2}(w, b) = \mathcal{L}(w, b) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\,\|w\|_2^2
$$

The penalty's gradient is $\lambda w$, so the update becomes

$$
w \leftarrow w - \eta\,(\nabla_w \mathcal{L} + \lambda w) = (1 - \eta\lambda)\,w - \eta\,\nabla_w \mathcal{L}
$$

Here $\lambda$ is the penalty strength, not the eigenvalue it stood for in
post 1. Every step first shrinks every weight by the factor $(1 -
\eta\lambda)$, then takes the usual gradient step. This is why L2 regularization is also
called **weight decay**. With $\eta = 0.5$ and $\lambda = 0.003$, each weight
loses 0.15% of itself per step unless the data keeps pushing it back. On
separable data, the pull toward infinity now meets a pull back toward zero,
and they balance at a finite $w$. The loss has a true minimum again. There's a
second, quieter benefit that connects to post 1. The penalty adds $\lambda I$
to the Hessian, so it raises every curvature eigenvalue by $\lambda$. The
flattest directions of the valley are lifted most in relative terms, which
lowers the condition number and makes gradient descent converge faster.

The bias $b$ is left out of the penalty on purpose. It sets the base rate
(here, "a quarter of questions are serving") and shrinking it toward zero
would bias every prediction toward 50%.

### Where the penalty comes from

L2 isn't an arbitrary add-on. It's what you get from a belief about the
weights *before* seeing data. Suppose each weight is drawn from a Gaussian
**prior** centered at zero, $w_j \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$. Choosing
the most probable weights given both the data and the prior is **maximum a
posteriori** (MAP) estimation:

$$
\hat w = \arg\max_w \; p(\text{data} \mid w)\, p(w)
= \arg\min_w \; \Big[ -\log p(\text{data} \mid w) + \frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\sum_j w_j^2 \Big]
$$

The first term is the log-loss, summed over examples. The second is the L2
penalty. Dividing through by $n$ to use the mean loss gives $\lambda =
1/(n\sigma^2)$. A strong penalty is a confident belief that weights are
small. As $n$ grows, the data term dominates and the prior matters less,
which is why regularization matters most exactly when data is scarce, as
it is here.

## L1: set most weights to zero

Replace the square with an absolute value:

$$
\mathcal{L}_\text{L1}(w, b) = \mathcal{L}(w, b) + \lambda\,\|w\|_1 = \mathcal{L}(w, b) + \lambda \sum_j |w_j|
$$

This looks like a small change and behaves completely differently. The
L2 penalty's pull, $\lambda w_j$, fades as a weight gets small, so weights
shrink toward zero but never reach it. The L1 penalty's pull is $\lambda$
times the sign of $w_j$: the same size whether the weight is 5 or 0.001. So
it can push a weight *all the way* to zero and hold it there.

Gradient descent can't use that gradient directly, because $|w_j|$ has no
derivative at zero, which is exactly where we want weights to land. The
clean way is to split each step in two. Take the usual gradient step on the
log-loss, getting a candidate $v_j$. Then solve the one-dimensional problem
"stay close to $v_j$, but pay $\lambda$ per unit of size":

$$
w_j = \arg\min_u \; \frac{1}{2\eta}(u - v_j)^2 + \lambda |u|
$$

For $u > 0$ the derivative is $(u - v_j)/\eta + \lambda$, which is zero at
$u = v_j - \eta\lambda$. That's only valid if $v_j > \eta\lambda$, and the
case $u < 0$ is the mirror image. Otherwise the minimum is at $u = 0$. So:

$$
w_j = \operatorname{sign}(v_j)\,\max\!\big(|v_j| - \eta\lambda,\; 0\big)
$$

This is the **soft-threshold** (the step is a *proximal gradient* step).
With $\eta = 0.5$ and $\lambda = 0.008$, the threshold is 0.004 per step. A
candidate weight of 0.30 becomes 0.296. A candidate of 0.003 becomes exactly
0. A weight at zero stays there as long as the size of its gradient is below
$\lambda$, so the pull of the data can't beat the pull of the penalty. The
`else` branch of `train()` above is this line.

The difference is easiest to see with two weights. Suppose the data alone
would put them at $v = (2,\ 0.3)$, and the loss near there is the round bowl
$\frac{1}{2}\|w - v\|^2$. Add each penalty with strength $0.5$:

- **L1** applies the soft-threshold to each coordinate: $(2 - 0.5,\ 0) =
  (1.5,\ 0)$. The small weight is not shrunk. It is *removed*.
- **L2** scales the whole vector: $w = v/(1 + 0.5) = (1.333,\ 0.2)$. Both
  weights shrink by the same factor, and neither reaches zero, however large
  $\lambda$ gets.

The prior behind L1 is the **Laplace** distribution, $p(w_j) \propto
e^{-|w_j|/s}$, which has a sharp peak at zero. It encodes the belief that
most weights *are* zero and a few are not. Geometrically, the set of
weights with $\|w\|_1 \le t$ is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the
loss's contours usually first touch a diamond at a corner, where some
coordinates are exactly zero. The L2 ball is round, with no corners to
prefer.

## The sweep

Now run both penalties at several strengths, each averaged over 20 splits:

```python

from router_data import split, featurize
from overfit import sigmoid, log_loss, train

# 2. Average every setting over 20 random splits: one 40-question
#    validation set is too small to trust on its own.
def evaluate(lam, penalty, seeds=range(20)):
    tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc, nonzero = [], [], [], []
    for seed in seeds:
        ((Xtr, ytr), (Xva, yva), _), _ = featurize(*split(seed))
        w, b = train(Xtr, ytr, lam, penalty)
        p = sigmoid(Xva @ w + b)
        tr_acc.append(((sigmoid(Xtr @ w + b) >= 0.5) == ytr).mean())
        va_loss.append(log_loss(p, yva))
        va_acc.append(((p >= 0.5) == yva).mean())
        nonzero.append((np.abs(w) > 0).sum())
    se = np.std(va_loss) / np.sqrt(len(va_loss))
    return (f"{penalty} λ={lam:<6}: train acc {np.mean(tr_acc):.3f}  "
            f"val loss {np.mean(va_loss):.3f} ± {se:.3f}  "
            f"val acc {np.mean(va_acc):.3f}  nonzero weights {np.mean(nonzero):.0f}")

for lam in [0.0, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1]:
    print(evaluate(lam, "l2"))
for lam in [0.001, 0.004, 0.008, 0.016]:
    print(evaluate(lam, "l1"))
```

```text
l2 λ=0.0   : train acc 1.000  val loss 0.480 ± 0.034  val acc 0.818  nonzero weights 383
l2 λ=0.001 : train acc 1.000  val loss 0.421 ± 0.021  val acc 0.804  nonzero weights 383
l2 λ=0.003 : train acc 1.000  val loss 0.416 ± 0.015  val acc 0.794  nonzero weights 383
l2 λ=0.01  : train acc 0.987  val loss 0.435 ± 0.010  val acc 0.784  nonzero weights 383
l2 λ=0.03  : train acc 0.887  val loss 0.473 ± 0.006  val acc 0.753  nonzero weights 383
l2 λ=0.1   : train acc 0.751  val loss 0.516 ± 0.002  val acc 0.750  nonzero weights 383
l1 λ=0.001 : train acc 1.000  val loss 0.530 ± 0.029  val acc 0.790  nonzero weights 112
l1 λ=0.004 : train acc 1.000  val loss 0.514 ± 0.022  val acc 0.767  nonzero weights 51
l1 λ=0.008 : train acc 0.893  val loss 0.502 ± 0.012  val acc 0.768  nonzero weights 27
l1 λ=0.016 : train acc 0.772  val loss 0.532 ± 0.005  val acc 0.742  nonzero weights 10
```

(The vocabulary is rebuilt from each split's training questions, so it
averages 383 words rather than split 0's 379.)

One caution before reading the table. Every run stops at 4,000 steps, so the
"no penalty" row is not the limit it looks like. It's *early-stopped*, and
early stopping is itself a regularizer. Train that model 4× longer and its
validation loss is 0.548, not 0.480 (the next section shows it). The two
weakest L1 settings haven't converged either. At 16,000 steps, $\lambda =
0.001$ keeps 73 weights, not 112. The L2 rows are converged, and
$\lambda = 0.003$ is identical at 16,000 steps.

**L2 traces the classic U.** Validation loss falls from 0.480 with no
penalty to 0.416 at $\lambda = 0.003$, then climbs as the penalty starts
erasing real signal. At $\lambda = 0.1$ the model has decayed almost to
"always predict the base rate". Its training accuracy is 0.751, barely above
the 0.75 that answer gets. Too little penalty overfits, and too much
**underfits**, failing to learn even the training data.

**Accuracy doesn't follow the loss.** This is the surprise in the table. The
best-loss setting, $\lambda = 0.003$, has *lower* validation accuracy
(0.794) than no penalty at all (0.818). Accuracy only asks which side of 0.5
each prediction falls on. Log-loss also asks how *confident* the prediction
was. Unpenalized weights are huge, so the model's wrong answers come with
probabilities like 0.99. L2 mostly fixes that confidence without changing
many decisions. Which of the two numbers you should optimize depends on
whether anything downstream uses the probability. For a router that falls
back to a slower, more careful search when it's unsure, the probability is
the whole point. That's the subject of post 2.2.

Notice also the ± column. The unpenalized model's validation loss varies a
lot from split to split (± 0.034), and the spread falls steadily as
$\lambda$ grows. That column is only a rough proxy for what regularization
is for. It measures how much the *result* depends on which questions landed
where. The **variance** in the bias–variance trade-off is narrower: how much
the model's prediction for a fixed question would move if it were trained on
a different sample of 120 questions. Regularization trades a little
**bias** (weights pulled away from what the data wants) for less of that
variance, and the column shrinks for the same reason. Every regularizer,
including early stopping, dropout, and data augmentation later in the
series, makes that trade in some form.

**L1 is sparser, and worse here.** At $\lambda = 0.008$ it keeps 27 of 383
weights on average (30 on the split below) and reaches a validation loss of
0.502, clearly worse than L2's 0.416. In fact every L1 setting is worse even
than the early-stopped no-penalty row. With many weak, correlated words that
each carry a little evidence, L1 keeps one word from each group and drops
the rest, where L2 spreads the weight across all of them. (The **elastic
net** adds both penalties to get sparsity without that loss.) L1's choice is
also unstable: which of two correlated words survives can flip from one split
to the next. So the list below is one split's answer, not a property of the
data. Still, it's the most revealing output in this post:

```python

from router_data import split, featurize, tokens
from overfit import sigmoid, log_loss, train

# 3. Which words does L1 keep? (one split, λ = 0.008)
((Xtr, ytr), _, _), vocab = featurize(*split(seed=0))
w, b = train(Xtr, ytr, 0.008, "l1")
kept = sorted((w[j], vocab[j]) for j in np.flatnonzero(w))
print(f"{len(kept)} of {len(vocab)} weights are nonzero; those of size >= 0.01:")
print("toward serving:", ", ".join(f"{t} {v:+.2f}" for v, t in kept[::-1] if v >= 0.01))
print("away:          ", ", ".join(f"{t} {v:+.2f}" for v, t in kept if v <= -0.01))
```

```text
30 of 379 weights are nonzero; those of size >= 0.01:
toward serving: batching +1.70, to +1.60, token +1.34, prefix +1.26, model +1.16, memory +1.14, decode +0.91, my +0.81, tokens +0.80, draft +0.74, one +0.68, vllm +0.63, request +0.61, for +0.50, does +0.33, on +0.28, throughput +0.22, cache +0.22, time +0.12
away:           agent -1.80, need -0.87, what -0.74, attention -0.39, how -0.37, should -0.12, layer -0.02
```

Half of these are what a person would pick: *batching*, *prefix*, *decode*,
*vllm*, *throughput* toward serving, and *agent*, *layer* away. The other
half are words like *to*, *my*, *one*, *what* and *how*, which carry no
meaning about the topic. Some reflect mild phrasing habits: *to* appears in 7
of the 50 serving questions and in only 3–4 of each other route's 50, from
questions like "How do I stream tokens to the browser?". Others are pure
accident. *my* appears in 3 serving questions and 5 others across the whole
dataset, but split 0's training sample happened to put it mostly with
serving, so this split learned *my* as serving evidence. With 120 training
questions, the model can't tell a real correlation from a lucky draw, and
some of these would reverse on a different sample.

Two lessons in one output:

- **Sparsity makes a model readable.** You can inspect 30 weights, not 383.
  That's how we found the problem in the first place.
- **Readable doesn't mean right.** What you read is what the data taught,
  including its accidents.

## One good feature matches 379

Post 1's router used one feature: the count of 18 hand-picked serving words.
How does it compare on exactly the same splits? This block continues the
previous one (save both as `compare.py`):

```python
# 4. Post 1's hand-picked keyword count vs the learned bag of words.
SERVING = {"kv", "cache", "caching", "batch", "batching", "latency",
           "throughput", "serve", "serving", "vllm", "sglang", "tensorrt",
           "gpu", "decode", "prefill", "paged", "quantization", "memory"}
def hits(rs, words=SERVING):
    return np.array([[sum(t in words for t in tokens(r["question"]))]
                     for r in rs], dtype=float)
scores = {"keyword count": [], "keyword count, seen words only": [],
          "bag of words": [], "both": []}
for seed in range(20):
    tr, va, te = split(seed)
    ((Xtr, ytr), (Xva, yva), _), vocab = featurize(tr, va, te)
    seen = SERVING & set(vocab)             # keywords that occur in training
    designs = {"keyword count": (hits(tr), hits(va), 0.0),
               "keyword count, seen words only": (hits(tr, seen), hits(va, seen), 0.0),
               "bag of words": (Xtr, Xva, 0.003),
               "both": (np.c_[Xtr, hits(tr)], np.c_[Xva, hits(va)], 0.003)}
    for name, (A, B, lam) in designs.items():
        w, b = train(A, ytr, lam)
        p = sigmoid(B @ w + b)
        scores[name].append((log_loss(p, yva), ((p >= 0.5) == yva).mean()))
for name, s in scores.items():
    s = np.array(s)
    print(f"{name:31s} val loss {s[:, 0].mean():.3f}  val acc {s[:, 1].mean():.3f}")
```

```text
keyword count                   val loss 0.381  val acc 0.878
keyword count, seen words only  val loss 0.436  val acc 0.851
bag of words                    val loss 0.416  val acc 0.794
both                            val loss 0.347  val acc 0.866
```

On average the single keyword feature does at least as well as the
best-regularized bag of words: 0.381 against 0.416 in loss, 0.878 against
0.794 in accuracy. It has just two parameters, a weight and a bias, so it has
almost no room to overfit the training questions. (The list itself, though,
was chosen by someone who had seen them.)

Where does its edge come from? The second row answers that. Restrict the
keyword list to words that actually occur in each split's training questions
and it scores **0.436**, *worse* than the bag of words. So the edge comes
from keywords that appear in *no* training question at all, about 2.7 of the
18 per split, like *sglang* or *prefill*. The bag of words can only learn
weights for words it has seen, and a hand-written list can know about words
the training data never showed. That's the real lesson: with little data,
**knowledge built into a feature can supply what the data doesn't contain**.

Two cautions keep this honest.

- **The edge is small and rests on a few questions.** Those unseen keywords
  hit about 2 of the 40 validation questions per split. The next section
  shows that differences this size are within the noise.
- **The same person wrote the keyword list and the questions**, so this
  dataset may flatter the list.

Treat the comparison as an illustration of the principle, not proof of it.
Real readers' questions will be the proper test.

**Both** features together give the lowest loss, 0.347, though slightly
lower accuracy (0.866) than the keywords alone. That accuracy difference is
noise at this sample size. The keyword count carries prior knowledge, and the
bag of words picks up what the list missed.

## How sure are we?

Every comparison so far is an average over the same 20 splits. How big does a
difference have to be before we believe it? The usual recipe is to compute
the standard deviation of the 20 results and divide by $\sqrt{20}$. That
assumes the 20 are independent, and they aren't. Every split draws from the
same 200 questions, so a question that happens to be hard for everyone pulls
all 20 results the same way. Nadeau and Bengio worked out a correction for
exactly this setting. Multiply the variance of the per-split *differences* by
$\frac{1}{J} + \frac{n_\text{val}}{n_\text{train}}$ instead of
$\frac{1}{J}$, where $J = 20$ splits. Here that makes the standard error
**2.8 times larger**:

```python

from router_data import split, featurize
from overfit import sigmoid, log_loss, train

# 6. How sure are we? Compare two settings on the same 20 splits (paired),
#    with the Nadeau-Bengio correction for splits that share questions.
def val_loss(lam, steps=4000):
    out = []
    for seed in range(20):
        ((Xtr, ytr), (Xva, yva), _), _ = featurize(*split(seed))
        w, b = train(Xtr, ytr, lam, steps=steps)
        out.append(log_loss(sigmoid(Xva @ w + b), yva))
    return np.array(out)

def compare(a, b, label):
    d = a - b
    naive = d.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(d))
    honest = d.std(ddof=1) * np.sqrt(1 / len(d) + 40 / 120)   # n_val / n_train
    print(f"{label:37s} {d.mean():+.3f}   naive SE {naive:.3f}   corrected SE {honest:.3f}")

l2 = val_loss(0.003)
compare(l2, val_loss(0.0), "L2 0.003 - no penalty (4,000 steps)")
compare(l2, val_loss(0.0, steps=16000), "L2 0.003 - no penalty (16,000 steps)")
compare(l2, val_loss(0.001), "L2 0.003 - L2 0.001")
compare(l2, val_loss(0.01), "L2 0.003 - L2 0.01")
```

```text
L2 0.003 - no penalty (4,000 steps)   -0.064   naive SE 0.020   corrected SE 0.055
L2 0.003 - no penalty (16,000 steps)  -0.131   naive SE 0.030   corrected SE 0.082
L2 0.003 - L2 0.001                   -0.005   naive SE 0.006   corrected SE 0.017
L2 0.003 - L2 0.01                    -0.019   naive SE 0.006   corrected SE 0.016
```

Save it as `honest.py`. Read the corrected column and several conclusions
soften.

- **L2 versus no penalty.** Against the early-stopped no-penalty model, L2's
  gain is 0.064 ± 0.055, barely more than one standard error: suggestive,
  not decisive. Against the same model trained to 16,000 steps, the gain is
  0.131 ± 0.082. That's the fair comparison, because longer training is
  what "no penalty" means, and it's the clearer result.
- **The exact λ.** 0.003 versus 0.001 or 0.01 is a tie. The U-shape is real,
  but its bottom is flat.
- **The features.** The same correction puts the keyword-versus-bag-of-words
  gap at 0.036 ± 0.050, a tie. *Both* versus the keywords alone is 0.034 ±
  0.030.

The general rule for data this size: treat differences under about 0.03 in
log-loss as ties, and report error bars that account for reused data. The
shape of the results is solid: overfitting without a penalty, a U-shaped
sweep, L1 sparsity. Most of the small margins between settings are not.

## Don't let the test set make decisions

What if we skip the validation set and pick $\lambda$ by the test set
directly? To isolate the effect of *where* the choice is made, both sides use
the same criterion, log-loss, and both report log-loss on the test set:

```python

from router_data import split, featurize
from overfit import sigmoid, log_loss, train

# 5. Choose λ by the test set instead of the validation set, using the SAME
#    criterion (log-loss) on both sides, and report test log-loss.
LAMBDAS = [0.0, 0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1]
peek = []
for seed in range(20):
    ((Xtr, ytr), (Xva, yva), (Xte, yte)), _ = featurize(*split(seed))
    fits = [train(Xtr, ytr, lam) for lam in LAMBDAS]
    test_loss = [log_loss(sigmoid(Xte @ w + b), yte) for w, b in fits]
    val_loss = [log_loss(sigmoid(Xva @ w + b), yva) for w, b in fits]
    peek.append((min(test_loss), test_loss[int(np.argmin(val_loss))]))
peek = np.array(peek)
print(f"test loss, λ chosen on test: {peek[:, 0].mean():.3f};"
      f" chosen on validation: {peek[:, 1].mean():.3f}")
```

```text
test loss, λ chosen on test: 0.403; chosen on validation: 0.439
```

Save it as `peek.py`. Choosing on the test set reports a test loss of 0.403.
Choosing honestly on validation and then measuring on test reports 0.439.
The 0.036 gap isn't a better model. It's the *selection* fitting the noise
in 40 test questions. Among six settings, one will do a little better on
this particular test set by chance, and picking it bakes that luck into the
reported number. Six settings on one split already inflate the result. A
real project that tunes dozens of choices against the same test set can
inflate it much further.

This is a form of **leakage**: information about the evaluation data
reaching the model through a decision rather than through training. The
common forms:

- **tuning on the test set**, as above;
- **duplicates and near-duplicates across splits**, such as the same
  question reworded, which make the test set partly a training set;
- **preprocessing on all the data**: computing the standardization mean, or
  a vocabulary with IDF weights, from rows that include the test set;
- **features that exist only in hindsight**, like a game's final move count
  used to predict its winner.

The [chess post](/posts/disciplined-ml-chess-outcomes/#encoding-the-leakage-contract-as-code)
encodes that last kind as a written contract that the pipeline enforces.
The general rule is simple: every decision uses training and validation data
only, and the test set is touched once.

## Where this leads

- **How good is the combined router, really?** Accuracy treats every mistake the same, and
  a quarter of the questions are positive, so "always no" already scores
  0.75. Post 2.2 measures the router with precision, recall and a confusion
  matrix, picks a threshold by what each mistake costs, and asks whether its
  probabilities can be trusted (calibration, which is exactly what L2
  improved here). It also runs the router on the 20 Vietnamese questions,
  whose words aren't in its vocabulary at all.
- **Features the model builds itself.** Both of this post's lessons, that
  features cap a linear model and that a hand-built feature matched learned
  ones, point the same way. We want a model that learns its *own* features
  from raw input. That's a neural network, and training one needs
  backpropagation (post 3).
- **Weight decay grows up.** L2 is the weight decay that appears, in its
  corrected form, in the AdamW optimizer (post 4.1). Dropout (post 4.2) is
  another regularizer that makes the same bias–variance trade.
- **Words as vectors.** A bag of words treats *token* and *tokens*, or
  *cache* and *caching*, as unrelated. Embeddings (Part II) put related words
  near each other, so knowledge about one transfers to the other.

> [!note] The Notebook Assistant, step 2
> The router now has two kinds of features: the 18-word keyword count from
> post 1, and a bag of words over the training vocabulary with an L2 penalty
> ($\lambda = 0.003$). Together they reach a validation log-loss of 0.347,
> the lowest of anything tried here. That number is optimistic, because the
> design and $\lambda$ were both chosen on it. On held-out test questions,
> which post 2.2 uses, the same router scores 0.333. It's trained on 120
> hand-labeled English questions from a 200-question dataset that the rest
> of the series reuses.

## Takeaways

- Features decide what a model *can* learn. A bag of words turns text into a
  0/1 vector over the training vocabulary, and drops any word it hasn't
  seen.
- Split the data by job. Training fits, validation decides, and test reports
  once. With small sets, average over many splits. The splits share data,
  though, so correct the standard error for it: here it was 2.8× too small.
- With more features than examples, the data is usually linearly separable.
  The log-loss then has no finite minimum, and gradient descent walks the
  weights toward infinity: training loss goes to 0 while validation loss
  turns back up. That is overfitting.
- L2 adds $\frac{\lambda}{2}\|w\|^2$, which is weight decay and a Gaussian
  prior. It restores a finite minimum and adds $\lambda$ to every curvature
  eigenvalue. Against unpenalized training run to 16,000 steps it cut
  validation loss by 0.131 ± 0.082, mostly by taming overconfidence rather
  than by changing decisions. Early stopping at 4,000 steps got part of the
  way on its own.
- L1 adds $\lambda\|w\|_1$, a Laplace prior. The soft-threshold step
  $\operatorname{sign}(v)\max(|v| - \eta\lambda, 0)$ sets most weights to
  exactly zero, which makes the model readable. Reading it exposed words like
  *to* and *my* that mean nothing. Here every L1 setting lost to L2, because
  L1 keeps one of each group of correlated weak words.
- One feature with domain knowledge (0.381) matched 383 learned ones (0.416,
  a tie within the corrected error). Its edge came from keywords that no
  training question contained. Combining both did best (0.347).
- Choosing a setting by the test set made the test loss look 0.036 better
  than an honest choice. That is leakage through a decision.

  and the combined L1 + L2 penalty.

  (ACM TKDD, 2012) — a taxonomy of leakage.

  (Information Processing & Management, 1988) — bag-of-words weighting and
  TF-IDF.
- Hastie, Tibshirani and Friedman, [_The Elements of Statistical Learning_](https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/)
  (2nd ed., 2009) — shrinkage methods (§3.4) and cross-validation (§7.10).
Attention, written the way [post 11](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/)
derived it, is three steps: scores $S = QK^\top / \sqrt{d}$, weights $P =
\operatorname{softmax}(S)$ row by row, output $O = PV$. For a sequence of
$n$ tokens, $S$ and $P$ are $n \times n$ matrices. At 32,768 tokens that's
a billion numbers per head, per layer: 2 GiB in 16-bit floats, for one
head of one layer of one sequence.

Nothing about the *output* needs that matrix to exist all at once. Each
output row is a weighted average of value rows, and FlashAttention (Dao et
al., 2022) computes it while looking at only a block of keys at a time,
never storing $S$ or $P$. It isn't an approximation: the result is the
same attention, to the last few bits of floating point. What it changes is
how much the GPU has to move between its large slow memory and its small
fast one, which [post 6](/posts/how-a-gpu-runs-deep-learning/) showed is
usually what decides the speed.

## Table of contents

## Where standard attention's time goes

A GPU has two kinds of memory ([post 6](/posts/how-a-gpu-runs-deep-learning/)). **HBM**, the GPU's main memory,
holds tens of gigabytes and delivers about 3.35 TB/s on an H100. **SRAM**,
the shared memory inside each streaming multiprocessor, holds up to 228 KB
per SM on an H100 and is roughly ten times faster: on the A100 the
FlashAttention paper used, 192 KB per SM, it estimates about 19 TB/s across
all SMs against 1.5–2.0 TB/s for HBM. Arithmetic happens on data in
registers and SRAM; anything bigger lives in HBM and has to be brought in.

A straightforward implementation runs attention as separate operations,
each reading its inputs from HBM and writing its result back: the matrix
multiply writes $S$, the softmax reads $S$ and writes $P$, the second
multiply reads $P$. Counted for one head, in 16-bit numbers, against what
FlashAttention moves:

```python
# Memory traffic of one attention head's forward pass, in 16-bit numbers
# (2 bytes each), for sequence length n and head size d.
#
# Standard attention runs three separate kernels, and each one reads its
# inputs from GPU memory (HBM) and writes its result back:
#   S = Q K^T       reads Q, K (2nd), writes S (n^2)
#   P = softmax(S)  reads S, writes P (2 n^2)
#   O = P V         reads P, V (n^2 + nd), writes O (nd)
#
# FlashAttention, in the loop order FlashAttention-2 uses, keeps a block of
# B_r query rows in fast on-chip memory and streams K and V past it in
# blocks: Q and O cross HBM once, K and V once per block of query rows, and
# S and P never do. (This charges every re-read of K and V to HBM, a worst
# case: on a real GPU many of them hit the L2 cache.)
H100_SMEM = 228 * 1024                                    # bytes of shared memory per SM (post 6)

def standard(n, d):
    return 2 * (2 * n * d + n * n + 2 * n * n + n * n + n * d + n * d)

def flash(n, d, B_r):
    return 2 * (2 * n * d + (n // B_r) * 2 * n * d)       # Q and O once; K and V once per row block

d = 128
B_r = 128                                                 # 128 query rows of 128: 32 KB in 16 bits; fits with K, V blocks
                                                          # (the score tile and output accumulator live in registers)
print(f"one block of Q, K and V at {B_r} x {d} in 16 bits: {3 * B_r * d * 2 / 1024:.0f} KB of the {H100_SMEM // 1024} KB")
for n in (4096, 32768, 131072):
    s, f = standard(n, d), flash(n, d, B_r)
    print(f"n = {n:>7,}: standard {s / 2**20:9,.0f} MiB, flash {f / 2**20:7,.0f} MiB ({s / f:4.1f}x less); "
          f"the score matrix alone {n * n * 2 / 2**20:9,.0f} MiB per head")

# Bigger on-chip memory means bigger row blocks and fewer passes over K and V.
n = 32768
print(f"n = {n:,}: flash traffic with row blocks of " + ", ".join(
    f"{b}: {flash(n, d, b) / 2**20:,.0f} MiB" for b in (64, 128, 256)))

# What training keeps for the backward pass: standard attention saves P,
# n^2 numbers per head; FlashAttention saves only O and one number per row
# (the softmax's log-sum-exp) and recomputes the blocks of P when needed.
for n in (4096, 32768):
    print(f"n = {n:>6,}: saved for backward per head: standard {n * n * 2 / 2**20:7,.0f} MiB, "
          f"flash {(n * d + n) * 2 / 2**20:5.1f} MiB")
```

```text
one block of Q, K and V at 128 x 128 in 16 bits: 96 KB of the 228 KB
n =   4,096: standard       132 MiB, flash      66 MiB ( 2.0x less); the score matrix alone        32 MiB per head
n =  32,768: standard     8,224 MiB, flash   4,112 MiB ( 2.0x less); the score matrix alone     2,048 MiB per head
n = 131,072: standard   131,200 MiB, flash  65,600 MiB ( 2.0x less); the score matrix alone    32,768 MiB per head
n = 32,768: flash traffic with row blocks of 64: 8,208 MiB, 128: 4,112 MiB, 256: 2,064 MiB
n =  4,096: saved for backward per head: standard      32 MiB, flash   1.0 MiB
n = 32,768: saved for backward per head: standard   2,048 MiB, flash   8.1 MiB
```

Three things in that output:
- **The score matrix dominates.** At 4,096 tokens it's 32 MiB per head; at
  32,768, 2 GiB; at 131,072, 32 GiB, for one head; a 32-head layer
  computed at once would need about a terabyte. Everything else attention touches, $Q$, $K$, $V$ and $O$, is $n
  \times d$, a few MiB.
- **The traffic falls, by a factor set by the block size.** FlashAttention
  still reads $K$ and $V$ many times, once per block of query rows, so its
  traffic grows as $n^2 d / B_r$: with 128-row blocks it's half the
  standard count here, with 256-row blocks a quarter. This count is a
  worst case: it charges every re-read of $K$ and $V$ to HBM, while thread
  blocks working on neighbouring query blocks stream the same tiles at
  about the same time, so many re-reads are served from the 50 MB L2
  cache. Measured, the paper's GPT-2 medium attention moved 4.4 GB against
  standard attention's 40.3 GB. The bigger the
  on-chip memory, the bigger the blocks and the fewer the passes; the
  paper states it as $\Theta(n^2 d^2 / M)$ bytes for an SRAM of $M$ bytes,
  against $\Theta(nd + n^2)$ for standard attention.
- **The storage falls much more.** For training, standard attention keeps
  $P$ for the backward pass: $n^2$ numbers per head. FlashAttention keeps
  the output it produces anyway plus one number per row, about 64 KB at
  32,768 tokens, instead of $P$'s 2 GiB.

(This count is for unfused kernels in 16-bit numbers; real implementations
fuse some steps and often keep scores in 32 bits. The shape of the
comparison doesn't change.)

## The obstacle: softmax needs the whole row

The reason the standard version materializes $S$ is softmax. Row $i$ of
the output is

$$
O_i = \sum_j \frac{e^{S_{ij}}}{\sum_k e^{S_{ik}}} V_j
$$

and the denominator sums over *every* key. You can't finish weighting
the first value until you've seen the last score. Worse, a stable softmax
([post 3.2](/posts/softmax-and-cross-entropy/)) subtracts the row's
maximum before exponentiating, and the maximum is also known only at the
end. So the obvious order is: compute the whole row of scores, find its
max, exponentiate, sum, divide, multiply by $V$. Each step needs the whole
row, and a row is $n$ numbers.

## The online softmax

The way out is to keep a summary that can be corrected later. Process the
keys in blocks, and for each query row keep three running quantities:
$m$, the largest score seen so far; $\ell$, the sum of $e^{S_{ij} - m}$
over keys seen so far; and $o$, the sum of $e^{S_{ij} - m} V_j$ over the
same keys. When a new block arrives with scores $s$:

$$
m' = \max(m, \max_j s_j), \qquad
\ell' = \ell\, e^{m - m'} + \sum_j e^{s_j - m'}, \qquad
o' = o\, e^{m - m'} + \sum_j e^{s_j - m'} V_j
$$

The factor $e^{m - m'}$ is the correction: everything accumulated so far
was computed relative to the old maximum, and multiplying by it re-expresses
it relative to the new one. If the max didn't change, the factor is 1.
After the last block, $o / \ell$ is exactly the softmax-weighted average,
because $o$ and $\ell$ are the numerator and denominator of the formula
above, both scaled by the same $e^{-m}$, which cancels. (The running
normalizer is Milakov and Gimelshein's, 2018; carrying $o$ along with it
is Rabe and Staats', 2021, and FlashAttention's.)

A worked example first, with one query and four keys in two blocks, then
the same thing at full size, against standard attention:

```python

# Attention one block of keys at a time, never holding a full row of scores.
# The running state per query row: m, the largest score seen so far; l, the
# sum of exp(score - m) so far; o, the weighted sum of values so far, also
# relative to m. When a new block raises the max from m to m', everything
# accumulated is rescaled by exp(m - m') (Milakov and Gimelshein, 2018).
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def attention(Q, K, V):
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(Q.shape[1])                     # the full n x n score matrix
    P = np.exp(S - S.max(1, keepdims=True))
    return (P / P.sum(1, keepdims=True)) @ V

def tiled_attention(Q, K, V, block):
    n, d = Q.shape
    m = np.full(n, -np.inf)                               # running max per row
    l = np.zeros(n)                                       # running sum of exponentials
    o = np.zeros((n, V.shape[1]))                         # running (unnormalized) output
    for j in range(0, K.shape[0], block):
        S = Q @ K[j:j + block].T / np.sqrt(d)             # only n x block scores at a time
        m_new = np.maximum(m, S.max(1))
        scale = np.exp(m - m_new)                         # how much the old max overstated
        P = np.exp(S - m_new[:, None])
        l = l * scale + P.sum(1)
        o = o * scale[:, None] + P @ V[j:j + block]
        m = m_new
    return o / l[:, None]

# The worked example: one query, four keys, two blocks of two.
q = np.array([[1.0, 0.0]])
k = np.array([[2.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], [4.0, 0.0], [0.0, 0.0]]) * np.sqrt(2)   # scores 2, 1, 4, 0
v = np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [4.0]])
s = (q @ k.T / np.sqrt(2))[0]
print("scores", s, "-> softmax", np.round(np.exp(s - s.max()) / np.exp(s - s.max()).sum(), 4))
m, l, o = -np.inf, 0.0, 0.0
for j, blk in enumerate(((0, 1), (2, 3))):
    sb = s[list(blk)]
    m_new = max(m, sb.max())
    scale = np.exp(m - m_new)
    p = np.exp(sb - m_new)
    l, o, m = l * scale + p.sum(), o * scale + (p * v[list(blk), 0]).sum(), m_new
    print(f"after block {j + 1}: max {m:.0f}, sum {l:.4f}, output so far {o:.4f} -> {o / l:.4f}")
print(f"standard attention gives {attention(q, k, v)[0, 0]:.4f}")

for n, d, block in ((1024, 64, 128), (4096, 128, 256)):
    Q, K, V = (rng.normal(size=(n, d)) for _ in range(3))
    err = np.abs(tiled_attention(Q, K, V, block) - attention(Q, K, V)).max()
    print(f"n = {n}, d = {d}, blocks of {block}: largest difference from standard attention {err:.1e}")
```

```text
scores [2. 1. 4. 0.] -> softmax [0.1125 0.0414 0.831  0.0152]
after block 1: max 2, sum 1.3679, output so far 1.7358 -> 1.2689
after block 2: max 4, sum 1.2034, output so far 3.3082 -> 2.7489
standard attention gives 2.7489
n = 1024, d = 64, blocks of 128: largest difference from standard attention 7.8e-16
n = 4096, d = 128, blocks of 256: largest difference from standard attention 6.8e-16
```

In the worked example the first block sees scores 2 and 1, so $m = 2$
and the running answer is 1.27, a weighted average of the first two values.
The second block brings a score of 4: the max rises to 4, the first block's
contributions are scaled down by $e^{2 - 4} = 0.135$, the new block is
added, and the result, 2.7489, is the exact softmax average. At full size
the tiled version and the standard one agree to $10^{-15}$: the same
answer up to the order of floating-point additions. Step through it, with
blocks of different sizes; the answer at the end never changes:

## FlashAttention: tiles in fast memory

FlashAttention combines the online softmax with **tiling**. Here it is in
the form FlashAttention-2 settled on, which is how it's usually taught.
Each block of GPU threads takes a block of $B_r$ query rows: the queries
go into shared memory, their running $m$, $\ell$ and $o$ into registers.
It then streams the keys and values through in blocks of $B_c$ rows: load
a block of $K$ and $V$ into shared memory, compute that block's $B_r \times
B_c$ scores, update the running quantities, discard the scores, load the
next block. When all the keys have passed, it divides $o$ by $\ell$ and
writes the output rows to HBM. (The 2022 original put the loops the other
way round: it streamed blocks of $K$ and $V$ in the outer loop and, for
each one, revisited every block of queries, reading and rewriting their
partial outputs in HBM. Both orders move $\Theta(n^2 d^2 / M)$ bytes;
swapping them is part of what made version 2 faster.)

<figure>
<svg viewBox="0 0 375 230" role="img" aria-label="The score matrix split into a 6 by 6 grid of tiles, rows for query blocks and columns for key blocks. </figure>

The full $n \times n$ matrix never exists anywhere. At any moment, a
block of threads holds one $B_r \times B_c$ tile of it, in fast memory,
for as long as it takes to use it. The figure also shows what a **causal
mask** does to the work: a tile entirely above the diagonal, where every
key comes after every query, is skipped outright; a tile on the diagonal
is computed and masked element by element; a tile below it needs no mask.
For a language model, that skips about half the tiles. (A row that is
entirely masked needs care: with $m = -\infty$, $e^{m - m'}$ is
undefined, so implementations special-case it.)

## Measured

```python

# Standard attention (score matrix, softmax, weighted sum: three operations)
# against PyTorch's fused scaled_dot_product_attention, which on the CPU
# runs a FlashAttention-style tiled kernel. One head of size 64, 32-bit
# floats. Each measurement runs in a fresh process so its peak memory can
# be read on its own. Run on an otherwise idle machine: under memory
# pressure the standard version's big matrices get swapped, and its times
# become meaningless.
def run(kind, n, d=64):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    q, k, v = (torch.randn(1, 1, n, d) for _ in range(3))
    def standard():
        s = q @ k.transpose(-1, -2) / d ** 0.5
        return torch.softmax(s, -1) @ v
    def fused():
        return F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v)
    f = standard if kind == "standard" else fused
    f()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(3):
        out = f()
    t = (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 3
    peak = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss / 2**20        # bytes on macOS -> MiB
    print(f"{t * 1e3:.1f} {peak:.0f}")

if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    torch.set_num_threads(4)
    run(sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]))
else:
    base = None
    for n in (2048, 8192, 16384):
        row = {}
        for kind in ("standard", "fused"):
            out = subprocess.run([sys.executable, __file__, kind, str(n)], capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.split()
            row[kind] = (float(out[0]), float(out[1]))
        (ts, ms), (tf, mf) = row["standard"], row["fused"]
        print(f"n = {n:>6,}: standard {ts:7.1f} ms, peak {ms:6,.0f} MiB;  fused {tf:7.1f} ms, peak {mf:6,.0f} MiB;  "
              f"the n x n score matrix is {n * n * 4 / 2**20:5,.0f} MiB")
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    a = torch.randn(1, 1, 4096, 64); b = torch.randn(1, 1, 4096, 64); c = torch.randn(1, 1, 4096, 64)
    ref = torch.softmax(a @ b.transpose(-1, -2) / 8, -1) @ c
    print(f"largest difference between the two at n = 4,096: {(ref - F.scaled_dot_product_attention(a, b, c)).abs().max():.1e}")
```

```text
n =  2,048: standard     3.9 ms, peak    228 MiB;  fused     1.1 ms, peak    197 MiB;  the n x n score matrix is    16 MiB
n =  8,192: standard    44.4 ms, peak    716 MiB;  fused    14.7 ms, peak    206 MiB;  the n x n score matrix is   256 MiB
n = 16,384: standard   175.6 ms, peak  2,263 MiB;  fused    57.7 ms, peak    215 MiB;  the n x n score matrix is 1,024 MiB
largest difference between the two at n = 4,096: 6.6e-07
```

PyTorch's `scaled_dot_product_attention` picks a fused, tiled kernel
when one is available; on the CPU it runs a FlashAttention-style
implementation (`_scaled_dot_product_flash_attention_for_cpu`). Against the
three-step version, on one head:
- **The fused kernel is about 3 times faster at every length**, 57 ms
  against 175 at 16,384 tokens. Both do the same $n^2$ work, and both
  times grow as $n^2$; the standard version also writes a 1 GiB score
  matrix to memory, reads it back for the softmax, writes the
  probabilities and reads them again.
- **Its memory stays flat**, about 200 MiB, most of it the Python process,
  while the standard version's peak tracks the score matrix: 2.2 GiB at
  16,384 tokens, the process plus two copies of a 1 GiB matrix.
- **The two agree** to $7 \times 10^{-7}$ in 32-bit floats, rounding
  error.

(Three repeated runs agree to within a few percent. A first run, taken
while a training job filled the machine's memory, showed a 28 times gap:
the standard version's large matrices were being swapped to disk. Timings
of memory-heavy code mean nothing on a machine that's under memory
pressure. On GPUs the original paper reports GPT-2 training 3 times faster
at 1,024 tokens than the Hugging Face implementation, and BERT-large
training 15% faster than the MLPerf 1.1 record.)

## The backward pass: recompute instead of store

Training needs gradients, and the backward pass of attention needs $P$:
the softmax's gradient (post 3.2) is $dS = P \circ (dP - D)$, where $dP =
dO\, V^\top$ and $D_i$ is the row sum of $dP \circ P$. Storing $P$ is
exactly what FlashAttention avoided, so it doesn't. It keeps the output
$O$ and one number per row, the log-sum-exp $m + \log \ell$. The row sum
$D_i$ equals $dO_i \cdot O_i$, one dot product per row, which is why $O$ is
kept. And each tile of $P$ is rebuilt as $e^{S - \text{LSE}}$ from $Q$ and
$K$ when it's needed, with no running max, since the log-sum-exp is
already known.

That's more arithmetic: one of the forward pass's two matrix multiplies,
$QK^\top$, done again.
It's still faster, because the extra multiply runs at full speed on data
already in SRAM, while reading a stored $n \times n$ matrix from HBM
would be limited by bandwidth (post 6's roofline). Trading compute for
memory traffic is the same idea as activation checkpointing (Part VII),
at the scale of one kernel.

## FlashAttention 2 and 3, and Flash-Decoding

The math hasn't changed since 2022; the implementations have, following
the hardware.
- **FlashAttention-2** (Dao, 2023) swapped the loops, so each thread block
  owns a block of query rows, which parallelizes a long single sequence
  across the GPU's SMs as well as across batch and heads; kept $o$
  unnormalized until the end and stored only the log-sum-exp; and cut the
  work that isn't matrix multiplication, which can't use the tensor cores
  (an A100 does 312 TFLOPS of 16-bit matrix multiply but 19.5 TFLOPS of
  other 32-bit arithmetic, so each such operation costs about 16 times as
  much). About twice as fast as the first version, 50–73% of an A100's
  peak.
- **FlashAttention-3** (Shah et al., 2024) is built for the H100. Warp
  specialization splits the work: producer warps issue the asynchronous
  memory copies (TMA) while consumer warpgroups run the tensor-core
  multiplies (WGMMA). Ping-pong scheduling lets one warpgroup's softmax run
  while another's multiplies do, and within a warpgroup the softmax of one
  tile overlaps the next multiply. For FP8 it adds block quantization and
  "incoherent processing", a random rotation that spreads outliers before
  rounding. 740 TFLOPS in 16-bit, 75% of the GPU's peak, and about 1.2
  PFLOPS in FP8.
- **Flash-Decoding** (Dao et al., 2023) handles generation. When decoding,
  there is one query per sequence, so a kernel that parallelizes over
  query blocks has almost nothing to parallelize. Flash-Decoding splits the
  *keys* instead: blocks of the KV cache are processed in parallel, each
  producing its own $m$, $\ell$ and $o$, and the partial results are
  combined with the same rescaling as the online softmax. Up to 8 times
  faster decoding at long contexts. The KV cache's layout in memory, which
  this kernel reads, is the subject of [the paged attention
  post](/posts/paged-attention-explained/).

## What FlashAttention doesn't change

- **The FLOPs, asymptotically.** Attention is still $4 n^2 d$ per head in
  the forward pass, quadratic in the context. FlashAttention does somewhat
  more in training, since the backward pass recomputes $QK^\top$: about
  25% more backward and 13–17% more overall. With a causal mask it does
  about *half* as much as a naive implementation, which computes every
  score and then masks half of them, because it skips the tiles above the
  diagonal. Either way it makes long contexts affordable in memory and in
  bandwidth, not in compute. Reducing the compute is what [the attention
  alternatives](/posts/attention-alternatives/) are for.
- **The KV cache.** Generation still keeps every earlier token's keys and
  values ([post 20](/posts/kv-cache-explained/)); FlashAttention only reads
  them more efficiently.
- **The result.** It's exact attention, the same output up to the order
  of floating-point additions. Unlike sparse or linear attention, nothing
  about the model or its outputs changes, which is why it spread so
  quickly: it's a drop-in replacement. (Its backward pass can be
  nondeterministic from run to run, where gradients are summed with atomic
  additions.)

## Using it

In practice nobody writes this kernel. PyTorch's
`F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, is_causal=True)` picks a fused
backend by itself, FlashAttention, a memory-efficient kernel or cuDNN's on
NVIDIA GPUs, and falls back to the three-step version only when none
applies; the `flash_attn` package exposes the kernels directly. Things
worth knowing when using them:
- **Head sizes are limited**, to 256 in FlashAttention-2 and 3.
- **Variable-length batches** can be packed without padding: the kernels
  take the cumulative sequence lengths and keep sequences from attending
  to each other.
- **Custom masks** (sliding windows, document boundaries, prefixes) are
  what FlexAttention (Dong et al., 2024) is for: it compiles a mask or a
  score modification into a FlashAttention-style kernel.
- **Contexts too long for one GPU** are split across several with ring
  attention (Liu et al., 2023), which merges partial results with the same
  $(m, \ell, o)$ rescaling as the online softmax.
- **The most readable implementation** is Triton's fused-attention
  tutorial, about a hundred lines.

## Where this leads

- **Post 23**, the Part V capstone, reads a frontier model's design as the
  sum of this part's ideas.
- **Part XII** comes back to these kernels from the serving side: paged
  KV caches, and the batching that decides how full each kernel's work is.

## Takeaways

- Standard attention writes an $n \times n$ score matrix to GPU memory and
  reads it back: 2 GiB per head at 32,768 tokens. At long contexts that
  traffic and storage, not the arithmetic, sets the speed.
- The online softmax keeps a running max, sum and output per row, and
  rescales them by $e^{m - m'}$ when the max rises, so attention can be
  computed one block of keys at a time with an exactly equal result.
- FlashAttention tiles the computation so a block of queries stays in fast
  on-chip memory while keys and values stream past; the score matrix never
  exists, and with a causal mask the tiles above the diagonal are skipped.
  Measured here: about 3 times faster on a CPU, with memory flat
  instead of growing as $n^2$.
- The backward pass recomputes the score tiles instead of storing them:
  more arithmetic, less traffic, a good trade on a GPU.
- Versions 2 and 3 follow the hardware (loop order and work partitioning,
  Hopper's asynchrony, FP8); Flash-Decoding splits the KV cache for
  one-query decoding. None of them change attention's quadratic FLOPs or
  the KV cache's size.

[Post 29](/posts/rlhf-from-comparisons/)'s reward model was needed because
"helpful" can't be computed. Some things can. A math answer can be compared
with the known result, code can be run against tests, a response's format
can be parsed. **Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards** (RLVR)
trains on those checks directly: no human comparisons, no reward model,
and no learned reward to overoptimize. It is how DeepSeek-R1 and other
reasoning models (post 32) were trained, most often with **GRPO**, an
algorithm that removes PPO's value model.

## Table of contents

## Verifiable rewards

A verifiable reward is a program. For DeepSeek-R1 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) it
had two parts, both rule-based: an **accuracy** reward, checking the final
answer of a math problem (in a required format, such as a box) or running
code against test cases, and a **format** reward for putting the reasoning
between thinking tags. They deliberately didn't use a neural reward model,
for two reasons: as post 29 showed, a large-scale RL run will find
whatever a learned reward gets wrong, and retraining a reward model during
the run would cost compute and complicate the pipeline.

A checker can be gamed too, just differently. A test suite that doesn't
cover a case rewards code that special-cases the tests; an answer checker
that accepts any string containing the right number rewards listing many
numbers. The reward is only as good as the check.

## The group-relative advantage

[Post 28](/posts/policy-gradient-to-ppo/)'s PPO needs an advantage per
token, and estimates it with a value model as large as the policy. GRPO
(Shao et al., 2024) drops the value model. It was introduced in
DeepSeekMath with a *learned* reward model, so it isn't tied to verifiable
rewards; DeepSeek-R1 later paired it with rule-based ones.
For each question it samples a **group** of $G$ answers, scores each, and
uses the group as its own baseline:

$$
\hat{A}_i = \frac{r_i - \text{mean}(r_1, \dots, r_G)}{\text{std}(r_1, \dots, r_G)},
$$

the same advantage for every token of answer $i$. Worked with $G = 4$ and
rewards $(1, 0, 0, 1)$: the mean is 0.5 and the standard deviation 0.5
(the population form, dividing by $G$), so the two right answers get
$+1$ and the two wrong ones $-1$. With rewards $(1, 0, 0, 0)$, the mean is
0.25 and the deviation 0.433: the one right answer gets $+1.73$ and each
wrong one $-0.58$. A rare success is pushed up hard; a common failure
gently. It is post 28's mean baseline, computed over answers to the *same*
question, so that question difficulty cancels.

The objective is PPO's clipped one with this advantage, averaged over each
answer's tokens and over the group, plus a KL penalty to the reference
policy added directly to the loss, rather than to the reward as in post
29. In practice the loss takes several PPO passes over each batch, which
is why the ratio and clip still matter. For the penalty, GRPO estimates
$\text{KL}(\pi_\theta \,\|\, \pi_\text{ref})$ per token from the sampled
token's probability ratio alone, the token being drawn from the policy
(Schulman's "k3" estimator):

$$
\mathbb{D}_\text{KL} \approx \frac{\pi_\text{ref}(o_t)}{\pi_\theta(o_t)} - \log \frac{\pi_\text{ref}(o_t)}{\pi_\theta(o_t)} - 1 .
$$

Its average under $\pi_\theta$ is exactly that KL, because the ratio
$\pi_\text{ref} / \pi_\theta$ averages to 1 under $\pi_\theta$, and it is
never negative, because $x - 1 \ge \log x$. Recent work (DAPO among it)
drops the KL term altogether, on the grounds that a reasoning model is
meant to move far from where it started.

## What it saves

PPO for RLHF held four models ([post 28](/posts/policy-gradient-to-ppo/)):
policy, reference, reward model, value model. With a verifier and a group
baseline, GRPO holds two: the policy, trained, and the reference, frozen.
For a 7B policy in mixed-precision AdamW, 112 GB plus 14 GB, against about
250 GB for PPO with a 7B reward model. The cost moves elsewhere: every
question now needs $G$ sampled answers per step, typically 8 to 64, and
for reasoning models those answers are thousands of tokens long, so
generation dominates the run.

## Groups that all agree teach nothing

If every answer in a group gets the same reward, every advantage is zero
(and the standard deviation in the denominator is zero too, which
implementations guard with a small constant). The group contributes no
gradient. For a question the model gets right with probability $p$, that
happens with probability $p^G + (1 - p)^G$. At $p = 0.9$ with $G = 4$,
that's 66% of groups wasted; with $G = 16$, 19%. Larger groups keep
learning from questions the model mostly gets right or mostly gets wrong,
which is where most questions end up as training goes on. DAPO (Yu et al.,
2025) also filters such groups out and samples more questions to keep the
batch full ("dynamic sampling").

## An experiment: the length bias

Two details of GRPO's loss were questioned by Liu et al. (2025) in "Dr.
GRPO": dividing each answer's loss by its own length, and dividing the
advantage by the group's standard deviation. The first, they argued,
biases the model's length: a short answer's tokens each get a larger share
of its advantage, so short right answers are reinforced more per token
than long right ones, and long wrong answers are penalized less per token
than short wrong ones. The second creates a difficulty bias: dividing by a
small spread up-weights questions the model almost always gets right or
almost always gets wrong. A toy where length can't matter tests both, with
two hybrids that change one detail at a time. To isolate the
normalizations, every learner takes one gradient step per batch, so the
ratio and clip never come into play, and there is no KL term. The first
token can also be the end token, an empty answer, which is wrong:

```python

# GRPO on a toy with checkable answers and free length. 16 "questions";
# the answer is a sequence of up to 8 tokens from {0, 1, 2, 3}, ended by an
# end token (or cut off at 8). It is correct if its first token equals the
# question's hidden answer: reward 1, else 0. Length never affects the
# reward, so any change in length comes from the loss alone. The policy is
# a table of logits per (question, position, previous token).
# Per update: 16 questions x a group of G answers each.
#   GRPO:     advantage (R - group mean) / group std; each answer's loss is
#             its tokens' -A log pi averaged over its own length, then
#             averaged over the group (Shao et al., 2024);
#   Dr. GRPO: advantage R - group mean; token losses summed and divided by
#             a constant, the maximum length (Liu et al., 2025);
# and two hybrids that change one of the two at a time. Length counts the
# end token, so an answer that ends at once has length 1 (and is wrong).
Q, V, LMAX, END = 16, 4, 8, 4

def run(method, G, seed, updates=400, lr=0.05):
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)
    answer = torch.randint(0, V, (Q,), generator=g)
    logits = torch.zeros(Q, LMAX, V + 2, V + 1, requires_grad=True)   # prev token index V+1 = "start"
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([logits], lr=lr)
    hist = []
    for _ in range(updates):
        with torch.no_grad():                                         # sample Q x G answers
            q = torch.arange(Q).repeat_interleave(G)
            toks = torch.full((Q * G, LMAX), END)
            alive = torch.ones(Q * G, dtype=torch.bool)
            prev = torch.full((Q * G,), V + 1)
            length = torch.zeros(Q * G, dtype=torch.long)
            for t in range(LMAX):
                p = logits[q, t, prev].softmax(-1)
                a = torch.multinomial(p, 1, generator=g)[:, 0]
                toks[alive, t] = a[alive]
                length += alive.long()
                alive = alive & (a != END)
                prev = torch.where(a == END, prev, a)
        R = (toks[:, 0] == answer[q]).float()
        Rg = R.view(Q, G)
        adv = (Rg - Rg.mean(1, keepdim=True))
        if method in ("GRPO", "GRPO, summed"):
            adv = adv / (Rg.std(1, keepdim=True, unbiased=False) + 1e-4)   # population std, as in the worked example
        adv = adv.reshape(-1)
        # log-probs of the sampled tokens, recomputed with gradients
        prev = torch.cat([torch.full((Q * G, 1), V + 1), toks[:, :-1]], 1)
        for t in range(1, LMAX):                                      # an end token doesn't change "previous"
            prev[:, t] = torch.where(toks[:, t - 1] == END, prev[:, t - 1], toks[:, t - 1])
        lp = logits[q[:, None], torch.arange(LMAX)[None], prev].log_softmax(-1).gather(-1, toks[..., None])[..., 0]
        mask = torch.arange(LMAX)[None] < length[:, None]
        tok_loss = -(adv[:, None] * lp) * mask
        if method in ("GRPO", "Dr. GRPO, per answer"):
            loss = (tok_loss.sum(1) / length).mean()
        else:
            loss = tok_loss.sum(1).mean() / LMAX
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        L = length.float()
        hist.append((R.mean().item(), L[R == 1].mean().item() if (R == 1).any() else np.nan,
                     L[R == 0].mean().item() if (R == 0).any() else np.nan))
    return np.array(hist)

for G in (4, 16):
    print(f"group size {G}: accuracy / mean length of right answers / of wrong answers, 5 seeds, at update")
    print(f"{'':22s}" + "".join(f"{u:>22d}" for u in (1, 50, 100, 400)))
    for method in ("GRPO", "GRPO, summed", "Dr. GRPO, per answer", "Dr. GRPO"):
        H = np.stack([run(method, G, seed) for seed in range(5)])
        at = lambda u: np.nanmean(H[:, max(0, u - 10):u], axis=(0, 1))
        print(f"{method:22s}" + "".join(f"{at(u)[0]:8.2f} {at(u)[1]:6.2f} {at(u)[2]:6.2f}" for u in (1, 50, 100, 400)))
```

```text
group size 4: accuracy / mean length of right answers / of wrong answers, 5 seeds, at update
                                           1                    50                   100                   400
GRPO                      0.22   5.02   4.03    0.78   4.27   4.53    0.96   3.59   4.43    0.99   2.83   5.46
GRPO, summed              0.22   5.02   4.03    0.84   5.03   4.07    0.97   5.03   3.89    1.00   4.98   5.00
Dr. GRPO, per answer      0.22   5.02   4.03    0.78   4.28   4.50    0.96   3.58   4.44    0.99   2.83   5.15
Dr. GRPO                  0.22   5.02   4.03    0.84   5.02   4.03    0.97   5.04   3.83    1.00   5.00   5.46
group size 16: accuracy / mean length of right answers / of wrong answers, 5 seeds, at update
                                           1                    50                   100                   400
GRPO                      0.20   4.95   3.97    0.91   3.28   4.50    0.99   2.55   4.38    1.00   2.30   5.08
GRPO, summed              0.20   4.95   3.97    0.93   4.92   4.01    0.99   4.86   4.05    1.00   4.84   3.95
Dr. GRPO, per answer      0.20   4.95   3.97    0.91   3.26   4.51    0.98   2.62   4.57    1.00   2.35   4.58
Dr. GRPO                  0.20   4.95   3.97    0.92   4.93   3.97    0.98   4.88   3.99    1.00   4.85   3.40
```

Every learner solves the task, from about 21% right to 99% or more. But
the reward never depends on length, so an unbiased learner has no reason
to change it, and they differ:
- **Right answers get shorter with per-answer normalization, and only with
  it.** Under GRPO, from 5.0 tokens on average to 2.8 with groups of 4 and
  2.3 with groups of 16. Dr. GRPO with per-answer normalization put back
  does the same (2.8 and 2.35); GRPO with summed losses doesn't (5.0 and
  4.8), and neither does Dr. GRPO (5.0 and 4.85). Dividing by the
  standard deviation changes nothing about length, as expected: it scales
  a whole group's advantages equally. The shortening is the per-answer
  length normalization.
- **Wrong answers get longer with it.** They start at 4.0 tokens, shorter
  than right ones because empty answers are wrong. At update 50, with
  accuracy near 80% for groups of 4, wrong answers average 4.5 tokens with
  per-answer normalization and stay at 4.0 to 4.1 without it, for both
  group sizes. By update 400 wrong answers are 1% or fewer, and their
  average length is too noisy to compare.
- **Larger groups learn faster per update**, though they also sample four
  times as many answers: with 16 per question, accuracy is 98 to 99% by
  update 100, against 96 to 97% with 4, and the GRPO length drift is
  faster too (2.6 against 3.6 tokens at update 100).

In real reasoning training, the second half of the bias matters most:
wrong answers that grow longer look like the model "thinking longer" while
it isn't getting anything right. DAPO divides by the total number of
tokens in the batch; Dr. GRPO divides by a constant, the generation budget,
as the code above does. Neither divides each answer by its own length.

## What came after

- **DAPO** (Yu et al., 2025) collected four changes to GRPO for long
  reasoning: a higher upper clip bound than lower ("clip-higher", $\epsilon$
  0.2 below and 0.28 above, so that unlikely but useful tokens can grow),
  dynamic sampling, a token-level loss, and a soft penalty on answers that
  run past the length limit. It also drops the KL penalty.
- **DeepSeek-R1-Zero** (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) applied GRPO with only rule-based
  rewards to a base model, with no supervised fine-tuning first. Its pass@1
  on AIME 2024 rose from 15.6% to 71.0%, and its answers grew longer as
  training went on, which DeepSeek read as the model learning to think
  longer. Liu et al. (2025) argue part of that growth is the length bias
  measured above: with Dr. GRPO, length grows far less at similar accuracy.
  Post 32 picks up the story.

## Where this leads

- **Post 32**: reasoning models and test-time compute, what RLVR trains a
  model to do with its tokens.

## Takeaways

- When an answer can be checked by a program, RL can train on the check
  directly: no human labels, no reward model. The check can still be gamed.
- GRPO samples a group of answers per question and uses the group's mean
  (and spread) as the baseline, so it needs no value model: two models in
  memory instead of PPO's four.
- A group in which every answer gets the same reward teaches nothing:
  $p^G + (1-p)^G$ of groups, 66% at $p = 0.9$ with 4 answers.
- GRPO's per-answer length normalization biases length. On a toy where
  length never affects the reward, it shortened right answers from 5.0
  tokens to 2.3 to 2.8, and made wrong ones longer; without it, right
  answers stayed at about 5 tokens, with or without the standard
  deviation.
