Part III built a Transformer the way it's built in 2026, and along the way
it kept saying "the 2017 paper did X; modern models do Y". This post
collects those changes in one place. The striking thing about them is how
few there are. GPT-2's diagram from 2019 still describes a 2026 model: a
token embedding, $L$ blocks of attention and MLP reading from and adding
to a residual stream ([post 13](/posts/residual-stream-explained/)), a final norm and an unembedding. What
changed is a list of **substitutions** inside that skeleton, and each one
stuck because it bought something that could be measured: stability,
memory, speed, or quality at the same cost.

## Table of contents

## The substitutions

| | 2017 Transformer | 2026 default | why it changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| **norm placement** | post-norm: normalize after each residual add | pre-norm: normalize the sublayer's input | stable training without long warmup, at higher learning rates |
| **norm type** | LayerNorm | RMSNorm | as good, and simpler; fused, about the same cost |
| **biases** | in every linear layer | none | little value; stability at scale |
| **MLP** | ReLU, $4D$ wide | SwiGLU, $\tfrac83 D$ or wider (often $3.5$–$4D$) | better at matched cost |
| **position** | sinusoids added to the input | RoPE inside attention | relative position, nothing to learn |
| **attention heads** | multi-head (MHA) | grouped-query (GQA), or latent (MLA) | a far smaller KV cache |
| **MLP capacity** | one dense MLP | a mixture of experts (MoE) at the largest scales | more parameters at the same FLOPs per token |
| **attention span** | every token sees every earlier token | some layers sliding-window, sparse or linear | cost at long context |
| **stability extras** | — | QK-norm (and, in some models, a z-loss) | fewer loss spikes in very large runs |

The rest of this post goes through them, grouped by what they're for.
Several have their own posts already, so here each gets its reason and
its number.

## Training stability: where the norms go, and which norms

**Pre-norm** moved the normalization off the residual stream's main path
([posts 4.2](/posts/dropout-and-normalization/) and 13). With post-norm, gradients near the output are large at
initialization and training needs a careful warmup (Xiong et al., 2020);
with pre-norm the identity path stays clean. [Post 14](/posts/tiny-gpt-from-scratch/) measured the swap on
its 4-layer model: post-norm cost 0.06–0.08 bits per byte, with that post's
caveats (a learning rate tuned for pre-norm, an unscaled embedding). The
published evidence is that the gap grows with depth (Xiong et al., 2020),
which is why almost every model since 2019 is pre-norm.
Some recent ones add a second norm on each sublayer's *output* before the
add (Gemma 2 and later), or use only that one (OLMo 2); both keep the main
path free of normalization.

**RMSNorm** (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019) drops LayerNorm's mean subtraction
and shift (post 4.2). It matches LayerNorm's quality and is simpler: one
statistic instead of two, no shift parameters, a slightly cheaper backward
pass. Normalization is memory-bound ([post
6](/posts/how-a-gpu-runs-deep-learning/)), and in naive code RMSNorm saves
a pass over memory; with the fused kernels production models use, the two
cost about the same (post 4.2 works this out). It won because it is no
worse, no more expensive, and simpler. **Dropping biases** (T5, 2019;
PaLM, 2022) removes parameters that bought little; PaLM reports it also
improved training stability at scale. (Qwen2 and 2.5 are an exception: they
keep biases on the query, key and value projections.)

The last group, **QK-norm** (normalizing queries and keys before their dot
product; ViT-22B, Dehghani et al., 2023, and now OLMo 2, Qwen3 and Gemma
3), the **z-loss** (a small penalty on the log of the softmax's
normalizer, used by PaLM) and **logit soft-capping** (Gemma 2, which Gemma
3 replaced with QK-norm), all keep softmaxes from growing extreme in very
large runs, where a single loss spike can cost days of compute. QK-norm is
the one that has become standard. They matter at a scale this blog can't
reproduce.

## Quality at the same cost: SwiGLU and RoPE

**SwiGLU** (Shazeer, 2020) replaces the MLP's ReLU with a gated unit,
shrinking the hidden width to $\tfrac83 D$ so the weights stay at $8D^2$
(post 13). Shazeer's matched-cost comparison found it better, and nearly
every model since 2023 uses it or the GELU-gated variant. Newer models
often go wider than $\tfrac83 D$: Llama 3 and Mistral use $3.5D$, Gemma 2
9B $4D$, Qwen2.5-7B about $5.3D$.

**RoPE** ([post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/)) moved position from an added input vector into a
rotation of queries and keys, so attention scores depend on relative
distance, with no parameters at all. (Some recent models leave a few
layers without it, as in Llama 4.) Post 14 measured it against a learned
position table at the same context length: 0.1 bits per byte better at
4,000 steps, with the gap still closing.

Both can be measured on post 14's tiny GPT, trained the same way on the
dev slice, two seeds each, swapping one piece at a time. GELU at $4D$
against SwiGLU at $\tfrac83 D$ has exactly the same parameter count;
LayerNorm adds a bias per norm:

```bash
P=../embenv/bin/python
BASE='"kind": "char", "steps": 4000, "dropout": 0.2, "checkpoints": [1000, 2000, 3000, 4000]'
for seed in 0 1; do
  $P train.py "SwiGLU + RMSNorm (baseline) s$seed" "{$BASE, \"seed\": $seed}"
  $P train.py "GELU MLP, 4D wide         s$seed" "{$BASE, \"seed\": $seed, \"mlp\": \"gelu\"}"
  $P train.py "LayerNorm instead of RMS  s$seed" "{$BASE, \"seed\": $seed, \"norm\": \"layer\"}"
done
```

```text
SwiGLU + RMSNorm (baseline) s0: 1000: 2.147 / 2000: 2.053 / 3000: 2.034 / 4000: 2.027  (61 passes)
GELU MLP, 4D wide         s0: 1000: 2.233 / 2000: 2.077 / 3000: 2.039 / 4000: 2.020  (61 passes)
LayerNorm instead of RMS  s0: 1000: 2.134 / 2000: 2.047 / 3000: 2.060 / 4000: 2.029  (61 passes)
SwiGLU + RMSNorm (baseline) s1: 1000: 2.140 / 2000: 2.030 / 3000: 2.023 / 4000: 2.006  (61 passes)
GELU MLP, 4D wide         s1: 1000: 2.246 / 2000: 2.074 / 3000: 2.022 / 4000: 2.009  (61 passes)
LayerNorm instead of RMS  s1: 1000: 2.127 / 2000: 2.051 / 3000: 2.028 / 4000: 2.017  (61 passes)
```

At this scale, with the 600 KB of text repeated 61 times, where training
ends up is set by the data, and neither substitution changes it. After
4,000 steps GELU scores 2.020 and 2.009 against SwiGLU's 2.027 and 2.006,
and LayerNorm 2.029 and 2.017: differences of 0.01 or less, either way,
the size of the gap between two seeds. What SwiGLU does change is the
speed of getting there: after 1,000 steps (already about 15 passes over
the data) it is ahead of GELU by 0.09 and 0.11 bits per byte on the two
seeds, and by 0.02 to 0.04 after 2,000. In a run that sees each token
about once, as large runs do, being ahead at a given step *is* the final
result, and that is the regime Shazeer's comparison measured. LayerNorm
and RMSNorm tie within the seed spread at every checkpoint, as they should
if RMSNorm's case is its simplicity, not its quality. (All these runs use
the constant learning rate, like post 14's ablations.)

These are small models on small data, and the published comparisons are
at far larger scale. What the experiment shows is the kind of evidence
each substitution rests on: a measurable gain at matched cost (SwiGLU,
here in speed), the same quality more simply (RMSNorm), or stability
(pre-norm, which post 14 measured).

## Memory at inference: GQA and MLA

Every generated token reads the keys and values of every earlier token, the
KV cache ([post 20](/posts/kv-cache-explained/)), and for long contexts and large batches that cache, not
the weights, fills GPU memory. Standard multi-head attention stores a key
and a value per head per layer. Two substitutions cut that:
- **Multi-query** and **grouped-query attention** (Shazeer, 2019; Ainslie
  et al., 2023) let groups of query heads share one key head and one value
  head. With 8 groups for 64 query heads, the cache shrinks 8 times.
- **Multi-head latent attention** (MLA; DeepSeek-AI, 2024) caches one
  compressed vector per token and layer, from which every head's keys and
  values are reconstructed (at inference, by folding the up-projections
  into the query and output projections rather than rebuilding them), plus
  a small key carrying RoPE (post 12 explains why that part can't be
  compressed).

```python
# What the attention substitutions save: the KV cache per generated token
# (post 20), in 16-bit numbers, for published configurations, and the
# attention weights per layer. MHA keeps a key and a value per head; GQA one
# per group of query heads; MLA a compressed vector per token plus a small
# rotated key (DeepSeek-AI, 2024).
def kv_bytes(layers, per_layer_elements, bytes_per=2):
    return layers * per_layer_elements * bytes_per

configs = [
    # name, layers, model width, query heads, key/value heads, head size
    ("GPT-3 175B (MHA)", 96, 12288, 96, 96, 128),
    ("Llama 2 70B (GQA, 8 groups)", 80, 8192, 64, 8, 128),
    ("Llama 3 8B (GQA, 8 groups)", 32, 4096, 32, 8, 128),
]
for name, L, D, nq, nkv, h in configs:
    cache = kv_bytes(L, 2 * nkv * h)
    attn = D * nq * h * 2 + D * nkv * h * 2                     # Q and output, then K and V
    print(f"{name:30s} KV cache {cache / 1024:7.0f} KiB per token; attention weights per layer "
          f"{attn / 1e6:6.1f}M (with full MHA: {4 * D * nq * h / 1e6:6.1f}M)")

# DeepSeek-V2: 60 layers, 128 heads of 128, KV compression 512, rotated key 64.
L, nh, dh, dc, dr = 60, 128, 128, 512, 64
mla, mha = kv_bytes(L, dc + dr), kv_bytes(L, 2 * nh * dh)
print(f"{'DeepSeek-V2 (MLA)':30s} KV cache {mla / 1024:7.0f} KiB per token; the same heads with MHA: "
      f"{mha / 1024:,.0f} KiB, {mha / mla:.0f} times as much")

# Mixture of experts: parameters held vs parameters used per token.
for name, total, active in (("Mixtral 8x7B", 47e9, 13e9), ("DeepSeek-V2", 236e9, 21e9)):
    print(f"{name:30s} {total / 1e9:5.1f}B parameters, {active / 1e9:4.1f}B used per token "
          f"({active / total:.0%}): per-token FLOPs of a {active / 1e9:.0f}B model, memory of a {total / 1e9:.0f}B one")
```

```text
GPT-3 175B (MHA)               KV cache    4608 KiB per token; attention weights per layer  604.0M (with full MHA:  604.0M)
Llama 2 70B (GQA, 8 groups)    KV cache     320 KiB per token; attention weights per layer  151.0M (with full MHA:  268.4M)
Llama 3 8B (GQA, 8 groups)     KV cache     128 KiB per token; attention weights per layer   41.9M (with full MHA:   67.1M)
DeepSeek-V2 (MLA)              KV cache      68 KiB per token; the same heads with MHA: 3,840 KiB, 57 times as much
Mixtral 8x7B                    47.0B parameters, 13.0B used per token (28%): per-token FLOPs of a 13B model, memory of a 47B one
DeepSeek-V2                    236.0B parameters, 21.0B used per token (9%): per-token FLOPs of a 21B model, memory of a 236B one
```

GPT-3's full multi-head attention needs 4.5 MiB of cache per token, so
4,096 tokens of context for one user would be 18 GiB (GPT-3's own context
was 2,048). Llama 2 70B, a smaller but comparable width, needs 320 KiB per
token with GQA. DeepSeek-V2's
MLA stores 68 KiB, 57 times less than the same heads with MHA would. GQA
also removes attention weights (151M per layer instead of 268M for Llama 2
70B), but the point is the cache: its size decides how many users and how
long a context fit on a GPU, which is post 20's and Part XII's subject.

## Parameters without FLOPs: mixtures of experts

A **mixture of experts** replaces each block's MLP with many MLPs, the
experts, and a router that sends each token to a few of them (post 19). The
model holds all the experts' parameters but uses only a few per token:
Mixtral 8x7B has 47B parameters and uses 13B per token, DeepSeek-V2 236B
and 21B. Per token it costs the FLOPs of the smaller number and the memory
of the larger. At the largest scales, where quality is limited by
parameters and compute is the budget, that trade has won: most frontier
open models of 2025–2026 are MoE (DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-235B, Llama 4, Kimi
K2, gpt-oss, GLM-4.5).

## Cost at long context: sliding-window, sparse and linear attention

Attention's own work grows with the context, and post 13 showed it
overtaking the MLP's at about $T = 8D$ tokens. The responses, covered in
[the attention alternatives post](/posts/attention-alternatives/) (post
21), keep full attention in some layers and replace it in others:
**sliding-window** layers that see only a recent window (Mistral 7B used
one in every layer; Gemma 2 alternates local and global layers, Gemma 3
uses five local layers of 1,024 tokens per global one, gpt-oss alternates
with 128-token windows), **sparse** attention that selects which earlier
tokens to read (DeepSeek-V3.2's DSA), and **linear-attention** or
state-space layers with a fixed-size state, interleaved with full
attention (Jamba, Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear, Nemotron-H). Not every hybrid
stuck: MiniMax went back from a linear hybrid to full attention. The
skeleton stays; only some layers' mixing changes.

## How big, on how much data: the scaling laws

The other half of a model's design is its size, and the scaling laws are
how that's decided. Fit, across many training runs, a formula for the
final loss of a model with $N$ parameters trained on $D$ tokens:

$$
L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{\alpha}} + \frac{B}{D^{\beta}}
$$

Here $D$ is tokens, not the model width it meant above. $E$ is the loss no
model can beat (roughly, the entropy of the text under this tokenizer),
and the two other terms shrink as the model and the data grow. Training
compute is about $C = 6ND$ ([post 3.1](/posts/backpropagation-by-hand/)).
For a fixed budget $C$, which $N$ minimizes the loss? Substituting $D = C /
6N$ and setting the derivative in $N$ to zero gives $\alpha A / N^{\alpha}
= \beta B / D^{\beta}$, the two terms falling at matched rates, and so
$N^* \propto C^{\beta / (\alpha + \beta)}$: the optimal model grows
with the budget at a rate set by how fast each term falls.

The history is a correction, and then a correction of the correction.
- **Kaplan et al. (2020)** found the optimal model size growing fast with
  compute, $N^* \propto C^{0.73}$, and data only as $C^{0.27}$: spend extra
  compute mostly on a bigger model. GPT-3 (175B parameters on 300B tokens)
  followed that advice. (Later analyses add other reasons for Kaplan's
  answer: it counted only non-embedding parameters, and its models were
  small; Pearce and Song, 2024.)
- **Hoffmann et al. (2022)**, "Chinchilla", found that parameters and data
  should grow about equally, $N^* \propto C^{0.5}$ by their first two
  methods (0.46 by the third), with a constant that works out to about
  **20 tokens per parameter**. Their 70B model, trained on 1.4T
  tokens, beat their own 280B Gopher, trained on 300B, at the same compute.
  One reason for the difference, the Chinchilla paper argues, was the
  learning rate schedule: Kaplan used one fixed schedule for every run,
  whatever its number of tokens, while a cosine schedule matched to each
  run's length gives a lower final loss (post 14 saw the same at small
  scale).
- **Besiroglu et al. (2024)** refit Chinchilla's third method on data
  reconstructed from the paper's own figure. The published constants fit
  that data badly, mostly because they were rounded in the paper (a data
  exponent of 0.28 for 0.2849) and partly because the original fit
  stopped before converging; the refit agrees with the paper's other two
  methods.

The fit as printed, with its unrounded constants, and refit, worked
through:

```python
# Compute-optimal training from a fitted scaling law,
#     L(N, D) = E + A / N^alpha + B / D^beta,
# the loss of a model with N parameters trained on D tokens (here D is
# tokens, not width), with training compute C = 6 N D (post 3.1). Three
# versions of one fit: Hoffmann et al.'s (2022, "Chinchilla", approach 3) as
# printed in the paper, the same with the unrounded constants from the
# paper's source, and Besiroglu et al.'s (2024) refit of the same data.
FITS = {"Hoffmann, as printed": dict(E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7, alpha=0.34, beta=0.28),
        "Hoffmann, unrounded": dict(E=1.6934, A=406.4, B=410.7, alpha=0.3392, beta=0.2849),
        "Besiroglu refit": dict(E=1.8172, A=482.01, B=2085.43, alpha=0.3478, beta=0.3658)}

def loss(f, N, D):
    return f["E"] + f["A"] / N ** f["alpha"] + f["B"] / D ** f["beta"]

def optimal(f, C):
    """Minimizing L subject to 6ND = C. Setting dL/dN = 0 along the
    constraint gives alpha A / N^alpha = beta B / D^beta, so
    N* = G (C/6)^(beta/(alpha+beta)), G = (alpha A / (beta B))^(1/(alpha+beta))."""
    a, b = f["alpha"], f["beta"]
    G = (a * f["A"] / (b * f["B"])) ** (1 / (a + b))
    N = G * (C / 6) ** (b / (a + b))
    return N, C / 6 / N

for name, f in FITS.items():
    rows = []
    for C in (1e21, 1e23, 1e25):
        N, D = optimal(f, C)
        rows.append(f"{D / N:5.1f}")
    print(f"{name:21s} tokens per parameter at C = 1e21 / 1e23 / 1e25 FLOPs: {' / '.join(rows)}")

# Llama 3 8B: about 8 billion parameters, trained on about 15 trillion tokens.
N8, D8 = 8e9, 15e12
C = 6 * N8 * D8
print(f"\nLlama 3 8B: {D8 / N8:,.0f} tokens per parameter, C = {C:.1e} FLOPs")
for name, f in FITS.items():
    No, Do = optimal(f, C)
    target = loss(f, N8, D8)
    lo, hi = 1e18, C                                    # least compute whose optimal model reaches the 8B's loss
    for _ in range(100):
        mid = (lo * hi) ** 0.5
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if loss(f, *optimal(f, mid)) > target else (lo, mid)
    Nm, _ = optimal(f, hi)
    print(f"  {name:21s} same compute: optimal {No / 1e9:3.0f}B on {Do / 1e12:4.1f}T tokens, loss {loss(f, No, Do):.3f} "
          f"vs the 8B's {target:.3f}; same loss: a {Nm / 1e9:.0f}B model with {hi / C:.2f}x the 8B's training compute")

# For the chart: loss against model size at the 8B's training compute.
for name, f in FITS.items():
    pts = [(n, loss(f, n * 1e9, C / 6 / (n * 1e9))) for n in (2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256)]
    print(f"curve {name}: " + " ".join(f"{n}:{l:.4f}" for n, l in pts))
```

```text
Hoffmann, as printed  tokens per parameter at C = 1e21 / 1e23 / 1e25 FLOPs:  50.1 /  78.2 / 122.1
Hoffmann, unrounded   tokens per parameter at C = 1e21 / 1e23 / 1e25 FLOPs:  34.0 /  50.7 /  75.7
Besiroglu refit       tokens per parameter at C = 1e21 / 1e23 / 1e25 FLOPs:  21.6 /  19.2 /  17.1

Llama 3 8B: 1,875 tokens per parameter, C = 7.2e+23 FLOPs
  Hoffmann, as printed  same compute: optimal  36B on  3.4T tokens, loss 1.923 vs the 8B's 1.949; same loss: a 26B model with 0.50x the 8B's training compute
  Hoffmann, unrounded   same compute: optimal  45B on  2.7T tokens, loss 1.911 vs the 8B's 1.944; same loss: a 29B model with 0.40x the 8B's training compute
  Besiroglu refit       same compute: optimal  81B on  1.5T tokens, loss 1.968 vs the 8B's 2.022; same loss: a 34B model with 0.18x the 8B's training compute
curve Hoffmann, as printed: 2:2.0266 4:1.9801 8:1.9485 16:1.9299 32:1.9228 64:1.9264 128:1.9405 256:1.9654
curve Hoffmann, unrounded: 2:2.0266 4:1.9777 8:1.9435 16:1.9221 32:1.9119 64:1.9121 128:1.9223 256:1.9426
curve Besiroglu refit: 2:2.1169 4:2.0622 8:2.0221 16:1.9941 32:1.9766 64:1.9688 128:1.9703 256:1.9813
```

Chinchilla's published formula, taken literally, says 50 to 122 tokens per
parameter. The same formula with its unrounded constants says 34 to 76:
rounding a data exponent from 0.2849 to 0.28 moves the answer by a factor
of 1.5. The refit gives 17 to 22, consistent with the paper's other
methods and its 20-tokens-per-parameter rule. Constants quoted to two
digits are worth checking against the claim they're quoted for.

Each curve is one fit's predicted loss for models of different sizes, all
trained with the same compute (smaller models on more tokens). The minimum
is the compute-optimal size. Note how flat the valley is: the curves change
by a few hundredths across a factor of eight in size.

**And then everyone overtrained.** Llama 3 8B was trained on about 15
trillion tokens, 1,875 per parameter, nearly a hundred times the
compute-optimal ratio. Applied to it (with a caveat: these fits were made
on DeepMind's data and tokenizer, so the losses are illustrative, not
Llama 3's), every fit says a 36B to 81B model on fewer tokens would have
reached a lower loss for the same compute. Turned around: a compute-optimal
model of 26B to 34B would match the 8B's loss with a fifth to a half of
its training compute. Meta's own fit, on its own data, makes the same
point: the Llama 3 paper puts its 405B flagship near compute-optimal and
says the smaller models were trained "much longer than is compute-optimal"
— on purpose, since they "perform better than compute-optimal models at
the same inference budget". Compute-optimal means optimal for *training*,
and a popular model is trained once and used for billions of tokens. Each
generated token costs about $2N$ FLOPs, so the 8B serves at roughly a
quarter to a tenth of the cost of the compute-optimal model for the same
budget. Paying extra once in training to save on every token served is the
trade (Sardana et al., 2024, formalize it), and small open models since
2023 have been trained that way.

## What hasn't changed

Embeddings, causal attention with a softmax in at least some layers, an
MLP per position, residual additions, a norm, next-token cross-entropy
(with an extra multi-token prediction objective in some, like DeepSeek-V3),
and warmup with decay: every 2026 language model still has them. Even the
optimizer has mostly stayed AdamW, though Muon has started to replace it
in some 2025 frontier runs (Kimi K2, GLM-4.5). Two smaller trends also run
through these years: vocabularies grew, from 32K tokens (Llama 2) to 128K
(Llama 3) and 256K (Gemma), and large models stopped tying the embedding
and unembedding, while small ones still tie. The substitutions
above changed what each piece costs, not what the pieces are. That is
also why the next posts can each take one substitution and go deep:
mixtures of experts (19), the KV cache that GQA and MLA shrink (20),
alternatives to full attention (21), FlashAttention (22), and a frontier
model that combines them all (23).

## Takeaways

- The Transformer's skeleton is unchanged since GPT-2. What changed is a
  short list of substitutions, each kept because it bought something
  measurable.
- Stability: pre-norm (0.06–0.08 bits per byte at only 4 layers, in post
  14), no biases, and at the largest scales QK-norm. Simplicity: RMSNorm,
  which matched LayerNorm here.
- Quality at the same cost: SwiGLU (it learned faster at the same cost
  here) and RoPE (it beat a learned table in post 14).
- Inference memory: GQA and MLA shrink the KV cache by 4 to 8 times (the
  ratio of query heads to key-value heads) and 57 times against multi-head
  attention.
- Parameters without FLOPs: mixtures of experts use 9–28% of their
  parameters per token.
- Scaling laws set the size: compute-optimal is about 20 tokens per
  parameter (Chinchilla's printed formula says more, mostly because its
  constants were rounded; the refit agrees). Models are now trained far past it, because inference, not
  training, dominates a popular model's cost.

A model's context window is the number of tokens it *accepts*. Whether it
*uses* them all equally is a different question, and the answer is no.
Liu et al. (2024) gave models a set of documents, one of which held the
answer to a question, and moved that document from the start of the
prompt to the end. Accuracy was highest with the answer at the start or
the end, and lowest in the middle: a U-shaped curve, **lost in the
middle**. The models had the information in their context and didn't
find it.

This post reproduces the effect on a small model, shows why the most
famous long-context test doesn't see it, and works through the causes,
each of which suggests a different fix.

## Table of contents

## The experiment

Two tasks, each at four prompt lengths, with the thing to find placed at
five depths, from the very start (0%) to the very end (100%):
- **Key-value lookup** (after Liu et al.'s second task): a JSON object of
  random UUID keys and values, and a question asking for one key's value.
  Every other pair is a distractor that looks exactly like the answer.
- **Needle in a haystack**: one out-of-place sentence, "The passphrase for
  the notebook assistant is blue-heron-417.", inserted into this blog's
  own prose, and a question asking for the passphrase.

The model is [post 15](/posts/decoding-from-logits-to-text/)'s Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, greedy, which accepts 32,768
tokens; its chat template also puts a short default system prompt first.
A trial counts as right if the answer contains the exact value. Depth is
measured among the pairs (or the words of prose), not in tokens.

```python

from lm import model, tok, DEVICE

# Where in a long prompt does a model find things? Two tasks, each at four
# prompt lengths, with the thing to find at five depths:
#   kv:     a JSON object of random UUID keys and values; give the value for
#           one key. Every other pair is a near-identical distractor
#           (after Liu et al., 2024).
#   needle: one out-of-place sentence hidden in this blog's own prose; give
#           the passphrase it states ("needle in a haystack").
# Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, greedy, chat template; a trial counts as right if
# the answer contains the exact value.
TASK = sys.argv[1]
TRIALS = 12 if TASK == "kv" else 6
SIZES = {"kv": (10, 30, 60, 120), "needle": (750, 2000, 4000, 8000)}[TASK]    # pairs, or prose tokens
SALT = ""
if len(sys.argv) > 2:                     # python position.py kv <sizes> <trials> <salt>: more trials, new draws
    SIZES, TRIALS, SALT = tuple(int(x) for x in sys.argv[2].split(",")), int(sys.argv[3]), sys.argv[4]
DEPTHS = (0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0)
blog = open("blog_train.txt").read()
blog_ids = tok(blog).input_ids
m = model()

def ask(content):
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": content}], add_generation_prompt=True,
                                  return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True)["input_ids"].to(DEVICE)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = m.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=60, do_sample=False, repetition_penalty=1.0)
    return ids.shape[1], tok.decode(out[0, ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)

def kv_trial(n, depth, rng):
    pairs = [(str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128))), str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128)))) for _ in range(n)]
    key, value = pairs[round(depth * (n - 1))]
    data = "{" + ", ".join(f'"{k}": "{v}"' for k, v in pairs) + "}"
    return ask(f"Extract the value corresponding to the specified key in the JSON object below. "
               f"Answer with the value only.\n\nJSON data:\n{data}\n\nKey: \"{key}\"\nValue:"), value

def needle_trial(n, depth, rng):
    start = rng.randrange(0, len(blog_ids) - n)
    words = tok.decode(blog_ids[start:start + n]).split(" ")
    secret = f"{rng.choice(['blue', 'red', 'amber', 'grey'])}-heron-{rng.randrange(100, 1000)}"
    words.insert(round(depth * len(words)), f"(The passphrase for the notebook assistant is {secret}.)")
    return ask(f"Read the text below, then answer the question.\n\n{' '.join(words)}\n\n"
               f"What is the passphrase for the notebook assistant? Answer with the passphrase only."), secret

trial = kv_trial if TASK == "kv" else needle_trial
results = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for n in SIZES:
    for depth in DEPTHS:
        rng = random.Random(f"{TASK}-{n}-{depth}{SALT}")
        right, lengths = 0, []
        for _ in range(TRIALS):
            (length, answer), value = trial(n, depth, rng)
            right += value in answer; lengths.append(length)
        results[(n, depth)] = (right, sum(lengths) / len(lengths))
    row = " ".join(f"{results[(n, d)][0]:>2}/{TRIALS}" for d in DEPTHS)
    print(f"{TASK:6s} ~{results[(n, 0.5)][1]:5.0f} prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: {row}"
          f"   ({time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s so far)", flush=True)
```

```text
kv     ~  763 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12 12/12 12/12 11/12 12/12   (128 s so far)
kv     ~ 2106 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12 11/12 12/12 12/12 12/12   (340 s so far)
kv     ~ 4106 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12 11/12 10/12  8/12 12/12   (705 s so far)
kv     ~ 8151 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12 10/12  6/12 11/12 12/12   (1411 s so far)
needle ~  822 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%:  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6   (40 s so far)
needle ~ 2072 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%:  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6   (122 s so far)
needle ~ 4072 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%:  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6  6/6   (269 s so far)
needle ~ 8072 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%:  6/6  5/6  6/6  6/6  6/6   (581 s so far)
```

The key-value lookup at 8,000 tokens loses things in the middle. To firm
that up, and to see what happens further out, the same script with 12
more trials at 8,000 tokens (new random objects) and a 16,000-token
length:

```text
kv     ~ 8142 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12  7/12  9/12  9/12 12/12   (936 s so far)
kv     ~16189 prompt tokens: right at depth 0 / 25 / 50 / 75 / 100%: 12/12  2/12 10/12  5/12 12/12   (2448 s so far)
```

Together:

(The 8,100-token line pools both runs, 24 trials per depth; the others
have 12. The 2,100-token line is left out: it sits on the 800-token one.)

Three things stand out:
- **The ends held.** With the key first or last, the model was right in
  all 144 trials, at every length.
- **The middle fails more as the prompt grows.** Pooling the three middle
  depths: 97% right at 800 and at 2,100 tokens, 81% at 4,100, 72% at
  8,100 and 47% at 16,200, half the model's 32,768-token window.
- **The shape within the middle isn't settled.** At 8,100 tokens the two
  runs (independent draws) disagree on which middle depth is worst: at
  25%, 10 then 7 of 12; at 50%, 6 then 9. At 16,200 tokens the key at 25%
  was found 2 times in 12 and at 50% 10 times, a gap larger than chance,
  which this post doesn't explain. What holds at every length is the U's
  outline: ends that hold, and a middle that gets worse as the prompt
  grows. It's the shape Liu et al. report for much larger models.

How does it fail? Logging the answers for the 12 objects of the 8,100-token,
50%-depth cell that scored 6 of 12, and asking the same questions with the
key stated before the data as well as after:

```python

from lm import model, tok, DEVICE

# The 12 key-value objects of position.py's 8,100-token, 50%-depth cell
# (the first run's random draws, regenerated from the same seed), asked two
# ways: as in position.py, and with the key also stated before the data.
# Every answer is classified: right, another pair's value, the right value
# with a character or two wrong, or none of these.
m = model()

def ask(content):
    ids = tok.apply_chat_template([{"role": "user", "content": content}], add_generation_prompt=True,
                                  return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True)["input_ids"].to(DEVICE)
    with torch.no_grad():
        out = m.generate(ids, max_new_tokens=60, do_sample=False, repetition_penalty=1.0)
    return tok.decode(out[0, ids.shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()

def close(a, b):                              # equal length and at most 2 characters differ
    return len(a) == len(b) and sum(x != y for x, y in zip(a, b)) <= 2

n, depth = 120, 0.5
rng = random.Random(f"kv-{n}-{depth}")
target = round(depth * (n - 1))
counts = {"after only": {}, "before and after": {}}
for trial in range(12):
    pairs = [(str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128))), str(uuid.UUID(int=rng.getrandbits(128)))) for _ in range(n)]
    key, value = pairs[target]
    data = "{" + ", ".join(f'"{k}": "{v}"' for k, v in pairs) + "}"
    task = "Extract the value corresponding to the specified key in the JSON object below. Answer with the value only."
    for way, content in (("after only", f"{task}\n\nJSON data:\n{data}\n\nKey: \"{key}\"\nValue:"),
                         ("before and after", f"{task}\n\nKey: \"{key}\"\n\nJSON data:\n{data}\n\nKey: \"{key}\"\nValue:")):
        answer = ask(content)
        values = [v for _, v in pairs]
        if value in answer:
            kind = "right"
        elif any(v in answer for v in values):
            kind = f"another pair's value (pair {next(i for i, v in enumerate(values) if v in answer)}, target {target})"
        elif any(close(w.strip('"`.'), value) for w in answer.split()):
            kind = "right value, a character or two wrong"
        else:
            kind = f"none of these: {answer[:40]!r}"
        counts[way][kind] = counts[way].get(kind, 0) + 1
for way, c in counts.items():
    print(f"{way}: " + "; ".join(f"{k}: {v}" for k, v in sorted(c.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])))
```

```text
after only: right: 6; none of these: '57615999-1111-2222-3333-444444444444': 1; right value, a character or two wrong: 1; another pair's value (pair 40, target 60): 1; another pair's value (pair 55, target 60): 1; another pair's value (pair 52, target 60): 1; another pair's value (pair 50, target 60): 1
before and after: right: 12
```

Of the six misses, four were the value of *another* pair, 5 to 20 pairs
before the target; one was the right value with a character wrong; one
was made up. "Lost" mostly means found the wrong neighbor: the model
located roughly the right region and then matched imprecisely. The second
line is the subject of the last section.

## Why the needle test is too easy

The needle task is the most famous long-context test, and here it's nearly
perfect: 119 of 120 right, at every length and depth up to 8,000 tokens. Long-context models
advertise needle results at a million tokens with the same all-green grid.
The key-value task, at the same lengths, loses things in the middle.

The difference is what the model has to tell apart. The needle is the
only sentence about a passphrase, in prose about something else: a
question about passphrases matches it and nothing else, so any attention
head that compares the question with the text finds it. In the key-value
task, every pair looks like the answer: same format, same length, random
characters. The model has to match 36 characters of key exactly, among
up to 240 candidates of identical form. Real long-context work looks more
like the second task: find the clause that applies in a long contract,
the right function among similar ones in a codebase, the one relevant
paragraph among many on the same topic.

Benchmarks since have moved that way. **RULER** (Hsieh et al., 2024) adds
needles with distractors, several needles, chains of references to
follow, and counting and aggregation tasks; of the models tested, all of
which claimed 32K tokens or more, only half stayed satisfactory at 32K.
**Context Rot** (Hong et al., 2025) showed degradation with length across
18 models on tasks as simple as repeating a list of words, worse when the
question resembles the answer less and when distractors are present, and,
unexpectedly, worse when the irrelevant text is coherent than when it's
shuffled (a vendor's technical report, which measures the effects without
pinning down their causes). RULER also gives the effect a name: a model's
**effective context length** is the longest input at which it still scores
as well as a reference model does at 4K tokens, and it's typically far
below the advertised window.

## Causes

### Softmax dilution

Attention spreads one unit of weight over every earlier token ([post 11](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/)).
Suppose one key, the relevant one, scores $\delta$ above $n - 1$ others
that all score the same. Its share of the attention is

$$
\frac{e^{\delta}}{e^{\delta} + (n - 1)}
$$

which, for a fixed margin, falls as the context grows:

```python

# Softmax dilution: one relevant key scores delta above n - 1 others that all
# score the same. Its share of the attention is e^delta / (e^delta + n - 1).
for delta in (4, 8):
    shares = ", ".join(f"{n:>7,} keys {math.exp(delta) / (math.exp(delta) + n - 1):6.1%}" for n in (100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000))
    print(f"score margin {delta}: {shares}")
print(f"margin needed for half the attention among 100,000 keys: ln(99,999) = {math.log(99_999):.1f}")
```

```text
score margin 4:     100 keys  35.5%,   1,000 keys   5.2%,  10,000 keys   0.5%, 100,000 keys   0.1%
score margin 8:     100 keys  96.8%,   1,000 keys  74.9%,  10,000 keys  23.0%, 100,000 keys   2.9%
margin needed for half the attention among 100,000 keys: ln(99,999) = 11.5
```

A margin of 8 in the scores gives the relevant key three quarters of the
attention among 1,000 keys and 3% among 100,000. To hold half the
attention among 100,000 keys, it needs a margin of 11.5, so the queries and
keys have to become sharper as the context grows, and a model trained
mostly on short texts never had to learn that. With many similar
distractors the problem is worse: they don't score equally low, they score
almost as high as the answer. The margin needed grows as $\ln n$, which
is the link to [post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/): a model
with no position information lost a "seen before" task at four times its
training length, and scaling the scores by $\log n$, at test time only,
brought it back from 81% to 96%. Similar in spirit, some models scale
their attention scores with the log of the length (Qwen's LogN scaling),
and YaRN adjusts the attention temperature when extending context.

Dilution explains why longer prompts are harder, but not why the middle is
harder than the ends: the formula has no position in it. With the key
first or last, this model kept enough margin at 16,000 tokens to be right
every time, so something position-dependent has to sit on top of it.

### Attention sinks

```python

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from lm import PATH, tok, DEVICE

# Where does attention go? For 1,024 tokens of this blog, the share of each
# layer's attention (averaged over heads and over every query position past
# the first 64) that lands on the very first token, on the 4 most recent
# tokens, and on everything in between.
# 32-bit floats: with the explicit ("eager") attention needed to read the
# weights out, 16-bit scores overflow in this model.
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(PATH, dtype=torch.float32, attn_implementation="eager").to(DEVICE).eval()
text = open("blog_train.txt").read()
ids = torch.tensor([tok(text[200_000:206_000]).input_ids[:1024]], device=DEVICE)
with torch.no_grad():
    attn = model(ids, output_attentions=True).attentions          # per layer: (1, heads, T, T)
T = ids.shape[1]
rows = []
for layer, a in enumerate(attn):
    a = a[0, :, 64:, :].float().mean(0)                         # heads averaged; queries 64..T-1
    q = torch.arange(64, T, device=a.device)
    first = a[:, 0].mean().item()
    recent = torch.stack([a[i, max(0, int(qi) - 3):int(qi) + 1].sum() for i, qi in enumerate(q)]).mean().item()
    rows.append((layer, first, recent, 1 - first - recent))
for layer, first, recent, rest in rows:
    if layer % 3 == 0 or layer == len(rows) - 1:
        print(f"layer {layer:2d}: first token {first:5.1%}, last 4 tokens {recent:5.1%}, the other ~1,000 {rest:5.1%}")
print(f"averaged over all {len(rows)} layers: first token {sum(r[1] for r in rows) / len(rows):.1%}, "
      f"last 4 tokens {sum(r[2] for r in rows) / len(rows):.1%}; a uniform split would give the first token "
      f"{sum(1 / (q + 1) for q in range(64, T)) / (T - 64):.2%}")

# Per head rather than per layer (layers 1 to 26, 12 heads each).
per_head = torch.stack([a[0, :, 64:, 0].float().mean(-1) for a in attn[1:27]]).flatten()
print(f"heads in layers 1-26 putting over half their attention on the first token: "
      f"{int((per_head > 0.5).sum())} of {per_head.numel()}; under 5%: {int((per_head < 0.05).sum())}")

# Is it that token, or the first position? Four passages starting with
# different tokens, and the first one again with its first token moved to
# the end: which position gets the most attention, and how much.
def most_attended(ids):
    with torch.no_grad():
        att = model(torch.tensor([ids], device=DEVICE), output_attentions=True).attentions
    share = sum(a[0, :, 64:, :].float().mean((0, 1)) for a in att) / len(att)   # each key's average weight
    v, i = share.max(0)
    return int(i), tok.decode([ids[int(i)]]), v.item()

first = ids[0].tolist()
for name, x in [(f"passage at character {k:,}", tok(text[k:k + 6000]).input_ids[:1024]) for k in (100_000, 200_000, 300_000, 400_000)] \
               + [("first passage, first token moved to the end", first[1:] + first[:1])]:
    pos, token, share = most_attended(x)
    print(f"{name:44s} starts with {tok.decode(x[:1])!r:12s}: most attention on position {pos} ({token!r}), {share:.1%}")

# The digit: the first passage with one token put in front of it.
for lead in ("7", "3", "A", ".", "\n", "the"):
    x = tok(lead).input_ids + first
    pos, token, share = most_attended(x[:1024])
    print(f"first passage with {lead!r:6s} in front: most attention on position {pos} ({token!r}), {share:.1%}")
```

```text
layer  0: first token  0.0%, last 4 tokens 60.4%, the other ~1,000 39.6%
layer  3: first token 35.1%, last 4 tokens 21.5%, the other ~1,000 43.4%
layer  6: first token 49.5%, last 4 tokens 17.3%, the other ~1,000 33.3%
layer  9: first token 31.7%, last 4 tokens 20.2%, the other ~1,000 48.1%
layer 12: first token 34.9%, last 4 tokens 14.3%, the other ~1,000 50.8%
layer 15: first token 16.8%, last 4 tokens 28.7%, the other ~1,000 54.4%
layer 18: first token 20.2%, last 4 tokens 33.0%, the other ~1,000 46.9%
layer 21: first token 30.6%, last 4 tokens 12.1%, the other ~1,000 57.3%
layer 24: first token 46.8%, last 4 tokens 17.3%, the other ~1,000 36.0%
layer 27: first token  0.1%, last 4 tokens 13.0%, the other ~1,000 86.9%
averaged over all 28 layers: first token 30.5%, last 4 tokens 21.1%; a uniform split would give the first token 0.29%
heads in layers 1-26 putting over half their attention on the first token: 48 of 312; under 5%: 19
passage at character 100,000                 starts with 'rive'      : most attention on position 0 ('rive'), 29.0%
passage at character 200,000                 starts with ' then'     : most attention on position 0 (' then'), 30.5%
passage at character 300,000                 starts with 'Parameter' : most attention on position 0 ('Parameter'), 32.3%
passage at character 400,000                 starts with '7'         : most attention on position 1 ('"'), 30.9%
first passage, first token moved to the end  starts with ' climbs'   : most attention on position 0 (' climbs'), 30.4%
first passage with '7'    in front: most attention on position 1 (' then'), 30.4%
first passage with '3'    in front: most attention on position 1 (' then'), 30.4%
first passage with 'A'    in front: most attention on position 0 ('A'), 30.3%
first passage with '.'    in front: most attention on position 0 ('.'), 30.4%
first passage with '\n'   in front: most attention on position 0 ('\n'), 30.4%
first passage with 'the'  in front: most attention on position 0 ('the'), 30.4%
```

Averaged over the 28 layers, the very first token of a 1,024-token passage
receives 30% of all attention, a hundred times its share if attention were
spread evenly, and the four most recent tokens another 21%. The rest of
the context, about a thousand tokens, gets half. Some layers are
different: the first layer looks mostly at the last few tokens (the
query's own included), and the last layer spreads widely. In most layers,
on average, a third of the attention goes to the first position, and it's
concentrated in some heads: 48 of the 312 heads in layers 1 to 26 put more
than half of theirs there.

It's mostly not the token's meaning. Passages beginning with "rive",
" then" and "Parameter", the first passage rotated so it begins with
" climbs", and the same passage behind "A", ".", a newline or "the" all
put about 30% on their first token. The exception is telling: a passage
that starts with a digit ("7", or "3" in its place) puts the sink on the
second token instead. Xiao et al. (2024) called these **attention sinks**:
since softmax must put its weight somewhere, heads that have nothing
useful to attend to learn to park it on a token every query can see.
Which token gets the role is something the model builds, unusually large
activations on that token (Sun et al., 2024), normally for whatever comes
first; why a leading digit doesn't get it in this model, this post can't
say. The sink is harmless, even useful: it lets a head effectively switch
itself off. It matters for long context in one concrete way: evicting the
first tokens' keys and values from a model trained with full attention
breaks it, which is why streaming methods pin them ([post
21](/posts/attention-alternatives/) is the home of this topic). It is
*not* where content is read: in the key-value prompts the sink is the
chat template's first token, dozens of tokens before the first key.

### Position and training data

Two more causes, which this small experiment can't separate from the
others:
- **Position.** Beyond a model's training length, RoPE's rotation makes
  far-apart query-key pairs land at angles training never produced (post
  12, which also covers position interpolation and YaRN for extending
  context). At 16,000 tokens this model is inside its trained length, so
  that doesn't apply here. What can apply is that long distances are rare
  in training even within the window: An et al. (2024) trace short
  effective context lengths to how seldom far relative positions occur in
  training.
- **Training data.** Most documents are short. A model trained on text
  where the relevant context is usually nearby learns a prior for the
  nearby, and for the start, where instructions and titles go.
  Long-context training sets are built by packing or synthesizing long
  documents, and how many tasks in them truly need distant information
  decides what the model learns to use.

The U shape itself is consistent with two position effects: the end of the
prompt is closest to the question, where recency helps, and early tokens
are visible to every later position in every layer, which biases a causal
model toward them (Wu et al., 2025). Attention sinks are a separate fact
about the start: they mark where heads park attention, not where content
is read.

## What to do about it

Each cause suggests its own remedy, and in practice they're combined:
- **Put the question where it helps.** On the objects that scored 6 of 12
  above, stating the key before the data as well as after scored 12 of 12.
  In a causal model a token can only use what came before it, so with the
  question first, every data token is processed already knowing what's
  being looked for (Liu et al. found the same for key-value lookup, though
  little gain on document QA). Providers' guides differ in detail:
  Anthropic's says to put long documents first and the query last, and
  reports up to 30% better answers that way; OpenAI's GPT-4.1 guide says
  instructions at both ends work best, and if only once, before the
  context. One trade-off: a question placed before a fixed block of
  documents changes every request's prefix, which defeats prompt caching
  of those documents (post 34); documents first, question last is the
  cache-friendly order.
- **Send less.** Retrieval (Part IX) selects the relevant passages instead
  of sending everything, so there's less middle to get lost in, and a
  reranker can put the best ones first or last.
- **Compact.** Summarize old turns and tool outputs and drop what's done
  (post 35, and post 44 for agents), so the context holds what's needed
  now.
- **Train for it.** Longer training sequences, data whose answers depend on
  distant text, and position schemes that extend gracefully. That's the
  model builder's fix; the others are the application builder's.
- **Measure on your task.** A needle grid says little. Test the model on
  your own documents, with the relevant part at several depths, at the
  lengths you'll actually send.

## Where this leads

- **Part V** turns to the architecture: post 21's alternatives to full
  attention exist largely because of attention's long-context cost, and
  [post 20](/posts/kv-cache-explained/)'s KV cache is what a long context costs in memory.
- **Part VIII**, context engineering, and **Part IX**, retrieval, are the
  application-side answers to this post: deciding what goes into the
  context, and where.

## Takeaways

- A context window is what a model accepts, not what it uses evenly. On
  a key-value lookup, a 1.5B model was always right with the key at the
  start or end, and in the middle went from 97% right at 2,000 tokens to
  47% at 16,000.
- Needle-in-a-haystack tests miss this: one odd sentence is easy to find
  (119 of 120 here). Distractors that look like the answer, several
  needles, and reasoning over what's found are what break models, and
  RULER and Context Rot measure them.
- Most misses weren't blanks but neighbors: another pair's value, a few
  pairs away. Stating the question before the data as well fixed every
  miss in the cell tested (6 of 12 to 12 of 12).
- Softmax dilution: with a fixed score margin, the relevant token's share
  of attention falls toward $e^{\delta}/n$ once $n$ is much larger than
  $e^{\delta}$; holding it needs a margin that grows as $\ln n$. It
  explains why long prompts are harder, not why the middle is.
- Attention sinks: about 30% of attention goes to the first token, almost
  whatever it is (a leading digit is an exception in this model). They
  mark where heads park attention, not where content is read.
- Position extrapolation and short training documents add to it. The
  fixes are on both sides: put important text at the ends, send less
  (retrieve, compact), train on long documents that need their length,
  and test at your own lengths and depths.

  (TACL, 2024) — the U-shaped curve.
- Hsieh et al., [_RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654)
  (COLM, 2024) — tasks beyond retrieval, and effective context length.
- Hong, Troynikov and Huber, [_Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance_](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot)
  (Chroma, 2025) — degradation with length on simple tasks, 18 models.
- An et al., [_Why Does the Effective Context Length of LLMs Fall Short?_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.18745)
  (2024) — short effective context from rarely trained long distances.
- Wu, Wang, Jegelka and Jadbabaie, [_On the Emergence of Position Bias in Transformers_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01951)
  (ICML, 2025) — the causal mask's bias toward early positions.
- Sun, Chen, Kolter and Liu, [_Massive Activations in Large Language Models_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17762)
  (COLM, 2024) — the huge activations behind attention sinks.
- Anthropic, [_Prompting best practices_: long context](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices)
  — documents first, the query last. OpenAI, [_GPT-4.1 prompting guide_](https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt4-1_prompting_guide)
  — instructions at both ends of long context.
- Xiao, Tian, Chen, Han and Lewis, [_Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.17453)
  (ICLR, 2024) — attention sinks.
An agent's context fills as it works ([post
35](/posts/context-engineering-compaction-clearing-memory/)): every file
it reads and every tool result stays, and a long task pushes out what it
needs. One answer is to compress the context. Another is to split the
work: hand pieces of the task to other agents, each with its own fresh
context, and collect what they find. This post covers that second answer,
its patterns and protocols, and an honest accounting of what it costs.

## Table of contents

## Why subagents

A **subagent** is an agent started by another agent to do part of its
task, with its own context window, its own instructions, and often its
own tools. It returns a result, usually a summary, and its working
context disappears. Three things follow:
- **Context isolation.** The fifty files a subagent read to find one fact
  never enter the main agent's context; only the fact does. This is the
  same benefit as compaction, achieved by never filling the context in
  the first place.
- **Parallelism.** Independent subtasks can run at the same time, which cuts
  wall-clock time.
- **Specialization.** Each subagent can get a focused prompt, a smaller tool
  set, or a different model (cheaper for search, stronger for synthesis).

## Roles and topologies

Multi-agent systems assign **roles**: a planner or **lead** that decomposes
the task, **workers** or specialists that execute parts, sometimes a
**critic** or verifier that checks results. AutoGen (Wu et al., 2023)
popularized writing systems as conversations among such agents.

How they talk is the **topology**:
- **Direct**: agents message each other pairwise, as in a chain where each
  passes its output to the next, or a **handoff**, where one agent
  transfers the whole conversation to another better suited to continue
  (a triage agent handing a billing question to a billing agent).
- **Central**: every message goes through one coordinator, which assigns
  work and collects results. Easiest to reason about, and the coordinator
  is a bottleneck and a single point of failure.
- **Broadcast**: every agent sees every message, as in a group chat or a
  debate. Maximal information sharing, and every agent's context fills
  with everyone else's work.
- **Shared memory**: agents read and write a common store (a file, a
  database, a scratchpad, [post 42](/posts/agent-memory/)'s memory)
  instead of messaging, which decouples them in time.
- **Hierarchical**: central coordination nested, with leads of leads, for
  tasks too big for one coordinator.

The choice decides what each agent sees, which is the main lever: too
little and they duplicate or contradict each other; too much and the
context isolation that justified splitting is gone. [Post
47](/posts/learned-orchestration-sakana-fugu/)'s "orchestration collapse",
where agents sharing one transcript all follow the first one's lead, is
what too much sharing looks like.

## Protocols: A2A

Inside one application, agents can pass Python objects. Across vendors
and services they need a protocol. **A2A** (Agent2Agent), announced by
Google in April 2025 and moved to the Linux Foundation that June, is the
main one. Its pieces, as its specification describes them:
- an **Agent Card**, a JSON document at a well-known URL
  (`/.well-known/agent-card.json`) that advertises what an agent can do,
  its endpoint and how to authenticate;
- **tasks**, the unit of delegated work, with a lifecycle (submitted,
  working, input-required, completed, failed, canceled, among others) and
  the messages and output artifacts that belong to them;
- transport over HTTP, with JSON-RPC 2.0 the original binding (gRPC and a
  REST-style binding came later), Server-Sent Events for streaming
  progress, and push notifications to a webhook for tasks that run long.

A2A and MCP ([post 45](/posts/mcp-skills-and-okf/)) are complementary: MCP
connects an agent to tools and data, which do what they're told; A2A
connects an agent to other agents, which have their own judgment and may
take a while, ask questions, or fail in ways a tool doesn't.

## Orchestration patterns

The common shapes, from simplest to most general:
- **Sequential**: a pipeline; each agent's output is the next one's input
  (draft, then review, then edit).
- **Parallel**: independent agents work at the same time and their results
  are merged (several searches, or several answers to vote on).
- **Conditional**: a router sends the task to one of several agents based on
  its type ([post 47](/posts/learned-orchestration-sakana-fugu/)'s Fugu is a
  learned router).
- **Loop**: an agent and a checker alternate until the checker passes the
  result (write, test, fix).
- **Orchestrator-worker**: a lead plans, spawns workers for the subtasks it
  decided on, reads their results, and decides what to do next, possibly
  spawning more. The plan is made at run time, which makes this the most
  flexible pattern and the one used for open-ended research.

## What it costs: a model on real sizes

Take one research question over this blog that needs six posts: how do
the inference posts trade memory bandwidth against compute? One agent
could read all six; or a lead could brief six workers, one per post, and
synthesize their summaries. A cost model, with the posts' real sizes:

```python

from transformers import AutoTokenizer

# One research question over this blog, "How do the inference posts trade
# memory bandwidth against compute?", needs six posts. Their real sizes
# (Qwen2.5's tokenizer, standing in for any model's):
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("/Users/tanle/.cache/huggingface/hub/models--Qwen--Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct/"
                                    "snapshots/989aa7980e4cf806f80c7fef2b1adb7bc71aa306")
slugs = ["kv-cache-explained", "flashattention-explained", "serving-metrics-and-disaggregation",
         "kv-cache-compression", "speculative-decoding", "quantization-from-scratch"]
docs = []
for s in slugs:
    body = open(f"/Users/tanle/Developer/residual-stream/src/content/posts/{s}.mdx").read().split("---", 2)[-1]
    docs.append(len(tok(re.sub(r"^import .*$", "", body, flags=re.M)).input_ids))
print("posts to read:", ", ".join(f"{d:,}" for d in docs), f"(total {sum(docs):,} tokens)")

# A cost model of input tokens (output tokens, fewer but pricier, are left
# out). Each model call rereads its whole context. With prompt caching
# (post 34), a call reads what the previous call sent at 0.1x the price and
# writes only what's new at 1.25x. Assumed: a 2,000-token system prompt and
# task; each post read over STEPS calls; 300 tokens of reasoning per call;
# workers get a 200-token brief and return 600-token summaries; the lead
# writes the briefs in one call and, once all workers have returned in
# parallel, synthesizes in one more.
SYS, THINK, BRIEF, SUMMARY = 2000, 300, 200, 600
def agent(prefix, chunks):
    """(input tokens read, cost with caching in uncached-token equivalents,
    largest context, model calls) for one agent reading chunks in order."""
    read, cached, context, prev = 0, 0.0, prefix, 0
    for c in list(chunks) + [0]:                     # the last call writes the answer
        read += context
        cached += 0.1 * prev + 1.25 * (context - prev)
        prev = context
        context += c + THINK if c else 0
    return read, cached, prev, len(chunks) + 1

def compare(steps, explore):
    """explore: how much each worker reads relative to its share (searching
    finds overlapping and irrelevant material)."""
    single = agent(SYS, [d / steps for d in docs for _ in range(steps)])
    workers = [agent(SYS + BRIEF, [d * explore / steps] * steps) for d in docs]
    lead_plan = agent(SYS, [])                                          # one call: write the six briefs
    lead_synth = agent(SYS + len(docs) * (BRIEF + SUMMARY), [])         # one call: read the summaries, answer
    multi = [sum(x[i] for x in [lead_plan, lead_synth] + workers) for i in (0, 1)]
    seq_multi = 1 + max(w[3] for w in workers) + 1
    return single, multi, max(w[2] for w in workers + [lead_synth]), seq_multi

print(f"\n{'assumptions':38s} {'':10s} {'tokens read':>12s} {'cached cost':>12s} {'largest context':>16s} {'sequential calls':>17s}")
for steps, explore, label in ((4, 1.0, "each post in 4 reads, no extra search"), (1, 1.0, "each post in 1 read"),
                              (4, 2.0, "workers search twice as much")):
    single, multi, wmax, seq = compare(steps, explore)
    print(f"{label:38s} {'single':10s} {single[0]:>12,.0f} {single[1]:>12,.0f} {single[2]:>16,.0f} {single[3]:>17d}")
    print(f"{'':38s} {'lead + 6':10s} {multi[0]:>12,.0f} {multi[1]:>12,.0f} {wmax:>16,.0f} {seq:>17d}")
print(f"\nwhat reaches the lead: {len(docs) * SUMMARY:,} tokens of summaries for {sum(docs):,} tokens of posts "
      f"({len(docs) * SUMMARY / sum(docs):.1%})")
```

```text
posts to read: 5,972, 8,695, 5,638, 5,703, 8,117, 8,626 (total 42,751 tokens)

assumptions                                        tokens read  cached cost  largest context  sequential calls
each post in 4 reads, no extra search  single          651,186      124,862           51,951                25
                                       lead + 6        199,678      102,711           12,095                 7
each post in 1 read                    single          164,128       69,946           46,551                 7
                                       lead + 6         79,751       84,509           11,195                 4
workers search twice as much           single          651,186      124,862           51,951                25
                                       lead + 6        306,555      162,563           20,790                 7

what reaches the lead: 3,600 tokens of summaries for 42,751 tokens of posts (8.4%)
```

The three blocks change the assumptions: how many separate reads each
post takes, and how much extra searching workers do on top of their
share. Some conclusions survive all three; one doesn't.
- **The token bill can go either way.** Without caching, the single agent
  reads more in every case, because each call rereads a context that keeps
  growing. With prompt caching (post 34), rereads
  cost a tenth, and the comparison flips with the assumptions: the lead and
  workers are cheaper in the first case, more expensive when each post is
  read in one go, and 30% more expensive when workers search twice as much
  as their share strictly requires. Splitting is not a reliable way to save
  tokens. (The single agent here also never compacts its context, which
  [post 35](/posts/context-engineering-compaction-clearing-memory/) would
  have it do.)
- **The largest context is about a quarter the size** in every case: no
  worker's context exceeds 21,000 tokens, against 47,000 to 52,000 for the
  single agent. Models use long contexts worse than short ones ([post
  17](/posts/long-context-lost-in-the-middle/)), so that difference is
  about quality, not price.
- **Latency drops** because the workers run at the same time: the longest
  chain of sequential model calls is the lead's briefing, one worker's
  reads, and the lead's synthesis, 7 calls against 25.
- **Information is lost.** The lead sees 3,600 tokens of summaries for
  42,751 tokens of posts, 8%. Whatever a worker didn't think to include is
  gone, and if the question needs a connection between two posts that only
  appears when both are read side by side, no worker can make it.

Real systems do more work, not less, when they split. Anthropic's account
of its multi-agent research system reports that a Claude Opus 4 lead with
Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single Claude Opus 4 agent by
90.2% on its internal research evaluation, while multi-agent runs used about 15 times as many tokens as
a chat interaction (single agents about 4 times). On a browsing
benchmark, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in
performance. Read together: much of the gain comes from spending more
tokens, in parallel, across more separate contexts than one agent could
hold, and that pays only when the task is worth it.

## When multi-agent loses

The same report is direct about poor fits: tasks where all agents need
the same context, or where subtasks depend on each other in many ways.
Most coding tasks, it notes, involve fewer truly parallelizable parts
than research does. The model above shows why. Splitting pays when
subtasks are independent (each worker's summary is enough), when the
context one agent would need is too large to use well, and when the value
of the result covers the extra tokens. It loses when the answer depends
on details only visible across pieces, when coordination messages grow
faster than the work, and on easy tasks, where a single agent with good
context management is cheaper and just as good.

The case against multi-agent designs has been made directly. Cognition's
"Don't Build Multi-Agents" (2025) argues that subagents working from
partial context make conflicting decisions, and that a single agent with a
well-managed context is more reliable for most tasks. A study of failures
in multi-agent systems (Cemri et al., 2025) found that many come not from
the models but from the system design: badly specified roles, agents
ignoring each other's output, and no one verifying the result. Two
practices address both: write each subagent's brief as carefully as a
prompt for a person (the objective, the output format, what's out of
scope, where to look), and verify what subagents return rather than
trusting it, with a check or a separate reviewer.

## Takeaways

- Subagents buy context isolation, parallelism and specialization; the
  price is coordination and whatever doesn't make it into a summary.
- Topology (direct, central, broadcast, shared memory) decides what each
  agent sees, and too much sharing undoes the isolation.
- A2A standardizes agent-to-agent delegation (agent cards, tasks, JSON-RPC
  over HTTP); MCP connects agents to tools.
- On real sizes, a lead with six workers kept every context near a
  quarter of the single agent's and cut the sequential calls from 25 to 7;
  its token bill, with caching, was lower or higher depending on the
  assumptions; and it passed only 8% of the source material to the lead.
- Published results show large gains from multi-agent research at about
  15 times the tokens of chat; tasks with shared context or tight
  dependencies, including most coding, favor a single agent.
