[Post 24](/posts/small-and-specialized-models/) found that decoding one
sequence is memory-bound: tokens per second are capped by how many bytes
of weights must be read per token. Halve the bytes and the cap doubles.
**Quantization** stores weights in fewer bits, 8 or 4 instead of 16, and
it is the single biggest reason large models run on small hardware. This
post builds it from the rounding step up, and measures each refinement on
real layers of a real model.

## Table of contents

## Scale and zero-point

To store a number in $b$ bits, map it onto the integers $0$ to $2^b - 1$.
For a block of weights with minimum $w_{\min}$ and maximum $w_{\max}$, the
**scale** is the step between grid points and the **zero-point** is the
integer that represents zero:

$$
s = \frac{w_{\max} - w_{\min}}{2^b - 1}, \qquad z = \text{round}\Big(\frac{-w_{\min}}{s}\Big), \qquad q = \text{clip}\Big(\text{round}\Big(\frac{w}{s}\Big) + z,\ 0,\ 2^b - 1\Big),
$$

and the weight is read back as $\hat{w} = (q - z)\, s$. Storing $z$ makes
zero exactly representable, which matters because zero padding and many
activations are exactly zero. Worked for eight weights at 4 bits, in the
first lines of the output below: the scale is 0.052, so every weight
moves to the nearest multiple of 0.052, and 0.47 becomes 0.468. The
**rounding error** is at most half a step, $s/2$, and the step is set by
the block's range: one large weight in a block makes the step large for
every other weight in it.

A **symmetric** grid drops the zero-point: it spans $[-\max|w|, \max|w|]$
with $2^{b-1} - 1$ levels on each side (15 levels at 4 bits, here; many
kernels use the 16th as an extra negative level), so zero is a grid point
by construction and dequantizing is a single multiplication. The price is
range: if a block's weights run from $-0.1$ to $+0.3$, a third of a
symmetric grid covers $[-0.3, -0.1]$, where there are no weights at all.

The widget quantizes 128 real weights, one group from layer 22 of
Qwen2.5-0.5B. Try the group with an outlier at 4 bits: with the range taken
from the group, the outlier stretches the grid and most weights share a
handful of levels; with the range taken from the whole row, as one scale
per channel would, it gets worse; switch to symmetric and watch half the
grid go unused:

## Where to put the scales

That last point decides the first design choice, how many weights share a
scale:
- **Per tensor**: one scale for a whole matrix. Cheapest, and ruined by the
  largest weight anywhere in it.
- **Per channel**: one scale per output row.
- **Per group**: one scale per run of, typically, 128 consecutive weights
  in a row. The scales cost a little memory, one 16-bit scale and a
  4-bit zero-point per 128 weights, about 0.16 bits per weight (0.25 if
  the zero-point is kept in 16 bits), and the step adapts to local ranges.

## Formats beyond integers

Integers aren't the only small grid:
- **NF4** (Dettmers et al., 2023, for QLoRA): 16 levels placed at
  quantiles of a normal distribution, scaled per block of 64 by the
  block's largest magnitude. Weights are roughly normal, so the levels sit
  where the weights are, and no zero-point is stored. The 32-bit block
  scales cost 0.5 bits per weight; QLoRA's double quantization of the
  scales cuts that to 0.127. QLoRA (post 26) fine-tunes on top of it.
- **FP8** (Micikevicius et al., 2022): an 8-bit floating-point number, in
  two variants: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits, up to 448) for
  weights and activations, and E5M2 (up to 57,344) where range matters
  more, as in gradients. Ada, Hopper and later GPUs multiply FP8 natively;
  Blackwell also runs the MX formats below.
- **MX formats** (the OCP Microscaling specification, 2023): blocks of 32
  values share one 8-bit power-of-two scale, with the values themselves in
  FP8, FP6, FP4 or INT8. A block scale in hardware is what group-wise
  quantization does in software.

## Post-training quantization or quantization-aware training

Everything in this post is **post-training quantization** (PTQ): take a
trained model, quantize its weights, perhaps with some calibration data.
It costs minutes to a few GPU-hours and no gradient updates. **Quantization-aware training** (QAT)
inserts the rounding into training itself: the forward pass uses quantized
weights, and the backward pass treats the rounding as if it were the
identity, the straight-through estimator, so the model learns weights that
survive rounding. It recovers more quality at very low bit widths, at the
cost of a training run.

## GPTQ: rounding with error compensation

Rounding each weight to its nearest grid point minimizes each weight's
own error. It doesn't minimize what matters, the error in the layer's
*output* on real inputs, $\|XW^\top - X\hat{W}^\top\|^2$, because errors in
different weights can cancel or add up depending on the inputs. **GPTQ**
(Frantar et al., 2023), descended, via Optimal Brain Quantization, from
Optimal Brain Surgeon (Hassibi and Stork, 1993), quantizes one input column at a time and, after rounding
each, adjusts the columns not yet quantized to compensate. The adjustment
comes from the second derivative of the output error, the Hessian $H =
2X^\top X$, estimated on **calibration** text:

$$
\delta = \frac{w_i - \hat{w}_i}{[H^{-1}]_{ii}}, \qquad W_{:, j} \leftarrow W_{:, j} - \delta\, [H^{-1}]_{ij} \quad \text{for every later column } j .
$$

Here $H^{-1}$ is the inverse Hessian over the columns not yet quantized,
which changes after every step; row $i$ of the Cholesky factor of
$H^{-1}$ gives all of these at once, which is why GPTQ uses it. Columns
whose inputs are correlated with column $i$ absorb its error. The
whole layer is processed in one pass, using a Cholesky factor of
$H^{-1}$, in blocks of 128 columns to keep it fast on a GPU; Frantar et
al. quantized 175-billion-parameter models to 3 and 4 bits in about four
GPU hours.

## AWQ: protect the channels that matter

Activations are not uniform: a few input channels carry much larger
values than the rest, so errors in the weights that multiply them cost
more. **AWQ** (Lin et al., 2024) scales those weights *up* before
quantizing, and the corresponding inputs *down* by the same factor:
$W x = (W \operatorname{diag}(s)) (\operatorname{diag}(s)^{-1} x)$, exact
in full precision. The scaled-up weights get finer relative steps. With
$s_j = \overline{|x_j|}^{\alpha}$, one exponent $\alpha$ per layer is
chosen on calibration data, and the inverse scaling is folded into the
previous operation, so it costs nothing at inference. The full method
also searches, for each group, how far to clip its largest weights before
rounding: a smaller range with a few clipped weights can beat a wider one
with a coarser step. Both halves are measured below.

## Measured on two real layers

All four, implemented from the descriptions above, on the MLP
down-projections of layers 12 and 22 of Qwen2.5-0.5B, with their real
inputs from this blog's text. Error is measured on the layer's output,
on 2,048 tokens that calibration never saw:

```python

# Quantizing real layers: Qwen2.5-0.5B's MLP down-projections (896 x 4,864)
# in layers 12 and 22, with their real inputs from this blog's text. Quality is the
# layer's output error on 2,048 held-out tokens, relative to the output's
# size: ||X W^T - X Q^T|| / ||X W^T||. Calibration (GPTQ, AWQ) uses
# 32,768 other tokens, kept as H = 2 X^T X and each channel's mean |x|
# (capture_big.py), or, to show what too little does, 2,048.
def quantize(w, bits, axis=None):
    """Asymmetric round-to-nearest: an integer grid 0 .. 2^bits - 1, a scale
    and a zero-point so the grid spans [min, max] along `axis`."""
    lo, hi = w.min(axis=axis, keepdims=True), w.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    scale = (hi - lo) / (2 ** bits - 1)
    scale = np.where(scale == 0, 1, scale)
    zero = np.round(-lo / scale)
    q = np.clip(np.round(w / scale) + zero, 0, 2 ** bits - 1)
    return (q - zero) * scale

def symmetric(w, bits, axis):
    """Symmetric (absmax): a grid centred on zero, -(2^(b-1) - 1) .. 2^(b-1) - 1,
    scale = max|w| / that; no zero-point to store."""
    top = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1
    scale = np.abs(w).max(axis=axis, keepdims=True) / top
    scale = np.where(scale == 0, 1, scale)
    return np.clip(np.round(w / scale), -top, top) * scale

# NF4 (Dettmers et al., 2023): 16 levels at quantiles of a normal
# distribution, scaled per block by the block's absmax (QLoRA's values).
NF4 = np.array([-1.0, -0.6961928009986877, -0.5250730514526367, -0.39491748809814453, -0.28444138169288635,
                -0.18477343022823334, -0.09105003625154495, 0.0, 0.07958029955625534, 0.16093020141124725,
                0.24611230194568634, 0.33791524171829224, 0.44070982933044434, 0.5626170039176941,
                0.7229568362236023, 1.0])
def nf4(w, axis):
    m = np.abs(w).max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    m = np.where(m == 0, 1, m)
    x = w / m
    return NF4[np.abs(x[..., None] - NF4).argmin(-1)] * m

def rtn(W, bits, granularity):
    if granularity == "per tensor":
        return quantize(W, bits)
    if granularity == "per channel":
        return quantize(W, bits, axis=1)                      # one scale per output row
    G = W.reshape(W.shape[0], -1, 128)                        # groups of 128 inputs per row
    return quantize(G, bits, axis=2).reshape(W.shape)

def gptq(W, bits, H, block=128, damp=0.01):
    """GPTQ (Frantar et al., 2023): quantize one input column at a time, in
    groups of 128, and push each column's rounding error onto the columns
    not yet quantized, weighted by the inverse Hessian of the layer's
    squared output error, H = 2 X^T X."""
    W = W.copy(); n = W.shape[1]
    H = H.copy()
    H += damp * np.mean(np.diag(H)) * np.eye(n)
    Hinv = np.linalg.cholesky(np.linalg.inv(H)).T              # upper Cholesky factor of H^-1
    Q = np.zeros_like(W)
    for i1 in range(0, n, block):
        i2 = i1 + block
        W1, E1 = W[:, i1:i2].copy(), np.zeros((W.shape[0], block))
        lo, hi = W1.min(1), W1.max(1)                             # this group's grid, from current weights
        scale = np.where(hi > lo, (hi - lo) / (2 ** bits - 1), 1); zero = np.round(-lo / scale)
        for i in range(block):
            col = W1[:, i]
            q = (np.clip(np.round(col / scale) + zero, 0, 2 ** bits - 1) - zero) * scale
            Q[:, i1 + i] = q
            e = (col - q) / Hinv[i1 + i, i1 + i]
            W1[:, i:] -= np.outer(e, Hinv[i1 + i, i1 + i:i2])     # compensate within the block
            E1[:, i] = e
        W[:, i2:] -= E1 @ Hinv[i1:i2, i2:]                        # and in the columns after it
    return Q

def awq(W, bits, H, mag, grid=np.linspace(0, 1, 11)):
    """AWQ (Lin et al., 2024): scale input channel j of the weights up by
    s_j = mean|x_j|^alpha and its inputs down by the same factor, so the
    channels that matter most get finer steps; alpha chosen on calibration
    data. The scaling is exact in full precision."""
    best = None
    for a in grid:
        s = mag ** a; s /= np.sqrt(s.max() * s.min())
        Q = rtn(W * s, bits, "group 128") / s
        D = W - Q
        e = np.sum((D @ H) * D)                                   # calibration output error, from H
        if best is None or e < best[0]:
            best = (e, a, Q)
    return best[2], best[1]

def awq_clip(W, bits, H, mag, alpha, n_grid=20, max_shrink=0.5):
    """The second half of AWQ: after the scaling, for every group of 128
    weights in a row, search how far to clip its range before rounding
    (shrinking it by up to half), keeping whichever gives the least output
    error, here measured with the group's block of H."""
    s = mag ** alpha; s /= np.sqrt(s.max() * s.min())
    Ws = W * s
    Hs = H / s[:, None] / s[None, :]                               # H for the scaled inputs
    Q = np.zeros_like(Ws)
    for g in range(0, Ws.shape[1], 128):
        w, h = Ws[:, g:g + 128], Hs[g:g + 128, g:g + 128]
        top = np.abs(w).max(1, keepdims=True)
        best_err, best_q = np.full(w.shape[0], np.inf), np.zeros_like(w)
        for i in range(n_grid):
            t = top * (1 - max_shrink * i / n_grid)
            q = quantize(np.clip(w, -t, t), bits, axis=1)
            d = q - w
            e = np.sum((d @ h) * d, axis=1)
            better = e < best_err
            best_err[better], best_q[better] = e[better], q[better]
        Q[:, g:g + 128] = best_q
    return Q / s

# Worked: 8 weights to 4 bits.
w = np.array([-0.31, -0.12, 0.0, 0.04, 0.09, 0.18, 0.22, 0.47])
s, z = (w.max() - w.min()) / 15, np.round(-w.min() / ((w.max() - w.min()) / 15))
print(f"worked, 8 weights to 4 bits: scale {s:.4f}, zero-point {z:.0f}")
print(f"  integers {np.clip(np.round(w / s) + z, 0, 15).astype(int).tolist()}")
print(f"  back     {np.round(quantize(w, 4), 3).tolist()}")

for L in (12, 22):
    X, W = np.load(f"X_{L}.npy").astype(np.float64), np.load(f"W_{L}.npy").astype(np.float64)
    Xcal, Xtest = X[:2048], X[2048:]
    H_big, mag_big = np.load(f"H_big_{L}.npy"), np.load(f"mag_big_{L}.npy")
    ref = Xtest @ W.T
    err = lambda Q: np.linalg.norm(ref - Xtest @ Q.T) / np.linalg.norm(ref)
    print(f"\n=== layer {L}: input channels' mean |x|: median {np.median(mag_big):.3f}, largest "
          f"{mag_big.max():.2f} ({mag_big.max() / np.median(mag_big):.0f}x); top 1% of channels carry "
          f"{np.sort(mag_big)[-49:].sum() / mag_big.sum():.0%} of the total")
    print("round-to-nearest, output error (held-out tokens):")
    print(f"{'':12s}" + "".join(f"{b:>8d} bits" for b in (8, 4, 3)))
    for g in ("per tensor", "per channel", "group 128"):
        print(f"{g:12s}" + "".join(f"{err(rtn(W, b, g)):13.2%}" for b in (8, 4, 3)))
    G64 = W.reshape(W.shape[0], -1, 64)
    print(f"4 bits, blocks of 64: asymmetric {err(quantize(G64, 4, axis=2).reshape(W.shape)):.2%}, "
          f"symmetric {err(symmetric(G64, 4, 2).reshape(W.shape)):.2%}, NF4 {err(nf4(G64, 2).reshape(W.shape)):.2%}")
    print("group 128, output error (held-out tokens):")
    H_small = 2 * Xcal.T @ Xcal
    for b in (4, 3):
        Qa, a = awq(W, b, H_big, mag_big)
        print(f"  {b} bits: round-to-nearest {err(rtn(W, b, 'group 128')):.2%}; GPTQ {err(gptq(W, b, H_big)):.2%}; "
              f"AWQ scaling only {err(Qa):.2%} (alpha {a:.1f}), with clipping {err(awq_clip(W, b, H_big, mag_big, a)):.2%}")
    print("  GPTQ at 4 bits with 2,048 calibration tokens, by damping (fraction of H's mean diagonal): " +
          ", ".join(f"{d:g}: {err(gptq(W, 4, H_small, damp=d)):.2%}" for d in (0.01, 0.1, 1.0)) +
          f"; on its own calibration tokens (0.01): "
          f"{np.linalg.norm(Xcal @ W.T - Xcal @ gptq(W, 4, H_small).T) / np.linalg.norm(Xcal @ W.T):.2%}")
```

```text
worked, 8 weights to 4 bits: scale 0.0520, zero-point 6
  integers [0, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 15]
  back     [-0.312, -0.104, 0.0, 0.052, 0.104, 0.156, 0.208, 0.468]

=== layer 12: input channels' mean |x|: median 0.067, largest 0.52 (8x); top 1% of channels carry 3% of the total

                   8 bits       4 bits       3 bits

  3 bits: round-to-nearest 23.31%; GPTQ 19.44%; AWQ scaling only 23.25% (alpha 0.2), with clipping 20.52%

=== layer 22: input channels' mean |x|: median 0.146, largest 8.53 (58x); top 1% of channels carry 12% of the total
round-to-nearest, output error (held-out tokens):
                   8 bits       4 bits       3 bits
per tensor          3.69%       57.74%       85.07%
per channel         1.03%       17.38%       36.14%
group 128           0.63%       10.64%       22.62%
4 bits, blocks of 64: asymmetric 9.40%, symmetric 11.53%, NF4 8.51%
group 128, output error (held-out tokens):
  4 bits: round-to-nearest 10.64%; GPTQ 6.87%; AWQ scaling only 8.15% (alpha 0.4), with clipping 7.70%
  3 bits: round-to-nearest 22.62%; GPTQ 15.06%; AWQ scaling only 17.13% (alpha 0.4), with clipping 15.47%
  GPTQ at 4 bits with 2,048 calibration tokens, by damping (fraction of H's mean diagonal): 0.01: 8.23%, 0.1: 7.03%, 1: 6.95%; on its own calibration tokens (0.01): 2.64%
```

- **8 bits is nearly free; 4 bits needs care; 3 bits hurts.** With group
  scales, 8-bit weights change the output by 0.6%, 4-bit by about 11%, and
  3-bit by about 23%, in both layers.
- **Granularity matters more than anything else at low bits.** At 4 bits
  in layer 12, one scale per tensor gives 73% output error, per channel
  18%, per group of 128 11%. Smaller blocks mean a smaller range per
  block, so a smaller step.
- **GPTQ's compensation helps, given enough calibration.** At 4 bits it
  cuts the group-128 error from 11.0% to 9.0% in layer 12 and from 10.6% to
  6.9% in layer 22; at 3 bits, from 23% to 19% and 15%. The counterfactual
  is calibration size. With 2,048 calibration tokens instead of 32,768,
  GPTQ in layer 12 is *worse* than plain rounding (12.8% against 11.0%).
  $X^\top X$ from 2,048 tokens of 4,864-dimensional inputs has rank at most
  2,048; in the directions those tokens never exercised, the Hessian is
  only the small damping term, so GPTQ treats them as free and pushes
  rounding error into them, and held-out text does use them. On its own
  calibration tokens it scored 3.8%: overfitting. Raising the damping from
  1% to 100% of the Hessian's mean diagonal brings it back to 9.5%; in
  layer 22, the 2,048-token run still beat rounding (8.2% against 10.6%).
  For scale, the GPTQ paper calibrates on 128 sequences of 2,048 tokens,
  262,000 tokens.
- **AWQ's scaling helps where there are outliers, and only there.** Layer
  12's largest input channel averages 8 times the median, and the scaling
  changes nothing (10.9% against 11.0%). Layer 22's largest is 58 times
  the median, the top 1% of channels carry 12% of the input's size, and
  the scaling cuts the 4-bit error from 10.6% to 8.2% and the 3-bit from
  22.6% to 17.1%. Its clipping search helps both layers: with it, AWQ
  reaches 10.4% in layer 12 and 7.7% in layer 22 at 4 bits. GPTQ is still
  ahead in both.

At 4 bits with QLoRA's blocks of 64, the formats line up as the theory
says: symmetric absmax is worst (11.7% and 11.5%): its range is set by
whichever side of zero is larger, and its grid has 15 levels, not 16,
which together make its step about 20% coarser than the asymmetric grid's
in these blocks, and the error about 20% higher. Asymmetric with a
zero-point gets 9.7% and 9.4%, paying a few bits for its zero-points;
NF4, with levels shaped like the weights, 9.3% and 8.5%, without one.

Output error in one layer isn't the model's quality: errors compound
through 24 layers, and the papers' own numbers are perplexity over whole
models on WikiText-2 and C4. These per-layer errors, on two of the 24
layers and one of the seven linear layers in each, are a proxy for that,
good for seeing the mechanisms, not for ranking the methods on a model.

## What it buys at decode

```python
# What 4-bit weights buy at decode, by batch size, for an 8B model on an
# H100 (3.35 TB/s; 989 TFLOP/s dense BF16). One decode step for a batch of
# B sequences reads every weight once and does 2 FLOPs per weight per
# sequence; its time is at least the larger of the two (post 6's roofline;
# KV-cache reads and dequantization ignored). INT4 weights with group
# scales take about 4.25 bits each.
N, BW, FLOPS = 8e9, 3.35e12, 989e12
print(f"{'batch':>6s} {'BF16 step':>10s} {'INT4 step':>10s} {'speedup':>8s}   bound by")
for B in (1, 8, 64, 128, 256, 1024):
    compute = 2 * N * B / FLOPS
    bf16, int4 = max(2 * N / BW, compute), max(4.25 / 8 * N / BW, compute)
    print(f"{B:6d} {bf16 * 1e3:8.2f} ms {int4 * 1e3:8.2f} ms {bf16 / int4:7.1f}x   "
          f"BF16 {'memory' if 2 * N / BW > compute else 'compute'}, INT4 {'memory' if 4.25 / 8 * N / BW > compute else 'compute'}")
print(f"compute-bound from a batch of {4.25 / 8 * N / BW * FLOPS / (2 * N):.0f} (INT4) and "
      f"{2 * N / BW * FLOPS / (2 * N):.0f} (BF16)")
```

```text
     1     4.78 ms     1.27 ms     3.8x   BF16 memory, INT4 memory
     8     4.78 ms     1.27 ms     3.8x   BF16 memory, INT4 memory
    64     4.78 ms     1.27 ms     3.8x   BF16 memory, INT4 memory
   128     4.78 ms     2.07 ms     2.3x   BF16 memory, INT4 compute
   256     4.78 ms     4.14 ms     1.2x   BF16 memory, INT4 compute
  1024    16.57 ms    16.57 ms     1.0x   BF16 compute, INT4 compute
compute-bound from a batch of 78 (INT4) and 295 (BF16)
```

At small batches a decode step only reads weights, so 4-bit weights make
it 3.8 times faster. As the batch grows, the same weights serve more
sequences per read and compute catches up: 4-bit weights are
compute-bound from a batch of about 80, so at 128 the speedup is 2.3 and
at 256, 1.2. At 1,024 both are
compute-bound and weight-only quantization buys nothing. Hence the split
in practice: weight-only 4-bit for local and low-batch serving, and 8-bit
weights *and* activations, using the GPU's integer or FP8 units, for
high-throughput serving. Two things this arithmetic ignores both shrink
the gain: dequantizing in the kernel costs time, and the KV cache is read
too. At a batch of 64 with 4,000-token contexts, an 8B model with GQA
reads about 34 GB of KV cache per step, twice its 16-bit weights, and
4-bit weights then speed the step up only about 1.3 times. The KV cache
has its own quantization (post 52).

## Weights only, or activations too

Everything above quantizes weights only: they are stored in 4 bits and
expanded to 16 for the multiplication, which helps exactly where post 24
said the bottleneck is, reading weights during decode. Quantizing the
*activations* too, to run the multiplication itself in 8-bit integers,
also speeds up compute-bound prefill and large batches, but activation
outliers make it harder: LLM.int8() (Dettmers et al., 2022) keeps the few
outlier dimensions in 16 bits, and SmoothQuant (Xiao et al., 2023)
migrates the outliers' range from activations into weights with the same
per-channel scaling trick as AWQ.

## Where this leads

- **Post 57** runs quantized models on a laptop: GGUF formats and
  llama.cpp, with measured speed against post 24's bandwidth bound.

## Takeaways

- Quantization stores each weight as an integer on a grid set by a scale
  and a zero-point; the error is up to half a step, and the step is set
  by the range of the block sharing the scale.
- Group-wise scales (128 weights) are what make 4 bits workable: 11% output
  error on a real layer, against 73% with one scale per tensor.
- GPTQ rounds column by column and pushes each error onto correlated
  columns, cutting 4-bit output error by a fifth to a third here, given
  enough calibration text; with 2,048 tokens and default damping it
  overfit, and in layer 12 was worse than plain rounding.
- AWQ's scaling by activation size helped only in the layer with large
  activation outliers (10.6% to 8.2%); its clipping search helped both.
- At 4 bits in blocks of 64, NF4 beat asymmetric and symmetric integer
  grids on both layers (9.3% and 8.5% output error).
- Weight-only quantization speeds up memory-bound decoding, 3.8 times at
  small batches for 4-bit weights, and nothing once the batch makes the
  step compute-bound; quantizing activations as well has to handle their
  outliers.

[Post 37](/posts/semantic-and-hybrid-search/) ranked every section of this
blog with BM25 and with embeddings, and fused the two. Both are cheap per
document, because a search has to score every document. That cheapness
has a price: the query and the document never meet. Each is reduced to
its own vector, or its own bag of words, before they are compared. A
**reranker** lets them meet, which costs far more per document, so it
reads only the top few that a cheap first stage returns.

## Bi-encoders and cross-encoders

A **bi-encoder**, post 8's embedding model, encodes the query and each
document separately; the documents can be encoded once, ahead of time,
and a query costs one encoding plus a dot product per document. A
**cross-encoder**, first used for passage ranking by Nogueira and Cho
(2019), reads the query and a document
together, as one input, and outputs a relevance score. Every attention
layer can then compare each query token with each document token, which
is where its accuracy comes from, but nothing can be computed ahead of
time: every query needs one full forward pass per document. Worked for
this blog's sections:

```python

from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from sections import sections

# Cost per query of the three designs, for this blog's 309 English
# sections, with a MiniLM-sized encoder: 22.7M parameters, about 11M of
# them the token-embedding table (a lookup), so roughly 2 x 11M FLOPs per
# token for the rest, ignoring attention. Queries are the section headings.
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
secs = sections("en")
full = np.array([len(tok(s["body"]).input_ids) for s in secs])
read = np.minimum(full, 512)                                   # what a 512-token encoder reads
q = np.mean([len(tok(s["heading"]).input_ids) for s in secs])
N, flop_tok, K = len(secs), 2 * 11e6, 50
print(f"{N} sections, {full.mean():.0f} tokens each on average ({read.mean():.0f} read at most 512); "
      f"queries average {q:.1f} tokens")
bi = q * flop_tok + N * 384 * 2
cross = K * (q + read.mean()) * flop_tok
late = q * flop_tok + N * q * full.mean() * 128 * 2
print(f"bi-encoder: encode the query, then {N} dot products           {bi / 1e6:10.1f} MFLOPs per query")
print(f"cross-encoder, top {K}: {K} passes over query + section        {cross / 1e6:10.1f} MFLOPs per query")
print(f"late interaction (ColBERT, 128-d): every query x section token {late / 1e6:10.1f} MFLOPs per query")
print(f"  roughly K (q + L) / q = {K * (q + read.mean()) / q:,.0f}: the cross-encoder's multiple of one query encoding")
for n_docs in (1e4, 1e6):
    print(f"  at {n_docs:,.0f} documents: bi-encoder {(q * flop_tok + n_docs * 384 * 2) / 1e9:6.2f} GFLOPs, "
          f"MaxSim over every document {(q * flop_tok + n_docs * q * full.mean() * 256) / 1e9:8.1f} GFLOPs")
print("\nindex size, every token indexed, 16-bit numbers:")
print(f"  bi-encoder, one 384-d vector per section:              {N * 384 * 2 / 2**20:7.2f} MiB")
print(f"  ColBERT, one 128-d vector per token:                   {full.sum() * 128 * 2 / 2**20:7.2f} MiB")
for b in (2, 1):
    print(f"  ColBERTv2, 4-byte centroid id + {b}-bit residuals:       {full.sum() * (4 + 128 * b / 8) / 2**20:7.2f} MiB")
```

```text
309 sections, 426 tokens each on average (361 read at most 512); queries average 9.0 tokens
bi-encoder: encode the query, then 309 dot products                198.3 MFLOPs per query
cross-encoder, top 50: 50 passes over query + section          407149.5 MFLOPs per query
late interaction (ColBERT, 128-d): every query x section token      501.3 MFLOPs per query
  roughly K (q + L) / q = 2,056: the cross-encoder's multiple of one query encoding
  at 10,000 documents: bi-encoder   0.21 GFLOPs, MaxSim over every document     10.0 GFLOPs
  at 1,000,000 documents: bi-encoder   0.97 GFLOPs, MaxSim over every document    981.6 GFLOPs

index size, every token indexed, 16-bit numbers:
  bi-encoder, one 384-d vector per section:                 0.23 MiB
  ColBERT, one 128-d vector per token:                     32.12 MiB
  ColBERTv2, 4-byte centroid id + 2-bit residuals:          4.52 MiB
  ColBERTv2, 4-byte centroid id + 1-bit residuals:          2.51 MiB
```

Reranking only 50 sections with a cross-encoder costs about 2,000 times
the bi-encoder's whole search; over all 309 it would be six times more
again, and over a million documents, out of the question. The ratio is
roughly $K (q + L) / q$ for $K$ candidates of length $L$ and a query of
length $q$, since encoding the query dominates the bi-encoder's cost: it
grows with longer documents and shorter queries. Hence **two-stage
retrieval**: a cheap first stage narrows the collection to $k$ candidates,
and the expensive stage orders only those. The first stage's recall at $k$
caps the whole pipeline: a document it misses can never be reranked into
first place.

## Late interaction: ColBERT

**ColBERT** (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020) sits between the two. Like a
bi-encoder it encodes documents ahead of time, but it keeps *one vector per
token* instead of one per document. At query time it encodes the query's
tokens and scores each document by **MaxSim**: every query token takes its
best match among the document's tokens, and the score is the sum of those
best matches,

$$
s(q, d) = \sum_{i \in q} \max_{j \in d} \, q_i \cdot d_j .
$$

Worked on a three-word query, which becomes four word pieces, against two
short documents. The token vectors here are from MiniLM, which wasn't
trained for this, so only the arithmetic is ColBERT's:

```python

from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

# Late interaction (ColBERT's MaxSim), worked on a 3-word query (4 word pieces). Every
# token of the query and of each document gets its own vector; each query
# token takes its best match among the document's tokens, and the score is
# the sum of those maxima. The token vectors here are all-MiniLM-L6-v2's,
# which was not trained for this: the arithmetic is ColBERT's, the numbers
# only illustrate it.
path = "sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2"
tok, enc = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(path), AutoModel.from_pretrained(path).eval()
def vectors(text):
    ids = tok(text, return_tensors="pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        h = enc(**ids).last_hidden_state[0, 1:-1]                     # drop [CLS] and [SEP]
    return tok.convert_ids_to_tokens(ids.input_ids[0, 1:-1]), torch.nn.functional.normalize(h, dim=-1).numpy()

q_tokens, Qv = vectors("paged kv cache")
for doc in ("vllm stores the kv cache in fixed-size pages, like virtual memory",
            "the cache line of a cpu holds sixty-four bytes"):
    d_tokens, Dv = vectors(doc)
    S = Qv @ Dv.T                                                     # every query token vs every document token
    best = S.argmax(1)
    print(f'document: "{doc}"')
    for i, t in enumerate(q_tokens):
        print(f"  {t:7s} best match {d_tokens[best[i]]!r:12s} {S[i, best[i]]:.2f}   (mean over the document {S[i].mean():.2f})")
    print(f"  MaxSim score {S.max(1).sum():.2f}; mean-of-similarities score {S.mean(1).sum():.2f}")
```

```text
document: "vllm stores the kv cache in fixed-size pages, like virtual memory"
  page    best match 'pages'      0.75   (mean over the document 0.29)
  ##d     best match 'like'       0.46   (mean over the document 0.30)
  kv      best match 'kv'         0.92   (mean over the document 0.30)
  cache   best match 'cache'      0.92   (mean over the document 0.35)
  MaxSim score 3.06; mean-of-similarities score 1.24
document: "the cache line of a cpu holds sixty-four bytes"
  page    best match 'cache'      0.35   (mean over the document 0.22)
  ##d     best match 'cache'      0.36   (mean over the document 0.24)
  kv      best match 'cpu'        0.24   (mean over the document 0.14)
  cache   best match 'cache'      0.87   (mean over the document 0.35)
  MaxSim score 1.81; mean-of-similarities score 0.95
```

The second document matches "cache" almost as well as the first (0.87
against 0.92), but nothing in it matches "kv" or "paged", and MaxSim
scores it far lower, 1.81 against 3.06. **Why max and not mean**: a query
token should be judged by its best match, not diluted by every unrelated
word in the document; averaging cuts both scores and the gap between them,
to 1.24 against 0.95, and it would punish long documents for being long.

ColBERT gets most of a cross-encoder's token-level matching; the original
paper reports reranking more than 170 times faster than BERT, with 13,900
times fewer FLOPs per query. On this blog's 309 sections its cost is close
to a bi-encoder's, because encoding the query dominates. On a large
collection, scoring every document by MaxSim would not be: at a million
documents it is about a thousand times a bi-encoder's search, by the
table's last lines. So ColBERT doesn't score everything. It first gathers
candidates with a nearest-neighbor search per query token, through
centroids in ColBERTv2's engine, PLAID (Santhanam et al., 2022b), and runs
MaxSim only on those. (ColBERT also pads every query to 32 tokens with a
special mask token, which its ablations show helps.)

The other price is the index: one vector per token, 32 MiB for this
blog's sections against a quarter of a MiB for one vector per section,
both in 16 bits. **ColBERTv2** (Santhanam et al., 2022a) compresses each
128-number token vector to the 4-byte ID of its nearest centroid plus a
1- or 2-bit residual per dimension: 20 or 36 bytes instead of 256, about
13 or 7 times smaller here, with little loss. On why max and not mean,
ColBERT's own ablation is the evidence: swapping the maximum for an
average lost noticeably on MS MARCO.

## Training rerankers and retrievers: hard negatives

A reranker is trained on queries paired with relevant and irrelevant
documents: scored one at a time against a label (Nogueira and Cho's
pointwise cross-entropy), or relevant against irrelevant (pairwise or
listwise losses). What it learns depends on the irrelevant ones. Random
documents are too easy: almost anything beats a random document. **Hard
negatives**, documents a first stage ranked high but that aren't
relevant, teach the distinctions a reranker exists to make; Nogueira and
Cho took theirs from BM25's top thousand. The same technique trains
retrievers.

Hard negatives carry a risk: some are relevant passages nobody labeled,
and training against them teaches the wrong thing. ColBERTv2's answer is
denoised supervision. A first ColBERT model retrieves the top passages for
each training query; a cross-encoder scores them; and ColBERT is trained
to match those scores across 64 passages per query rather than trusting
the binary labels, distillation from a teacher (post
27). The teacher was ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2,
the very cross-encoder measured below.

## LLM rerankers

A language model can rerank too: ask for a relevance score per document
(pointwise; monoT5 reads it from the probability of the word "true",
Nogueira et al., 2020), or show it the query and the candidates and ask
for an ordering (listwise; RankGPT, Sun et al., 2023). Listwise reranking
has to fit the candidates in the context window, so it slides a window
over them, and it is sensitive to the order they are shown in. It brings
everything the model knows, and the cost is a language model's: hundreds
of tokens per candidate, through a model hundreds of times larger than a
MiniLM. In practice it is a third stage, over the cross-encoder's top few,
or a way to label training data for a smaller reranker, which is what
RankGPT's authors did.

## Measured: reranking post 37's benchmark

```python

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
exec(open("retrieval.py").read().split("# How much each encoder reads")[0])   # post 37's data, BM25, dense, RRF

# Two-stage retrieval on post 37's benchmark. Stage 1, cheap, over every
# section: post 37's best ranker for the language (English: BM25 fused with
# dense passages; Vietnamese: BM25). Stage 2, expensive, over its top 50
# only: a cross-encoder reads query and section together and scores the
# pair (English: ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2; multilingual:
# mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1). Sections it ranks are cut to its input
# limit, 512 tokens; one run instead scores 80-word passages and keeps each
# section's best.
K = 50
def two_stage(title, corpus, queries, stage1, ce_name, passages=False):
    ce = CrossEncoder(ce_name, device="cpu")
    docs = [s["body"] for s in corpus]
    before, after, seconds = [], [], []
    for q, target in queries:
        s1 = stage1(q)
        top = np.argsort(-s1)[:K]
        before.append(int((s1 >= s1[target]).sum()))
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        if passages:                                                     # score each 80-word passage, keep the best
            pairs, owner = [], []
            for j, i in enumerate(top):
                w = docs[i].split()
                for p in range(0, len(w), 80):
                    pairs.append((q, " ".join(w[p:p + 80]))); owner.append(j)
            sc = ce.predict(pairs, batch_size=64)
            s2 = np.full(K, -np.inf); np.maximum.at(s2, np.array(owner), sc)
        else:
            s2 = ce.predict([(q, docs[i]) for i in top], batch_size=K)
        seconds.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        if target in top:
            after.append(int((s2 >= s2[list(top).index(target)]).sum()))
        else:
            after.append(before[-1])                                     # stage 1 missed it; rerank can't help
    b, a = np.array(before), np.array(after)
    d = 1 / a - 1 / b
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    lo, hi = np.percentile([d[rng.integers(0, len(d), len(d))].mean() for _ in range(2000)], [2.5, 97.5])
    print(f"{title} ({len(queries)} queries), cross-encoder {ce_name.split('/')[1]}"
          f"{', best 80-word passage' if passages else ''}:")
    print(f"  stage 1 alone:    recall@1 {np.mean(b == 1):4.0%}  MRR {np.mean(1 / b):.3f}  (right section in its top {K}: {np.mean(b <= K):.0%})")
    print(f"  + re-rank top {K}: recall@1 {np.mean(a == 1):4.0%}  MRR {np.mean(1 / a):.3f}  "
          f"difference {d.mean():+.3f} [{lo:+.3f}, {hi:+.3f}]")
    print(f"  re-ranking time: {np.median(seconds) * 1e3:.0f} ms per query on the CPU ({K} pairs)")

en_docs, vi_docs = [s["body"] for s in en], [s["body"] for s in vi]
en_q = [(s["heading"], i) for i, s in enumerate(en) if s in unique(en)]
vi_q = [(s["heading"], i) for i, s in enumerate(vi) if s in unique(vi)]
en_stage1 = rrf(BM25(en_docs).scores, dense_passages("MiniLM (English)", en_docs))
vi_stage1 = BM25(vi_docs).scores
two_stage("English", en, en_q, en_stage1, "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2")
two_stage("English", en, en_q, en_stage1, "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2", passages=True)
two_stage("English", en, en_q, en_stage1, "cross-encoder/mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1")
two_stage("Vietnamese", vi, vi_q, vi_stage1, "cross-encoder/mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1")
two_stage("Vietnamese", vi, vi_q, vi_stage1, "cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2")
```

```text
English (297 queries), cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2:
  stage 1 alone:    recall@1  40%  MRR 0.530  (right section in its top 50: 90%)
  + re-rank top 50: recall@1  45%  MRR 0.575  difference +0.045 [+0.012, +0.079]
  re-ranking time: 1468 ms per query on the CPU (50 pairs)
English (297 queries), cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2, best 80-word passage:
  stage 1 alone:    recall@1  40%  MRR 0.530  (right section in its top 50: 90%)
  + re-rank top 50: recall@1  40%  MRR 0.535  difference +0.004 [-0.032, +0.040]
  re-ranking time: 1737 ms per query on the CPU (50 pairs)
English (297 queries), cross-encoder mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1:
  stage 1 alone:    recall@1  40%  MRR 0.530  (right section in its top 50: 90%)
  + re-rank top 50: recall@1  39%  MRR 0.516  difference -0.014 [-0.054, +0.025]
  re-ranking time: 2377 ms per query on the CPU (50 pairs)
Vietnamese (257 queries), cross-encoder mmarco-mMiniLMv2-L12-H384-v1:
  stage 1 alone:    recall@1  42%  MRR 0.539  (right section in its top 50: 91%)
  + re-rank top 50: recall@1  41%  MRR 0.529  difference -0.010 [-0.055, +0.037]
  re-ranking time: 2317 ms per query on the CPU (50 pairs)
Vietnamese (257 queries), cross-encoder ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2:
  stage 1 alone:    recall@1  42%  MRR 0.539  (right section in its top 50: 91%)
  + re-rank top 50: recall@1  35%  MRR 0.487  difference -0.053 [-0.098, -0.007]
  re-ranking time: 976 ms per query on the CPU (50 pairs)
```

Five runs, one per pairing of language and reranker, plus one that
reads passages:
- **A reranker trained on the right data helps.** The English MS MARCO
  cross-encoder lifts English first-place hits from 40% to 45%, MRR
  $+0.045$ with a 95% interval of $[+0.012, +0.079]$ over queries. The first
  stage had the right section in its top 50 for 90% of queries, the
  ceiling on first-place hits for a reranker over 50; it gets part of the
  way.
- **It needs to read the section.** Scoring 80-word passages and keeping
  each section's best, instead of reading the whole section cut at 512
  tokens, erases the gain ($+0.004$, $[-0.032, +0.040]$): the relevant
  evidence for a heading is spread through its section.
- **A bigger, multilingual reranker isn't automatically better.** The
  multilingual cross-encoder, twelve layers against six and twice the
  compute per pair, doesn't improve English ($-0.014$, $[-0.054, +0.025]$),
  and on Vietnamese it only matches BM25 ($-0.010$, $[-0.055, +0.037]$).
  Both rerankers were trained on the same web questions, the multilingual
  one on mMARCO, MS MARCO machine-translated into 13 languages including
  Vietnamese, from a model distilled from one covering about a hundred
  languages. So the gap is in the model, not the domain; this experiment
  can't say whether translation noise or capacity spread over many
  languages is to blame.
- **A reranker in the wrong language hurts.** The English cross-encoder on
  Vietnamese drops first-place hits from 42% to 35% ($-0.053$, $[-0.098,
  -0.007]$): it overrides a good first stage with scores it can't compute
  well.
- **Reranking is the expensive step.** About 1 to 1.5 seconds per query
  for the six-layer model over 50 sections, 2.3 seconds for the
  twelve-layer one, on this laptop's CPU while other jobs ran on its GPU,
  so treat them as rough. The first stage is a dot product and a word-count
  lookup per section; the cost table above puts the ratio between them in
  the thousands.

A reranker is a model, with a training distribution. Check it on your own
queries against the first stage alone before putting it in the pipeline,
as for any other model.

## Where this leads

- **Post 39** assembles retrieval-augmented generation: chunking, query
  rewriting and caching, around the pipeline built in posts 36 to 38.

## Takeaways

- A cross-encoder reads query and document together and scores more
  accurately than a bi-encoder, at one forward pass per document: about
  2,000 times the bi-encoder's whole search, for 50 documents here.
- Two-stage retrieval lets the cheap stage pick the candidates and the
  expensive one order them; the first stage's recall at $k$ is the ceiling.
- ColBERT keeps one vector per token and scores by MaxSim, near a
  bi-encoder's cost with token-level matching; its index is per token, and
  ColBERTv2's compression cut it 7 to 13 times here.
- On this blog, the English MS MARCO reranker added $+0.045$ MRR in English,
  but only reading whole sections; the same model hurt Vietnamese
  ($-0.053$), and a multilingual one helped neither. Rerankers have
  training distributions too.
