  (2021) — MS MARCO machine-translated into 13 languages, Vietnamese among them; the data behind the multilingual cross-encoder.
Every Transformer post on this blog is, underneath its own topic, a story
about one object: a single vector, per token position, that starts as an
embedding and ends as a prediction. This blog is named after it. Posts 8 to
12 built the pieces: embeddings, attention, position. This post puts them
into one picture, the floor that KV caches and serving engines stand on.

Picture a relay race where every runner, instead of handing off the baton
and stepping aside, *keeps running alongside it*, adding their own stride to
its path without ever taking it away from anyone else. Nothing is ever
overwritten; every layer just adds its contribution to a path that started
at the very first token embedding and keeps accumulating all the way to the
end. That accumulating path is the **residual stream**, and this post is
about what lives on it, why it's shaped that way, and how it turns into a
next-token prediction.

## Table of contents

## Tokens become vectors: embedding

A model never sees text. A tokenizer first splits it into a sequence of
discrete IDs from a fixed vocabulary — word pieces, not necessarily whole
words — and an **embedding matrix** $W_E$ turns each ID into a learned
vector: row $i$ of $W_E$ *is* the vector for token $i$.

Take a toy 4-token vocabulary and a 2-dimensional embedding, small enough to
write out in full:

$$
\text{vocab} = [\texttt{the},\ \texttt{cat},\ \texttt{sat},\ \texttt{.}],
\qquad
W_E = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Embedding the token `cat` just reads off row 1:

$$
x_0 = W_E[\texttt{cat}] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

That's it — no computation yet, just a table lookup. (Models also need
**positional information**, so that attention knows *where* each token
sits, not just *what* it is. Older models add it at this step, as
sinusoidal functions or learned position embeddings; most current ones
instead rotate the queries and keys inside attention, rotary embeddings,
and leave $x_0$ alone. [Post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/)
covers all of them; the [attention patterns post](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/#limitations-what-attention-doesnt-give-you-for-free)
flags *why* they're needed.)

$x_0$ is the residual stream's very first value — for this one token
position, at layer 0, before anything else has touched it.

## The residual stream: one running vector, read and written by everything

Here's the idea this whole post is named after, stated precisely. Every
component of a Transformer works on the *same* vector at the *same*
position: the embedding writes its first value, every attention sublayer
and every MLP sublayer reads it and writes back by **addition**, and the
unembedding reads the result:

$$
x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(x_l)
$$

$F_l$ is everything block $l$ adds: its attention update plus its MLP
update (the next section splits it into those two steps). Blocks never
replace $x_l$ outright; they each read it, compute an update,
and add that update back in. After $L$ layers, $x_L$ is the *sum* of the
original embedding plus every single layer's contribution:

$$
x_L = x_0 + \sum_{l=0}^{L-1} F_l(x_l)
$$

This is exactly the framing Anthropic's interpretability team made precise
in 2021, and it's worth reading in their own words:

> [!note] Where the term comes from
> "All components of a transformer (the token embedding, attention heads,
> MLP layers, and unembedding) communicate with each other by reading and
> writing to different subspaces of the residual stream." — Elhage et al.,
> [_A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits_](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html)
> (Anthropic, 2021)

That "different subspaces" detail matters: because every layer's output is
just *added in*, nothing forces two layers' contributions to occupy
different directions of the vector, and they often overlap. Models pack
more features into the stream than it has dimensions, at the cost of some
interference between them (Elhage et al., 2022, call this superposition).
Whatever separation exists is learned and soft, not an architectural
guarantee. That's precisely what makes the residual
stream interesting to study: it's a shared, additive workspace, not a neatly
labeled set of slots.

## Each block: attention sublayer + MLP sublayer, both additive

A Transformer stacks $L$ identical **blocks**, and every block does the
exact same two-step read-compute-add:

1. **Attention sublayer.** The stream is normalized (LayerNorm — rescales
   the vector so training stays stable; its formula, and RMSNorm's, are in
   [the normalization post](/posts/dropout-and-normalization/)), the
   normalized copy goes into the attention computation, and
   attention's output is added back onto the *un-normalized* stream:
   $x_l' = x_l + \text{Attn}(\text{LN}(x_l))$. What attention actually
   computes there — the $Q$, $K$, $V$ projections, the scaled dot product,
   the softmax — is what [post 11](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/)
   derived; nothing here depends on those details, only on the fact that
   whatever it computes gets *added*.
2. **MLP sublayer.** The (now-updated) stream is normalized again, fed
   through a small feed-forward network — expand to a wider hidden
   dimension, apply a nonlinearity, project back down — and that output is
   added back the same way: $x_{l+1} = x_l' + \text{MLP}(\text{LN}(x_l'))$.
   The MLP works on each position separately, processing whatever the
   attention step just mixed in; [its section below](#inside-the-mlp-sublayer)
   opens it up.

Both sublayers follow the identical contract: read the stream (through a
normalization step), compute something, add it back. Nothing about that
contract cares *what* the something is — which is exactly why attention and
the MLP can be swapped for other mechanisms in a Transformer variant without
changing anything about the stream itself.

One historical note, because it changes how you should read diagrams of the
original Transformer: the 2017 paper (Vaswani et al.) normalized *after*
each addition — "Post-LN," $x_{l+1} = \text{LN}(x_l + F_l(x_l))$. By
2018–19, implementations and papers (Wang et al., 2019) had moved the
normalization *inside* the branch — "Pre-LN," the version described above
— and GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) adopted it, adding one final norm before
the unembedding because the un-normalized stream keeps growing through the
layers. Xiong et al. (2020) later showed why the placement matters: with
Post-LN the norm sits on the main path, gradients near the output are large
at initialization, and training needs a careful warmup. Pre-LN leaves an
unbroken additive path from the first token embedding to the last block.
[Post 14](/posts/tiny-gpt-from-scratch/#taking-pieces-out) measured the
swap on a small model: post-norm cost 0.06–0.08 bits per byte at 4 layers.
Pre-LN is what essentially every modern LLM (GPT-3 onward, Llama, and this
blog's own inference-serving series) uses, most of them with RMSNorm in
place of LayerNorm. Some also, or instead, normalize each sublayer's *output*
before the add (Gemma 2 does both, OLMo 2 only the output); the main path
stays free of normalization either way. [The normalization post](/posts/dropout-and-normalization/#where-the-norms-go-in-a-transformer)
covers why the position matters for training.

## Inside the MLP sublayer

Attention is the only place where positions exchange information. The MLP
never looks at another position: it applies the same small network to each
position's vector on its own. Write $D$ for the stream's width, the
length of $x$ (`d_model` in the code below). In the 2017 Transformer that
network expands the vector to four times its width, applies a
nonlinearity, and projects it back, with $x$ a row vector as in the rest
of this post:

$$
\text{MLP}(x) = \phi(x W_1)\, W_2, \qquad W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times 4D},\;
W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{4D \times D}
$$

with $\phi$ a ReLU in the original and GELU, a smooth version of it
(Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016), from GPT and BERT (2018) on. Most current
models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek) use a **gated** version instead,
SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020). A second projection of the input multiplies the
activated one element by element ($\odot$), so each hidden unit's output is
scaled by a learned, input-dependent gate:

$$
\text{SwiGLU}(x) = \big( \text{SiLU}(x W_{\text{gate}}) \odot x W_{\text{up}}
\big) W_{\text{down}}, \qquad \text{SiLU}(z) = z \cdot \sigma(z)
$$

where $\sigma(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$ is the sigmoid.

That is three matrices instead of two, so to keep the cost the same the
hidden width shrinks from $4D$ to $\tfrac{8}{3}D$: $3 \cdot \tfrac{8}{3} D
\cdot D = 8D^2$ weights, the same as $2 \cdot 4D \cdot D$. Shazeer's
comparison, at matched cost on a T5-base encoder–decoder, found the gated
variants better: held-out log-perplexity 1.944 with SwiGLU against 1.997
with ReLU after 65,536 steps, 1.636 against 1.677 after 524,288, and the
gated variants also did best on most GLUE and SuperGLUE tasks. The paper
offers no explanation beyond the results. Counted, for a model of Llama 1
7B's width, and for the newer Llama 3 8B layout:

```python

# Two MLP sublayers of the same size. The 2017 one expands D to 4D, applies
# a nonlinearity, and projects back. SwiGLU (Llama and most current models)
# has three matrices: a gate, an "up" projection, and the way back down, with
# a hidden width of about 8/3 D so it costs the same.
class SwiGLU(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, D, F):
        super().__init__()
        self.gate = torch.nn.Linear(D, F, bias=False)
        self.up = torch.nn.Linear(D, F, bias=False)
        self.down = torch.nn.Linear(F, D, bias=False)
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.down(torch.nn.functional.silu(self.gate(x)) * self.up(x))

count = lambda m: sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
D = 4096
with torch.device("meta"):                                  # shapes only, no memory
    gelu_mlp = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(D, 4 * D, bias=False), torch.nn.GELU(),
                                   torch.nn.Linear(4 * D, D, bias=False))
    swiglu = SwiGLU(D, 11008)                               # Llama 1 7B: 8/3 * 4096, rounded up to a multiple of 256
    attention = torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(D, D, bias=False) for _ in range(4)])  # Q, K, V, output
print(f"D = {D}: GELU MLP {count(gelu_mlp) / 1e6:.1f}M weights (8 D^2 = {8 * D * D / 1e6:.1f}M), "
      f"SwiGLU {count(swiglu) / 1e6:.1f}M, attention {count(attention) / 1e6:.1f}M (4 D^2)")

# Forward FLOPs per token for one block: 2 per weight for every matrix, plus
# attention's own work: for each earlier token, D multiply-adds (2D FLOPs)
# for its score and 2D more for adding in its value. With the causal mask a
# token sees, on average over a sequence of length T, T/2 earlier tokens.
for T in (2048, 8192, 32768, 131072):
    weights = 2 * (count(swiglu) + count(attention))
    mixing = 4 * D * T / 2
    print(f"context {T:>7,}: MLP {2 * count(swiglu) / (weights + mixing):.0%} of the block's FLOPs, "
          f"attention's projections {2 * count(attention) / (weights + mixing):.0%}, "
          f"scores and weighted sums {mixing / (weights + mixing):.0%}")

# A newer layout: Llama 3 8B widens the MLP to 14,336 and shares each key and
# value head among 4 query heads (grouped-query attention), so K and V
# project to 1,024 dimensions instead of 4,096.
with torch.device("meta"):
    mlp3 = SwiGLU(D, 14336)
    attn3 = torch.nn.ModuleList([torch.nn.Linear(D, n, bias=False) for n in (D, 1024, 1024, D)])
print(f"Llama 3 8B block: MLP {count(mlp3) / 1e6:.1f}M, attention {count(attn3) / 1e6:.1f}M, "
      f"MLP share {count(mlp3) / (count(mlp3) + count(attn3)):.0%}")
```

```text
D = 4096: GELU MLP 134.2M weights (8 D^2 = 134.2M), SwiGLU 135.3M, attention 67.1M (4 D^2)
context   2,048: MLP 64% of the block's FLOPs, attention's projections 32%, scores and weighted sums 4%
context   8,192: MLP 57% of the block's FLOPs, attention's projections 28%, scores and weighted sums 14%
context  32,768: MLP 40% of the block's FLOPs, attention's projections 20%, scores and weighted sums 40%
context 131,072: MLP 18% of the block's FLOPs, attention's projections 9%, scores and weighted sums 73%
Llama 3 8B block: MLP 176.2M, attention 41.9M, MLP share 81%
```

Two things follow. At matched cost a block holds about $12D^2$ weights,
$4D^2$ in attention's four projections and $8D^2$ in the MLP, so **two
thirds of the block is MLP**. That is the parameter count [post
14](/posts/tiny-gpt-from-scratch/) builds a model from: $12 L D^2$ plus the
embeddings. Newer models tilt further: Llama 3 and Mistral widen the
SwiGLU to $3.5D$, and grouped-query attention (Part V) shrinks the key and
value projections, so in Llama 3 8B the MLP holds about four fifths of
each block.

And at the context lengths most text is trained at, the MLPs also do most
of the arithmetic. Attention's own work, the scores and weighted sums,
grows with the context: $2DT$ FLOPs per token against the MLP's $16D^2$, so
it overtakes the MLP at about $T = 8D$, 32,768 tokens at this width. That
counts only the half of the $T \times T$ scores the causal mask keeps;
post 14 counts all of them, as the PaLM paper does, which moves the
crossover to $4D$. FLOPs aren't time, either: how fast attention runs
depends on its memory traffic as much as its arithmetic. This growing part
is what the long-context methods of Part V are built to cut.

## Why "residual"? Fixing a wall deep networks used to hit

The name isn't decorative. **Residual connections** — the identity shortcut
$y = x + F(x)$ — were introduced by He et al. for image models in
[_Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)
(2015), to fix something that looked at first like overfitting but wasn't:
plain deep networks, past a certain depth, got systematically *worse* on
both training and test data as more layers were added. Depth wasn't
learning to be a better function — it was struggling to learn even an
identity function through dozens of stacked nonlinearities. He et al. were
careful about the cause: their plain networks used batch normalization,
and they checked that the gradients had healthy norms, so the problem
wasn't simply vanishing gradients. Deep plain networks were just much
harder to optimize.

The residual add fixes this directly, and the reason is a one-line
derivative. For a single block $y = x + F(x)$:

$$
\frac{\partial y}{\partial x} = I + \frac{\partial F}{\partial x}
$$

with $I$ the identity matrix. That leading $I$ is the trick. Across many
blocks the derivative is a product, $\partial x_L / \partial x_l = \prod_k
(I + \partial F_k / \partial x_k)$, and expanding the product always leaves
a bare $I$ term: part of the gradient at the top reaches block $l$
unchanged, whatever the branches do in between (He et al., 2016). It
doesn't stop the other terms from growing or shrinking, but it means a
block can start out doing almost nothing and still pass the signal
through, and learning a near-identity function becomes the easy default
rather than something to discover. In a plain network every path goes
through every layer's Jacobian. The identity path only stays clean if
nothing sits on it after the addition, which is the Pre-LN argument above.

Transformers inherited this trick wholesale: the "Add" in every sublayer's
"Add & Norm" is exactly He et al.'s residual connection, which, together
with normalization and careful initialization, is what makes a 96-layer
model trainable. [Post 14](/posts/tiny-gpt-from-scratch/#what-happens-without-the-residual-stream)
removes it from a 4-layer model: at a normal learning rate the model
collapses to predicting the same character distribution whatever its
input.

## From the stream to a prediction: unembedding

After the last block, one more normalization and one more matrix
multiplication turn the stream back into something over the vocabulary.
The **unembedding matrix** $W_U$ projects the final stream vector to one
raw score — a **logit** — per vocabulary entry, and softmax turns those
logits into a probability distribution to sample or argmax from.

($W_U$ is sometimes literally $W_E^\top$ — "weight tying," from
[Press & Wolf, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.05859) — reusing the
embedding table backwards instead of learning a second one. Many large open
models (Llama 3 8B and 70B, DeepSeek-V3) use a separate $W_U$, though Gemma
ties at every size. A common reason: embedding parameters grow with
vocabulary size × width and the rest with layers × width², so at scale the
saving from tying is small. Post 14's tiny model ties, where the saving is
large.)

Continuing the toy example, take the stream after some number of blocks to
be $x_L = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 1.1 \end{bmatrix}$ and unembed with:

$$
W_U = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
\text{logits} = x_L W_U = \begin{bmatrix} 0.4 & 1.1 & -0.4 & -1.1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Softmax turns those four raw scores into a distribution that sums to 1. It
appears throughout this blog; [post 3.2](/posts/softmax-and-cross-entropy/)
derives it with cross-entropy, and here is the short version.

### What softmax actually computes

Given a vector of $n$ real numbers $z$ — the logits — softmax exponentiates
each one and divides by the sum of all the exponentials:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(z)_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{n} e^{z_j}}
$$

Exponentiating makes every entry positive, whatever sign the logit had;
dividing by the total makes them sum to exactly 1. So the output is always a
valid probability distribution, and it preserves order — the largest logit
gets the largest probability. Worked on the toy logits:

$$
e^{z} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{0.4} & e^{1.1} & e^{-0.4} & e^{-1.1} \end{bmatrix}
      = \begin{bmatrix} 1.492 & 3.004 & 0.670 & 0.333 \end{bmatrix},
\qquad \textstyle\sum_j e^{z_j} = 5.499
$$

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(z) = \frac{1}{5.499}\begin{bmatrix} 1.492 & 3.004 & 0.670 & 0.333 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 0.271 & 0.546 & 0.122 & 0.061 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Two properties follow directly from the formula and matter everywhere
softmax appears:

- **Only differences between logits matter.** Adding the same constant $c$
  to every $z_i$ multiplies numerator and denominator by $e^{c}$, which
  cancels: $\operatorname{softmax}(z + c) = \operatorname{softmax}(z)$. This
  is why the code below computes `np.exp(logits - logits.max())` —
  subtracting the maximum changes nothing mathematically but keeps $e^{z}$
  from overflowing when logits are large.
- **Scale controls sharpness.** Multiplying every logit by $s > 1$ stretches
  the differences, so the largest entry takes more of the mass; as $s$ grows
  the output approaches one-hot (all mass on the argmax) and the derivative
  $\partial p_i / \partial z_i = p_i(1 - p_i)$ collapses toward zero.
  Multiplying by $s < 1$ flattens it toward uniform. That sensitivity is
  exactly why attention divides its scores by $\sqrt{d_k}$ ($d_k$, the
  per-head key size) before the
  softmax — [the attention post](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/)
  derives the scale it is correcting.

Drag the logits below to see all of this at once — the exponentials, the
normalizer, the probabilities — and use the scale and shift controls to
check the two properties:

`cat` is the most likely next token here — not because of anything
meaningful (these are arbitrary toy numbers), but because that's
mechanically all a prediction is: whatever accumulated on the stream,
projected onto the vocabulary and normalized into probabilities. Every
Transformer, at every step of generation, ends exactly here.

## Reproducing this in code

The embedding and unembedding steps above are real matrices; the "layers in
between" step is deliberately a stand-in, not real attention or a real MLP:
post 11 derived attention, and post 14 trains real blocks. What matters
here is only the shape: read the stream, compute something, add it back,
repeat:

```python

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

vocab = ["the", "cat", "sat", "."]
d_model = 4
W_E = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d_model)).round(2)   # embedding table
W_U = rng.normal(size=(d_model, len(vocab))).round(2)    # unembedding (untied)

def toy_layer(x, seed):
    """Stand-in for one block's attention+MLP sublayers combined. The real
    versions are far more structured than a random projection, but every
    one of them has this exact shape: read the stream, compute an update,
    add it back."""
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    W = r.normal(scale=0.3, size=(d_model, d_model))
    return x + np.tanh(x @ W)                            # <-- the residual add
                                                         # (real blocks also normalize first; omitted here)

token_ids = [0, 1, 2]                                    # "the cat sat"
x = W_E[token_ids[-1]]                                   # stream at the last position only
print("after embedding:  ", x.round(3))

for layer in range(3):                                   # 3 toy blocks
    x = toy_layer(x, seed=layer)
    print(f"after block {layer + 1}:   ", x.round(3))

logits = x @ W_U
probs = np.exp(logits - logits.max())
probs /= probs.sum()
print("logits: ", logits.round(3))
print("probs:  ", probs.round(3), "-> predicted next token:", vocab[probs.argmax()])
# after embedding:   [-0.7   -1.27  -0.62   0.04]
# after block 1:    [-0.426 -1.148 -1.106 -0.339]
# after block 2:    [-0.808 -1.475 -0.925 -0.608]
# after block 3:    [-1.505 -1.556 -1.035 -0.269]
# logits:  [ 0.207 -1.803  1.463 -1.101]
# probs:   [0.203 0.027 0.714 0.055] -> predicted next token: sat
```

Notice the stream keeps accumulating — it never resets between blocks — and
that the entire prediction machinery at the end (`x @ W_U`, softmax, argmax)
is identical regardless of what ran inside `toy_layer`. That's the whole
point of building the stream this way: everything upstream of the
unembedding can be replaced, extended, or studied independently, because the
interface between "the layers" and "the prediction" is just one accumulated
vector.

## Where this leads

This post stays at the level of the stream; the pieces it connects have
their own posts:

- **What attention computes** inside its sublayer — the $Q$, $K$, $V$
  projections and the scaled dot product — is [post
  11](/posts/transformer-attention-patterns/).
- **Training a real block.** `toy_layer` above is a stand-in.
  [Post 14](/posts/tiny-gpt-from-scratch/) builds real blocks, attention
  plus SwiGLU with RMSNorm before each, trains a small GPT on this blog, and
  removes the residual connection and moves the normalization to see what
  each costs.
- **Tokenization** (how text becomes IDs in the first place) is [post
  10](/posts/bpe-tokenizer-explained/), the floor beneath this one.
  **Positional encoding**, how the model knows where each token is, is
  [post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/); in current models it
  isn't added to $x_0$ at all but applied inside attention.
- **LayerNorm's exact formula** is in [post
  4.2](/posts/dropout-and-normalization/), which derives LayerNorm and
  RMSNorm and what normalizing does to training; all that matters here is
  *where* it sits (Pre-LN, inside each branch, not in the stream's main
  path).
- **Part V** comes back to the block: grouped-query and latent attention,
  mixtures of experts in place of the MLP, and attention's long-context
  cost.

Each of those is a well-defined, separate topic precisely because the
residual stream decouples them — that decoupling is the architectural
payoff this whole post has been building toward.

## Takeaways

- A Transformer's core object is the **residual stream**: one vector per
  token position, starting at the embedding, updated only by **addition**
  at every subsequent layer.
- Every sublayer follows the same contract — normalize, compute, add back —
  regardless of whether it's attention, an MLP, or something else entirely.
  That uniform contract is what lets each piece be studied, replaced, or
  extended independently.
- Residual (skip) connections exist because deep plain networks are hard to
  optimize; the residual add's identity term leaves part of the gradient,
  and the signal, passing through every block unchanged, so a block can
  start near the identity and learn from there.
- The MLP processes each position on its own. Current models use a gated
  MLP, SwiGLU: $\tfrac{8}{3}D$ wide at matched cost (Llama 1 and 2), wider
  in newer ones. In a matched-cost block the weights are about $12D^2$, two
  thirds of them in the MLP, and the MLP does most of the arithmetic until
  the context reaches about $8D$ tokens.
- Modern LLMs normalize *before* each sublayer (Pre-LN, standard since GPT-2),
  not after (Post-LN, the original 2017 design) — Pre-LN keeps the stream's
  main path free of normalization entirely.
- Prediction is mechanical once the stream is built: unembed, softmax,
  sample — the exact same three steps regardless of how many layers or what
  kind of layers produced the final stream value.

## References

- Vaswani et al., [_Attention Is All You Need_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) (NeurIPS, 2017) — the original Transformer; Post-LN, the encoder-decoder block structure this post's Pre-LN description is contrasted against.
- He, Zhang, Ren & Sun, [_Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385) (CVPR, 2016; arXiv 2015) — the residual/skip connection Transformers inherited, and the degradation problem it fixes.
- He, Zhang, Ren & Sun, [_Identity Mappings in Deep Residual Networks_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05027) (ECCV, 2016) — the identity-path analysis, and why nothing should sit on the path after the addition.
- Radford et al., [_Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners_](https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf) (GPT-2, 2019) — adopted Pre-LN plus a final norm.
- Wang et al., [_Learning Deep Transformer Models for Machine Translation_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.01787) (ACL, 2019) — pre-norm for deep Transformers.
- Xiong et al., [_On Layer Normalization in the Transformer Architecture_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.04745) (ICML, 2020) — why Post-LN needs warmup and Pre-LN doesn't.
- Elhage et al., [_A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits_](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2021/framework/index.html) (Anthropic, 2021) — the residual-stream framing this post (and this blog) is named after.
- Elhage et al., [_Toy Models of Superposition_](https://transformer-circuits.pub/2022/toy_model/index.html) (Anthropic, 2022) — more features than dimensions.
- Hendrycks & Gimpel, [_Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.08415) (2016) — GELU.
- Touvron et al. (Meta AI), [_LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13971) (2023) — SwiGLU at 8/3 D (11,008 for the 7B model).
- Shazeer, [_GLU Variants Improve Transformer_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202) (2020) — SwiGLU and the other gated MLPs, compared at matched cost.
- Press & Wolf, [_Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1608.05859) (EACL, 2017) — weight tying between the embedding and unembedding matrices.
[Post 28](/posts/policy-gradient-to-ppo/) trained a policy on a reward
it could compute. For "a helpful, honest answer" there is nothing to
compute: nobody can write that function down. What people can do, quickly
and fairly reliably, is look at two answers and say which is better.
**Reinforcement learning from human feedback** (RLHF) turns those
judgments into a reward, and trains the model on it with post 28's PPO.

## Table of contents

## From comparisons to a reward: Bradley–Terry

Bradley and Terry (1952) modeled paired comparisons with a hidden score
per item: item $i$ beats item $j$ with probability

$$
P(i \succ j) = \sigma(r_i - r_j) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-(r_i - r_j)}},
$$

the sigmoid of a difference ([post 1](/posts/learning-is-optimization/)'s
logistic function). Only differences matter: adding a constant to every
score changes nothing. Fitting the scores is logistic regression on
comparisons. Worked on three answers:

```python

# Bradley-Terry on three answers, A, B and C. People compared them in pairs:
# A beat B in 3 of 4 comparisons, B beat C in 3 of 4, A beat C in 4 of 5.
# Model: P(i beats j) = sigmoid(r_i - r_j). Fit r by maximizing the log-
# likelihood of the 13 outcomes. Only differences matter, so fix r_C = 0.
wins = {("A", "B"): (3, 1), ("B", "C"): (3, 1), ("A", "C"): (4, 1)}    # (i wins, j wins)
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))
r = {"A": 0.0, "B": 0.0, "C": 0.0}
for _ in range(5000):
    grad = {k: 0.0 for k in r}
    for (i, j), (wi, wj) in wins.items():
        p = sigmoid(r[i] - r[j])
        grad[i] += wi * (1 - p) - wj * p                  # d/dr_i of wi log p + wj log(1 - p)
        grad[j] -= wi * (1 - p) - wj * p
    for k in ("A", "B"):
        r[k] += 0.05 * grad[k]
print("rewards: " + ", ".join(f"r_{k} = {v:+.2f}" for k, v in r.items()))
for (i, j), (wi, wj) in wins.items():
    print(f"P({i} beats {j}) = sigmoid({r[i]:.2f} - {r[j]:.2f}) = {sigmoid(r[i] - r[j]):.2f}   observed {wi}/{wi + wj} = {wi / (wi + wj):.2f}")
```

```text
rewards: r_A = +1.67, r_B = +0.84, r_C = +0.00
P(A beats B) = sigmoid(1.67 - 0.84) = 0.70   observed 3/4 = 0.75
P(B beats C) = sigmoid(0.84 - 0.00) = 0.70   observed 3/4 = 0.75
P(A beats C) = sigmoid(1.67 - 0.00) = 0.84   observed 4/5 = 0.80
```

The fit doesn't reproduce every observed rate, and it shouldn't. Three
win rates are tied together by only two free differences, so the model
finds the single set of scores most consistent with all of them: A beat C
"only" 4 of 5 times, but A beat B and B beat C, so the model believes A
is well ahead of C.

A **reward model** is the same thing with a neural network for the score:
a language model whose next-token head is replaced by a linear head that
outputs a single number,
$r_\phi(x, y)$ for prompt $x$ and response $y$. Given a comparison where
people preferred $y_w$ to $y_l$, its loss is the negative log-likelihood
of that preference,

$$
\mathcal{L}(\phi) = -\log \sigma\big( r_\phi(x, y_w) - r_\phi(x, y_l) \big),
$$

which is [post 1](/posts/learning-is-optimization/)'s binary
cross-entropy with the reward difference as the logit. The reward model
never sees an absolute score, so its scores mean something only relative
to each other. InstructGPT kept all the pairs from one prompt's ranking in
the same batch element, each weighted by one over the number of pairs:
shuffled, those correlated pairs made the reward model overfit within one
epoch.

## The 2017 paper: a backflip from comparisons

Christiano et al. (2017) showed this works for control. An agent in a
simulator produced pairs of 1-to-2-second video clips of its behavior; a
person picked the better clip; a reward model was fitted to those choices,
and the agent was trained with RL on the reward model, with new
comparisons collected as the agent improved. With 900 comparisons, under
an hour of a person's time, a simulated robot learned to do a backflip, a
behavior nobody could easily specify as a reward function. With feedback
on under 1% of the agent's interactions, it nearly matched RL on the true
reward on the robotics tasks, and came close on some Atari games but not
others.

## InstructGPT's three steps

Ziegler et al. (2019) first applied the method to language models, adding
the KL penalty below; Stiennon et al. (2020) scaled it to summarization,
and Ouyang et al. (2022) to following instructions in general, with the
recipe still used today:
1. **Supervised fine-tuning** (post 25):
   about 13,000 prompts with answers written by labelers.
2. **Reward model**: for about 33,000 prompts, labelers ranked 4 to 9 of
   the SFT model's answers; every pair from a ranking is one comparison.
   InstructGPT's reward model had 6B parameters.
3. **PPO** against the reward model on about 31,000 prompts, with a
   penalty for moving away from the SFT model, below.

Labelers preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT model's answers to those of the
175B GPT-3, a model over 100 times larger, even when GPT-3 was given a
few-shot prompt. The usual reading is that RLHF mostly changes how a model
uses what it already knows, rather than adding knowledge.

## The KL leash, and the policy it implies

Maximize the reward model's score with nothing else, and the policy finds
whatever the reward model overrates: answers that are long, flattering, or
odd in ways the reward model never saw in training. RLHF therefore
maximizes reward minus a penalty for moving away from the reference
policy $\pi_\text{ref}$ (the SFT model):

$$
\max_\pi\ \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi}\big[ r(x, y) \big] - \beta\, \text{KL}\big( \pi(\cdot \mid x) \,\|\, \pi_\text{ref}(\cdot \mid x) \big).
$$

In practice the penalty is applied per token: each token's reward gets
$-\beta \log \frac{\pi(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_\text{ref}(a_t \mid s_t)}$, and the
reward model's score is added at the end. Summed over a sampled response,
these terms are a one-sample estimate of the sequence's KL divergence, so
the two forms agree on average.

This objective has an exact solution, worth deriving because DPO (post
30) is built on it. Write the objective for one prompt as a sum over
responses, and divide by $\beta$:

$$
\sum_y \pi(y) \Big[ \frac{r(y)}{\beta} - \log \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y)} \Big]
= -\sum_y \pi(y) \log \frac{\pi(y)}{\pi_\text{ref}(y)\, e^{r(y) / \beta}}
= -\text{KL}\big( \pi \,\|\, \pi^* \big) + \log Z,
$$

where $\pi^*(y) = \pi_\text{ref}(y)\, e^{r(y)/\beta} / Z$ and $Z = \sum_y
\pi_\text{ref}(y)\, e^{r(y)/\beta}$ makes it a distribution. $\log Z$
doesn't depend on $\pi$, and a KL divergence is zero only when the two
distributions are equal, so the best policy, over all possible policies
(a real network can only approximate it), is

$$
\pi^*(y \mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\, \pi_\text{ref}(y \mid x)\, \exp\!\Big( \frac{r(x, y)}{\beta} \Big).
$$

The reference policy, reweighted by exponentiated reward: a **Boltzmann
distribution** with temperature $\beta$. Large $\beta$ keeps $\pi^*$ close
to $\pi_\text{ref}$; small $\beta$ piles probability onto the highest
reward. PPO can't compute this distribution, because $Z$ sums over every
possible response; it climbs toward it with sampled gradient steps on a
parametric policy. On a space small enough to enumerate, it can be computed
exactly, which the experiment below does.

## An experiment: overoptimization, exactly

Everything in RLHF can be done exactly on a small enough space: 512
possible responses, a hidden **gold** reward standing in for what people
actually prefer, 300 noisy comparisons drawn from it through
Bradley–Terry, a reward model fitted to them, and the KL-regularized
optimum $\pi^*$ for a range of $\beta$, with no sampling noise from PPO,
in 100 random worlds of each kind:

```python

# RLHF end to end on a space small enough to enumerate: every "response" is
# 3 tokens from a vocabulary of 8, 512 in all. A hidden gold reward stands
# in for what people actually prefer. People never report it; they compare
# two responses and prefer one with probability sigmoid(gold_a - gold_b),
# the Bradley-Terry model.
#   1. Reward model: fit a proxy reward to 300 comparisons of responses
#      sampled from the starting policy, by maximizing the Bradley-Terry
#      likelihood. It sees one feature per (position, token), so it can't
#      represent anything that depends on two tokens together.
#   2. Policy: the KL-regularized optimum, pi(y) ~ pi_ref(y) exp(r(y) / beta)
#      (derived in the post), computed exactly for a range of beta.
# Two worlds, the same except for one term in the gold reward.
#   "random": gold = a score per (position, token) + effects of some token
#     pairs, of either sign: errors the proxy can't represent, but with no
#     direction to them;
#   "in moderation": the same, plus one token (7) that is good once and bad
#     in excess, +b for one occurrence, 0 for two, -4 for three, the way
#     detail or length is in a real answer. The starting policy rarely
#     writes it twice, so comparisons teach the proxy "7 is good" at every
#     position. Two strengths, b = 2 and b = 4.
# 100 random worlds each.
V, L = 8, 3
Y = np.array(list(itertools.product(range(V), repeat=L)))          # (512, 3)
X = np.zeros((len(Y), L * V))
X[np.arange(len(Y))[:, None], np.arange(L) * V + Y] = 1             # one-hot per position
sigmoid = lambda z: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

def world(kind, seed, bonus=0.0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    w = rng.normal(0, 1, L * V)
    pair = rng.normal(0, 2.5, (V, V)) * (rng.random((V, V)) < 0.15)
    gold = X @ w + pair[Y[:, 0], Y[:, 2]]
    if kind == "in moderation":
        gold = gold + np.array([0.0, bonus, 0.0, -4.0])[(Y == 7).sum(1)]
    tok = np.exp(rng.normal(0, 0.5, (L, V)))
    tok /= tok.sum(1, keepdims=True)
    ref = tok[0, Y[:, 0]] * tok[1, Y[:, 1]] * tok[2, Y[:, 2]]
    return rng, gold, ref

def fit_reward_model(rng, gold, ref, n=300, steps=3000, lr=0.5, l2=1e-3):
    a, b = rng.choice(len(Y), n, p=ref), rng.choice(len(Y), n, p=ref)
    prefer_a = rng.random(n) < sigmoid(gold[a] - gold[b])          # noisy human labels
    win, lose = np.where(prefer_a, a, b), np.where(prefer_a, b, a)
    D = X[win] - X[lose]
    theta = np.zeros(L * V)
    for _ in range(steps):                                          # gradient ascent on the BT log-likelihood
        p = sigmoid(D @ theta)
        theta += lr * (D.T @ (1 - p) / n - l2 * theta)
    return X @ theta

betas = [3, 1, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02]
for kind, bonus in (("random", 0.0), ("in moderation", 2.0), ("in moderation", 4.0)):
    rows = []                                                        # (seed, beta, KL, proxy gain, gold gain, 7s)
    for seed in range(100):
        rng, gold, ref = world(kind, seed, bonus)
        proxy = fit_reward_model(rng, gold, ref)
        for beta in betas:
            logits = np.log(ref) + proxy / beta
            logpi = logits - logits.max() - np.log(np.exp(logits - logits.max()).sum())
            pi = np.exp(logpi)
            rows.append((seed, beta, pi @ (logpi - np.log(ref)), pi @ proxy - ref @ proxy, pi @ gold - ref @ gold,
                         pi @ (Y == 7).sum(1)))
    rows = np.array(rows)
    G = rows[:, 4].reshape(100, len(betas))                         # gold gain, per world and beta
    fell = np.mean(G.max(1) - G[:, -1] > 0.5)
    name = kind if kind == "random" else f"{kind}, +{bonus:g} for one 7"
    print(f"\nworld \"{name}\": means over 100 worlds; the starting policy writes "
          f"{np.mean([world(kind, s, bonus)[2] @ (Y == 7).sum(1) for s in range(100)]):.2f} sevens per answer")
    print(f"{'beta':>6s} {'KL from ref':>12s} {'proxy gain':>11s} {'gold gain':>10s} {'7s per answer':>14s}")
    for beta in betas:
        r = rows[rows[:, 1] == beta]
        print(f"{beta:6g} {r[:, 2].mean():12.2f} {r[:, 3].mean():11.2f} {r[:, 4].mean():10.2f} {r[:, 5].mean():14.2f}")
    print(f"worlds whose gold gain ends more than 0.5 below its peak: {fell:.0%}")
```

```text

world "random": means over 100 worlds; the starting policy writes 0.37 sevens per answer
  beta  KL from ref  proxy gain  gold gain  7s per answer
     3         0.11        0.69       0.70           0.37
     1         0.88        1.87       1.88           0.37
   0.5         2.39        2.92       2.91           0.37
   0.3         3.76        3.46       3.45           0.36
   0.2         4.67        3.68       3.67           0.35
   0.1         5.64        3.83       3.82           0.34
  0.05         6.10        3.86       3.87           0.33
  0.02         6.37        3.87       3.88           0.32
worlds whose gold gain ends more than 0.5 below its peak: 6%

world "in moderation, +2 for one 7": means over 100 worlds; the starting policy writes 0.37 sevens per answer
  beta  KL from ref  proxy gain  gold gain  7s per answer
     3         0.11        0.68       0.74           0.47
     1         0.91        1.89       1.92           0.71
   0.5         2.42        2.95       2.75           0.95
   0.3         3.78        3.48       3.10           1.07
   0.2         4.66        3.70       3.24           1.11
   0.1         5.62        3.85       3.35           1.12
  0.05         6.10        3.88       3.40           1.12
  0.02         6.36        3.89       3.41           1.11
worlds whose gold gain ends more than 0.5 below its peak: 22%

world "in moderation, +4 for one 7": means over 100 worlds; the starting policy writes 0.37 sevens per answer
  beta  KL from ref  proxy gain  gold gain  7s per answer
     3         0.12        0.71       0.88           0.55
     1         1.06        2.15       1.92           1.02
   0.5         2.83        3.39       1.69           1.55
   0.3         4.20        3.93       1.05           1.85
   0.2         4.94        4.12       0.67           1.98
   0.1         5.66        4.22       0.35           2.07
  0.05         6.03        4.25       0.19           2.10
  0.02         6.29        4.26       0.10           2.11
worlds whose gold gain ends more than 0.5 below its peak: 71%
```

Read each table top to bottom as optimizing harder: $\beta$ falls, and
the policy moves further from where it started (KL, in nats).
- **When the reward model's errors have no direction, optimizing it is
  mostly safe.** In the "random" world the reward model can't represent the
  pair effects, so it is wrong about many responses, but its errors point
  every which way. Gold reward rises with the proxy, from 0.70 to 3.88 on
  average, and only 6% of worlds end more than 0.5 below their best.
- **A direction the policy can reach is what hurts.** The "in moderation"
  worlds add one term: token 7 is good once and bad three times. The reward
  model, trained on the starting policy's answers, which average about a
  third of a 7, learns "7 is good" at every position. When a single 7 is
  worth $+4$, that direction usually wins: the policy goes from 0.37 sevens
  per answer to 2.1, proxy reward climbs from 0.71 to 4.26, and gold
  reward peaks at 1.92, at $\beta = 1$ and about 1 nat of KL, then falls to
  0.10. In 71% of worlds it ends more than 0.5 below its peak.
- **Whether the policy goes there depends on the competition.** When a
  single 7 is worth only $+2$, the proxy's "7 is good" is usually weaker
  than the best ordinary token at the same position, and the policy writes
  a 7 there only in some worlds: 1.1 sevens per answer on average, gold
  still rising on average (to 3.41), and 22% of worlds ending more than 0.5
  below their peak. Five worlds would not have shown this: in the first
  five, three happened to fall.

The shape is qualitatively the one Gao et al. (2023) measured, in a setup
much like this one: a large "gold" reward model labeled the comparisons
that a smaller proxy reward model was trained on. Plotted against the
square root of the KL divergence, proxy reward kept rising while gold
reward rose, peaked and fell, with different curve shapes for best-of-$n$
and for RL. It is **Goodhart's law** for RLHF, and the worlds above show
what makes it bite: not that a reward model is wrong, but that it's wrong
in a direction the policy can push and that wins against the alternatives.
In real RLHF the best-known such direction is length: reward models tend
to prefer longer answers, and policies learn to pad (Singhal et al.,
2024). Gao et al. also found that the KL penalty acted much like stopping
early: it moved where the policy ended up on the curve, not the curve
itself. Either one, chosen by watching a held-out measure of quality and
not the reward model's score, is what keeps the policy before the peak.

## What it costs: the alignment tax

RLHF optimizes for what labelers prefer, which can cost abilities they
weren't judging. InstructGPT measured this as an **alignment tax**:
performance on some public NLP benchmarks dropped after PPO. Mixing
pretraining gradients back into the PPO updates (they called it PPO-ptx)
recovered most of it, though not all, the same replay that limited
forgetting in post 25.

## What changed since

- **AI feedback.** Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) replaced human
  harmlessness labels entirely: a model critiqued and revised its own
  answers against a written list of principles (a supervised stage), then
  judged pairs of answers against those principles to train the preference
  model for RL, called RL from AI feedback (RLAIF). Human labels were still
  used for helpfulness.
- **No reward model.** DPO (post 30) shows the reward model and the RL loop
  can be folded into one supervised loss on the comparisons.
- **Verifiable rewards.** For math and code, a checker replaces the reward
  model entirely, so there's no learned reward to overoptimize (post 31),
  though verifiers can be gamed too.

## Where this leads

- **Post 30** derives DPO from the Boltzmann optimum above.
- **Post 31** replaces the reward model with a checker, and the value model
  with a group of samples.

## Takeaways

- People can't write down a reward for "helpful", but they can compare.
  Bradley–Terry turns comparisons into scores, $P(i \succ j) =
  \sigma(r_i - r_j)$, and a reward model is that, with a network for $r$.
- RLHF is three steps, SFT, a reward model on comparisons, PPO against it.
  InstructGPT's 1.3B model was preferred to the 175B GPT-3.
- The KL-regularized objective has an exact optimum: the reference policy
  reweighted by $e^{r/\beta}$. PPO approximates it; DPO (post 30) uses it
  directly.
- A reward model's error is mostly harmless when it has no direction and
  harmful when it has one the policy can reach: over 100 exact toy worlds,
  gold reward kept rising with random errors (6% of worlds fell back), and
  peaked and fell, 1.92 to 0.10 on average, when the reward model
  overrated a token that was good once and bad in excess (71% fell back).
- The KL penalty or early stopping, chosen against a held-out measure of
  quality, keeps the policy before that peak; replaying pretraining data
  pays back some of the alignment tax.

  (2019) — the first RLHF on language models, with the KL penalty.

  (NeurIPS, 2020).

  (NeurIPS, 2022) — InstructGPT.

  (arXiv, 2022).
- Singhal, Goyal, Xu and Durrett, [_A Long Way to Go: Investigating Length Correlations in RLHF_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03716)
  (COLM, 2024) — length as a reward-hacking direction.
Part I built models that take a fixed-size input: a question's bag of
words, four routes out. Language isn't fixed-size. A sentence can be three
tokens or three thousand, and meaning depends on order: "the model trains
the data" isn't "the data trains the model". This part of the series is
about models that read sequences, and it starts with the design that
dominated neural sequence modeling in the years before the Transformer:
the **recurrent neural network**.

The idea fits in one sentence: *read one token at a time, and keep one
fixed-size vector that summarizes everything read so far.* Both halves of
that sentence turn out to be problems.
- **One at a time** means the computation is serial, and the gradient has
  to travel back through every step, where it shrinks or explodes.
- **One fixed-size vector** means everything the model will ever know about
  the past has to fit in it.

This post builds an RNN by hand, measures both problems, and shows the two
fixes that came before the Transformer: gates (LSTM, GRU) for the first, and
attention for the second. Attention then turns out to be the whole answer,
which is where Part III picks up.

## Table of contents

## A state that carries the past

An **Elman RNN** (Elman, 1990) keeps a **hidden state** $h_t$, a vector, and
updates it at every step from the previous state and the new input $x_t$:

$$
h_t = \tanh(x_t W_x + h_{t-1} W_h + b)
$$

The same weights $W_x$, $W_h$ and $b$ are used at every step. That's what
lets one network read a sequence of any length, and it's also where the
trouble starts. A prediction at step $t$ reads $h_t$, through an output
layer like the router's. Here are three steps with a 2-number state, every
number shown, and the gradient computed backward through all three:

```python

# An Elman RNN with a 2-number state, run for 3 steps:
#   h_t = tanh(x_t W_x + h_{t-1} W_h + b),   and a prediction y = h_3 w_out at the end.
W_x = np.array([[0.5, -0.3]])                # one input number per step
W_h = np.array([[0.8, 0.2], [-0.4, 0.6]])    # the same matrix at every step
b, w_out = np.array([0.1, 0.0]), np.array([1.0, -1.0])
xs = [1.0, 0.0, -1.0]

def forward(W_h):
    h, hs = np.zeros(2), [np.zeros(2)]
    for x in xs:
        h = np.tanh(x * W_x[0] + h @ W_h + b)
        hs.append(h)
    return hs, hs[-1] @ w_out

hs, y = forward(W_h)
for t, h in enumerate(hs[1:], 1):
    print(f"h_{t} = {np.round(h, 4)}")
print(f"prediction y = h_3 . w_out = {y:.4f}")

# Backprop through time: run post 3.1's rules backward through the 3 steps.
# The same W_h was used at every step, so its gradient is the sum over steps.
dW_h, dh = np.zeros_like(W_h), w_out.copy()          # dy/dh_3
for t in range(3, 0, -1):
    dz = dh * (1 - hs[t] ** 2)                        # back through tanh
    dW_h += np.outer(hs[t - 1], dz)                   # this step's share of the gradient
    dh = dz @ W_h.T                                   # pass back to h_{t-1}
    print(f"gradient reaching h_{t - 1}: {np.round(dh, 4)}")
eps, numeric = 1e-6, np.zeros_like(W_h)
for i in np.ndindex(W_h.shape):
    E = np.zeros_like(W_h); E[i] = eps
    numeric[i] = (forward(W_h + E)[1] - forward(W_h - E)[1]) / (2 * eps)
print(f"dy/dW_h = {np.round(dW_h, 4).tolist()}; largest gap to finite differences "
      f"{np.abs(dW_h - numeric).max():.1e}")
```

```text
h_1 = [ 0.537  -0.2913]
h_2 = [ 0.5691 -0.0673]
h_3 = [0.082 0.357]
prediction y = h_3 . w_out = -0.2750
gradient reaching h_2: [ 0.6201 -0.9208]
gradient reaching h_1: [ 0.1521 -0.7177]
gradient reaching h_0: [-0.0448 -0.4374]
dy/dW_h = [[0.7904, -0.9888], [-0.189, 0.3257]]; largest gap to finite differences 4.6e-11
```
