  (EMNLP, 2024).
[Post 15](/posts/decoding-from-logits-to-text/) turned a model's
distributions into tokens, one forward pass each. A 300-word answer is
about 400 tokens, and at 20 to 50 milliseconds a token that's eight to
twenty seconds of generation. Nothing about decoding can change that the tokens
come out one at a time. What can change is when the reader sees them.

**Streaming** sends each piece of text as soon as it exists, instead of the
whole answer at the end. It doesn't make generation faster: the last token
arrives when it would have anyway. It changes which wait the reader feels.
This post builds a streaming server from the standard library, measures
what it buys, and goes through what breaks it in practice.

## Table of contents

## Five ways to get text to a browser

The web was built for request and response: the client asks, the server
answers, the connection is done. Generated text doesn't fit that shape,
since the answer exists only gradually. There are five standard ways to
deal with it:

| | how it works | first text after | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **request/response** | one answer, sent when complete | the whole generation | simplest; nothing to show meanwhile |
| **polling** | the client asks "anything new?" every $\Delta t$ | up to $\Delta t$ late, each time | many requests, most of them empty |
| **long polling** | the server holds each request open until there's something new | about one round trip late | a new request per piece |
| **server-sent events (SSE)** | one long HTTP response, the server writes events into it | immediately | one direction only, server to client |
| **WebSocket** | the connection upgrades to a two-way message channel | immediately | its own protocol; proxies and load balancers must support it |

Nearly every model API streams with **SSE**: OpenAI's, Anthropic's and
Google's all do. It's plain HTTP, so it passes through the same infrastructure as
everything else, and generation only needs the server-to-client direction.
WebSockets come in when the client must also talk during the stream, as
voice interfaces do (post 71); OpenAI's Realtime API, for voice, uses
WebSockets or WebRTC.

## The SSE wire format

An SSE response is an ordinary HTTP response with the content type
`text/event-stream`, kept open, into which the server writes **events** as
lines of text (WHATWG, *HTML Living Standard*):
- `data: ...` lines carry the payload; several `data` lines in one event
  are joined with newlines;
- `event: ...` names the event's type, `id: ...` gives it an identifier,
  and `retry: ...` tells the client how long to wait before reconnecting;
- a **blank line** ends the event and dispatches it;
- a line starting with `:` is a comment, ignored, which makes it the way
  to send keep-alive pings through proxies that close idle connections.

If the connection drops, the browser's `EventSource` reconnects by itself
and sends the last `id` it saw in a `Last-Event-ID` header, so the server
can resume. But `EventSource` can only make GET requests, with no request
body and no custom headers, and a model API needs to POST a prompt and an
API key (which belongs on your backend, never in the browser). So clients
for model APIs read the response stream with `fetch` and parse the events
themselves, and those conveniences don't apply. They'd need help anyway:
`EventSource` reconnects after a stream ends *normally* too, unless the
server answers with status 204, and resuming at `Last-Event-ID` only works
if the server kept what it already generated. Otherwise a reconnect starts
generation over, and bills it again.

How the stream says it's finished is a convention, not part of SSE:
- **OpenAI**'s Chat Completions end with a last event whose data is the
  literal `[DONE]`; its Python SDK stops reading when an event's data
  starts with `[DONE]`. OpenAI's newer Responses API uses named, typed
  events instead (`response.output_text.delta`, ..., `response.completed`).
- **Anthropic**'s Messages API names every event: `message_start`, then for
  each content block `content_block_start`, a series of
  `content_block_delta`, and `content_block_stop`, then one or more
  `message_delta` and a final `message_stop`, with `ping` events anywhere
  and an `error` event if something fails mid-stream. New event types may
  be added, so a client should ignore ones it doesn't know.

The server below uses the OpenAI-style sentinel, with one JSON object per
piece of text.

## A streaming server, from the standard library

The whole server, on `asyncio` and no web framework, with post 15's
`choose` for sampling and Qwen2.5-1.5B as the model. Generation runs in a
thread and hands each piece of text to the network side through a queue;
before every token it checks a stop flag:

```python

from lm import model, tok, DEVICE
from sampling import choose
from detokenizer import Detokenizer

# One model, three ways to deliver its tokens, on Python's standard library:
#   POST /complete  the whole answer as one JSON response, at the end;
#   POST /stream    server-sent events, one event per piece of text;
#   GET  /ws        a WebSocket, which also lets the client say "stop";
#   GET  /log       what was generated for each request so far.
# Generation runs in a thread and checks a stop flag before every token.
# With --naive the server never notices that a client has left.
NAIVE = "--naive" in sys.argv
LOG = []                                                  # (endpoint, tokens generated, client left?)

def generate(prompt, n, out, stop, loop):
    """Sample up to n tokens (top-p 0.9, seeded), pushing text pieces to the
    asyncio queue `out`; a None marks the end."""
    m, ids = model(), torch.tensor([tok(prompt).input_ids], device=DEVICE)
    g = torch.Generator(device=DEVICE).manual_seed(0)
    d, history, produced = Detokenizer(), [], 0
    with torch.no_grad():
        result = m(ids, use_cache=True)
        for _ in range(n):
            if stop.is_set():
                break
            token = choose(result.logits[0, -1], history, g, p=0.9)
            history.append(token); produced += 1
            if token == tok.eos_token_id:
                break
            loop.call_soon_threadsafe(out.put_nowait, d.push(token))
            result = m(torch.tensor([[token]], device=DEVICE), past_key_values=result.past_key_values, use_cache=True)
    loop.call_soon_threadsafe(out.put_nowait, None)
    return produced

async def start(prompt, n):
    out, stop, loop = asyncio.Queue(), threading.Event(), asyncio.get_running_loop()
    job = loop.run_in_executor(None, generate, prompt, n, out, stop, loop)
    return out, stop, job

async def handle(reader, writer):
    head = (await reader.readuntil(b"\r\n\r\n")).decode()
    method, path, _ = head.split("\r\n")[0].split(" ")
    headers = {k.lower(): v for k, v in (l.split(": ", 1) for l in head.split("\r\n")[1:] if ": " in l)}
    if path == "/ws":
        return await websocket(reader, writer, headers)
    if path == "/log":                                    # what the server did, for the experiments
        payload = json.dumps(LOG).encode()
        writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" % len(payload) + payload)
        return writer.close()
    body = json.loads(await reader.readexactly(int(headers["content-length"])))
    out, stop, job = await start(body["prompt"], body.get("max_tokens", 100))
    left = False
    if path == "/complete":
        pieces = []
        while (piece := await out.get()) is not None:
            pieces.append(piece)
        payload = json.dumps({"text": "".join(pieces)}).encode()
        writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: application/json\r\n"
                     b"Content-Length: %d\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n" % len(payload) + payload)
    else:
        writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Type: text/event-stream\r\nCache-Control: no-cache\r\n"
                     b"X-Accel-Buffering: no\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n")
        if not NAIVE:                                     # the client closing its side means it's gone
            asyncio.create_task(watch(reader, stop))
        while (piece := await out.get()) is not None:
            if piece:
                writer.write(b"data: " + json.dumps({"text": piece}).encode() + b"\n\n")
                try:
                    await writer.drain()
                except ConnectionError:
                    left = True
                    if not NAIVE:
                        stop.set()
        writer.write(b"data: [DONE]\n\n")
        left = left or stop.is_set()
    LOG.append((path, await job, left))
    print(f"{path}: generated {LOG[-1][1]} tokens, client left early: {left}", flush=True)
    try:
        await writer.drain(); writer.close()
    except ConnectionError:
        pass

async def watch(reader, stop):
    await reader.read()                                   # returns b"" when the client disconnects
    stop.set()

# --- WebSocket (RFC 6455), by hand: an HTTP upgrade, then framed messages.
async def websocket(reader, writer, headers):
    accept = base64.b64encode(hashlib.sha1((headers["sec-websocket-key"] +
                              "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11").encode()).digest())
    writer.write(b"HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n"
                 b"Sec-WebSocket-Accept: " + accept + b"\r\n\r\n")
    request = json.loads(await read_frame(reader))
    out, stop, job = await start(request["prompt"], request.get("max_tokens", 100))
    async def listen():                                   # the client can talk while the server streams
        while True:
            message = await read_frame(reader)
            if message is None or json.loads(message).get("stop"):
                stop.set(); return
    listener = asyncio.create_task(listen())
    while (piece := await out.get()) is not None:
        if piece:
            writer.write(frame(json.dumps({"text": piece}).encode()))
    writer.write(frame(json.dumps({"done": True}).encode()))
    await writer.drain()
    LOG.append(("/ws", await job, stop.is_set()))
    print(f"/ws: generated {LOG[-1][1]} tokens, client said stop: {stop.is_set()}", flush=True)
    listener.cancel(); writer.close()

def frame(payload, opcode=0x1):
    """A server-to-client frame: FIN + opcode, then the length, then the data."""
    n = len(payload)
    head = bytes([0x80 | opcode]) + (bytes([n]) if n < 126 else bytes([126]) + n.to_bytes(2, "big"))
    return head + payload

async def read_frame(reader):
    """A client-to-server frame; clients must mask their data with 4 random bytes."""
    try:
        b0, b1 = await reader.readexactly(2)
    except asyncio.IncompleteReadError:
        return None
    n = b1 & 0x7F
    if n == 126:
        n = int.from_bytes(await reader.readexactly(2), "big")
    mask, data = await reader.readexactly(4), await reader.readexactly(n)
    if b0 & 0x0F == 0x8:                                  # a close frame
        return None
    return bytes(b ^ mask[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(data)).decode()

async def main():
    model()                                               # load the weights before taking requests
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 8765)
    print("listening on 8765" + (" (naive)" if NAIVE else ""), flush=True)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

The SSE response has neither a `Content-Length` nor chunked encoding, so
its end is the connection closing. That's legal HTTP/1.1, but it means a
dropped connection looks like a finished answer at the HTTP level, which
is one thing the `[DONE]` event is for: it tells the client the end was
meant. Frameworks send chunked encoding instead, and HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
carry the body in frames. This is a teaching server, not a production one:
it parses headers loosely and handles few errors.

The WebSocket part is the protocol written out (RFC 6455). The client asks
to upgrade with a random key; the server proves it understood by hashing
the key with a fixed string from the RFC and sending the hash back, and
from then on both sides exchange **frames**: a byte with the frame's type
and a "final fragment" bit, the payload's length in one, three or nine
bytes, and the payload. Frames from the client must be **masked**: XORed
with four random bytes the browser chooses and the page's script can't
predict. Without that, a script could send bytes that an old proxy which
doesn't understand WebSockets reads as a fresh HTTP request, and the proxy
would then cache the attacker's reply as the response for some other
site's URL (RFC 6455, §10.3).

This server leaves out what a real WebSocket server needs. It doesn't
answer pings (opcode 9) with pongs, and since it treats every frame as
text, a client library that sends a ping, as Python's `websockets` does
every 20 seconds by default, would break its "stop" listener. It doesn't
send its own close frame at the end, so a browser reports an unclean
close. It has no 64-bit lengths, no fragmented messages, and no check of
the `Origin` header, which matters because browsers don't apply CORS to
WebSockets and do send cookies: without that check, any page can open a
socket to it as the user.

### A trap in sending text one token at a time

The server doesn't send `tok.decode([token])` for each token. A token is a
piece of a *byte* sequence, and one character can span several tokens:

```python
from lm import tok

# Streaming text one token at a time has a trap: a token is a piece of a
# byte sequence, not of a string, and one character can span two tokens.
# Decoding each token alone then prints broken characters. The fix is
# incremental: decode everything so far, and emit only the new text once it
# no longer ends in a half-finished character.
class Detokenizer:
    def __init__(self):
        self.ids, self.sent = [], ""
    def push(self, token_id):
        """Add a token; return the new text that is safe to send (may be '')."""
        self.ids.append(token_id)
        text = tok.decode(self.ids)
        if text.endswith("�"):            # the last character isn't complete yet
            return ""
        new, self.sent = text[len(self.sent):], text
        return new
```

```python
from lm import tok
from detokenizer import Detokenizer

# A character split across tokens, decoded one token at a time and
# incrementally.
text = "Con vẹt 🦜 nói: mô hình sinh văn bản từng token một 🫠"
ids = tok(text).input_ids
naive = [tok.decode([i]) for i in ids]
print(f"{len(ids)} tokens; decoded one by one:")
print("  " + " | ".join(naive))

d = Detokenizer()
pieces = [d.push(i) for i in ids]
print("incremental:")
print("  " + " | ".join(pieces))
print(f"broken pieces one by one: {sum('�' in p for p in naive)}, incremental: "
      f"{sum('�' in p for p in pieces)}; joined text equal to the original: {''.join(pieces) == text}")
```

```text
20 tokens; decoded one by one:
  Con |  v | ẹ | t |  � | � | � |  nói | : |  mô |  hình |  sinh |  văn |  bản |  từng |  token |  một |  � | � | �
incremental:
  Con |  v | ẹ | t |  |  |  🦜 |  nói | : |  mô |  hình |  sinh |  văn |  bản |  từng |  token |  một |  |  |  🫠
broken pieces one by one: 6, incremental: 0; joined text equal to the original: True
```

The parrot and the melting face are each split across three tokens, and
decoding them one at a time produces replacement characters `�` that no
later token can repair, since each piece was already sent. The
incremental version holds a piece back until its last character is
complete. The Vietnamese words in this sentence happen to split only
between whole characters ("v", "ẹ", "t"), but emoji, rarer scripts and
unusual accented letters hit this constantly with a byte-level tokenizer.
Three caveats. Decoding the whole text every step costs time proportional
to its length; production detokenizers decode only a short window of
recent tokens (vLLM's offsets, Hugging Face's `DecodeStream`). This one
never flushes: whatever it holds back when generation ends must be sent
then. And it assumes decoding a prefix of the tokens gives a prefix of the
text, which holds for byte-level BPE like Qwen's but not for every
tokenizer.

## Measured: the first text, and the bytes

A client written on raw sockets, so it can time every byte and count it:

<Reveal label="Show the client and the measurement script">

```python

# Measuring the server from the outside, over raw sockets, so every byte on
# the wire is counted: when the first text arrives, when the last does, and
# how many bytes it took.
PORT = int(os.environ.get("PORT", 8765))

async def post(path, prompt, n, stop_after=None):
    """POST a prompt; returns (seconds to first text, seconds to the end,
    bytes received, pieces of text). Closes early after `stop_after` events."""
    r, w = await asyncio.open_connection("127.0.0.1", PORT)
    body = json.dumps({"prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": n}).encode()
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    w.write(b"POST %s HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\n\r\n" % (path.encode(), len(body)) + body)
    first, received, pieces, buffer = None, 0, [], b""
    head_done = False
    while chunk := await r.read(65536):
        received += len(chunk); buffer += chunk
        if not head_done and b"\r\n\r\n" in buffer:
            head_done, buffer = True, buffer.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)[1]
        if head_done and path == "/stream":
            while b"\n\n" in buffer:
                event, buffer = buffer.split(b"\n\n", 1)
                data = event[len(b"data: "):]
                if data != b"[DONE]":
                    first = first or time.perf_counter() - t0
                    pieces.append(json.loads(data)["text"])
            if stop_after and len(pieces) >= stop_after:
                w.close(); await asyncio.sleep(1.0)       # leave, then give the server a moment to notice
                return first, time.perf_counter() - t0, received, pieces
    if path == "/complete":
        first = time.perf_counter() - t0
        pieces = [json.loads(buffer)["text"]]
    return first, time.perf_counter() - t0, received, pieces

def ws_frame(payload):
    """A client-to-server text frame, masked as RFC 6455 requires."""
    mask, n = os.urandom(4), len(payload)
    size = bytes([0x80 | n]) if n < 126 else bytes([0x80 | 126]) + n.to_bytes(2, "big")
    return bytes([0x81]) + size + mask + bytes(b ^ mask[i % 4] for i, b in enumerate(payload))

async def websocket(prompt, n, stop_after=None):
    r, w = await asyncio.open_connection("127.0.0.1", PORT)
    key = base64.b64encode(os.urandom(16))
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    w.write(b"GET /ws HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nUpgrade: websocket\r\nConnection: Upgrade\r\n"
            b"Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13\r\nSec-WebSocket-Key: " + key + b"\r\n\r\n")
    received = len(await r.readuntil(b"\r\n\r\n"))
    w.write(ws_frame(json.dumps({"prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": n}).encode()))
    first, pieces = None, []
    while True:
        b0, b1 = await r.readexactly(2)
        size = b1 if b1 < 126 else int.from_bytes(await r.readexactly(2), "big")
        message = json.loads(await r.readexactly(size))
        received += 2 + (2 if b1 >= 126 else 0) + size
        if message.get("done"):
            break
        first = first or time.perf_counter() - t0
        pieces.append(message["text"])
        if stop_after and len(pieces) == stop_after:
            w.write(ws_frame(b'{"stop": true}'))           # same connection, other direction
    w.close()
    return first, time.perf_counter() - t0, received, pieces
```

```python

from client import post, websocket

# Five prompts from post 15's set, 100 tokens each, delivered three ways.
prompts = [p["prompt"] for p in json.load(open("../post15/prompts.json"))][:5]

async def main():
    rows = {"/complete": [], "/stream": [], "/ws": []}
    for prompt in prompts:
        rows["/complete"].append(await post("/complete", prompt, 100))
        rows["/stream"].append(await post("/stream", prompt, 100))
        rows["/ws"].append(await websocket(prompt, 100))
    for name, rs in rows.items():
        first = sum(r[0] for r in rs) / len(rs); total = sum(r[1] for r in rs) / len(rs)
        text = ["".join(r[3]) for r in rs]
        received = sum(r[2] for r in rs); chars = sum(len(t.encode()) for t in text)
        print(f"{name:10s} first text after {first:5.2f} s, all of it after {total:5.2f} s; "
              f"{received / 5:6.0f} bytes on the wire per answer, for {chars / 5:4.0f} bytes of text "
              f"({received / chars:.1f}x)")
    same = all("".join(a[3]) == "".join(b[3]) == "".join(c[3]) for a, b, c in zip(*rows.values()))
    print(f"the same text all three ways: {same}")

asyncio.run(main())
```

</Reveal>

Five of post 15's prompts, 100 tokens each, delivered all three ways:

```text
/complete  first text after  4.68 s, all of it after  4.68 s;    596 bytes on the wire per answer, for  488 bytes of text (1.2x)
/stream    first text after  0.13 s, all of it after  4.75 s;   2626 bytes on the wire per answer, for  488 bytes of text (5.4x)
/ws        first text after  0.13 s, all of it after  5.12 s;   2038 bytes on the wire per answer, for  488 bytes of text (4.2x)
the same text all three ways: True
```

The same text arrives all three ways, and it finishes at about the same
time, 4.7 to 5.1 seconds; repeated runs on this laptop vary by more than
the gap between the three. What differs is the **first text**: 4.68
seconds without streaming, about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds with either kind of
streaming (0.13 on average here). That is the **time to first token**
(TTFT), measured from sending the request: the prompt's forward pass plus
one sampling step. These prompts are short, about 40 tokens. With a
10,000-token prompt, or a queue of other requests ahead, TTFT grows, and
that is where post 51 picks it up.

Streaming costs bytes. Each piece of text, about 5 bytes, travels inside
an event: `data: {"text": "..."}` and a blank line. For this server that's
5.4 times the text's own size, 4.2 with WebSocket frames, against 1.2 for
one JSON response. Real APIs carry more per event:

```python

# What one streamed piece of text, "Two", costs on the wire in different
# formats, as compact JSON. The Anthropic event is the documented example's
# shape; the OpenAI chunk has the fields of the example in OpenAI's cookbook
# (current chunks also carry a padding field, below).
text = "Two"
ours = b"data: " + json.dumps({"text": text}).encode() + b"\n\n"
anthropic = (b"event: content_block_delta\ndata: " + json.dumps(
    {"type": "content_block_delta", "index": 0, "delta": {"type": "text_delta", "text": text}},
    separators=(",", ":")).encode() + b"\n\n")
openai = b"data: " + json.dumps(
    {"id": "chatcmpl-9lMgfRSWPHcw51s6wxKT1YEO2CKpd", "object": "chat.completion.chunk", "created": 1721075653,
     "model": "gpt-july-test", "system_fingerprint": "fp_e9b8ed65d2",
     "choices": [{"index": 0, "delta": {"content": text}, "logprobs": None, "finish_reason": None}]},
    separators=(",", ":")).encode() + b"\n\n"
payload = json.dumps({"text": text}).encode()
websocket = bytes([0x81, len(payload)]) + payload            # a server-to-client frame: 2 bytes of header
for name, b in (("this post's SSE event", ours), ("Anthropic content_block_delta", anthropic),
                ("OpenAI chat.completion.chunk", openai), ("this post's WebSocket frame", websocket)):
    print(f"{name:31s} {len(b):4d} bytes for {len(text.encode())} bytes of text")
```

```text
this post's SSE event             23 bytes for 3 bytes of text
Anthropic content_block_delta    118 bytes for 3 bytes of text
OpenAI chat.completion.chunk     257 bytes for 3 bytes of text
this post's WebSocket frame       17 bytes for 3 bytes of text
```

An OpenAI chunk repeats the response's identifier, model name and
timestamp in every event: about 257 bytes to carry three bytes of text.
Current chunks are larger still, and vary: OpenAI now pads each one with a
random-length `obfuscation` field by default, because otherwise the size
of each encrypted event reveals each token's length to anyone watching the
network, enough to infer much of what a response says (Weiss et al.,
2024).
That sounds wasteful and mostly isn't: at 20 to 100 events a second it's
tens of kilobytes a second, nothing next to what a web page loads. Bytes
start to matter for many concurrent streams through one proxy, and for
compression, below.

## What the reader feels

Streaming helps because people read slower than models write:

```python

from lm import tok

# Is generation faster than reading? Tokens per word on the blog's own
# prose (post 15's 20 real continuations), against a reader's speed: 238
# words a minute for non-fiction, the average across studies (Brysbaert,
# 2019). Generation speed is from measure.py: 100 tokens in about 4.7 s.
texts = [p["human"] for p in json.load(open("../post15/prompts.json"))]
tokens = sum(len(tok(t).input_ids) for t in texts)
words = sum(len(t.split()) for t in texts)
per_word = tokens / words
reading = 238 / 60 * per_word                              # tokens a second a reader gets through
generating = 100 / 4.7
print(f"{per_word:.2f} tokens per word; a reader at 238 words a minute takes in {reading:.1f} tokens a second; "
      f"this laptop generates {generating:.0f}, {generating / reading:.1f} times as fast")
for n_words in (50, 300):
    n = n_words * per_word
    print(f"a {n_words}-word answer ({n:.0f} tokens): {n / generating:.1f} s to generate, {n_words / 238 * 60:.0f} s to read; "
          f"without streaming the reader waits {n / generating:.1f} s before the first word, with it about 0.13 s")
```

```text
1.38 tokens per word; a reader at 238 words a minute takes in 5.5 tokens a second; this laptop generates 21, 3.9 times as fast
a 50-word answer (69 tokens): 3.2 s to generate, 13 s to read; without streaming the reader waits 3.2 s before the first word, with it about 0.13 s
a 300-word answer (415 tokens): 19.5 s to generate, 76 s to read; without streaming the reader waits 19.5 s before the first word, with it about 0.13 s
```

A reader takes in about 5.5 tokens a second; even a laptop generates four
times that. So once the first piece arrives, the reader is never waiting:
the text runs ahead of them. Without streaming, a 300-word answer means 20
seconds of nothing. With it, 0.13 seconds, then reading. The **perceived
latency** is the time to first token, not the total, as long as
generation stays ahead of reading. That second condition is the one
serving systems have to protect under load: post 51's time per output
token, TPOT, is the number that must stay below about 180 ms (one token
per $1/5.5$ seconds) for a reader never to catch up. That's an average,
and averages hide stalls: a pause while the server runs someone else's
long prompt is what a reader notices, so post 51 looks at the slowest
gaps between tokens, not only the mean. (And 238 words a minute is for
English prose; the tokens per word differ for code and for other
languages, and readers skim.)

## When the user leaves

A user closes the tab halfway through an answer. What should the server
do? Stop: every further token costs a forward pass, and the request's KV
cache, which can be gigabytes for a long context (post 20), stays
allocated until generation ends. Two runs of the same experiment, one
against the server above, which watches its connection, and one against
the same server started with `--naive`, which doesn't:

<Reveal label="Show the experiment script">

```python

from client import post, websocket

# Three experiments against the running server (and, for the last, through
# the proxy on port 8766):
#   leave:   the client goes away after 10 pieces of text. Does the server stop?
#   stop:    over a WebSocket, the client asks it to stop after 10 pieces.
#   proxy:   when does the first text arrive through a buffering proxy?
PROMPT = json.load(open("../post15/prompts.json"))[3]["prompt"]

async def server_log():
    r, w = await asyncio.open_connection("127.0.0.1", 8765)
    w.write(b"GET /log HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\n\r\n")
    return json.loads((await r.read()).split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)[1])

async def main(which):
    if which == "leave":
        await post("/stream", PROMPT, 100, stop_after=10)
        await asyncio.sleep(5)                            # let a server that didn't notice finish
        path, generated, left = (await server_log())[-1]
        print(f"SSE client left after 10 pieces: the server generated {generated} tokens in all")
    if which == "stop":
        await websocket(PROMPT, 100, stop_after=10)
        path, generated, stopped = (await server_log())[-1]
        print(f"WebSocket client said stop after 10 pieces: the server generated {generated} tokens in all")
    if which == "proxy":
        client.PORT = 8766
        first, total, received, pieces = await post("/stream", PROMPT, 100)
        print(f"through the proxy: first text after {first:.2f} s, the end after {total:.2f} s, "
              f"{len(pieces)} pieces, {received:,} bytes")

asyncio.run(main(os.environ["WHICH"]))
```

</Reveal>

Watching the connection:

```text
SSE client left after 10 pieces: the server generated 10 tokens in all
```

Started with `--naive`:

```text
SSE client left after 10 pieces: the server generated 100 tokens in all
```

The server that notices stops at 10 tokens; the naive one generates all
100, 90 of them for nobody. (The 11th forward pass was already running when
the client left, and its token was discarded: a check per token stops
within one token, and a batched serving engine checks once per step.)

How the server notices matters, and no signal works everywhere:
- **Writing**: after the client closes, the operating system accepts the
  next write and the one after fails, so on a direct connection a server
  that only watches for write errors stops about one token late.
- **Reading**, as here: the read returns end-of-file the moment the client
  closes, so the stop is immediate. But end-of-file isn't the same as gone:
  a client that half-closes its sending side after the request would look
  like it left.
- **Behind a proxy**, the server sees the proxy's connection, not the
  user's. nginx closes the upstream connection when its client aborts, by
  default; other hops vary.
- **Over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3**, cancelling one request resets one stream on a
  connection that stays open, so no end-of-file ever arrives; the server
  must watch for the stream reset.
- **A client whose network just vanishes**, a phone going to sleep, sends
  nothing at all, and neither signal fires until TCP gives up, minutes
  later.

Frameworks expose the transport's own signal (Starlette's
`request.is_disconnected()`, or the disconnect message that cancels a
`StreamingResponse`), serving engines abort the request on it, and a write
timeout or a heartbeat catches the rest. The same check belongs on the
non-streaming endpoint: a closed tab wastes a `/complete` request just as
much, and this server doesn't check there at all.

With a WebSocket the client doesn't have to leave to stop. It sends a
message on the same connection:

```text
WebSocket client said stop after 10 pieces: the server generated 10 tokens in all
```

With SSE, which only goes one way, "stop" means closing the connection, or
a second request to a cancel endpoint.

**Backpressure** is the other direction of the same problem: the client is
there but slow, a phone on a poor network. Here the generation thread puts
pieces into an unbounded queue, so a slow reader makes the queue grow
while the model runs at full speed. A bounded queue makes the generator
wait when the reader falls behind; whether that's wanted depends on
whether the GPU time is better spent on other users. Text is small enough
that most servers buffer it and move on, but it's a decision, not a
default.

## The proxy that undoes it all

Between a user and a model server there are usually several machines: a
CDN, a load balancer, a reverse proxy such as nginx. Proxies can
**buffer** responses, collecting upstream data before passing it on, which
is efficient for ordinary pages and fatal for a stream. Whether a given hop
does depends on the product and its configuration. nginx's
`proxy_buffering`, on by default, stores the response in buffers of one
memory page (4 or 8 KB) as it arrives, and often passes small SSE events
on promptly anyway; a response cache, a gzip filter, an
application server's own buffering, or some load balancers and CDNs hold
data back. A stand-in for the worst case: a proxy that forwards only in
8 KB blocks, and that, started with `--honor`, respects `X-Accel-Buffering:
no`, the response header nginx honors by default to turn buffering off for
one response:

```python

# A stand-in for a reverse proxy between the user and the server, the kind
# every deployment has (nginx, a load balancer, a CDN). This one buffers the
# worst way a hop can: it collects the upstream response and forwards it
# only in blocks of 8 KB, or when the upstream finishes.
# With --honor it skips buffering for responses that ask for that with the
# header nginx uses, X-Accel-Buffering: no.
HONOR = "--honor" in sys.argv
BLOCK = 8192

async def pipe_up(reader, writer):
    while data := await reader.read(65536):
        writer.write(data); await writer.drain()

async def handle(client_r, client_w):
    up_r, up_w = await asyncio.open_connection("127.0.0.1", 8765)
    asyncio.create_task(pipe_up(client_r, up_w))
    buffered, head, passthrough = b"", None, False
    while data := await up_r.read(65536):
        if head is None:
            head = data.split(b"\r\n\r\n", 1)[0]
            passthrough = HONOR and b"x-accel-buffering: no" in head.lower()
        if passthrough:
            client_w.write(data); await client_w.drain(); continue
        buffered += data
        while len(buffered) >= BLOCK:
            client_w.write(buffered[:BLOCK]); buffered = buffered[BLOCK:]; await client_w.drain()
    client_w.write(buffered); await client_w.drain(); client_w.close()

async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle, "127.0.0.1", 8766)
    print("proxy on 8766" + (", honoring X-Accel-Buffering" if HONOR else ""), flush=True)
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()

asyncio.run(main())
```

Buffering:

```text
through the proxy: first text after 4.91 s, the end after 4.91 s, 100 pieces, 2,583 bytes
```

With `--honor`:

```text
through the proxy: first text after 0.20 s, the end after 5.03 s, 100 pieces, 2,583 bytes
```

Through the buffering proxy the first text arrives after 4.91 seconds,
with the last: the whole 2.6 KB answer fit in one block, so the user got
none of streaming's benefit, and the server and the client both behaved
correctly. When the proxy honors the header, the first text arrives after
0.20 seconds, the same as this prompt gets with no proxy at all. The
header only helps where a hop honors it: Cloudflare, AWS's load balancers
and HAProxy ignore it, and have their own settings. The other usual
suspects:
- **compression**: gzip middleware buffers to compress well; streams must
  be excluded or flushed per event;
- **idle timeouts**: nginx closes an upstream connection that's silent for
  60 seconds by default, an AWS load balancer after 60, Cloudflare after
  about 100, and a long reasoning step can be that quiet. A comment line
  (`: ping`) every 15 seconds or so, as the SSE specification suggests,
  keeps the connection alive; Anthropic sends `ping` events for the same
  reason;
- **connection limits**: over HTTP/1.1 a browser opens at most six
  connections to one host, shared by all its tabs, and each open stream
  holds one. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex streams over one connection, up
  to a limit the server sets, usually 100.

The test is always the same: measure the time to the first *event*, not
the first byte (a buffering hop often passes the headers on at once),
through the whole path a user's request takes, not against the server
alone.

## What real streams also carry

Text deltas are the simple case. A production client also has to handle:
- **Usage at the end.** OpenAI sends token counts in a final chunk, when
  asked, whose `choices` list is empty, which crashes code that reads
  `choices[0]`; Anthropic's `message_delta` carries cumulative usage.
- **Tool calls as partial JSON.** A function call's arguments stream as
  fragments of a JSON string (OpenAI's `arguments` deltas, Anthropic's
  `input_json_delta`). Accumulate them and parse once the block ends,
  never per fragment.
- **Errors after success.** Once the 200 status and the headers are sent,
  the status can't change, so a failure mid-stream arrives as an event:
  Anthropic's `error` event, an OpenAI chunk with an `error` field.
- **Partial markdown.** The text arrives with unclosed code fences and
  half-written tables; rendering the whole answer again on every token is
  slow, and rendering it naively flickers.
- **Flushing in the framework.** FastAPI's `StreamingResponse` sends each
  yielded piece; a hand-written server should also disable Nagle's
  algorithm (`TCP_NODELAY`, which asyncio sets), or small events can wait
  tens of milliseconds for company.

## Where this leads

- **Post 51** measures TTFT and TPOT under real serving load, where
  batching trades one against the other.
- **Post 20**, the KV cache, is what a cancelled request should free.
- **Post 71**, voice agents, needs the two-way channel: the user
  interrupts while the model speaks.

## Takeaways

- Streaming doesn't make generation faster. It moves the wait the reader
  feels from the whole answer (4.7 s here for 100 tokens) to the time to
  first token (0.13 s).
- Readers take in about 5.5 tokens a second; generation runs several
  times faster, so with streaming the reader never waits after the first
  token, as long as time per output token stays under about 180 ms.
- Model APIs stream with server-sent events: one long HTTP response, a
  `data:` line per event, a blank line between. OpenAI's Chat Completions
  end with `[DONE]`; Anthropic, and OpenAI's Responses API, name every
  event. WebSockets add a channel back to the server.
- Send text, not tokens: decode incrementally, or characters split across
  tokens arrive broken.
- Stop generating when the user leaves, or a closed tab keeps the GPU and
  the KV cache busy: 90 of 100 tokens here. Use the transport's disconnect
  signal, plus a timeout or heartbeat, since no single signal works
  through proxies, over HTTP/2 and for vanished clients.
- A buffering hop turns a stream back into one late response. Test the
  time to the first event through the whole path, and turn off buffering,
  compression and short idle timeouts for streams.

The [vLLM](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/) and
[SGLang](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/) posts covered two engines
that are both, underneath everything else, dynamically-scheduled Python
runtimes — a scheduler decides what runs next, every step, against a live
execution graph. TensorRT-LLM started from a genuinely different premise:
instead of interpreting a model graph at runtime, compile it once, ahead of
time, into a fixed execution plan, and replay that plan on every request.
That was true for most of the project's life. It isn't fully true anymore,
and the story of why is as informative as the architecture itself — so this
post covers both: the ahead-of-time design that made TensorRT-LLM
distinctive, and the 2025–2026 pivot that moved it onto a PyTorch-native
runtime much closer to its two Python-native siblings in this series.

This is the third post in the series that started with
[vLLM's architecture](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/) and continued
with [SGLang's RadixAttention](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/). A
[final post](/posts/vllm-vs-sglang-vs-tensorrt-llm/) puts all three side by
side.

## Table of contents

## Compiling an engine: the architecture that defined TensorRT-LLM

[TensorRT-LLM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM) is NVIDIA's
open-source (Apache 2.0) LLM serving project, first released in October
2023. It's built on top of [TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt),
NVIDIA's general-purpose deep learning inference compiler, and it absorbed
the batching techniques of an earlier NVIDIA project,
[FasterTransformer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/FasterTransformer) — that
repo's own README now points readers to TensorRT-LLM for further
development instead. There's no single academic paper to cite here the way
there is for vLLM or SGLang; the closest things are the GitHub repo itself
and NVIDIA's own documentation.

For its first two years, TensorRT-LLM's defining workflow was a genuine
compile step. You'd describe a model using TensorRT-LLM's Python builder
API, then run `trtllm-build`, which:

- **Fused kernels and layers** — combining sequences of operations (a matmul,
  a bias add, an activation function) that would otherwise be separate GPU
  kernel launches into one fused kernel, cutting launch overhead and the
  memory traffic between them.
- **Calibrated precision ahead of time** — choosing and calibrating a
  quantization format (more on this below) as part of the build, not as a
  runtime decision.
- **Baked in a fixed shape profile** — the compiled engine targeted a
  specific GPU SKU and a chosen range of batch sizes and sequence lengths;
  it wasn't a portable artifact the way a HuggingFace checkpoint is.

The output was a `.engine` file: a serialized, hardware-specific execution
plan. Serving a model meant loading that engine and replaying its fixed plan
on every request, with no Python interpreter or dynamic graph traversal in
the hot path:

The trade was explicit: pay a compilation cost once, ahead of time, in
exchange for a hot path with no interpreter overhead and every kernel
already fused and tuned for the target GPU — the opposite bet from vLLM and
SGLang, which pay Python/PyTorch overhead on every step in exchange for
never needing a separate build step before serving a new model.

## In-flight batching and paged KV cache

TensorRT-LLM's own term for continuous batching is **in-flight batching**:
the same iteration-level idea covered in the [vLLM post](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/)
— sequences in their context (prefill) phase and sequences in their
generation (decode) phase are admitted and evicted from the batch every
step, rather than waiting for a whole static batch to finish together. If
that sounds familiar, it's the identical mechanism under NVIDIA's own name
for it.

TensorRT-LLM also adopted a paged KV cache — a later addition, converging
toward the same block-based memory layout PagedAttention introduced — with
configurable block sizes (8, 16, 32, 64, or 128 tokens). Its chunked-prefill
equivalent is called **Chunked Context**: a long prompt's context phase is
split into chunks and interleaved with other sequences' generation steps,
with one constraint that has no analogue in vLLM's version — the chunk size
must be an integer multiple of the KV-cache block size, since a chunk
boundary that split a block would leave that block only partially filled by
one sequence's context.

## Quantization: precision calibrated ahead of time

Precision calibration was the other pillar of the ahead-of-time philosophy.
Choosing and calibrating a quantization format is handled by a separate
NVIDIA tool, the
[TensorRT Model Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer)
("ModelOpt"), which has since become framework-agnostic — it now also
quantizes models for vLLM and SGLang, not just TensorRT-LLM, which is a
telling sign of how much of the "compile ahead of time" philosophy has
migrated out of TensorRT-LLM specifically and into shared tooling.

### What quantization does, in brief

[Post 56](/posts/quantization-from-scratch/) derives quantization from
scratch; the short version: map each real value to a small integer on a
grid set by a scale, $r \approx S(q - Z)$, and accept the rounding error in
exchange for memory. A parameter that costs 2 bytes in FP16 costs 1 byte
in INT8 and half a byte in INT4, so a 70B model goes from roughly
**140 GB → 70 GB → 35 GB** from the storage format alone, and decoding,
which is limited by reading weights, speeds up nearly in proportion. The
formats TensorRT-LLM's tooling targets:

| Format | Precision | Best-fit hardware |
| --- | --- | --- |
| FP8 | 8-bit float | Hopper, Blackwell |
| INT8 (SmoothQuant) | 8-bit int, activation-smoothed | Ada and earlier |
| INT4 (AWQ / GPTQ) | 4-bit int, weight-only | Memory-constrained deployments |
| NVFP4 / MXFP4 | 4-bit float | Blackwell |

Each row is a different answer to the same problem, one scale being too
coarse once weights or activations have outliers: SmoothQuant moves
activation outliers into the weights so both fit INT8; AWQ and GPTQ
quantize weights only, protecting salient channels or compensating
rounding error column by column; FP8 is a floating-point format with its
own dynamic range; and NVFP4 and MXFP4 share one scale per small block of
values, 16 or 32 of them. Post 56 works through symmetric and asymmetric
grids, group size, GPTQ and AWQ on a real model.

## Multi-GPU: tensor, pipeline, and expert parallelism

TensorRT-LLM supports the same tensor and pipeline parallelism covered in
the [vLLM post](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/) — sharding layer
weights across GPUs with an NCCL all-reduce combining partial results, or
assigning whole groups of layers to pipeline stages — plus expert
parallelism for mixture-of-experts models, with a ReduceScatter-plus-AllGather
optimization specifically for large MoE models split across many GPUs. One
property survived the entire architecture change discussed below unchanged:
the parallelism degree is fixed when a deployment is configured, not
adjusted per request the way vLLM's scheduler adjusts batch composition —
true of the original compiled-engine flow (baked into the build) and just
as true of the current PyTorch-native runtime (set at process launch).

## Speculative decoding

This is where TensorRT-LLM is the deepest of the three engines in this
series: it supports draft-model speculative decoding, **Medusa**, **EAGLE**
(EAGLE-1, EAGLE-2, and EAGLE-3, the last with disaggregated serving support
in the PyTorch backend), and **lookahead decoding** (a Jacobi-style method
that needs no extra draft model or training at all). The shared idea behind
all of them: a cheap step proposes several candidate tokens at once, and one
expensive forward pass through the full target model verifies all of them
together, accepting whichever prefix of the proposal the target model
agrees with and discarding the rest:

The accept/reject rule (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023) is the
same whichever method proposed the draft, and it makes the output exactly
the target model's distribution: accept each drafted token with
probability $\min(1, p_{\text{target}}/p_{\text{draft}})$, and at the first
rejection, resample from the leftover probability and discard the rest.
[Post 55](/posts/speculative-decoding/) derives the rule and proves it
exact, works out how many tokens a step yields and what the draft's cost
does to the speedup, and measures acceptance on real models. What matters
for TensorRT-LLM is the breadth of guessers it ships, because the right
one depends on the traffic: a separate draft model, Medusa heads,
EAGLE-1/2/3, and lookahead decoding, which needs no draft model at all.

## The 2025–2026 pivot: from compiled engines to a PyTorch-native runtime

Here's the part of the story that changes how you should read everything
above: TensorRT-LLM does not work this way by default anymore. Per the
project's own release notes and GitHub README:

| Version | Date | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| v0.17.0 | Jan 2025 | PyTorch backend added, experimental |
| v1.0.0 | Sep 2025 | PyTorch promoted to the default backend (breaking change) |
| v1.2.0 | Mar 2026 | TensorRT engine backend removed entirely — PyTorch is the sole execution backend |
| v1.2.1 | Apr 2026 | Current stable release |

As of v1.2.0, `trtllm-build`, `trtllm-refit`, `trtllm-prune`, and the
`TrtLlmArgs` configuration type are all gone from the codebase, and
requesting the old backend (`LLM(backend="tensorrt")`) raises a
`ValueError`. The project's own architecture documentation now describes a
`PyExecutor`-based dynamic runtime as the standard path, and files the old
compiled-engine flow under an explicit "Legacy" section. The GitHub README
states it plainly: TensorRT-LLM is "architected on PyTorch," with that
PyTorch-native design meant to let developers "experiment with the runtime
or extend functionality" — language that reads as a direct response to what
the old flow made hard.

One retrospective account of the change (not an official NVIDIA statement,
so treat it as informed color rather than a citable fact) attributes the
pivot to a "conversion tax": every new technique — a new speculative
decoding method, a new attention variant — had to be built twice, once
against PyTorch to validate it and once again against the separate
TensorRT graph-building API to ship it, and that tax slowed the project down
relative to vLLM and SGLang, which only ever had the one PyTorch-native
version to update.

What actually survives of the "compile ahead of time" philosophy today is
much narrower than a `.engine` file: `torch.compile`-based kernel fusion,
plus **piecewise CUDA graph** capture at process startup — a lightweight,
per-process JIT warmup that fuses and replays common execution shapes, not a
separate portable artifact tied to one GPU SKU and shape profile the way
`trtllm-build`'s output was. The idea of paying a cost once to save
repeated work didn't disappear; it shrank from "compile once, deploy the
artifact anywhere" down to "warm up once, per process."

The practical upshot: as of today, all three engines in this series —
vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM — are dynamically-scheduled, PyTorch-native
runtimes. The clean "two dynamic engines vs. one compiled one" framing this
post opened with described TensorRT-LLM's first two years accurately, but
it is no longer how any of the three actually work. The
[comparison post](/posts/vllm-vs-sglang-vs-tensorrt-llm/) picks this up from
here.

## Serving layer: trtllm-serve, Triton, and NIM

Three deployment paths coexist rather than one superseding the others.
**`trtllm-serve`** is a standalone, OpenAI-compatible HTTP/gRPC server that
needs no other serving framework, and supports disaggregated prefill/decode
serving — running the compute-bound prefill phase and the memory-bound
decode phase on separate GPU pools, an idea in the same spirit as the
[vLLM post](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/)'s point that mixing prefill
and decode work in one batch is exactly what chunked prefill has to manage
around. **Triton Inference Server**, paired with the `tensorrtllm_backend`,
remains a good fit when a deployment needs to route across multiple models
or backends on one server rather than serving TensorRT-LLM alone. **NVIDIA
NIM** — prebuilt inference containers — auto-selects an optimized backend
per target GPU and model, and as of NIM's current lineup that backend
selection can land on TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, *or* SGLang: NVIDIA's own
production packaging no longer treats TensorRT-LLM as the only option
inside it.

## What the benchmarks say

NVIDIA's MLPerf Inference v5.1 submission (published September 2025)
reported, for Blackwell Ultra GB300 NVL72 systems running DeepSeek-R1:
**5,842 tokens/sec/GPU** in the offline scenario and **2,907 tokens/sec/GPU**
in the server scenario — roughly **5× the per-GPU throughput of the prior
Hopper generation** on the same benchmark:

Separately, and more precisely, NVIDIA reported GB300 NVL72 delivering
**45% (offline) and 25% (server) higher per-GPU performance** than its own
immediate predecessor, the GB200 NVL72 — a closer generation-over-generation
comparison than the roughly-5×-vs-Hopper figure above, which spans a bigger
hardware jump. Both numbers are NVIDIA's own full-system MLPerf submission —
GPU and software stack together, with TensorRT-LLM as the serving software —
not an isolated "TensorRT-LLM vs. some other engine" comparison the way
Orca's number was for vLLM or SGLang's own paper benchmarks were. Like every
number in this series, treat it as that vendor's own dated, self-reported
figure for its own hardware generation, not a cross-engine verdict.

## Advantages and disadvantages

**Advantages:**

- The deepest speculative-decoding support of the three engines in this
  series — draft-model decoding, Medusa, EAGLE-1/2/3, and lookahead decoding
  all in one project.
- The broadest, most mature quantization tooling, via a Model Optimizer that
  has outgrown TensorRT-LLM specifically and now also serves vLLM and
  SGLang deployments.
- MLPerf-validated performance on NVIDIA's newest hardware generations,
  backed by full-system submissions rather than library-only claims.
- Multiple production-serving paths — a standalone server, Triton
  integration, and NIM packaging — for different deployment shapes.
- The PyTorch-native pivot removed the "conversion tax" that used to slow
  new techniques down, so recent additions (like EAGLE-3) are landing
  faster than the old compiled-engine era allowed.

**Disadvantages:**

- Still effectively NVIDIA-hardware-only — no AMD or TPU path the way vLLM
  and (more broadly still) SGLang document.
- The architecture changed twice in about a year and a half — experimental
  PyTorch backend, to default, to sole backend — which is real churn for
  anyone who built tooling against the old `trtllm-build` flow and has had
  to migrate off it entirely.
- For its first two years, the compiled-engine flow required a build step
  tied to one GPU SKU and a fixed batch/sequence-length shape profile before
  you could serve anything — a real, if now-historical, operational cost
  that was also the direct motivation for walking away from it.
- Being NVIDIA's own project, its integration with the broader open-source
  LLM ecosystem has at times lagged vLLM's, though that gap has narrowed
  since the PyTorch-native pivot.

## Where this leads

TensorRT-LLM's story doesn't end where it started: a genuinely different,
ahead-of-time-compiled architecture spent two years as the clearest
counterpoint to vLLM and SGLang's dynamic scheduling, then converged onto a
PyTorch-native runtime much like theirs — while keeping the deepest
speculative-decoding support and the most mature quantization tooling of the
three as what's left of its original bet on doing more work ahead of time.
The [comparison post](/posts/vllm-vs-sglang-vs-tensorrt-llm/) lines all
three up on the axes that actually still differ: prefix/cache reuse
strategy, quantization tooling, hardware portability, and deployment shape
— not "compiled vs. dynamic," which no longer separates any of them.

- [TensorRT-LLM Architecture Overview](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/architecture/overview.html) — the current `PyExecutor`-based runtime and the legacy compiled-engine flow.
- [TensorRT-LLM Release Notes](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/release-notes.html) — the v0.17.0 → v1.0.0 → v1.2.0 backend-migration timeline.
- [NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer) — the quantization/calibration toolchain, now framework-agnostic.
- Jacob et al., [_Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.05877) (CVPR 2018) — the affine quantization scheme (scale, zero-point) every format in this post's table builds on.
- Xiao et al., [_SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10438) (ICML 2023) — migrating quantization difficulty from activations to weights.
- Frantar et al., [_GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323) (2022) — Hessian-based column-by-column weight quantization.
- Lin et al., [_AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978) (MLSys 2024) — protecting salient weight channels identified by activation magnitude.
- [TensorRT-LLM: torch.compile and Piecewise CUDA Graphs](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/features/torch_compile_and_piecewise_cuda_graph.html) — what remains of ahead-of-time compilation under the PyTorch backend.
