Every Transformer, from the original encoder-decoder in [_Attention Is All You
Need_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) to a modern decoder-only LLM, is built
from exactly three attention patterns: **self-attention**, **masked
(causal) self-attention**, and **cross-attention**. They share the same
underlying math. This post derives *why* attention takes the shape it does,
then works through each of the three patterns with real matrices, start to
finish.

Token embeddings are [post 8](/posts/embeddings-and-contrastive-learning/).
What it means for a layer to "add its output back into the stream" is
[the residual stream post](/posts/residual-stream-explained/), post 13,
which shows where attention sits in the full block; this post derives what
attention computes.

## Table of contents

## Why not just use RNNs?

An RNN builds a representation of token $i$ by folding token $i-1$'s hidden
state together with token $i$'s embedding, one step at a time. That has two
consequences that matter a lot at scale:

- **It's sequential.** Token $n$'s representation can't be computed until
  token $n-1$'s is, so there's no parallelism across the sequence during
  training.
- **Long-range context is indirect.** Information about token $0$ has to
  survive being repeatedly compressed through every intermediate hidden state
  to influence token $n$. In practice it fades.

([The RNN post](/posts/rnns-and-why-transformers-won/) measures both: the
gradient reaching 50 steps back, and a sequence-to-sequence model that
can't reverse 40 digits until it gets attention.)

This exact problem already had a partial fix by the time Transformers came
along. Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio introduced attention in 2014 as a patch on
top of an RNN encoder-decoder for machine translation — instead of
compressing the whole source sentence into one fixed-size hidden state, let
the decoder look back and weight every encoder position directly. It helped,
but the RNN was still doing the token-by-token folding underneath, so the
sequential bottleneck never went away. Vaswani et al.'s 2017 insight was more
radical: what if the RNN wasn't needed at all, and attention could stand on
its own?

What we'd actually like is for every token's new representation to be a
direct, *learned* combination of every other token's representation —
computed for all positions at once. That's the property self-attention is
designed to have.

## From a similarity score to Q, K, V

Start with the simplest version of "direct combination": say each input token
has a vector representation $D_i$, and we want a new representation $Y_i$
that's a weighted sum of *all* the $D_j$:

$$
Y_i = \sum_{j} \alpha_{ij} D_j
$$

The weights $\alpha_{ij}$ should say how much token $j$ matters to token $i$.
A natural way to measure that is a dot product — $D_i \cdot D_j$ is large
when the two vectors point in a similar direction — followed by a softmax so
the weights for each $i$ sum to 1:

$$
\alpha_i = \operatorname{softmax}(D_i D^\top)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Y = \operatorname{softmax}(D D^\top) D
$$

This already has the shape of attention, but it has a limitation: it reuses
the *same* vector $D_i$ for three different jobs at once — deciding what
token $i$ is looking for, deciding what token $j$ offers to be matched
against, and deciding what token $j$ actually contributes to the sum. Those
are three different roles, so give each one its own learned linear
projection instead of reusing $D$ directly:

$$
Q = XW_Q, \qquad K = XW_K, \qquad V = XW_V
$$

- $Q$ (query) — what this token is looking for
- $K$ (key) — what this token offers, to be matched against queries
- $V$ (value) — what this token actually contributes once matched

> [!note] The one idea to hold onto
> Query, key, and value are three different learned *views* of the same token.
> Every attention pattern in this post — self, masked, cross — is the **same**
> $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ formula; all that ever changes is
> *which sequence* $Q$, $K$, and $V$ are projected from.

Swapping $D$ for $Q$ and $K$ in the similarity score, and $D$ for $V$ in the
weighted sum, gives scaled dot-product attention:

$$
\operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V
$$

The one new ingredient is the division by $\sqrt{d_k}$, the key dimension,
and it is there for a reason you can derive in two lines. Suppose the
entries of a query $q$ and a key $k$ are independent with mean 0 and
variance 1. Their dot product is a sum of $d_k$ terms $q_j k_j$, each with
mean 0 and variance 1, so:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(q \cdot k) = \sum_{j=1}^{d_k} \operatorname{Var}(q_j k_j) = d_k,
\qquad \operatorname{std}(q \cdot k) = \sqrt{d_k}
$$

The typical size of a raw score grows with the square root of the key
dimension — about 2 at $d_k = 4$, 8 at $d_k = 64$, 32 at $d_k = 1024$ — for
no reason other than there being more terms to add up. Softmax is sensitive
to exactly that: scaling every input by $s$ sharpens the output toward
one-hot and shrinks its gradient $p_i(1 - p_i)$ toward zero (the [softmax
section of the residual stream
post](/posts/residual-stream-explained/#what-softmax-actually-computes) has
a slider for this). Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ restores unit variance
regardless of $d_k$, so the softmax sees scores of the same typical size
whether a head is 4-dimensional or 1,024-dimensional. A quick check with
20,000 random query–key pairs: the measured standard deviations of
$q \cdot k$ are 2.00, 4.01, 7.96, 16.06 and 31.94 for $d_k$ = 4, 16, 64,
256, 1024 — and after dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$, all five are 1.00 to two
decimals.

## Self-attention, worked through

Take two tokens with a 2-dimensional embedding each:

$$
X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

and three learned projection matrices:

$$
W_Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
W_K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
W_V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Projecting $X$ through each gives:

$$
Q = XW_Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
K = XW_K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
V = XW_V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Note that $Q$ and $K$ must share a dimension for $QK^\top$ to even be
defined — self-attention conventionally sets $d_q = d_k = d_v$, one shared
projection size for all three, though only $d_q = d_k$ is strictly required.

With $d_k = 2$, the similarity scores $QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k}$ are:

$$
\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{2}} =
\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0.707 \\ 0.707 & 0.707 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Softmax normalizes each row into weights that sum to 1:

$$
A = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{2}}\right) =
\begin{bmatrix} 0.330 & 0.670 \\ 0.500 & 0.500 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Softmax redistributes each row's scores into non-negative weights that sum to
1 — that's why the heatmap above looks "smoother" than the raw scores one:
softmax always narrows the range compared to arbitrary real-valued scores.
(The formula itself, $e^{z_i} / \sum_j e^{z_j}$, and its two key properties
are derived once on this blog, in [the residual stream
post](/posts/residual-stream-explained/#what-softmax-actually-computes).)
And the output is that weighted combination of $V$'s rows:

$$
Y = AV = \begin{bmatrix} 0.330 & 1.000 \\ 0.500 & 1.000 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Row 0 of $Y$ is 33% token 0's value plus 67% token 1's — token 1 mattered
more to token 0's new representation than token 0 did to itself, purely
because of how $Q$ and $K$ happened to align. That's the whole mechanism:
everything downstream (multi-head attention, masking, cross-attention) is a
variation on this same $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ computation.

### Multi-head attention

One set of $W_Q, W_K, W_V$ gives the model one "way" of relating tokens. Multi-head
attention runs $h$ independent copies of this — each with its own, smaller
projection matrices — in parallel, then concatenates their outputs and
projects back down with one more learned matrix $W_O$:

$$
\operatorname{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(XW_Q^{(i)}, XW_K^{(i)}, XW_V^{(i)})
\qquad
Y = \operatorname{concat}(\operatorname{head}_1, \dots, \operatorname{head}_h)\,W_O
$$

Each head can specialize — one might track syntactic relationships, another
coreference, another local position — and $W_O$ learns how to combine them.

## Masked (causal) self-attention

The encoder can let every token look at every other token — the whole input
is available up front. A decoder generating text one token at a time can't:
if token 2 could attend to token 3, it would be attending to a word that
hasn't been generated yet. So decoder self-attention needs every token to be
blind to anything after it in the sequence.

The trick is to zero out the disallowed positions *before* the softmax, not
after — add a mask matrix $M$ to the raw scores where allowed positions get
$0$ (no change) and disallowed positions get $-\infty$ (so $e^{-\infty} = 0$
after the exponential, and softmax assigns them exactly zero weight):

$$
A = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right), \qquad
M = \begin{bmatrix}
0 & -\infty & -\infty & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & -\infty & \cdots \\
0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\
\vdots & & & \ddots
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Extend the running example to three tokens, reusing the same $W_Q, W_K, W_V$:

$$
X = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad
V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

The unmasked scores $QK^\top/\sqrt{2}$ come out to:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 0.707 & -0.707 \\
0.707 & 0.707 & 0 \\
-0.707 & 0 & -0.707
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Every position can see every other position here — nothing above the
diagonal is off-limits yet. Adding the mask sends every entry above the
diagonal to $-\infty$, and softmax turns those into zero weight — each row
can only draw from itself and earlier positions:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}
1.000 & 0 & 0 \\
0.500 & 0.500 & 0 \\
0.248 & 0.504 & 0.248
\end{bmatrix}
$$

Reading a single row of that matrix as bars makes the "distribution" part
concrete — token 3's weights are non-negative and sum to exactly 1:

Compare the two heatmaps: the raw scores fill the whole grid, but masking
collapses everything above the diagonal to zero before it ever reaches $V$.
That lower-triangular shape is the signature of causal masking — token 1
only ever attends to itself, token 2 splits its attention between tokens 1
and 2, and only token 3, the last position, is free to attend across the
whole sequence so far.

> [!tip] The signature of causal masking
> A lower-triangular attention matrix *is* causality made visible: query row $t$
> can only draw from key columns $\leq t$. A full, non-triangular matrix in a
> decoder's self-attention means the future is leaking into the present.

Multiplying $A$ by $V$ gives the final masked output:

$$
Y = AV = \begin{bmatrix}
1.000 & 1.000 \\
0.500 & 1.000 \\
0.497 & 0.752
\end{bmatrix}
$$

## Cross-attention

Self-attention (masked or not) always keeps $Q$, $K$, and $V$ coming from the
*same* sequence. Cross-attention is the one place that changes: it's how a
decoder incorporates information from a different sequence — the encoder's
output — while generating its own. The query comes from the decoder; the key
and value come from the encoder:

$$
Q = D_{\text{dec}} W_Q, \qquad K = E_{\text{enc}} W_K, \qquad V = E_{\text{enc}} W_V
$$

where $D_{\text{dec}}$ is the decoder's hidden state and $E_{\text{enc}}$ is
the encoder's output for the source sequence. Everything else — scaled dot
product, softmax, weighted sum — is identical to self-attention; only where
$K$ and $V$ come from has changed.

Take the 3-token encoder output from the masking example as
$E_{\text{enc}}$, and a separate, 2-token decoder state:

$$
E_{\text{enc}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
D_{\text{dec}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.5 & 0.5 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Projecting each through its own weight matrix:

$$
Q = D_{\text{dec}}W_Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1.000 & 0.500 \\ 0 & 1.000 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
K = E_{\text{enc}}W_K = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
V = E_{\text{enc}}W_V = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Note the shapes: $Q$ is $2 \times 2$ (2 decoder tokens) while $K$ and $V$ are
$3 \times 2$ (3 encoder tokens) — cross-attention doesn't require the two
sequences to be the same length, which is exactly why it works for
translation, where source and target sentences rarely have the same number
of tokens. Only $d_q = d_k$ is required here — $d_v$ is free to differ, since
$V$'s width just becomes the output's width. The scores end up rectangular
too, $2 \times 3$:

$$
\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{2}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.354 & 0.707 & -0.354 \\ 0.707 & 0 & 0.707 \end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
A = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \begin{bmatrix} 0.343 & 0.488 & 0.169 \\ 0.401 & 0.198 & 0.401 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Unlike the causal case, there's no triangular structure here — each decoder
row is free to spread its attention across all three encoder columns, since
nothing needs to be hidden from a query that isn't generating this token
itself.

$$
Y = AV = \begin{bmatrix} 0.512 & 0.831 \\ 0.802 & 0.599 \end{bmatrix}
$$

Each of the decoder's 2 tokens now has a representation that's a learned,
weighted blend of all 3 encoder tokens — the decoder gets to look at the
entire source sequence at every generation step, not just a compressed
summary of it.

## Reproducing this in code

Every number in this post came from one function. Here it is, in full, using
the same $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$ from the three worked examples above — run it
and the printed arrays match every heatmap on this page:

```python

def attention(Q, K, V, mask=None):
    d_k = K.shape[-1]
    scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if mask is not None:
        scores = scores + mask
    weights = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    weights /= weights.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return weights, weights @ V

W_Q = np.array([[1, 0], [1, 1]], dtype=float)
W_K = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=float)
W_V = np.array([[1, 1], [0, 1]], dtype=float)

# self-attention (2 tokens)
X = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1]], dtype=float)
_, Y = attention(X @ W_Q, X @ W_K, X @ W_V)
print("self-attention Y:\n", Y.round(3))
# [[0.33  1.  ]
#  [0.5   1.  ]]

# masked self-attention (3 tokens): future positions get -inf before softmax
X3 = np.array([[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, -1]], dtype=float)
causal_mask = np.triu(np.full((3, 3), -np.inf), k=1)
np.fill_diagonal(causal_mask, 0)
_, Y3 = attention(X3 @ W_Q, X3 @ W_K, X3 @ W_V, mask=causal_mask)
print("masked self-attention Y:\n", Y3.round(3))
# [[1.     1.   ]
#  [0.5    1.   ]
#  [0.497  0.752]]

# cross-attention: Q from the decoder, K/V from the encoder
D_dec = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [-1, 1]], dtype=float)
_, Yc = attention(D_dec @ W_Q, X3 @ W_K, X3 @ W_V)
print("cross-attention Y:\n", Yc.round(3))
# [[0.512  0.831]
#  [0.802  0.599]]
```

The only thing that changes between the three calls is which matrices go
into `attention()` — self-attention passes the same sequence three times,
masking adds one array before the softmax, and cross-attention swaps in a
second sequence for $K$ and $V$. That's the entire implementation surface of
every attention pattern in a Transformer.

## Limitations: what attention doesn't give you for free

Three things fall out of the mechanism above that are easy to miss on a
first pass.

**Attention has no sense of order.** Look at the formula again:
$\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ treats the input as a *set* of
rows, not a *sequence* — swap two rows of $X$ and the corresponding rows of
$Y$ swap right along with them, but nothing else about the computation
changes. An RNN gets word order for free, just by processing tokens one at a
time; a Transformer has to be told the order explicitly, via a separate
**positional encoding**, either added to the input embeddings before they
ever reach $W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, or, in most current models, applied inside
attention to the queries and keys. Attention itself is
permutation-equivariant — position has to be smuggled in from outside (a
causal mask lets some leak in; [post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/)
covers both, and the methods).

**The cost is quadratic in sequence length.** Computing $QK^\top$ for $n$
tokens produces an $n \times n$ matrix — double the sequence length and the
attention computation (and the memory to store the score matrix) roughly
quadruples. That's invisible at the toy sizes above, and it's exactly the
constraint that motivates [the KV cache](/posts/kv-cache-explained/) and
[paged attention](/posts/paged-attention-explained/) once a real model is
generating thousands of tokens per request. Those posts manage the cost;
[the attention alternatives post](/posts/attention-alternatives/) asks what
happens if you change the mechanism instead.

**Scaled dot-product isn't the only kind of attention — it's the one that
won.** Bahdanau's original 2014 formulation used *additive* attention: a
small feed-forward network scored each query-key pair instead of a dot
product. Vaswani et al. picked the dot-product form instead because it
reduces to matrix multiplication, which GPUs were already extremely fast at
— the two formulations perform comparably in practice, but only one of them
turns attention into hardware Transformers were already built to
accelerate. The $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling exists purely to patch a side effect
of that choice: without it, the standard deviation of a raw score grows as
$\sqrt{d_k}$ (derived above), pushing softmax toward a near-one-hot,
vanishing-gradient regime.

## Putting the three together

A full encoder-decoder Transformer stacks these in a specific order: each
encoder layer applies self-attention (every source token sees every other
source token) followed by a feed-forward network; each decoder layer applies
masked self-attention (so generation stays autoregressive), then
cross-attention into the encoder's output, then its own feed-forward network.
Decoder-only LLMs — GPT-style models — drop the encoder and cross-attention
entirely and rely on masked self-attention alone, which is why "causal" and
"decoder-only" tend to go together in practice.

### Three families

Which of the three patterns a model uses defines its family.

- **Encoder-only** models, like BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), use only
  unmasked self-attention. Every token sees the whole input in both
  directions, which makes them good at understanding a fixed text,
  classifying it or embedding it, and unable to generate left to right.
  The sentence encoders of the [embeddings post](/posts/embeddings-and-contrastive-learning/)
  are of this kind.
- **Decoder-only** models, like GPT, use only masked self-attention. Each
  token sees only the past, so the same model scores text and generates
  it, one token at a time. Almost every large language model today is one.
- **Encoder–decoder** models, like the original Transformer and T5 (Raffel
  et al., 2020), use all three: an encoder reads the input, and a decoder
  generates the output while attending into it. They suit tasks with a
  clear input and output, like translation.

The projections themselves ($W_Q$, $W_K$, $W_V$, $W_O$) are the only learned
parameters in attention — everything else in this post is fixed math once
those are learned. What they *converge to* during training, and what that
does to inference cost at serving time (KV caching, paged attention), are
their own posts.

## Takeaways

- Every attention pattern in a Transformer — self, masked, cross — is the
  same $\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ computation; only
  *which sequence* $Q$, $K$, and $V$ come from changes.
- Causal masking is additive: add $-\infty$ to disallowed score positions
  before the softmax, and they contribute exactly zero weight afterward.
- Cross-attention is the only pattern where $Q$ comes from a different
  sequence than $K$ and $V$ — that's what lets a decoder read a source
  sequence of a different length than its own.
- Attention has no built-in notion of token order and costs $O(n^2)$ in
  sequence length — positional encodings and the KV cache/paged attention
  exist specifically to patch those two gaps.

## References

- Vaswani et al., [_Attention Is All You Need_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) (2017) — the original Transformer; introduces scaled dot-product attention and removes recurrence entirely.
- Devlin, Chang, Lee and Toutanova, [_BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805) (NAACL 2019) — the encoder-only family.
- Raffel et al., [_Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683) (JMLR 2020) — T5, the encoder–decoder family.
- Bahdanau, Cho & Bengio, [_Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate_](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473) (2014) — the original (additive) attention mechanism, introduced to fix the fixed-size bottleneck in RNN encoder-decoders.
A language model generates by writing its distribution down: the chain rule
splits $p(x)$ into one next-token distribution after another ([post
9](/posts/autoregression-and-perplexity/)), each a softmax you can compute
and sample from. The chain rule works for any data, images
included, and autoregressive image models exist (PixelCNN, ImageGPT). But
a 512×512 color image is 786,432 numbers, which means 786,432 sequential
steps in a pixel order that nothing about the picture picks out. So
generative models for images mostly took two other routes, both built on
the same idea: start from simple noise $z$, and learn a network that maps it to
data.

- The **variational autoencoder** (VAE) keeps a likelihood, but can't
  compute it exactly, so it maximizes a lower bound, with an encoder to make
  the bound tight.
- The **generative adversarial network** (GAN) gives up on likelihood
  altogether: a second network, the critic, learns to tell real data from
  generated, and the generator learns to fool it.

The choice shows up in what goes wrong. VAEs put samples where there is
no data; GANs drop modes, and sometimes fail to train at all. This post
derives both, checks the math numerically, and trains a VAE, a GAN and
one improved GAN (WGAN-GP) on the same small test where each failure is
visible.

## Table of contents

## Latent variables

A **latent-variable model** says each data point $x$ was made from a hidden
code $z$: draw $z$ from a simple prior $p(z)$, usually $\mathcal N(0, I)$,
then draw $x$ from $p_\theta(x \mid z)$, a distribution whose parameters a
neural network (the **decoder**) computes from $z$. Sampling is easy, two
steps. The likelihood of a data point is not:

$$
p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)\, dz,
$$

an integral over every code that could have produced $x$. With a neural
decoder it has no closed form, and estimating it by sampling $z$ from the
prior fails because almost no random code produces any particular $x$. Both
models below are ways of training $\theta$ without ever computing this
integral.

An ordinary **autoencoder** has the pieces but not the probability: an
encoder squeezes $x$ into a code, a decoder rebuilds $x$ from it, and the
two train to make the reconstruction match. Its codes land wherever
training puts them, so a random point in code space usually decodes to
nothing useful. You can't sample from it. The VAE fixes exactly that.

## The ELBO, derived

Give the model an **encoder** $q_\phi(z \mid x)$: a network that, for each
$x$, outputs a distribution over the codes that could have made it.
Multiply and divide by it inside the integral, and the likelihood becomes
an expectation under $q$:

$$
\log p_\theta(x) = \log \mathbb E_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\right]
\;\ge\; \mathbb E_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z)}{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\right].
$$

The inequality is Jensen's ($\log$ is concave, so the log of an average is
at least the average of the logs). Splitting the right side gives the
**evidence lower bound** (ELBO):

$$
\text{ELBO}(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb E_{q_\phi(z \mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big]}_{\text{reconstruction}}
\;-\; \underbrace{\operatorname{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p(z)\big)}_{\text{stay close to the prior}}.
$$

The first term rewards codes that decode back to $x$: it is the
autoencoder's reconstruction loss. With a Gaussian decoder of fixed
variance $s^2$ it is minus the squared error divided by $2s^2$, plus a
constant. The second term is the KL divergence from [post
3.2](/posts/softmax-and-cross-entropy/), and it is what makes sampling work:
it pulls every encoding toward $\mathcal N(0, I)$, so the region the prior
draws from is the region the decoder was trained on.

How loose is the bound? Bayes' rule says
$p_\theta(x \mid z)\, p(z) = p_\theta(z \mid x)\, p_\theta(x)$, so the
quantity inside the ELBO's expectation is
$\log p_\theta(x) - \log \big(q_\phi(z \mid x) / p_\theta(z \mid x)\big)$.
The first part doesn't depend on $z$; the second, averaged over $q$, is a
KL divergence. So the gap is exactly:

$$
\log p_\theta(x) - \text{ELBO}(x) = \operatorname{KL}\big(q_\phi(z \mid x) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)\big).
$$

The ELBO is the log-likelihood minus how far the encoder is from the true
posterior. Since $\log p_\theta(x)$ doesn't depend on $\phi$, maximizing
the ELBO over $\phi$ only shrinks that gap: it makes the encoder a better
posterior. Maximizing over $\theta$ can do either of two things: raise
$\log p_\theta(x)$, or move the model's true posterior toward whatever
the encoder outputs, which shrinks the gap without improving the model.

The second option has a known failure. If the decoder is powerful enough
to model $x$ without looking at $z$ (an autoregressive decoder for text,
say), the cheapest way to raise the ELBO is to ignore $z$ altogether: the
encoder outputs the prior for every input, the KL term drops to zero, and
the codes carry no information. This is **posterior collapse**. A related
knob is the weight on the KL term, written $\beta$ (the **$\beta$-VAE**,
Higgins et al., 2017): $\beta > 1$ pushes codes harder toward the prior,
$\beta < 1$ favors reconstruction, and at $\beta \ne 1$ the objective is no
longer a bound on $\log p(x)$.

## Checking the bound exactly

With a linear decoder, $p(x \mid z) = \mathcal N(Wz + b,\ s^2 I)$, everything
has a closed form: $p(x)$ is Gaussian with covariance $WW^\top + s^2 I$, and
so is the posterior. That makes the identity above checkable, in 2-D:

```python

# A linear-Gaussian latent model in 2-D, small enough to solve exactly:
#   p(z) = N(0, I),   p(x | z) = N(W z + b, s^2 I).
# Then p(x) = N(b, W W^T + s^2 I), and the true posterior p(z | x) is Gaussian.
# For any Gaussian q(z | x) the ELBO is reconstruction - KL(q || prior), and
# log p(x) - ELBO = KL(q || true posterior). Checked here three ways.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
W, b, s = np.array([[1.0, 0.5], [-0.3, 0.8]]), np.array([0.2, -0.1]), 0.5
x = np.array([1.0, 0.4])

def log_normal(v, mean, cov):
    d = v - mean
    return -0.5 * (len(v) * np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.linalg.slogdet(cov)[1] + d @ np.linalg.solve(cov, d))

def kl_gauss(m1, S1, m0, S0):                       # KL(N(m1, S1) || N(m0, S0))
    S0i = np.linalg.inv(S0)
    return 0.5 * (np.trace(S0i @ S1) + (m0 - m1) @ S0i @ (m0 - m1) - len(m1)
                  + np.linalg.slogdet(S0)[1] - np.linalg.slogdet(S1)[1])

def elbo(mu, sigma, n=200_000):
    """Reconstruction term by sampling (the reparameterization trick: z = mu +
    sigma * eps), KL to the prior in closed form."""
    z = mu + sigma * rng.standard_normal((n, 2))
    r = x - z @ W.T - b
    rec = (-0.5 * (r ** 2).sum(1) / s ** 2 - np.log(2 * np.pi * s ** 2)).mean()
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + sigma ** 2 - 1 - np.log(sigma ** 2)).sum()
    r0 = x - W @ mu - b                               # the same expectation, in closed form
    exact = -0.5 * (r0 @ r0 + (W ** 2 * sigma ** 2).sum()) / s ** 2 - np.log(2 * np.pi * s ** 2)
    return rec, exact, kl

log_px = log_normal(x, b, W @ W.T + s ** 2 * np.eye(2))
P = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(2) + W.T @ W / s ** 2)      # posterior covariance
m = P @ W.T @ (x - b) / s ** 2                        # posterior mean
print(f"log p(x), exact: {log_px:.4f}")
print(f"true posterior: mean ({m[0]:.3f}, {m[1]:.3f}), "
      f"std ({np.sqrt(P[0, 0]):.3f}, {np.sqrt(P[1, 1]):.3f}), correlation {P[0, 1] / np.sqrt(P[0, 0] * P[1, 1]):.3f}\n")
print(f"{'q(z|x)':36s} {'recon (sampled, exact)':>22s} {'KL to prior':>11s} {'ELBO':>8s} {'gap':>7s} {'KL to post':>10s}")
# The best diagonal q (smallest KL to the posterior) keeps the posterior's
# mean but takes std_j = 1 / sqrt(precision_jj), not the posterior's own
# marginal stds: Kingma and Welling's encoder can't do better than this.
best = 1 / np.sqrt(np.diag(np.linalg.inv(P)))
cases = [("best diagonal Gaussian", m, best),
         ("posterior's mean and marginal stds", m, np.sqrt(np.diag(P))),
         ("right mean, stds 3x too wide", m, 3 * np.sqrt(np.diag(P))),
         ("the prior, N(0, I)", np.zeros(2), np.ones(2))]
for name, mu, sigma in cases:
    rec, exact, kl = elbo(mu, sigma)
    print(f"{name:36s} {rec:10.4f} {exact:10.4f}  {kl:11.4f} {exact - kl:8.4f} {log_px - (exact - kl):7.4f} "
          f"{kl_gauss(mu, np.diag(sigma ** 2), m, P):10.4f}")

mu, sigma = np.array([1.0, -0.5]), np.array([0.5, 2.0])
print(f"\nKL(N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, I)) for mu = (1, -0.5), sigma = (0.5, 2): "
      f"{0.5 * (mu ** 2 + sigma ** 2 - 1 - np.log(sigma ** 2)).sum():.4f} nats")
```

```text
log p(x), exact: -2.3429
true posterior: mean (0.365, 0.618), std (0.442, 0.479), correlation -0.210

q(z|x)                               recon (sampled, exact) KL to prior     ELBO     gap KL to post
best diagonal Gaussian                  -1.3081    -1.3066       1.0590  -2.3655  0.0226     0.0226
posterior's mean and marginal stds      -1.3417    -1.3435       1.0231  -2.3666  0.0237     0.0237
right mean, stds 3x too wide            -8.0050    -8.0153       0.5245  -8.5398  6.1969     6.1969
the prior, N(0, I)                      -6.1847    -6.1916       0.0000  -6.1916  3.8487     3.8487

KL(N(mu, sigma^2) || N(0, I)) for mu = (1, -0.5), sigma = (0.5, 2): 1.7500 nats
```

Four encoders for the same $x$, and in each the gap between $\log p(x)$
and the ELBO equals the KL from $q$ to the true posterior, to four
decimals. (The ELBO column uses the closed-form reconstruction term; the
sampled one agrees with it to about 0.01, which is the Monte Carlo noise a
VAE trains with.)

The first two rows are the instructive ones. The true posterior's two
coordinates are correlated ($-0.21$), and a VAE encoder that outputs a
mean and one standard deviation per coordinate (a diagonal Gaussian, the
usual choice) can't represent that. The best it can do is the first row,
0.0226 nats short of $\log p(x)$, which for two coordinates with
correlation $\rho$ is $-\tfrac12 \log(1 - \rho^2)$. That shortfall, from
restricting $q$ to a simple family, is the **approximation gap**. Note
that the best diagonal $q$ isn't the one that copies the posterior's
own standard deviations (second row, 0.0237): minimizing
$\operatorname{KL}(q \,\|\, p)$ makes $q$ narrower than the posterior's
marginals, a general habit of this direction of KL. Making the stds three
times too wide costs 6.2 nats; using the prior as the encoder, ignoring
$x$ entirely, costs 3.8.

## The KL term, worked

For a diagonal Gaussian encoder, $q = \mathcal N(\mu, \operatorname{diag}\sigma^2)$,
against the prior $\mathcal N(0, I)$, the KL needs no sampling, and it
splits into a sum over coordinates:

$$
\operatorname{KL} = \tfrac12 \sum_j \left(\mu_j^2 + \sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2\right).
$$

Take $\mu = (1, -0.5)$ and $\sigma = (0.5, 2)$. The first coordinate gives
$1 + 0.25 - 1 - \log 0.25 = 0.25 + 1.386 = 1.636$; the second gives
$0.25 + 4 - 1 - \log 4 = 3.25 - 1.386 = 1.864$. Half their sum is
**1.75 nats**, the last line of the output above. Each part of the formula
has a job: $\mu_j^2$ charges for moving away from the origin, and
$\sigma_j^2 - 1 - \log \sigma_j^2$, which is zero at $\sigma_j = 1$ and
positive on both sides, charges for being narrower or wider than the
prior. A code that shrinks to a point to reconstruct perfectly pays
$-\log \sigma_j^2 \to \infty$, which is what keeps the codes spread out
enough to sample from.

## The reparameterization trick

The reconstruction term is an expectation over $z \sim q_\phi(z \mid x)$,
and training needs its gradient with respect to $\phi$. But $\phi$ sits
in the distribution the expectation is taken over, not in the thing being
averaged, so you can't just average the gradient of samples: a sampled
$z$ carries no record of how it depended on $\phi$. The fix is to move
the randomness outside the network:

$$
z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I).
$$

Now $z$ is an ordinary differentiable function of $\phi$, with $\varepsilon$
an input like any other, and backpropagation ([post
3.1](/posts/backpropagation-by-hand/)) flows through the sample. One draw of
$\varepsilon$ per example gives an unbiased gradient estimate, usually with far
less variance than the score-function estimator that policy gradients use
([post 28](/posts/policy-gradient-to-ppo/)), which needs only
$\nabla_\phi \log q$, not a path through the sample, and so works for
discrete choices where this trick can't. That one line, published at the
same time by Kingma and Welling (2013) and by Rezende, Mohamed and
Wierstra (2014), is what made VAEs train with plain SGD. It appears in the
experiment below as `z = mu + torch.randn_like(mu) * (0.5 * logvar).exp()`.

## GANs: learn a critic instead

A GAN keeps the generator, $x = G(z)$ with $z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$, and
drops the likelihood and the encoder. In their place is a **discriminator**
$D(x) \in (0, 1)$, trained to output the probability that $x$ is real.
The two play a minimax game (Goodfellow et al., 2014):

$$
\min_G \max_D \; V(D, G) = \mathbb E_{x \sim p_\text{data}}\big[\log D(x)\big] + \mathbb E_{z}\big[\log\big(1 - D(G(z))\big)\big].
$$

For $D$ this is just binary cross-entropy on real versus generated. Fix the
generator, whose samples follow some distribution $q$, and the best
discriminator can be found pointwise: maximizing $p \log D + q \log(1-D)$
over $D$ at each $x$ gives

$$
D^*(x) = \frac{p(x)}{p(x) + q(x)}.
$$

Put it back into $V$ and the value is a known divergence:

$$
V(D^*, G) = 2\, \operatorname{JS}(p \,\|\, q) - \log 4,
$$

where the **Jensen-Shannon divergence** $\operatorname{JS}$ is the average
KL from $p$ and from $q$ to their mixture $m = (p+q)/2$. So against a
perfect critic, the generator minimizes the JS divergence to the data,
reaching $-\log 4$ exactly when $q = p$. The experiment script checks the
identity on two 1-D Gaussians a distance 1.5 apart, by integrating on a
grid:

```text
optimal-discriminator value -0.9440; 2 JS - log 4 = -0.9440
```

## Why GANs are hard to train

The derivation assumes a perfect critic and smooth distributions; training
has neither, and three problems follow.

- **Saturation.** Early on, generated samples are easy to spot, so
  $D(G(z)) \approx 0$ and $\log(1 - D(G(z)))$ is flat: the generator gets
  almost no gradient. The fix from the original paper, used ever since, is
  the **non-saturating loss**: train $G$ to maximize $\log D(G(z))$
  instead, which has the same fixed point and a strong gradient exactly
  when the generator is losing. It does change what is minimized: against
  the optimal discriminator it works out to
  $\operatorname{KL}(q \,\|\, p) - 2\,\operatorname{JS}(p \,\|\, q)$
  (Arjovsky and Bottou, 2017). That reverse KL charges heavily for samples
  where there's no data, and almost nothing for data the generator never
  produces: one reason GANs drop modes.
- **Disjoint supports.** By the **manifold hypothesis**, real images lie
  near a thin, low-dimensional surface in pixel space, and generated ones
  lie on the image of a low-dimensional $z$. Two such surfaces generally
  meet only in a set of volume zero, and then JS sits at its maximum,
  $\log 2$, however close the surfaces are: its gradient is zero, and
  nothing says "move this way."
- **Mode collapse.** Nothing in the game rewards covering all the data. A
  generator that produces a few convincing kinds of output can win each
  round; the critic learns to reject them, the generator jumps to other
  ones, and the pair can cycle instead of converging.

**Wasserstein GANs** (Arjovsky et al., 2017) attack the second problem by
changing the distance. The **Wasserstein-1** (earth-mover's) distance is
the least average distance mass has to move to turn $q$ into $p$, and it
keeps shrinking smoothly as two distributions approach, overlapping or not.
By a duality theorem it equals the largest gap
$\mathbb E_p[f(x)] - \mathbb E_q[f(x)]$ over all functions $f$ with slope at
most 1 everywhere (1-Lipschitz). So the critic becomes $f$, outputs any real
number, and maximizes that gap; the generator minimizes it. Enforcing the
slope limit is the hard part. The original paper clipped weights; **WGAN-GP**
(Gulrajani et al., 2017) instead penalizes the critic's gradient norm for
straying from 1 at random points between real and generated samples, and
trains the critic several steps per generator step (five, in the paper
and below).

## Three models, one test

The standard test for all of this is small: eight Gaussian blobs on a ring
of radius 2, each with standard deviation 0.05. Collapse is easy to see in
2-D, and two numbers measure it from 2,000 samples: **modes covered** (a
mode counts if more than 1% of samples, over 20 of the 2,000, land within
3 standard deviations of it) and **share near a mode** (the fraction of
samples within 3 standard deviations of any mode). They are toy versions
of the two halves of every generative metric: **recall**, how much of the
data the model can produce, and **precision**, how much of what it
produces looks like data. On images the standard single number is the
**Fréchet Inception Distance** (FID), which compares the mean and
covariance of real and generated images' features in a pretrained
classifier, and mixes both halves; precision and recall measured
separately in the same feature space (Kynkäänniemi et al., 2019) keep them
apart.

The same MLP size for every network, 6,000 generator steps, three seeds
each. Two settings to flag: the VAE's decoder noise is set to 0.05, the
data's own spread, which I could only choose because I made the data; and
WGAN-GP gets five critic steps per generator step at half the learning
rate (with Adam's $\beta_1 = 0.5$ for both GANs, where the WGAN-GP paper
used 0), so equal generator steps are not equal compute:

```python

# Three generative models on the same 2-D data: 8 Gaussian modes on a ring
# of radius 2 (std 0.05 each), the standard test for mode collapse. Each is
# scored on 2,000 samples: modes covered (a mode counts if at least 1% of
# samples fall within 3 std of it) and quality (the share of samples within
# 3 std of some mode). Three seeds each.
centers = torch.tensor([[2 * math.cos(a), 2 * math.sin(a)] for a in np.arange(8) * math.pi / 4], dtype=torch.float32)
def data(n, g):
    return centers[torch.randint(0, 8, (n,), generator=g)] + 0.05 * torch.randn(n, 2, generator=g)
def score(x):
    d = torch.cdist(x, centers)
    near = d.min(1).values < 0.15
    hits = torch.bincount(d.argmin(1)[near], minlength=8)
    return int((hits > 0.01 * len(x)).sum()), near.float().mean().item()
mlp = lambda i, o: nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(i, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, o))

def vae(seed, steps=6000, beta=1.0):
    """Encoder gives q(z|x) = N(mu, sigma^2) in 2-D; decoder gives p(x|z) =
    N(f(z), 0.05^2 I). Loss: minus the ELBO = reconstruction + KL to N(0, I)."""
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    enc, dec = mlp(2, 4), mlp(2, 2)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([*enc.parameters(), *dec.parameters()], 1e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x = data(256, g)
        mu, logvar = enc(x).chunk(2, -1)
        z = mu + torch.randn_like(mu) * (0.5 * logvar).exp()            # the reparameterization trick
        rec = ((dec(z) - x) ** 2).sum(-1) / (2 * 0.05 ** 2)
        kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - 1 - logvar).sum(-1)
        loss = (rec + beta * kl).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return score(dec(torch.randn(2000, 2)))

def gan(seed, steps=6000, wgan=False):
    """Generator maps 2-D noise to points; the critic tells data from
    samples. Ordinary GAN: the non-saturating loss of Goodfellow et al.
    WGAN-GP: a critic score difference with a gradient penalty."""
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed); torch.manual_seed(seed)
    G, D = mlp(2, 2), mlp(2, 1)
    og = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters(), 1e-4 if wgan else 2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.9))
    od = torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), 1e-4 if wgan else 2e-4, betas=(0.5, 0.9))
    bce = nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss()
    for step in range(steps):
        for _ in range(5 if wgan else 1):
            x, fake = data(256, g), G(torch.randn(256, 2)).detach()
            if wgan:
                eps = torch.rand(256, 1)
                mix = (eps * x + (1 - eps) * fake).requires_grad_(True)
                grad = torch.autograd.grad(D(mix).sum(), mix, create_graph=True)[0]
                ld = D(fake).mean() - D(x).mean() + 10 * ((grad.norm(dim=1) - 1) ** 2).mean()
            else:
                ld = bce(D(x), torch.ones(256, 1)) + bce(D(fake), torch.zeros(256, 1))
            od.zero_grad(); ld.backward(); od.step()
        fake = G(torch.randn(256, 2))
        lg = -D(fake).mean() if wgan else bce(D(fake), torch.ones(256, 1))
        og.zero_grad(); lg.backward(); og.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        return score(G(torch.randn(2000, 2)))

# The GAN's value at the optimal discriminator is 2 JS(p, q) - log 4: checked
# for two 1-D Gaussians on a grid.
xs = np.linspace(-10, 10, 20001); dx = xs[1] - xs[0]
p = np.exp(-0.5 * xs ** 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi); q = np.exp(-0.5 * (xs - 1.5) ** 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
Dstar = p / (p + q)
value = (p * np.log(Dstar) + q * np.log(1 - Dstar)).sum() * dx
m = (p + q) / 2
js = 0.5 * ((p * np.log(p / m)).sum() + (q * np.log(q / m)).sum()) * dx
print(f"optimal-discriminator value {value:.4f}; 2 JS - log 4 = {2 * js - math.log(4):.4f}")

print(f"\n{'model':24s} modes covered (of 8), per seed   share of samples near a mode")
for name, fn in (("VAE", vae), ("GAN (non-saturating)", gan), ("WGAN-GP", lambda s: gan(s, wgan=True))):
    res = [fn(s) for s in range(3)]
    print(f"{name:24s} {'  '.join(str(r[0]) for r in res):>18s}            {'  '.join(f'{r[1]:.0%}' for r in res)}", flush=True)
```

```text
model                    modes covered (of 8), per seed   share of samples near a mode
VAE                                 8  8  8            52%  48%  51%
GAN (non-saturating)                8  7  8            89%  82%  88%
WGAN-GP                             8  8  1            72%  65%  2%
```

The same trainings drawn, for the four runs that show the differences
(1,000 of each run's 2,000 samples; the circles are the 3-standard-deviation
region around each true mode; points outside the square are not drawn,
about 6% for WGAN-GP seed 2 and none for the others):

**The VAE puts samples where there's no data.** It covers all eight modes
in every seed, because the reconstruction term punishes any training
point it can't rebuild: dropping a mode is expensive. But only about half
its samples land on a mode; most of the rest sit along the ring between
modes, and a few inside it. The textbook explanation is averaging: if
neighboring modes' codes overlap, the decoder's best guess under squared
error is a point between them. That predicts that even reconstructions
would blur, and it can be tested, by decoding three kinds of code from the
same trained models:

```python

# Where do the VAE's off-mode samples come from? gen2d.py's vae(), trained
# the same way, but returning the encoder and decoder instead of a score.
src = open("gen2d.py").read().split("# The GAN's value")[0]
ns = {}; exec(src.replace("return score(dec(torch.randn(2000, 2)))", "return enc, dec"), ns)
print(f"{'seed':>4s} {'reconstructions':>16s} {'z from the encoders':>20s} {'z from the prior':>17s}")
for seed in range(3):
    enc, dec = ns["vae"](seed)
    with torch.no_grad():
        x = ns["data"](2000, torch.Generator().manual_seed(99))
        mu, logvar = enc(x).chunk(2, -1)
        rec = dec(mu)                                                    # decode each point's mean code
        agg = dec(mu + torch.randn_like(mu) * (0.5 * logvar).exp())      # a code the encoder could give
        prior = dec(torch.randn(2000, 2))                                # what sampling the VAE does
    print(f"{seed:4d} " + "".join(f"{ns['score'](v)[1]:>{w}.0%}" for v, w in ((rec, 16), (agg, 21), (prior, 18))), flush=True)
```

```text
seed  reconstructions  z from the encoders  z from the prior
   0             100%                 100%               52%
   1             100%                  99%               50%
   2             100%                 100%               48%
```

Averaging is not what happens here. Every reconstruction lands on its
mode, and so do 99–100% of codes drawn from the encoders' own
distributions. Only codes drawn from the prior go wrong. The encoders
together use only part of the prior's space (the **aggregate posterior**,
the mix of all the $q(z \mid x)$, doesn't fill $\mathcal N(0, I)$), and a
prior sample that falls in a gap between the regions they use decodes to
whatever the continuous decoder passes through on its way from one mode
to the next: a point on the ring between them. The KL term pulls each
$q(z \mid x)$ toward the prior but can't close those gaps. On images both
causes are at work: decoders do average when a code is ambiguous, which
gives the familiar blur, and prior samples from the gaps give
implausible images. Later fixes target the gap: a learned prior, or a
second model that samples from the aggregate posterior, which is what
latent diffusion amounts to.

**The GAN is sharp and can drop modes.** 82–89% of its samples land on a
mode, because the critic rejects anything off the data, and an in-between
sample is the easiest thing for it to spot. But nothing makes it cover
them all: in seed 1 the lower-left mode fell below the 1% threshold, with
only a few stray samples near it. A generator is a continuous map from a
connected $z$-space, so it also has to cross the gaps between modes
somewhere; the GAN makes those crossings steep, and the trails of points
between modes in the figure are where it does.

**WGAN-GP, when it trains, keeps every mode.** Seeds 0 and 1 covered all
eight, with 72% and 65% of samples near a mode: less sharp than the plain
GAN at 6,000 generator steps. Seed 2 is a **training failure**, not a
collapse: after 6,000 steps only 2% of its samples are near any mode, and
the one mode it "covers" is one that a broad crescent of samples happens
to sweep past. To see whether it was merely slow, I ran it to 12,000
steps, scoring every 1,500:

```python

# WGAN-GP, seed 2, run to 12,000 generator steps and scored every 1,500:
# gen2d.py's gan() with a scoring hook. Scoring draws from the same global
# random generator as the generator's noise, so after the first checkpoint
# this run follows a different path from the one in the table.
src = open("gen2d.py").read().split("# The GAN's value")[0]
src = src.replace("        og.zero_grad(); lg.backward(); og.step()\n",
                  "        og.zero_grad(); lg.backward(); og.step()\n"
                  "        if (step + 1) % 1500 == 0: report(step + 1, G)\n")
ns = {}; exec(src, ns)
def report(step, G):
    with torch.no_grad():
        x = G(torch.randn(2000, 2))
    modes, near = ns["score"](x)
    print(f"step {step:6d}   modes {modes}   near a mode {near:5.1%}   "
          f"sample std ({x[:, 0].std():.2f}, {x[:, 1].std():.2f})", flush=True)
ns["report"] = report
ns["gan"](2, steps=12000, wgan=True)
```

```text
step   1500   modes 0   near a mode  0.1%   sample std (0.69, 0.43)
step   3000   modes 0   near a mode  0.8%   sample std (3.05, 2.17)
step   4500   modes 0   near a mode  0.0%   sample std (0.16, 0.24)
step   6000   modes 0   near a mode  0.0%   sample std (0.27, 0.63)
step   7500   modes 0   near a mode  1.0%   sample std (0.99, 2.04)
step   9000   modes 0   near a mode  0.2%   sample std (1.05, 1.03)
step  10500   modes 0   near a mode  0.4%   sample std (0.44, 0.83)
step  12000   modes 0   near a mode  1.4%   sample std (0.89, 1.00)
```

It never recovered: the samples' spread swings between 0.16 and 3 as the
generator chases the critic, without settling on the ring. The same code, step
count and learning rate trained fine for two other seeds, so the honest
reading is that this setup is fragile, not that WGAN-GP is worse. I didn't
tune it per seed, because that would be choosing settings after seeing
the results, and three seeds are too few to estimate how often it fails.
A real project would watch for this with sample quality during training,
not just the loss, and restart or lower the learning rate.

None of this is the clean "each objective predicts its failure" story:
the VAE's off-mode samples come from the prior, not the reconstruction
loss, and WGAN-GP's failure is an optimization failure that its objective
doesn't predict. These numbers are from one small test. On images, a well-tuned GAN with
the architectural tricks below is far sharper than a VAE of the same size,
and the gap here between the GAN and WGAN-GP at 6,000 steps says nothing
about which is better at scale.

## From blobs to faces: DCGAN and StyleGAN

Two architectures took GANs from toy data to photographs.

- **DCGAN** (Radford et al., 2015) found a convolutional recipe that trains
  stably: strided convolutions instead of pooling, batch normalization
  ([post 4.2](/posts/dropout-and-normalization/)) in both networks, ReLU in
  the generator and leaky ReLU in the discriminator, no fully connected
  hidden layers. It also showed the latent space had structure: arithmetic
  on $z$ vectors (a smiling woman's code, minus a neutral woman's, plus a
  neutral man's) produced a smiling man, when each code was the average of
  three examples; single codes were unstable.
- **StyleGAN** (Karras et al., 2019) stopped feeding $z$ in at the start. A
  mapping network turns $z$ into a style vector $w$, which modulates every
  layer of the generator through adaptive normalization, so coarse layers
  set pose and shape and fine layers set texture and color. It and its
  successors, StyleGAN2 and StyleGAN3, made 1024×1024 faces that were the
  state of the art for photorealism until diffusion.

## Where each is used now

Diffusion models ([post 68](/posts/diffusion-for-images-and-text/))
replaced both as the main way to generate images, by trading speed for
stability: many small denoising steps, each trained with a plain regression
loss and no adversary. Both ideas survive inside them.

- **The VAE is the latent space.** Stable Diffusion runs its diffusion not
  on pixels but on the latent grid of a VAE that shrinks the image 8 times
  along each side into 4 channels: a 512×512×3 image becomes 64×64×4,
  48 times fewer numbers. Its KL term is weighted very lightly (about
  $10^{-6}$), a $\beta$-VAE with tiny $\beta$, because the job is
  reconstruction, not sampling from the prior: the diffusion model learns
  to sample codes instead, which sidesteps the prior's gaps from the
  experiment above.
- **The adversarial loss sharpens.** That VAE's decoder was trained with a
  perceptual loss (distances between deep-network features, not pixels)
  and a patch discriminator on top of the reconstruction loss, which
  together keep its outputs from blurring. GAN losses are also used to
  distill many-step diffusion models into one- to four-step generators,
  as in adversarial diffusion distillation (SDXL Turbo).

## Takeaways

- A latent-variable model samples easily but can't compute its likelihood.
  The VAE maximizes a bound instead; the GAN trains a critic instead.
- The ELBO is reconstruction minus KL to the prior, and it falls short of
  $\log p(x)$ by exactly the KL from the encoder to the true posterior:
  checked to four decimals on a model small enough to solve.
- The reparameterization trick, $z = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon$, puts
  the randomness outside the network so gradients flow through the sample.
- Against the optimal discriminator $p/(p+q)$, the GAN objective is
  $2\,\operatorname{JS} - \log 4$. JS gives no gradient between
  distributions that barely overlap, which WGAN fixes with the earth-mover's
  distance and a critic limited to slope 1.
- The ELBO can rise without the model improving, by moving the true
  posterior toward the encoder; posterior collapse is the extreme case.
- On eight modes: the VAE kept every mode with half its samples off them,
  and the off-mode samples came from prior regions no encoder used, not
  from blurred reconstructions; the GAN was sharp and dropped a mode in
  one seed of three; WGAN-GP kept every mode in two seeds and failed to
  train in the third.
- Today VAEs are the compressed latent space diffusion runs in, and
  adversarial losses sharpen decoders and distill diffusion into fewer
  steps.

[Post 8](/posts/embeddings-and-contrastive-learning/) turned text into vectors whose
closeness means similar meaning. Retrieval, the subject of Part IX, starts
by finding the stored vectors closest to a query's vector: **nearest-neighbor
search**. Done exactly, it is one line of linear algebra and costs time in
proportion to the number of vectors. Every index built since trades a little
accuracy, a few true neighbors missed, for a large saving in that time, and
the right trade depends on how many vectors there are, how much memory
there is, and how often the data changes.

## Table of contents

## Similarity, three ways

Three measures are common: the **dot product** $q \cdot x$, the **cosine**
$\frac{q \cdot x}{\|q\| \|x\|}$, and the **Euclidean distance** $\|q - x\|$.
They usually agree, because embedding models are trained with normalized
vectors and their output is normalized before storing. For unit vectors
the cosine *is* the dot product, and

$$
\|q - x\|^2 = \|q\|^2 + \|x\|^2 - 2\, q \cdot x = 2 - 2\, q \cdot x,
$$

so the smallest distance is the largest dot product: all three rank
identically. (The measurement below confirms it on real embeddings, up to
ties between duplicate sentences.) Without normalization they don't: the
dot product favors long vectors, which some models use on purpose, so
search with the measure the model was trained for.

## Exact search, and why trees don't save it

Exact search computes the query's similarity to every stored vector:
$N \times d$ multiply-adds, 27.6 million for the 71,865 vectors of 384
dimensions below, 2.5 to 4 ms on one CPU core of this laptop, depending
on what else it is doing. That is fast enough for tens
of thousands of vectors, and it is always right. Below about a hundred
thousand vectors, it is usually the right choice.

For low-dimensional data, **k-d trees** (Bentley, 1975) cut the work by
splitting space into boxes and skipping boxes too far from the query. In
high dimensions this stops working, because distances stop telling points
apart (Beyer et al., 1999). For random points, the nearest and the
farthest neighbor of a query end up nearly equally far away:

```python

# Why trees fail in high dimensions: for 10,000 random points, the nearest
# and the farthest neighbor of a random query end up almost equally far away.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
for dim in (2, 10, 100, 384):
    P = rng.normal(size=(10_000, dim)); q = rng.normal(size=dim)
    dist = np.linalg.norm(P - q, axis=1)
    print(f"random points, {dim:3d} dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = {dist.min() / dist.max():.2f}")

# The real sentence embeddings of the next section (384 dimensions), for
# 200 of the query sentences: median of the same ratio.
X, Q = np.load("docs.npy"), np.load("queries.npy")
r = [np.sqrt(np.maximum(2 - 2 * (X @ q).max(), 0)) / np.sqrt(2 - 2 * (X @ q).min()) for q in Q[:200]]
print(f"real embeddings,   384 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = {np.median(r):.2f} (median of 200 queries)")
```

```text
random points,   2 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = 0.00
random points,  10 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = 0.19
random points, 100 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = 0.61
random points, 384 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = 0.78
real embeddings,   384 dimensions: nearest / farthest distance = 0.63 (median of 200 queries)
```

At 384 dimensions the nearest random point is 78% as far as the
farthest, so almost every box might hold a near neighbor and the tree
visits almost all of them. Real embeddings are less uniform: for the
sentence embeddings below the ratio is 0.63, like 100-dimensional random
data. That structure is why the approximate methods below work at all,
but it isn't enough for exact pruning.

## Locality-sensitive hashing

**LSH** (Indyk and Motwani, 1998) hashes vectors so that close vectors
probably share a hash, and looks only in the query's buckets. For cosine
similarity, the hash Charikar (2002) introduced takes random hyperplanes
and records which side of each a vector falls on, one bit each: two
vectors at angle $\theta$ disagree on each bit with probability $\theta /
\pi$. It has clean guarantees, but needs many bits or many tables for good
recall, and in practice the data-dependent methods below beat it. (The
measurement below uses such bit codes as a 128-byte sketch scanned
exhaustively, not as hash tables, so it shows their accuracy, not LSH's
speed.)

## IVF: search only the nearby lists

An **inverted file** index (IVF) runs k-means on the vectors, into 4 to 16
times $\sqrt{N}$ clusters by FAISS's guideline, and stores each vector in
the list of its
nearest centroid. A query is compared with the centroids, then searched
exhaustively in only the `nprobe` nearest lists. With 256 lists (about
$\sqrt{N}$ here) and 4 probes it scans about 1.6% of the vectors; the
measurement also tries 1,024 lists, about $4\sqrt{N}$. A true neighbor is missed when
it sits in a list whose centroid wasn't among the closest few, near a
boundary; probing more lists recovers it, at linear cost.

## Product quantization: an 8-byte vector, worked

IVF still stores every vector in full: 384 floats, 1,536 bytes. **Product
quantization** (PQ; Jégou et al., 2011) compresses them. Split each vector
into $m$ sub-vectors, run k-means with 256 centroids on each sub-space
separately, and store each sub-vector as the one-byte index of its nearest
centroid. With $m = 8$, a 384-dimensional vector becomes 8 sub-vectors of
48 dimensions and is stored as **8 bytes**, 192 times smaller, and the 8
codebooks, $8 \times 256$ centroids of 48 floats, are shared by all vectors.

Distances need no decompression, and the query itself is never
quantized (Jégou et al. call this asymmetric distance computation). For a
query, compute once the dot product
of each of its 8 sub-vectors with each of that sub-space's 256 centroids:
8 tables of 256 numbers. The approximate similarity to any stored vector
is then the sum of 8 table lookups, one per byte of its code. The answer
is approximate because each stored sub-vector was replaced by its
centroid; the more sub-vectors, the finer the approximation (the
measurement uses 48, 48 bytes a vector). PQ is usually combined with IVF
(IVF-PQ) for speed, and followed by **re-ranking**: re-score the best few hundred candidates with
the exact vectors, kept on disk or in cheaper memory. ScaNN (Guo et al.,
2020) improves the quantization itself: it penalizes the part of each
vector's quantization error parallel to the vector more than the part
orthogonal to it, since that is what changes large inner products.

## HNSW: a navigable small world

**HNSW** (hierarchical navigable small world; Malkov and Yashunin, 2016)
is a graph. Every vector is a node linked to up to $M$ neighbors on each
upper layer and $2M$ on layer 0. Vectors are inserted one at a time, and
each new vector's links are chosen with a heuristic that prefers
neighbors in different directions over a tight cluster of near ones,
which keeps the graph connected and gives it some long links. To search, start somewhere, move to whichever neighbor is
closer to the query, and repeat until no neighbor is closer. On a plain
neighbor graph that walk is slow, because it takes many short steps. HNSW
adds layers: every node is on layer 0, about one in $M$ also on layer 1,
fewer again on layer 2, each layer a sparser graph with longer links. The
search starts on the top layer, crosses the space in a few long hops,
drops a layer, and refines, like zooming in on a map. On layer 0 it keeps
a beam of the `ef` best candidates rather than just one, which makes it
less likely to stop at a point that is only locally nearest.

The widget builds a simplified one over 200 points: each point links to
its $M$ nearest, and about one in six reaches each higher layer. Click to
move the query; the thick lines are the search's moves on the upper
layers, the thin ones on layer 0. Compare the distances computed with the
200 of brute force. With 2 links per point it misses often, mostly
because a plain nearest-neighbor graph that sparse falls apart into
islands the search can't cross, which HNSW's neighbor heuristic prevents;
with 8 it rarely misses:

## Measured: recall, speed and memory

All of the above, in FAISS (Johnson et al., 2017), on the sentences of
WikiText-2's training set embedded with post 8's MiniLM, searched with
1,000 sentences from its test set. **Recall@10** is the fraction of the
true 10 nearest neighbors an index returns:

```python

# Exact and approximate nearest-neighbor search over 71,865 real sentence
# embeddings (384 dimensions, normalized), 1,000 held-out queries, top 10.
# Truth: exact inner-product search. Every index is queried one query at a
# time on one CPU thread, the latency a single request sees; each setting
# is timed three times and the fastest kept, since other work on the
# machine only ever slows a run down.
faiss.omp_set_num_threads(1)
X, Q = np.load("docs.npy"), np.load("queries.npy")
N, d, k = *X.shape, 10
exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d); exact.add(X)
_, truth = exact.search(Q, k)

# On unit vectors, L2, dot product and cosine rank identically:
#    |q - x|^2 = 2 - 2 q.x.
l2 = faiss.IndexFlatL2(d); l2.add(X); _, by_l2 = l2.search(Q[:100], k)
same = all(set(a) == set(b) for a, b in zip(by_l2, truth[:100]))
swaps = [(i, j) for i in range(100) for j in range(k) if by_l2[i, j] != truth[i, j]]
ties = all(np.isclose(Q[i] @ X[by_l2[i, j]], Q[i] @ X[truth[i, j]]) for i, j in swaps)
print(f"L2 vs dot product, 100 queries: same top-10 sets: {same}; order differs at {len(swaps)} positions, "
      f"all between exactly tied scores (duplicate sentences): {ties}")

def measure(index, name, bytes_per_vector, setter=None, values=(None,)):
    for v in values:
        if setter:
            setter(v)
        times = []
        for _ in range(3):
            t0 = time.perf_counter()
            found = np.vstack([index.search(Q[i:i + 1], k)[1] for i in range(len(Q))])
            times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
        ms = min(times) / len(Q) * 1e3
        recall = np.mean([len(set(f) & set(t)) / k for f, t in zip(found, truth)])
        label = name if v is None else f"{name}, {v}"
        print(f"{label:32s} recall@10 {recall:6.3f}   {ms:6.3f} ms/query   {bytes_per_vector:5.0f} bytes/vector")

print(f"\n{N:,} vectors, {d} dimensions:")
measure(exact, "flat (exact)", 4 * d)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
ivf = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, 256, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); ivf.train(X); ivf.add(X)
print(f"  (IVF, 256 lists: built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
measure(ivf, "IVF 256 lists, probe", 4 * d + 8, lambda v: setattr(ivf, "nprobe", v), (1, 4, 16, 64))
# FAISS's guideline is 4 to 16 times sqrt(N) lists; sqrt(71,865) is 268.
ivf4 = faiss.IndexIVFFlat(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, 1024, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); ivf4.train(X); ivf4.add(X)
measure(ivf4, "IVF 1024 lists, probe", 4 * d + 8, lambda v: setattr(ivf4, "nprobe", v), (8, 16, 32, 64))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pq = faiss.IndexPQ(d, 48, 8, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); pq.train(X); pq.add(X)
print(f"  (PQ, 48 sub-vectors x 8 bits: built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
measure(pq, "PQ, 48-byte codes", 48)
ivfpq = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, 256, 48, 8, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); ivfpq.train(X); ivfpq.add(X)
measure(ivfpq, "IVF-PQ, probe", 48 + 8, lambda v: setattr(ivfpq, "nprobe", v), (4, 16, 64))
# PQ's recall is capped by its coarse codes; re-scoring the top 100
# candidates with the exact vectors (kept in memory, or on disk) lifts it.
base = faiss.IndexIVFPQ(faiss.IndexFlatIP(d), d, 256, 48, 8, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); base.train(X)
refine = faiss.IndexRefineFlat(base); refine.k_factor = 10; refine.add(X)
measure(refine, "IVF-PQ + re-rank 100, probe", 48 + 8 + 4 * d, lambda v: setattr(base, "nprobe", v), (16, 64))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
hnsw = faiss.IndexHNSWFlat(d, 32, faiss.METRIC_INNER_PRODUCT); hnsw.hnsw.efConstruction = 128; hnsw.add(X)
print(f"  (HNSW, M = 32: built in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s)")
measure(hnsw, "HNSW M=32, efSearch", 4 * d + 2 * 32 * 4, lambda v: setattr(hnsw.hnsw, "efSearch", v), (16, 32, 64, 128))
lsh = faiss.IndexLSH(d, 1024); lsh.add(X)
measure(lsh, "LSH, 1024-bit codes, scanned", 1024 / 8)
```

```text
L2 vs dot product, 100 queries: same top-10 sets: True; order differs at 4 positions, all between exactly tied scores (duplicate sentences): True

71,865 vectors, 384 dimensions:
flat (exact)                     recall@10  1.000    4.071 ms/query    1536 bytes/vector
  (IVF, 256 lists: built in 0.5 s)
IVF 256 lists, probe, 1          recall@10  0.496    0.026 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 256 lists, probe, 4          recall@10  0.812    0.076 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 256 lists, probe, 16         recall@10  0.955    0.279 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 256 lists, probe, 64         recall@10  0.994    1.098 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 1024 lists, probe, 8         recall@10  0.799    0.062 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 1024 lists, probe, 16        recall@10  0.886    0.098 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 1024 lists, probe, 32        recall@10  0.941    0.174 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
IVF 1024 lists, probe, 64        recall@10  0.974    0.293 ms/query    1544 bytes/vector
  (PQ, 48 sub-vectors x 8 bits: built in 13.6 s)
PQ, 48-byte codes                recall@10  0.626    0.835 ms/query      48 bytes/vector
IVF-PQ, probe, 4                 recall@10  0.568    0.067 ms/query      56 bytes/vector
IVF-PQ, probe, 16                recall@10  0.604    0.118 ms/query      56 bytes/vector
IVF-PQ, probe, 64                recall@10  0.608    0.291 ms/query      56 bytes/vector
IVF-PQ + re-rank 100, probe, 16  recall@10  0.942    0.162 ms/query    1592 bytes/vector
IVF-PQ + re-rank 100, probe, 64  recall@10  0.969    0.328 ms/query    1592 bytes/vector
  (HNSW, M = 32: built in 47.4 s)
HNSW M=32, efSearch, 16          recall@10  0.876    0.089 ms/query    1792 bytes/vector
HNSW M=32, efSearch, 32          recall@10  0.950    0.153 ms/query    1792 bytes/vector
HNSW M=32, efSearch, 64          recall@10  0.983    0.279 ms/query    1792 bytes/vector
HNSW M=32, efSearch, 128         recall@10  0.994    0.551 ms/query    1792 bytes/vector
LSH, 1024-bit codes, scanned     recall@10  0.631    0.364 ms/query     128 bytes/vector
```

Read it as a menu of trades. Timings are one query at a time on one core
of this laptop, the fastest of three repeats, while other jobs ran on its
GPU; absolute times moved by up to half between runs hours apart, so
compare rows within this run rather than across runs.
- **Exact search**: 4.1 ms a query in this run, always right. At 72,000
  vectors that is fast enough for most uses; an index starts to pay at
  hundreds of thousands or millions, or at many queries per second.
- **IVF** buys speed with the number of lists probed. With 256 lists, 4
  probes find 81% of the true top 10 in 0.08 ms, 54 times faster than
  exact; 16 find 96%; 64 find 99.4%, 3.7 times faster than exact. With
  1,024 lists, the guideline's size, each probe scans less: 94% recall
  takes 0.17 ms, where 256 lists need 0.28 ms for 96%. Memory is
  unchanged: it stores every vector in full.
- **PQ** buys memory: 48 bytes per vector instead of 1,536, 32 times
  smaller, but at 48 bytes the codes alone cap recall near 61 to 63%,
  however many lists IVF-PQ probes. Re-ranking its top 100 with the exact
  vectors lifts it to 94 to 97%, at the cost of keeping those vectors
  somewhere.
- **HNSW** reaches 95% at 0.15 ms, 98% at 0.28 ms and 99.4% at 0.55 ms.
  Against IVF with the guideline's 1,024 lists it is roughly level around
  95%, slightly ahead at 97 to 98%, and at 99.4% it is twice as fast as
  the 256-list IVF that reaches it. Its edge grows with the number of
  vectors and the recall target. It costs memory (about 270 bytes of
  links and bookkeeping per vector), build time (47 seconds, against half
  a second for IVF), and, being a graph, it is awkward to delete from.
- **Random-hyperplane codes** of 1,024 bits reach 63% recall:
  data-independent hashing loses to methods that learn the data's
  structure.

At this scale every method is fast in absolute terms. What the table is
for is the shape of the trade, which holds at larger scale: IVF and HNSW
trade recall for time, PQ trades recall for memory, and re-ranking buys
the recall back.

## What a vector database adds

An index answers "nearest vectors to this one". A **vector database**
wraps it with what an application needs around that:
- **Filtering**: "nearest, among this user's documents from this year".
  Filtering after the search can leave fewer than $k$ results; filtering
  before it can break a graph index's navigation, so databases build
  filters into the search itself.
- **Updates and deletes**: IVF and PQ take new vectors easily, but their
  centroids go stale as the data shifts; HNSW handles inserts, while
  deletes are tombstoned (marked and skipped) and reclaimed by reusing the
  slot or rebuilding.
- **Persistence, sharding and replication**, like any database.
- **Hybrid search**: combining vector similarity with keyword matching,
  the subject of post 37.

## Where this leads

- **Post 37** adds keyword search, BM25, and fuses the two rankings.
- **Post 38** re-ranks the top results with a more expensive model.
- **Post 39** builds retrieval-augmented generation on all of it.

## Takeaways

- On normalized embeddings, dot product, cosine and Euclidean distance
  rank identically; use the measure the model was trained with.
- Exact search costs $N \times d$ per query, a few milliseconds for 72,000
  vectors of 384 dimensions here, and is the right choice until it isn't
  fast enough. Trees don't help in high dimensions: distances concentrate.
- IVF searches only the nearest clusters (94% recall at about 1/24 of
  exact's time with 1,024 lists); PQ compresses vectors 32 times but, at
  48 bytes, caps recall near 62% until re-ranking with exact vectors (94
  to 97%); HNSW navigates a layered graph, roughly level with a well-sized
  IVF at 95% recall and ahead at the highest recall, at extra memory and
  build time.
- A vector database adds what an index doesn't: filtering, updates,
  persistence and hybrid search.
