## Table of contents

## Modalities

A **modality** is a kind of input: text, images, audio, video. Each needs
a way to become vectors, which is what an **encoder** does for it, and the
interesting question for multimodal systems is how vectors from different
modalities are made comparable. There are two answers in this post:
train two encoders so their outputs share one space (CLIP), or translate
one modality's vectors into the other's token space and let a language
model read them (vision-language models).

## Patches: an image as a sequence

The **Vision Transformer** (ViT; Dosovitskiy et al., 2020) uses the most
direct translation. Cut the image into a grid of small square patches,
flatten each patch's pixels into one vector, and project every patch with
the same learned linear layer, the **patch embedding**. Add position
embeddings ([post 12](/posts/rope-and-positional-encoding/)) so the model
knows where each patch came from (ViT learns one embedding per position
in the flattened sequence; later models use 2-D-aware schemes such as 2-D
RoPE so the same model can take images of different sizes), and the
result is a sequence like any other:

```python
# An image as a sequence. ViT-B/16 on a 224x224 RGB image: cut it into
# 16x16 patches, flatten each (16 * 16 * 3 numbers), and project each to the
# model's width with one shared linear layer, the patch embedding.
H = W = 224; P = 16; C = 3; D = 768
n = (H // P) * (W // P)
print(f"{H}x{W} image, {P}x{P} patches: {H // P} x {W // P} = {n} patches, each {P * P * C} numbers")
print(f"patch embedding: a {P * P * C} x {D} matrix + bias = {P * P * C * D + D:,} parameters")
print(f"sequence for the Transformer: {n} patch tokens + 1 [CLS] = {n + 1} positions, attention over {(n + 1) ** 2:,} pairs")
for res, p in ((224, 14), (336, 14), (448, 14), (1024, 16)):
    print(f"  {res}x{res} with {p}x{p} patches: {(res // p) ** 2:,} tokens")

# In a vision-language model the patch embeddings, after a projector, become
# tokens in the language model's context, and cost KV cache like text.
# LLaVA-1.5: a CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336x336 gives 576 image tokens, fed to a 7B
# language model (32 layers, width 4096, full multi-head attention, 16-bit).
kv_per_token = 32 * 2 * 4096 * 2                 # layers x (K and V) x width x bytes
print(f"\nLLaVA-1.5 (7B language model): {kv_per_token / 2 ** 10:.0f} KiB of KV cache per token")
print(f"  one image, 576 tokens: {576 * kv_per_token / 2 ** 20:.0f} MiB; a 20-image conversation: "
      f"{20 * 576 * kv_per_token / 2 ** 30:.1f} GiB")
print(f"  as text, 576 tokens is about {int(576 * 0.75)} English words")
```

```text
224x224 image, 16x16 patches: 14 x 14 = 196 patches, each 768 numbers
patch embedding: a 768 x 768 matrix + bias = 590,592 parameters
sequence for the Transformer: 196 patch tokens + 1 [CLS] = 197 positions, attention over 38,809 pairs
  224x224 with 14x14 patches: 256 tokens
  336x336 with 14x14 patches: 576 tokens
  448x448 with 14x14 patches: 1,024 tokens
  1024x1024 with 16x16 patches: 4,096 tokens

LLaVA-1.5 (7B language model): 512 KiB of KV cache per token
  one image, 576 tokens: 288 MiB; a 20-image conversation: 5.6 GiB
  as text, 576 tokens is about 432 English words
```

A 224×224 image in 16×16-pixel patches is 196 tokens (each "word" in the
paper's title, "an image is worth 16×16 words", is one such patch), plus
one extra. That extra is the **[CLS]
token**, borrowed from BERT: a learned vector prepended to the sequence
whose output, after every layer of attention to the patches, serves as
the representation of the whole image. The alternatives are to average
the outputs of all patch tokens (**mean pooling**), which the ViT paper
found works as well once tuned, or to pool with a small attention layer
(SigLIP does this). Models that feed a language model keep all the patch
outputs instead.

**Inductive bias.** A convolutional network builds in two assumptions:
that nearby pixels matter most to each other (locality), and that a
pattern means the same thing wherever it appears (translation
equivariance). ViT builds in almost none: from the first layer, every
patch can attend to every other, and spatial structure has to be learned
from data. The paper found that this costs ViT on small datasets, where a
CNN's assumptions are worth a lot, and pays off on very large ones (it
was pretrained, with labels, on about 300 million images), where learned
structure beats assumed structure. Part of that gap was the training
recipe: DeiT (Touvron et al., 2021) later trained ViTs well on ImageNet's
1.3 million images with heavy augmentation and distillation. The same
trade, data for priors, is the story of Transformers in text.

ViTs also learn well without labels or captions. **MAE** (He et al., 2021)
masks most patches and trains the model to reconstruct them; **DINO** and
**DINOv2** (Oquab et al., 2023) train a ViT to match its own outputs on
different views of an image, the self-distillation of post 72's JEPA
family. DINOv2's features capture spatial detail that CLIP's miss, and
some vision-language models use both encoders side by side.

## CLIP: images and text in one space

A classifier learns a fixed set of labels. **CLIP** (Radford et al., 2021)
learns from 400 million image–caption pairs collected from the web, with
no labels at all, using the contrastive objective of [post
8](/posts/embeddings-and-contrastive-learning/). An image encoder (a ViT)
and a text encoder (a Transformer) each produce a vector, both normalized
to unit length. In a batch of $N$ pairs, the $N \times N$ matrix of cosine
similarities should be large on the diagonal (each image with its own
caption) and small elsewhere. The loss treats each row as a classification
problem (which of these $N$ captions is mine?) and each column likewise
(which image is mine?), with cross-entropy over a softmax, and averages
the two directions: the **symmetric InfoNCE** loss. Worked on three
pairs:

```python

# CLIP's loss on a batch of 3 image-caption pairs. Embeddings are unit
# vectors; S[i, j] is the cosine similarity of image i and caption j, and the
# logits are S divided by a temperature. The matching pairs are on the diagonal.
S = np.array([[0.90, 0.20, 0.10],
              [0.30, 0.80, 0.40],
              [0.05, 0.35, 0.70]])
t = 0.07                                   # CLIP's initial temperature
L = S / t
def log_softmax(x, axis):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    return x - np.log(np.exp(x).sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True))
img_to_txt = -np.diag(log_softmax(L, axis=1))     # each image: which caption is mine? (cross-entropy over the row)
txt_to_img = -np.diag(log_softmax(L, axis=0))     # each caption: which image is mine? (over the column)
print("logits = similarities / 0.07:\n", L.round(2))
print("image -> caption losses:", img_to_txt.round(4), " caption -> image losses:", txt_to_img.round(4))
print(f"CLIP loss (symmetric InfoNCE) = mean of both directions = {(img_to_txt.mean() + txt_to_img.mean()) / 2:.4f}")

# SigLIP: no softmax over the batch. Every pair is its own binary question,
# match (label +1) or not (-1), scored with a sigmoid; a learned scale t
# (from log t, initialized at log 10) and bias b (initialized at -10).
tp, b = 10.0, -10.0
z = np.where(np.eye(3) == 1, 1, -1)
pair = np.log1p(np.exp(-z * (tp * S + b)))        # -log sigmoid(z * logit)
print("\nSigLIP per-pair losses:\n", pair.round(4))
print(f"SigLIP loss = sum over all 9 pairs / 3 images = {pair.sum() / 3:.4f}")
```

(The cosines here are illustrative; a trained CLIP's similarities between
matching pairs are typically far smaller, around 0.2 to 0.35, and it
learns the temperature, as the logarithm of its inverse, capped so the
scale never exceeds 100.)

```text
logits = similarities / 0.07:
 [[12.86  2.86  1.43]
 [ 4.29 11.43  5.71]
 [ 0.71  5.   10.  ]]
image -> caption losses: [0.0001 0.0041 0.0068]  caption -> image losses: [0.0002 0.0018 0.0139]
CLIP loss (symmetric InfoNCE) = mean of both directions = 0.0045

SigLIP per-pair losses:
 [[1.3133e+00 3.0000e-04 1.0000e-04]
 [9.0000e-04 2.1269e+00 2.5000e-03]
 [1.0000e-04 1.5000e-03 3.0486e+00]]
SigLIP loss = sum over all 9 pairs / 3 images = 2.1647
```

Dividing the similarities by a temperature of 0.07 (CLIP's starting value;
it is learned) turns differences of a few tenths into logit gaps of 5 to
10, so this well-aligned batch has a loss near zero. The softmax couples
every pair in the batch: each caption competes with all the others. That
is what makes large batches valuable (more negatives per example) and
what makes them expensive, since the softmax needs the whole similarity
matrix, which gets complicated to compute when the batch is split across
many devices.

**SigLIP** (Zhai et al., 2023) removes the coupling. Each of the $N^2$
pairs becomes its own yes-or-no question, scored with a sigmoid: is this
image this caption's? Matching pairs are labeled +1 and all others −1,
with a learned scale (multiplying the similarity, the inverse of a
temperature) and a learned bias. No softmax means no normalization over
the batch, so every pair can be scored independently, and it trains better
than CLIP's loss at batch sizes below about 16,000 (both saturate around
32,000). The worked numbers show a detail of its design: at the paper's
starting values (scale 10, from a learned log-scale initialized at
$\log 10$, and bias −10), even a matching pair with similarity 0.9 gets a
negative logit and a loss of 1.3. That is deliberate. In a batch of $N$,
only $N$ of the $N^2$ pairs match; starting near the prior of "no match"
keeps the huge initial loss from all those negatives from driving large,
destabilizing first steps.

Once trained, CLIP does things no classifier could. **Zero-shot
classification**: embed the image and the captions "a photo of a dog",
"a photo of a cat", and so on, and pick the closest. **Cross-modal
search**: find images by text and text by image. And its image encoder
became the eyes of most of the models below.

## CLIP on this blog's diagrams

CLIP learned from photographs and their captions. This blog's diagrams
are schematic: boxes, arrows and labels. Can it still match each one to
the alt text its post gives it? Each diagram is rendered whole into a
512×512 square, once as drawn and once with every text label hidden:

```python

# Render each diagram whole, fitted (aspect kept) into a 512x512 white
# square, with headless Chrome; and a second set with all text hidden.
CHROME = "/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome"
os.makedirs("fit", exist_ok=True); os.makedirs("notext", exist_ok=True)
for path in sorted(glob.glob("/Users/tanle/Developer/residual-stream/public/images/diagrams/*-light.svg")):
    if "-vi-" in path:
        continue
    name = os.path.basename(path)[:-len("-light.svg")]
    svg = open(path).read()
    svg = re.sub(r"<svg([^>]*?)\swidth=\"[^\"]*\"", r"<svg\1", svg, count=1)
    svg = re.sub(r"<svg([^>]*?)\sheight=\"[^\"]*\"", r"<svg\1", svg, count=1)
    svg = svg.replace("<svg", '<svg width="512" height="512" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet"', 1)
    for folder, extra in (("fit", ""), ("notext", "svg text, svg foreignObject { display: none !important; }")):
        html = (f"<html><body style='margin:0;background:#fff'><style>{extra}</style>"
                f"<div style='width:512px;height:512px'>{svg}</div></body></html>")
        open(f"/tmp/claude-501/r_{name}.html", "w").write(html)
        subprocess.run([CHROME, "--headless=new", "--disable-gpu", "--hide-scrollbars", "--window-size=512,512",
                        f"--screenshot={os.getcwd()}/{folder}/{name}.png", f"file:///tmp/claude-501/r_{name}.html"],
                       capture_output=True, timeout=60)
print(len(glob.glob("fit/*.png")), len(glob.glob("notext/*.png")))
```

```python

from PIL import Image
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor

# CLIP (ViT-B/32) on this blog's own diagrams. Each diagram's caption is the
# alt text its post gives it. Can CLIP find the right diagram from its
# caption, and the right caption from the diagram, among the 19? The
# diagrams are rendered whole into 512x512 squares (render.py), once as
# they are and once with every text label hidden.
alts = {}
for path in glob.glob("/Users/tanle/Developer/residual-stream/src/content/posts/*.mdx"):
    for m in re.finditer(r'light="/images/diagrams/([^"]+)-light\.svg"\s+dark="[^"]+"\s+alt="([^"]+)"', open(path).read()):
        alts[m.group(1)] = m.group(2)
names = sorted(n for n in alts if glob.glob(f"fit/{n}.png"))
model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32").eval()
proc = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
with torch.no_grad():
    def image(folder):               # each tower's pooled output, then CLIP's projection into the shared space
        px = proc(images=[Image.open(f"{folder}/{n}.png").convert("RGB") for n in names], return_tensors="pt")
        return model.visual_projection(model.vision_model(pixel_values=px["pixel_values"]).pooler_output)
    def text(captions):              # CLIP reads at most 77 tokens; longer alt texts are cut
        enc = proc(text=captions, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True)
        out = model.text_model(input_ids=enc["input_ids"], attention_mask=enc["attention_mask"])
        return model.text_projection(out.pooler_output)
    caps = {"the post's alt text": [alts[n] for n in names],
            "the file name as words": [n.replace("-", " ") for n in names]}
    print(f"{len(names)} diagrams; chance of the right match at random: 1 in {len(names)} ({1 / len(names):.0%})\n")
    print(f"{'diagrams':20s} {'caption':24s} {'caption -> diagram':>19s} {'diagram -> caption':>19s}  (right one first)")
    for folder, label in (("fit", "as drawn"), ("notext", "with labels hidden")):
        img = image(folder)
        for name, c in caps.items():
            S = torch.nn.functional.normalize(img, dim=-1) @ torch.nn.functional.normalize(text(c), dim=-1).T
            i2t = int((S.argmax(1) == torch.arange(len(names))).sum())
            t2i = int((S.argmax(0) == torch.arange(len(names))).sum())
            print(f"{label:20s} {name:24s} {t2i:>12d} of {len(names)} {i2t:>12d} of {len(names)}")
    n_tok = [len(proc.tokenizer(a).input_ids) for a in caps["the post's alt text"]]
    print(f"\nalt texts: median {sorted(n_tok)[len(n_tok) // 2]} tokens, {sum(x > 77 for x in n_tok)} of {len(n_tok)} cut at 77")
```

```text
19 diagrams; chance of the right match at random: 1 in 19 (5%)

diagrams             caption                   caption -> diagram  diagram -> caption  (right one first)
as drawn             the post's alt text                 5 of 19            4 of 19
as drawn             the file name as words              4 of 19            3 of 19
with labels hidden   the post's alt text                 1 of 19            2 of 19
with labels hidden   the file name as words              1 of 19            2 of 19

alt texts: median 40 tokens, 3 of 19 cut at 77
```

Given an alt text, CLIP ranks the right diagram first for 5 of the 19,
and the right alt text first for 4: better than the one in 19 chance would
give, not by much, and with 19 items the uncertainty is wide. Hide the
labels and it falls to chance. Whatever CLIP recognizes in these
diagrams, it recognizes in their text: CLIP is known to read words in
images (so well that a printed label can override what a photo shows,
the "typographic attack" of Goh et al., 2021), and boxes and arrows carry
little else it was trained on.

The first version of this experiment reported 47%, from thumbnails made
with macOS's Quick Look. Those thumbnails turned out to be crops: the
top-left corner of each diagram at full size, its labels large and
legible, the rest cut off. The model was reading enlarged text, which
also explains why the score fell with faithful renders. Looking at the
inputs a model actually receives is part of evaluating it. A vision-language
model that reads text in images properly should do much better on
documents like these than one CLIP vector, though that wasn't measured
here.

## Vision-language models

A **vision-language model** (VLM) lets a language model read images
alongside text. The common recipe, popularized by **LLaVA** (Liu et al.,
2023), has three parts:
1. a pretrained **image encoder**, usually a CLIP or SigLIP ViT, which
   turns the image into a grid of patch vectors (keeping all of them, not
   just one pooled vector);
2. a small **projector**, a linear layer or two-layer MLP, that maps each
   patch vector into the language model's embedding space;
3. a pretrained **language model**, which receives the projected patches
   as if they were tokens, placed in the prompt where the image goes.

Training is staged: first only the projector, on image–caption pairs,
with the language model frozen, so the projector learns to map image
features into the language model's embedding space; then the projector
and the language model together on instruction data (questions and
answers about images). The image encoder stays frozen in both. Larger
systems train end to end, handle high resolutions by tiling an image into
crops or by giving the encoder native-resolution input with 2-D position
encodings, and sometimes skip a separate encoder altogether. A different
family (Flamingo, Llama 3.2 Vision) doesn't put image tokens in the
context at all: the language model attends to image features through
added cross-attention layers, which changes the cost picture below.

## What image tokens cost

Those tokens cost what text tokens cost. In the output above, LLaVA-1.5's
CLIP ViT-L/14 at 336×336 produces 576 image tokens, and its 7B language
model stores 512 KiB of KV cache per token ([post
20](/posts/kv-cache-explained/)): 288 MiB for one image, about what 430
words of text would take, and 5.6 GiB for a conversation with twenty
images. Higher resolution multiplies it: 1,024 tokens at 448×448, 4,096 at
1024×1024 with 16-pixel patches. This is why VLMs compress image tokens
(pooling neighboring patches, or learned resamplers that turn hundreds of
patches into a few dozen query tokens), why APIs cap image resolution,
and why a computer-use agent's screenshots dominate its context ([post
66](/posts/computer-use-agents/)).

## Takeaways

- ViT turns an image into a sequence: 16×16 patches of a 224×224 image are
  196 tokens, each a linear projection of 768 pixel values, plus a [CLS]
  token or mean pooling for the whole image.
- ViT gives up a CNN's locality and translation priors and wins them back
  with data, the same trade Transformers made in text.
- CLIP trains an image and a text encoder with a symmetric contrastive
  loss over the batch; SigLIP scores every pair independently with a
  sigmoid, removing the batch-wide softmax.
- On this blog's diagrams, CLIP matched alt texts to the right diagram 5
  times in 19 and fell to chance with the labels hidden: it reads their
  text. A cropped rendering had first made it look nearly twice as good.
- A vision-language model is an image encoder, a projector and a language
  model; its image tokens cost KV cache like text, 288 MiB per image for
  LLaVA-1.5.

contiguous reservation per sequence. That's the memory layer. This post is
about the rest of the machine built on top of it — the scheduler that decides
which requests run *this step*, the batching scheme that keeps the GPU busy
between them, and the distributed-serving layer that spreads a model across
GPUs. Together they're what turns "we don't waste memory" into "we serve
thousands of requests per second."

This is also the first post in a short series comparing how the major
inference engines are put together. The next two look at
[SGLang](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/) and

[final post](/posts/vllm-vs-sglang-vs-tensorrt-llm/) lines all three up
side by side.

## Table of contents

## The problem: static batching leaves the GPU idle

Batching multiple requests together is what makes GPU inference efficient —
one big matrix multiply is far cheaper per token than N small ones. The naive
way to batch is **static batching**: group $N$ requests, run decode steps
together, and don't touch the batch again until every one of them is done.

The problem is that requests don't finish at the same time. Some prompts want
a two-token answer, others want six hundred. Under static batching, a request
that finishes early doesn't free its slot — the batch is fixed until the
*longest* sequence in it finishes, so that slot just sits there, computed on
every step, contributing nothing.

Here's a toy batch of 4 slots with sequences of length 3, 9, 2, and 6 tokens.
The batch can't advance to a new set of requests until the 9-token sequence
finishes, so the shorter ones sit idle (colored 0) for most of the run:

In this toy example, 16 of the 36 slot-steps (44%) are wasted — and none of
that waste shows up until you look at individual sequences, because the batch
as a whole is still "running." Worse, any new request that arrived at step 1
has to wait in a queue until step 9, even though three-quarters of the batch's
slots were free from step 3 onward.

## Continuous batching: one iteration at a time

**Continuous batching** (also called iteration-level scheduling) fixes this by
making the unit of scheduling one forward pass, not one whole batch lifetime.
After *every* step, the scheduler checks which sequences just finished, frees
their slots, and immediately admits new requests from the waiting queue to
fill them — mid-batch, without waiting for anyone else to finish.

Same toy scenario, but now the queue has requests E, F, G, and H ready to go.
The moment slot 1's request A finishes at step 3, request E takes over the
slot for the rest of the run; slot 3 cycles through C, then F, then G:

No idle cells — every slot is generating *some* request's tokens at every
step. (This assumes a steady queue of waiting work, which is the normal case
under real load; if the queue runs dry, slots do sit empty, but that's a
demand problem, not a scheduling one.)

This idea predates vLLM: it was introduced by
[Orca](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu) (Yu et al.,
OSDI 2022) under the name "iteration-level scheduling," paired with
"selective batching" (batching only the operations that tolerate different
sequence lengths in a step, running attention per-sequence). Orca measured a
**36.9× throughput improvement** over NVIDIA FasterTransformer at matched
190ms latency on a GPT-3 175B model:

vLLM adopted iteration-level scheduling and combined it with PagedAttention:
continuous batching decides *which* sequences run this step, PagedAttention
means admitting a new sequence mid-batch never requires a big contiguous
reservation — it just needs one free block.

## The engine loop: scheduler, block manager, workers

Concretely, vLLM's engine is built from a few pieces that repeat this cycle
every step:

- **Scheduler** — owns three queues (waiting, running, swapped) and decides,
  each step, which sequences from `running` continue, which from `waiting`
  get admitted, and whether anything needs to be preempted.
- **Block manager** — the PagedAttention bookkeeping from the previous post:
  tracks free physical blocks and each sequence's block table.
- **Worker(s)** — run the actual forward pass (one iteration of prefill or
  decode) on the GPU(s), using the block tables to gather the right KV blocks.
- **Cache engine** — moves KV blocks between GPU and CPU memory when the
  scheduler needs to swap a sequence out.

An `AsyncLLMEngine` wraps this loop for online serving, and an
OpenAI-compatible API server sits in front of that, handling HTTP requests,
tokenizing prompts, and streaming detokenized output tokens back over
server-sent events as they're generated:

Every arrow back into the waiting queue is what makes this "continuous" —
there's no separate "start a new batch" event; admission happens every step.
Stripped down to just the control flow the diagram shows, one step looks
like this — not vLLM's actual source (the real scheduler also tracks swap
queues and chunked-prefill budgets), but the shape of the decision it makes
every iteration:

```python
def scheduler_step(running, waiting, block_manager):
    for seq in list(running):
        if not block_manager.has_free_block():
            victim = pick_preemption_victim(running)  # default: most recently added
            block_manager.free(victim)
            running.remove(victim)
            waiting.insert(0, victim)                 # re-enters admission like any new request

    while waiting and block_manager.has_free_block():
        seq = waiting.pop(0)
        block_manager.allocate(seq, blocks=1)          # only needs ONE free block to start
        running.append(seq)

    return worker.forward_pass(running)                # one prefill/decode step over `running`
```

Two things worth noticing here that the rest of this post is really about:
admitting a new sequence only ever needs `block_manager` to find **one**
free block, not a reservation — that's PagedAttention paying off inside the
scheduler — and a preempted sequence re-enters `waiting` through the exact
same code path as a brand-new request, which is why the "Scheduling policy
and preemption" section below doesn't need a separate mechanism for it.

## Prefill vs. decode, and why mixing them is tricky

Two very different kinds of work flow through that same loop. **Prefill**
processes an entire prompt in one shot to build its initial KV cache — it's
compute-bound, since it's one big matmul over hundreds or thousands of
tokens. **Decode** generates one token per sequence per step — it's
memory-bound, since attention has to re-read the whole cached history for
comparatively little new compute.

Naively mixing them causes a real problem: if the scheduler admits a new
request with a 4,000-token prompt in the middle of a running batch, that
single prefill can dominate the step, stalling token generation for every
other sequence that was mid-decode. Every request in the batch feels a latency
spike, not just the new one.

vLLM's fix is **chunked prefill**: split a long prompt into fixed-size chunks
and interleave them with other sequences' decode steps, instead of running the
whole prompt at once. Each step has a token budget $B$ (vLLM's
`max_num_batched_tokens`, 512 by default); decode tokens — one per running
sequence — are scheduled first, and whatever budget is left over goes to the
next chunk of a pending prompt:

$$
\text{prefill chunk size} = \min(\text{remaining prompt tokens},\ B - \text{decode tokens this step})
$$

For a 2,000-token prompt arriving alongside 8 already-running sequences with
$B = 512$:

| Iteration | Decode tokens (8 running seqs) | Prefill chunk (new request) | Total |
| --------- | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------- | ----- |
| 1 | 8 | 504 (chunk 1 of 4) | 512 |
| 2 | 8 | 504 (chunk 2 of 4) | 512 |
| 3 | 8 | 504 (chunk 3 of 4) | 512 |
| 4 | 8 | 488 (chunk 4, remainder) | 496 |
| 5 | 9 (new request now decoding too) | – | 9 |

Decode never waits behind the full prompt — it's prioritized every step, and
the big prefill is smeared across four iterations instead of stalling
everyone for one giant one. In vLLM's V1 engine, chunked prefill is on by
default whenever possible, precisely because mixed batches (some sequences
decoding, one or two prefilling) are the normal case under load, not an edge
case to special-case around.

## Scheduling policy and preemption under memory pressure

Sometimes there just isn't a free block for a running sequence's next token —
every physical block is already owned by some sequence. When that happens,
the scheduler **preempts** one of the running sequences (by default, the most
recently added, to protect requests that have been running the longest) and
moves it out of the `running` queue. vLLM supports two ways to do this:

- **Recompute** — drop the sequence's KV blocks entirely. When it's
  re-admitted later, it just reruns prefill on the tokens it already
  generated. Zero memory-transfer cost, but it burns the compute again.
- **Swap** — copy the sequence's physical blocks out to CPU memory instead of
  discarding them, and copy them back over PCIe when it's re-admitted. Saves
  the recompute, costs host-device bandwidth.

vLLM's V1 engine defaults to recompute, since for typical sequence lengths
re-running prefill is cheap relative to a round-trip over PCIe. Either way,
a preempted sequence goes back into the waiting queue and re-enters the same
admission process as a brand-new request — preemption and normal scheduling
share the same machinery.

## Distributed serving: tensor and pipeline parallelism

Once a model doesn't fit on one GPU, vLLM has to split it across several.
**Tensor parallelism** shards each layer's weight matrices (the attention
projections, the MLP) column- or row-wise across $N$ GPUs; every GPU computes
its shard of a layer's math on the same input, and an NCCL all-reduce
combines the partial results before the next layer:

That all-reduce happens *every layer*, so tensor parallelism wants GPUs
connected by something fast (NVLink within a node) — it doesn't scale well
across nodes on ordinary networking. For multi-node serving, vLLM also
supports **pipeline parallelism**: instead of splitting each layer, whole
groups of layers are assigned to different GPU stages, and micro-batches flow
through the pipeline so no stage sits idle waiting on the next. The two
compose — tensor-parallel within a node, pipeline-parallel across nodes — and
vLLM also supports expert parallelism specifically for mixture-of-experts
models, routing each token to whichever GPU holds the expert it was routed to.

## Serving many fine-tunes: multi-LoRA

A LoRA fine-tune (post 26) changes a model by adding small low-rank
matrices beside its weights, a few megabytes against the model's
gigabytes. That makes a cheap kind of multi-tenancy possible: vLLM can
serve one copy of the base model with many adapters loaded, and each
request names the adapter it wants. In one continuous batch, requests for
different adapters share every pass over the base weights, and only the
small adapter products differ per request, computed by kernels that
gather each request's adapter (the approach of Punica and S-LoRA).
Adapters are loaded into GPU memory on demand and evicted like any other
cache. The cost is a modest slowdown per step, against running a separate
copy of the model for every fine-tune.

## The V1 rewrite: pulling the scheduler out of the hot path

Everything above describes the logical architecture, but where each piece
*runs as a process* has changed. In vLLM's original engine, the API server,
scheduler, and detokenizer all lived in one Python process alongside the
model workers — at high request rates, ordinary Python/CPU overhead
(tokenizing, scheduling, streaming responses) started to compete with the
GIL for time the model loop needed.

[vLLM V1](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-27-v1-alpha-release) (announced
January 2025) splits this into a separate `EngineCore` process, running just
the scheduler and model executor, talking to the API/frontend process over a
ZeroMQ socket instead of sharing a thread with it. The practical effect is
that CPU-side request handling can no longer stall the GPU loop, and the
scheduler treats prefill and decode uniformly under one token-budget policy —
which is exactly what makes chunked prefill vLLM's default behavior rather
than a special mode you opt into.

## Advantages and disadvantages

**Advantages:**

- Fully open-source and Python-native — easy to read, extend, and debug, and
  it tracks new Hugging Face model architectures quickly.
- Broad hardware support beyond NVIDIA: AMD ROCm, Google TPU, and Intel Gaudi
  backends exist alongside CUDA.
- PagedAttention plus prefix caching give it some of the best memory
  efficiency of any serving engine, which is what continuous batching needs
  to actually pack GPUs full.
- Chunked prefill and preemption are handled by the scheduler itself, so
  latency-sensitive and throughput-sensitive workloads share one engine
  without hand-tuned request routing.
- A large, active OSS ecosystem: quantization formats (AWQ, GPTQ, FP8), LoRA
  multi-adapter serving, and structured-output integrations all land in vLLM
  quickly.

**Disadvantages:**

- It's still a Python/PyTorch runtime under the hood. CUDA graphs and
  `torch.compile` claw back a lot of the interpreter overhead, but a
  dynamically-scheduled Python engine has a higher CPU-side floor than a
  compiled, static-graph runtime.
- More moving parts to reason about: scheduler, block manager, cache engine,
  and workers all interact, and tuning `max_num_batched_tokens`, preemption
  mode, and parallelism together is genuinely nontrivial.
- Being general-purpose across models and hardware means it's not as tightly
  co-optimized to one vendor's kernels as a compiled, hardware-specific
  engine — see the TensorRT-LLM post below.
- Its prefix reuse is block-level (paged blocks matching a hash of their
  content), not the radix-tree structure SGLang builds its whole scheduler
  around — see the next post.

## Where this leads

vLLM's story is: memory efficiency (PagedAttention) plus iteration-level
scheduling (continuous batching, chunked prefill) equals a Python-native
engine that keeps the GPU full without giving up flexibility. The next post
looks at [SGLang](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/), which pushes
prefix reuse further with a radix tree instead of independent per-sequence
block tables, then [TensorRT-LLM](/posts/tensorrt-llm-explained/), which
spent its first two years taking the opposite approach entirely — compiling
a fixed, optimized engine ahead of time instead of scheduling dynamically in
Python — before converging on a PyTorch-native runtime of its own. The
[comparison post](/posts/vllm-vs-sglang-vs-tensorrt-llm/) puts all three
side by side.

## References

- Kwon et al., [_Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention_](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180) (SOSP 2023) — PagedAttention and vLLM's original architecture.
- Yu et al., [_Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models_](https://www.usenix.org/conference/osdi22/presentation/yu) (OSDI 2022) — iteration-level scheduling and selective batching, the origin of continuous batching, with the 36.9× throughput figure.
- [vLLM Architecture Overview](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/arch_overview/) — the LLMEngine/scheduler/worker breakdown and the V1 multi-process design.
- [_vLLM V1: A Major Upgrade to vLLM's Core Architecture_](https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-01-27-v1-alpha-release) (vLLM Blog, Jan 2025) — the EngineCore/ZeroMQ rewrite and default chunked-prefill scheduling.
- [vLLM Optimization and Tuning](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/configuration/optimization/) — `max_num_batched_tokens`, chunked prefill, and preemption-mode configuration.
Three posts, three engines: [vLLM](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/)'s
scheduler and continuous batching,
[SGLang](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/)'s shared radix tree, and
[TensorRT-LLM](/posts/tensorrt-llm-explained/)'s arc from ahead-of-time
compilation to a PyTorch-native runtime of its own. That last post ended by
pointing out something that changes how this comparison has to be written:
as of today, all three are dynamically-scheduled PyTorch-native runtimes.
The clean "compiled vs. dynamic" split this series could have leaned on a
year ago no longer separates any of them. So this post doesn't crown a
throughput winner — cross-vendor benchmark numbers were never apples-to-apples
to begin with, and now the architectures aren't even different enough to
make that comparison meaningful. Instead, it lines the three up on what
actually still differs, and ends with a decision framework.

## Table of contents

## What's no longer a differentiator

All three engines now reach for the same lightweight JIT toolkit instead of
a separate ahead-of-time build step: `torch.compile`-based kernel fusion,
plus CUDA graph capture for common execution shapes. vLLM lists
"`torch.compile` optimizations" and "CUDA graph acceleration" as core
features. SGLang has both automatic CUDA graph capture and its own
`torch.compile` integration — plus a feature it calls **Piecewise CUDA
Graph**, the same name TensorRT-LLM uses for the equivalent optimization it
adopted once it moved off compiled `.engine` files. Two of the three engines
in this comparison independently converged on the same name for the same
idea. None of the three has a separate, portable, ahead-of-time build
artifact anymore — the "compile once, deploy anywhere" bet TensorRT-LLM
originally made didn't survive contact with how fast the other two could
iterate without it.

## Batching strategy

All three admit and evict sequences mid-batch every step rather than
waiting for a static batch to finish — the iteration-level idea from Orca
that the [vLLM post](/posts/vllm-architecture-explained/) covered in depth.
What differs is what else shapes the scheduling decision:

| Engine | Term | Distinguishing detail |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vLLM | Continuous batching + chunked prefill | Preemption (recompute or swap) when memory runs out |
| SGLang | Continuous batching + cache-aware scheduling | Queue ordered by longest-matched-prefix-first, not just arrival order |
| TensorRT-LLM | In-flight batching + Chunked Context | Chunk size must be a multiple of the KV-cache block size |

SGLang is the one that changes the scheduling policy itself around its
cache, rather than treating scheduling and caching as separate concerns.

## KV-cache and prefix reuse

This is where the three genuinely diverge, and it's the closest thing this
series has to a real architectural fork line:

| Engine | Structure | Reuse granularity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vLLM | Per-sequence block tables (PagedAttention) | Block-level, matched by content hash |
| SGLang | One shared radix tree, engine-wide | Automatic, cross-request, reference-counted eviction |
| TensorRT-LLM | Per-sequence paged KV cache | Block-level, no cross-request tree structure |

vLLM and TensorRT-LLM both reuse cache at block granularity, matched
per-sequence. SGLang is the outlier: RadixAttention makes reuse a property
of one shared structure the whole engine sees, not something each sequence
negotiates independently — the payoff being automatic reuse across
requests that share a prefix, with no application-level cache-key
management, at the cost of only recognizing exact prefix matches (see the
[SGLang post](/posts/sglang-radixattention-explained/) for the reference
counting and eviction mechanics).

## Quantization

All three support the major formats — FP8, INT8, and 4-bit weight-only
formats (AWQ/GPTQ) — and the tooling has converged as much as the
architectures have: NVIDIA's
[TensorRT Model Optimizer](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-Model-Optimizer),
originally TensorRT-LLM's own calibration tool, is now framework-agnostic
and also quantizes models for vLLM and SGLang deployments. The practical
difference by this point is less "which formats" and more which hardware
generation each format targets — FP8 on Hopper/Blackwell, INT4 for
memory-constrained deployments, NVFP4 on the newest Blackwell hardware —
which is really the hardware-portability question below wearing a
quantization hat.

## Structured-output support

Constrained decoding shows the same tooling-consolidation pattern as
quantization: a wave of engine-specific implementations converging onto
shared grammar engines.

| Engine | Backend(s) | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vLLM | `auto` — tries XGrammar first, falls back to Outlines | `lm-format-enforcer` also exists; the vLLM team found it unreliable on long-context cases and deprioritized it |
| SGLang | xgrammar (default since v0.4, Dec 2024) | Originally its own compressed FSM (see the SGLang post), since generalized into xgrammar |
| TensorRT-LLM | XGrammar or LLGuidance | No stated default — must be explicitly enabled via a `guided_decoding_backend` config |

vLLM's own numbers for the XGrammar integration: "up to 5× improvement in
TPOT under load" (vLLM Blog, Jan 2025) — another vendor-reported, dated
figure, not a cross-engine claim.

## Hardware and portability

This is the one dimension that hasn't blurred at all:

SGLang documents the broadest hardware support of the three. vLLM covers
the same set minus Huawei Ascend. TensorRT-LLM is NVIDIA-only — the direct
consequence of being NVIDIA's own project, and the clearest, least
contestable differentiator in this whole comparison.

## Deployment complexity

| Engine | Standard path | Multi-replica story |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vLLM | `AsyncLLMEngine` + OpenAI-compatible API server | Official **vLLM Production Stack** — Kubernetes-native, Helm-deployable, with prefix-aware routing across replicas |
| SGLang | Similar single-server story | Its own **cache-aware load balancer** (v0.4, Dec 2024), routing requests to whichever replica already has the matching prefix cached |
| TensorRT-LLM | `trtllm-serve` (standalone, supports disaggregated prefill/decode), or Triton + `tensorrtllm_backend` | **NVIDIA NIM** — prebuilt containers that can themselves select TensorRT-LLM, vLLM, *or* SGLang as the backend per target GPU/model |

vLLM's Production Stack router and SGLang's cache-aware load balancer solve
the identical problem the identical way: route each request to the
replica most likely to already hold its prefix cached. TensorRT-LLM's NIM
packaging solves a different problem — picking a backend at all, from a
menu that now includes its two competitors in this series.

All three converge on the same client-facing surface, too. Point the same
`openai` client at three different ports and the application code doesn't
change at all — everything this post has covered so far is what's running
behind that URL, not what the caller has to know about it:

```python
from openai import OpenAI

engines = {
    "vLLM": OpenAI(base_url="http://vllm-host:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY"),
    "SGLang": OpenAI(base_url="http://sglang-host:30000/v1", api_key="EMPTY"),
    "TensorRT-LLM": OpenAI(base_url="http://trtllm-host:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY"),
}

for name, client in engines.items():
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="my-model",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi in five words."}],
    )
    print(name, "->", resp.choices[0].message.content)
```

Nothing above names a scheduler, a cache structure, or a backend — the
`base_url` is the only line that differs. Everything this comparison has
covered lives entirely on the other side of that URL.

## Ecosystem and governance

Worth being precise here, since these terms get used loosely:

| Engine | Relationship to PyTorch | Named production users (self-reported) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| vLLM | **PyTorch Foundation-hosted project** (announced May 2025) — actual governance, not a listing | Amazon (Rufus), LinkedIn |
| SGLang | Joined the **PyTorch ecosystem** (Mar 2025) — an ecosystem listing, not a governance transfer | xAI (Grok 3), Microsoft Azure (DeepSeek R1 on AMD MI300X) |
| TensorRT-LLM | NVIDIA's own project, Apache 2.0, no foundation affiliation | Validated via NVIDIA's own MLPerf submissions rather than named third-party deployments |

vLLM's relationship to the PyTorch Foundation is categorically stronger
than SGLang's — "officially governed and administered under the PyTorch
Foundation's neutral and transparent governance model," per the
Foundation's own announcement, versus SGLang's ecosystem-directory listing.
By the same May 2025 announcement, vLLM had 46,500+ GitHub stars and 1,000+
contributors; its own year-in-review post put 2024 growth at 14k→32.6k
stars, 190→740 contributors, and 6k→27k monthly downloads.

## Decision framework

- **Choose vLLM** if you want the broadest hardware portability, the
  largest and most formally governed OSS ecosystem (PyTorch
  Foundation), and your workload doesn't have the kind of heavy
  cross-request prefix overlap that would specifically reward SGLang's
  radix tree.
- **Choose SGLang** if your workload has real prefix-sharing structure —
  shared system prompts and few-shot batches, multi-turn chat, or
  tree-of-thought/self-consistency agent programs built on `fork`/`join` —
  where RadixAttention's automatic cross-request cache reuse pays off, or
  if you need hardware support broader than NVIDIA and AMD.
- **Choose TensorRT-LLM** if you're already committed to NVIDIA hardware
  and want the deepest speculative-decoding support of the three (Medusa,
  EAGLE-1/2/3, lookahead decoding) or NVIDIA's own MLPerf-tuned performance
  work, and NVIDIA-only lock-in is an acceptable trade.

## Where this leaves the series

vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM started from three different bets: memory
efficiency plus iteration-level scheduling; one shared cache structure the
scheduler is built around; and compiling a fixed engine ahead of time. Only
the middle one still looks like its original bet today — the first
converged toward it from a simpler starting point, and the third abandoned
its founding architecture entirely to land in the same place. What's left
that actually distinguishes them isn't "how they schedule" anymore; it's
what they optimize the shared architecture *for* — SGLang for automatic
prefix reuse, TensorRT-LLM for NVIDIA-specific depth (quantization,
speculative decoding), and vLLM for being the broadly-portable,
formally-governed default. Pick the one whose bet matches your workload.

The earlier posts in this part looked at single components: how a GPU
serves a model ([post 51](/posts/serving-metrics-and-disaggregation/)),
how tokens reach a browser ([post 16](/posts/streaming-tokens-sse-websockets/)),
which chip to use ([post 69](/posts/beyond-the-gpu-tpus-and-lpus/)). This
one designs a whole system, the way a system-design interview or a real
project would: requirements first, then estimates, then components, each
chosen to fit the numbers. The system is a **real-time voice agent**: a
caller speaks, the agent answers out loud, and the conversation should
feel like talking to a person.

## Table of contents

## Requirements

Functional: hold a spoken conversation; understand the caller; answer from
a language model that can call tools (look up an order, book a slot); let
the caller interrupt.

Non-functional, and these drive the design:
- **Latency.** In conversation between people, the gap between one person
  stopping and the other starting is typically around 200 ms (Stivers et
  al., 2009, across ten languages). Machines don't have to match that, but
  past about a second the pause feels like the line dropped. The target
  here: the agent's first audio within about **1 s** of the caller
  stopping, at the median, and not much more at the tail.
- **Scale.** 1,000 simultaneous calls at peak.
- **Robustness.** Mobile networks with jitter and loss; background noise;
  callers who pause mid-sentence.
- **Observability and cost**: every stage's latency per turn, and a cost
  per call-minute.

## The latency budget

A **cascaded** voice agent chains three models: speech-to-text (STT), a
language model, and text-to-speech (TTS). Every stage between the caller's
last word and the agent's first sound spends part of the second. Here are
the stages with figures for a well-built system calling a hosted LLM over
the network. They are assumptions, stated so they can be argued with, not
measurements; small items (the VAD's own 30 ms analysis windows, audio
resampling, packetizing TTS output) are left out:

```python
# A cascaded voice agent's response time, stage by stage: from the moment
# the user stops speaking to the moment they hear the first syllable of the
# reply. Every figure is an assumption for a well-built system, stated so it
# can be changed, not a measurement.
stages = [  # (stage, milliseconds, why)
    ("audio frame + jitter buffer", 40, "20 ms Opus frames; a jitter buffer of about one frame"),
    ("network, user -> server",     30, "one way, same region, WebRTC over UDP"),
    ("end-of-turn detection",      400, "VAD waits for this much silence before deciding the user is done"),
    ("speech-to-text, final",      100, "a streaming recognizer has the words already; it finalizes"),
    ("LLM time to first token",    250, "prefill of a cached 2,000-token prompt plus queueing"),
    ("LLM, first clause",          150, "TTS needs a few words to start: ~8 tokens at ~19 ms each"),
    ("text-to-speech, first audio", 120, "streaming TTS, time to its first audio chunk"),
    ("network, server -> user",     30, "one way"),
    ("playback buffer",             40, "the client's own jitter buffer before audio plays"),
]
total = sum(ms for _, ms, _ in stages)
print(f"{'stage':30s} {'ms':>5s} {'cumulative':>11s}")
run = 0
for name, ms, _ in stages:
    run += ms
    print(f"{name:30s} {ms:5d} {run:11d}")
print(f"\ntotal {total} ms; end-of-turn detection alone is {400 / total:.0%} of it")

# Two levers, applied to the same budget.
for name, change in (("semantic turn detection (400 -> 150 ms of silence)", {"end-of-turn detection": 150}),
                     ("speech-to-speech model (STT + LLM + TTS -> 350 ms)", None)):
    if change:
        t = sum(change.get(n, ms) for n, ms, _ in stages)
    else:
        t = sum(ms for n, ms, _ in stages if not n.startswith(("speech-to-text", "LLM", "text-to-speech"))) + 350
    print(f"  with {name}: {t} ms")
```

```text
stage                             ms  cumulative
audio frame + jitter buffer       40          40
network, user -> server           30          70
end-of-turn detection            400         470
speech-to-text, final            100         570
LLM time to first token          250         820
LLM, first clause                150         970
text-to-speech, first audio      120        1090
network, server -> user           30        1120
playback buffer                   40        1160

total 1160 ms; end-of-turn detection alone is 34% of it
  with semantic turn detection (400 -> 150 ms of silence): 910 ms
  with speech-to-speech model (STT + LLM + TTS -> 350 ms): 890 ms
```

The total is over budget, and the largest single item isn't a model at
all. It's **end-of-turn detection**: deciding that the caller has finished.
A voice activity detector (VAD) knows when there is speech, but people
pause mid-sentence, so the system has to wait for some silence before
treating a pause as the end of a turn. Too short a wait and the agent
interrupts people who were thinking; too long and every reply starts late.
400 ms of silence is a third of the budget.

That makes it the first lever. **Semantic turn detection** uses a small
model that reads the transcript so far and judges whether the sentence is
complete ("I'd like to book a table for" is not; "That's all, thanks" is),
so the silence threshold can be short when the words say the turn is over
and long when they don't. Cutting the average wait to 150 ms brings the
budget to 910 ms.

A second lever overlaps stages instead of shrinking them. During the
silence wait, the system can already finalize the transcript and start
the LLM's prefill on it, **speculatively**, and throw the work away if the
caller keeps talking. Many streaming recognizers also do their own
endpointing, so "wait for silence" and "finalize the transcript" are
partly the same 400 ms rather than two items in series. Done well,
much of the STT and TTFT rows disappear behind the turn detection.

The LLM rows also depend on where the model runs. 250 ms is a typical time
to first token for a hosted API reached over the network; a self-hosted
model with the conversation cached, as in the capacity section below, can
start in tens of milliseconds, which takes another 200 ms off.

The rest of the budget follows from one design rule: **every stage
streams**. STT transcribes while the caller is still speaking, so when the
turn ends it only finalizes. The LLM's first tokens go to TTS as soon as
they form a clause, not when the reply is complete. TTS sends its first
audio chunk while it's still synthesizing the rest. A system that waited
for each stage to finish would spend several seconds.

## Transport: WebRTC

Phone-quality conversation needs audio delivered in tens of milliseconds,
and it tolerates a lost packet far better than a late one. That makes
TCP a poor fit for the audio's last mile, the caller's own network: TCP
retransmits a lost packet and holds back everything behind it, which is
right for a web page and wrong for a voice. (Between data centers, where
loss is rare, audio is often carried over WebSockets on TCP without
trouble.) **WebRTC** (RFC 8825) carries audio over UDP in encrypted
real-time transport packets (SRTP), compressed with the **Opus** codec in
20 ms frames, and the receiver keeps a **jitter buffer** to smooth out
uneven arrival: about one frame on a good connection, 60–150 ms on a
congested mobile one, which comes straight out of the budget. Getting a
UDP connection through home routers and corporate firewalls is its own
problem. **ICE** (interactive connectivity establishment, RFC 8445) tries
candidate paths in turn: direct, then via the public address a client
appears from, discovered with **STUN** (RFC 8489), and finally through a
**TURN** relay server (RFC 8656) when no direct path works. For phone
calls, a telephony provider bridges the phone network (over SIP, with the
narrowband G.711 codec on the phone side) to the same audio stream, and
that bridge adds 100–200 ms the budget above doesn't include. Servers in
several regions, close to the callers, keep the network legs at the 30 ms
the budget assumes.

The text side (transcripts, tool events, the agent's state) can travel on
a WebRTC data channel or a WebSocket ([post
16](/posts/streaming-tokens-sse-websockets/)); it's small and latency
tolerant by comparison.

## The three models

**Speech-to-text.** A streaming recognizer emits partial transcripts every
few hundred milliseconds and revises them as more audio arrives. Whisper
(Radford et al., 2022) set the accuracy bar for open models but processes
30-second windows, so real-time systems either use streaming-native
recognizers or run Whisper-style models on short overlapping chunks. What
matters for the budget is the time from the end of speech to a final
transcript, which a streaming recognizer keeps around 100 ms.

**The language model.** Two numbers from [post
51](/posts/serving-metrics-and-disaggregation/) matter: **time to first
token** (TTFT), which sits directly on the critical path, and the time per
output token, which matters only until the first clause is ready for TTS.
After that, the agent is limited by how fast it can *speak*: about 150
words a minute, roughly three or four tokens a second. A model that
generates 50 tokens a second is already twelve times faster than it needs
to be. Keeping TTFT low means a short uncached part of the prompt: the
system prompt, tools and conversation so far are reused from the prefix
cache, and only the newest turn is prefilled.

**Text-to-speech.** Streaming TTS starts producing audio from the first
few words. Its time to first audio, around 100–150 ms for a good streaming
system, is the last model cost on the path.

## Cascaded or speech-to-speech

The alternative is one model that takes audio in and produces audio out,
with no text in between. Moshi (Défossez et al., 2024) models the user's
and its own audio streams together and reported about 200 ms of latency in
practice; OpenAI reported that GPT-4o could answer audio in as little as
232 ms, 320 ms on average. Removing the STT and TTS hand-offs saves their
latency, and the model hears tone and emphasis that a transcript loses.
Swapping the three stages for one 350 ms stage brings the same budget to
890 ms, if the system still waits 400 ms for silence, as API-style
speech-to-speech services with server-side turn detection do by default.
Vendor figures like GPT-4o's don't include that wait, so they aren't
comparable to the budget's total. Moshi goes further: it is full-duplex,
listening and speaking at the same time with no separate turn detection,
much as people do.

The cascade keeps advantages that matter in production: each component
can be chosen, measured and replaced separately; the transcript is there
for logging, tools, guardrails and compliance; and the language model can
be any model, including one much stronger than the available
speech-to-speech models. Many production systems are still cascades, with
speech-to-speech used where latency and naturalness matter most.

## Barge-in and tool calls

**Barge-in** is the caller interrupting the agent. The VAD keeps listening
while the agent speaks; when the caller starts talking, the system stops
TTS playback immediately, cancels whatever the LLM and TTS were still
producing, and records how much of the reply the caller actually heard,
so the conversation history doesn't claim the agent said things that were
cut off. Not every sound is an interruption: "uh-huh", a cough or a
door shouldn't stop the agent, so systems require a minimum stretch of
speech, or actual words from STT, before cancelling. And echo cancellation
has to stop the agent's own voice, played through the caller's speaker,
from triggering the VAD; it runs on the caller's side (the browser's
built-in canceller, or the phone network's), because the server can't
easily separate the two voices once they're mixed.

**Tool calls mid-turn** (post 40)
add their own latency to the critical path. A lookup that takes 800 ms
breaks the budget on its own. The usual answers: start speaking a filler
clause the LLM produces before the tool call ("Let me check that for
you"), run slow tools in parallel with that speech, and prefer tools that
answer in tens of milliseconds for anything conversational. And plan for
the slow case: a timeout on every tool and on the LLM itself, with a
fallback (a smaller, faster model, or a scripted "I'm still looking")
when it fires, because silence on a call reads as failure.

## Capacity: 1,000 calls

How many GPUs does the LLM stage need, if the model is served in-house?
Two facts shape the answer. A call doesn't use the LLM most of the time:
the caller is speaking, or the agent is speaking a reply already
generated. But each call carries a conversation history, and to start the
next reply in tens of milliseconds, its keys and values (the **prefix
cache**, post 34) must be kept somewhere between
turns, or recomputed. A simulation of continuous batching, one iteration
at a time, with each call pinned to one GPU so its cache is where its
requests go. The model, an 8B model on H100s, and every assumption are in
the code:

```python

# How many GPUs does the LLM stage of 1,000 simultaneous voice calls need?
# An idealized simulation of continuous batching (post 51), one iteration
# at a time, for an 8B model in BF16 on H100s (80 GB).
#   Calls: each sends the LLM a request every ~20 s on average (the caller
#   talks for a few seconds; the agent speaks its ~45-word answer for ~17 s);
#   arrivals are random (Poisson), 50 per second in all.
#   A request: a 2,000-token conversation so far plus 150 new tokens, and
#   60 output tokens. Each call is pinned to one GPU, so its cache is there.
#   An iteration decodes one token for every active request and prefills the
#   requests admitted this iteration. Its time is the larger of reading the
#   weights and every KV cache it touches at 3.35 TB/s, and the arithmetic at
#   40% of 989 TFLOPS.
# Where the 2,000 tokens of each call's history live between turns decides
# everything (2,000 tokens x 128 KiB = 262 MB per call, 262 GB for 1,000):
#   "HBM"     : kept in GPU memory, so only the 150 new tokens are prefilled,
#               but every call's cache must fit beside the weights;
#   "re-prefill": nothing kept, all 2,150 tokens prefilled every turn;
#   "CPU"     : kept in host memory and copied back over PCIe (~25 GB/s
#               effective) when the call's next request arrives.
N, W, BW, FLOPS, HBM = 8e9, 16e9, 3.35e12, 0.4 * 989e12, 80e9
KV, CONTEXT, NEW, OUT, MAX_BATCH, PCIE = 131072, 2000, 150, 60, 200, 25e9
CALLS, TURN_S = 1000, 20.0

def simulate(gpus, mode, seconds=120, seed=0):
    calls_per_gpu = math.ceil(CALLS / gpus)
    if mode == "HBM" and W + calls_per_gpu * CONTEXT * KV + MAX_BATCH * (NEW + OUT) * KV > 0.9 * HBM:
        return None                                          # the caches don't fit
    prefill = NEW if mode != "re-prefill" else CONTEXT + NEW
    reload = CONTEXT * KV / PCIE if mode == "CPU" else 0.0  # copy the history back before prefill
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    t, arrivals = 0.0, []
    while t < seconds:
        t += rng.exponential(TURN_S / CALLS)
        arrivals.append((t + reload, int(rng.integers(CALLS))))  # (ready time, call)
    arrivals.sort(reverse=True)
    clock, waiting, active = [0.0] * gpus, [[] for _ in range(gpus)], [[] for _ in range(gpus)]
    ttft, itl = [], []
    while arrivals or any(waiting) or any(active):
        g = min(range(gpus), key=lambda i: clock[i])
        now = clock[g]
        while arrivals and arrivals[-1][0] <= now:
            ready, call = arrivals.pop()
            waiting[call % gpus].append(ready - reload)       # sticky: a call always goes to its GPU
        if not waiting[g] and not active[g]:
            nxt = [a for a, c in arrivals if c % gpus == g]
            clock[g] = min(nxt) if nxt else float("inf")
            if all(c == float("inf") for c in clock):
                break
            continue
        admit = waiting[g][: max(0, MAX_BATCH - len(active[g]))]
        waiting[g] = waiting[g][len(admit):]
        reads = W + (len(active[g]) + len(admit)) * CONTEXT * KV        # weights + every cache touched
        dt = max(reads / BW, 2 * N * (len(active[g]) + prefill * len(admit)) / FLOPS)
        clock[g] = now + dt
        if active[g]:
            itl.append(dt)
        active[g] = [r - 1 for r in active[g] if r > 1] + [OUT - 1] * len(admit)
        ttft += [clock[g] - a for a in admit]
    warm = len(ttft) // 10
    return np.array(ttft[warm:]), np.array(itl)

print(f"{CALLS} calls, a request every {TURN_S:.0f} s per call; 2,000 + 150 prompt tokens, {OUT} out")
print(f"{'history kept in':>15s} {'GPUs':>4s} {'TTFT p50':>9s} {'TTFT p99':>9s} {'ITL p50':>8s} {'ITL p99':>8s}")
for mode in ("HBM", "re-prefill", "CPU"):
    for gpus in (1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12):
        r = simulate(gpus, mode)
        if r is None:
            print(f"{mode:>15s} {gpus:4d}   {1000 // gpus + 1} calls' caches don't fit in 80 GB")
            continue
        ttft, itl = r
        if np.median(ttft) > 10:
            print(f"{mode:>15s} {gpus:4d}   overloaded: requests queue without bound")
            continue
        print(f"{mode:>15s} {gpus:4d} {np.median(ttft) * 1e3:6.0f} ms {np.percentile(ttft, 99) * 1e3:6.0f} ms "
              f"{np.median(itl) * 1e3:5.1f} ms {np.percentile(itl, 99) * 1e3:5.1f} ms", flush=True)
```

```text
1000 calls, a request every 20 s per call; 2,000 + 150 prompt tokens, 60 out
history kept in GPUs  TTFT p50  TTFT p99  ITL p50  ITL p99
            HBM    1   1001 calls' caches don't fit in 80 GB
            HBM    2   501 calls' caches don't fit in 80 GB
            HBM    4   251 calls' caches don't fit in 80 GB
            HBM    6      9 ms     16 ms   5.0 ms   6.2 ms
            HBM    8      8 ms     16 ms   4.9 ms   6.2 ms
            HBM   12      8 ms     14 ms   4.9 ms   6.1 ms
     re-prefill    1   overloaded: requests queue without bound
     re-prefill    2   overloaded: requests queue without bound
     re-prefill    4   8715 ms  22437 ms  20.4 ms 2440.8 ms
     re-prefill    6    194 ms   1321 ms   5.3 ms 261.2 ms
     re-prefill    8    106 ms    554 ms   5.0 ms  87.9 ms
     re-prefill   12     90 ms    349 ms   4.9 ms  87.1 ms
            CPU    1     22 ms     41 ms   6.5 ms  13.3 ms
            CPU    2     20 ms     31 ms   5.5 ms   6.8 ms
            CPU    4     19 ms     27 ms   5.1 ms   6.3 ms
            CPU    6     19 ms     27 ms   5.0 ms   6.2 ms
            CPU    8     19 ms     26 ms   4.9 ms   6.2 ms
            CPU   12     18 ms     24 ms   4.9 ms   6.1 ms
```

The compute is the easy part. With the histories offloaded to CPU memory
and copied back over PCIe when a call's turn comes, a single GPU keeps the
time to first token at 22 ms (median) and 41 ms (99th percentile),
including the copy. An iteration takes about 6.5 ms, so at 50 requests a
second, each decoding 60 tokens, only about 20 requests are decoding at
any moment. Speech is slow, so
the GPU spends most of each call serving someone else.

Memory is the hard part. 1,000 histories of 2,000 tokens are 262 GB of KV
cache. Kept in GPU memory, they need 6 GPUs just to fit, whatever the
compute needs. Recomputed every turn, they make each request a 2,150-token
prefill: 8 GPUs and the 99th percentile is still over half a second. Kept
in CPU memory, they cost host RAM and PCIe bandwidth instead (here about
13 GB/s of copies, half of what one GPU's link sustains), which is cheaper
than either. The design question is not "how many GPUs" but "where does
each call's state live between turns", and serving systems now support
exactly this kind of tiered KV storage.

This is a model, and the assumptions matter: an 8B model is small for
reliable multi-step tool use, and a 70B-class model needs about nine times
the compute, more than twice the KV cache per token, and at least two
GPUs per copy; real serving reaches a fraction of the roofline ([post
6](/posts/how-a-gpu-runs-deep-learning/)) assumed here; peak traffic is
burstier than random; and each tool call or turn-detection model adds
requests. A production deployment would multiply the answer for headroom
and failures. The STT and TTS models, which run continuously while anyone
is speaking, need the same sizing, and often more GPUs than the LLM.

Cost per call-minute follows from the GPU count. Six GPUs at an
illustrative \$2.50 an hour each serve 60,000 call-minutes an hour, about
\$0.00025 per call-minute for the LLM. Speech recognition, synthesis and
telephony, priced per minute, usually cost far more than that, which is
one more reason to size them as carefully.

## Observability

Every turn should produce a trace with one span per stage: VAD end of
turn, STT final, LLM time to first token (TTFT), first clause, TTS first
audio, plus the network legs measured from the client. The latency that matters is the
caller's, from their last word to the agent's first sound, at the 50th,
95th and 99th percentiles; any stage's distribution shifting shows up in
it. Barge-in rate (how often callers interrupt) and the share of turns
where the agent cut the caller off are the quality signals that pure
latency misses. Turn detection in particular is a trade-off curve:
replaying recorded calls through the detector at several silence
thresholds gives the false-cutoff rate against added latency, and the
operating point is a product decision.

## Takeaways

- Design from the latency budget: about a second, shared by transport,
  turn detection, STT, the LLM and TTS.
- End-of-turn detection, waiting for silence, is the largest single item
  in the budget; semantic turn detection cuts it.
- Every stage must stream: partial transcripts, clause-by-clause LLM
  output, chunked TTS audio.
- WebRTC over UDP, with ICE, STUN and TURN for connectivity, carries the
  audio; lost packets are cheaper than late ones.
- Speech-to-speech models cut latency and keep tone; cascades keep
  modularity, transcripts and a free choice of LLM.
- Speech is slow, about three or four tokens a second, so an 8B LLM is
  busy only a small fraction of each call; for 1,000 calls the binding
  constraint is where 262 GB of conversation caches live between turns:
  6 GPUs to hold them, 8 to recompute them, or one GPU with the caches in
  CPU memory, in an idealized simulation.

- [RFC 8489](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8489): Session Traversal Utilities for NAT (STUN).
- [RFC 8656](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8656): Traversal Using Relays around NAT (TURN).
- [RFC 8445](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8445): Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE).
